  • CMU 15-445 — #22 Distributed Database Architectures ~75 min — partitioning schemes as a database implementer sees them.
Chapter 6
Consensus — Getting Everyone to Agree
The hardest problem in distributed systems, explained from scratch.
⚡ Quick reference
Consensus is expensive. Buy the smallest amount that solves your problem.
If you need…Reach forBecauseUsed in
One leader, agreed by everyoneRaft or PaxosThe general solution: total order broadcast, leader election and linearizable CAS are all the same problem.etcd, Consul, CockroachDB, Spanner, ZooKeeper
Mutual exclusion across processesLease + fencing tokenA lease can expire while its holder is paused, so the token is what makes the stale holder harmless.ZooKeeper locks, Chubby, GFS D18
Membership and config, not dataA small consensus clusterBuy consensus for a few kilobytes of topology that changes weekly — never for the data path.Kafka controller, D12's ring, Kubernetes
Ordered delivery of eventsTotal order broadcastEquivalent to consensus. Recognising that stops you inventing a weaker, broken version.Kafka partition, replicated state machines
To avoid consensus entirelyPartition so the constraint is localOne shard, one row, one owner. The cheapest consensus is the one you did not need.D19 booking, D4 conversations

Imagine you need to elect a new president for a company of 100 employees spread across 10 offices. You need exactly one president — not zero, not two. The election must work even if some offices can't communicate with others at the moment. Some employees might crash mid-vote (they faint at the drama).

This is the consensus problem. In distributed systems, you need consensus for:

  • Leader election: Exactly one node is the leader at any time.
  • Atomic broadcast: All nodes deliver the same messages in the same order.
  • Distributed locking: Only one process holds the lock.
  • Configuration management: All nodes agree on the current config.

Why Is This Hard? The FLP Impossibility

In 1985, Fischer, Lynch, and Paterson proved something remarkable: in a fully asynchronous system where even one process can crash, there is no deterministic algorithm that always guarantees consensus.

This sounds devastating. But the key phrase is "fully asynchronous" — where messages can take arbitrarily long to arrive. In practice, messages don't take forever. We use timeouts to detect "probably failed" nodes. This introduces partial synchrony — and in partially synchronous systems, consensus is solvable. That's what Paxos and Raft do.

Raft — The Understandable Consensus Algorithm

Paxos was the original consensus algorithm (Lamport, 1998). It's proven correct but famously difficult to understand. In 2014, Diego Ongaro created Raft specifically to be easier to understand and implement, while providing equivalent guarantees. Today, Raft is used by etcd, CockroachDB, TiKV, and many others.

Raft operates in three phases. Let's walk through each:

Raft's three phases: election → replication → commitment. Safety is guaranteed by the election restriction.

Raft in Detail

1
Normal operation: heartbeats

The leader sends heartbeats (empty AppendEntries) to all followers every ~150ms. Followers reset their election timer on each heartbeat. As long as heartbeats arrive, followers stay as followers.

2
Leader failure: election begins

A follower's election timer fires (random 150-300ms). It increments its term number, becomes a Candidate, votes for itself, and sends RequestVote to all peers. The randomized timer prevents simultaneous candidates that split the vote.

3
Voters check the candidate's log

A node grants its vote only if: (a) it hasn't voted in this term already, and (b) the candidate's log is at least as up-to-date as the voter's log. "Up-to-date" means: higher term number in last entry, or same term but longer log. This ensures only candidates with all committed entries can win.

4
Winning the election

First candidate to collect votes from a majority of nodes (⌊N/2⌋ + 1) becomes the new leader. Immediately starts sending heartbeats to suppress other candidates.

5
Log replication

Client sends a command (e.g., x=5) to the leader. Leader appends it to its own log, then sends AppendEntries to all followers in parallel. Once a majority acknowledge, the entry is committed. Leader applies it to its state machine and responds to the client. Tells followers to apply it in the next heartbeat.

🔬 Google-Level Depth — Raft vs Paxos

Paxos and Raft provide the same safety guarantees, but differ in approach:

  • Raft: Strong leader. All entries go through the leader, in order. Easy to reason about. One leader handles all writes — can become a bottleneck. Used by: etcd, CockroachDB, TiKV.
  • Multi-Paxos: Stable leader is an optimization, not a requirement. Any node can be a proposer. More flexible. Can pipeline multiple in-flight proposals. Harder to implement correctly. Used by: Google Chubby, Spanner, Megastore.
  • Google's choice: Paxos, because at Google scale, the pipeline efficiency matters. Staff engineers working on Spanner or Borg should know Multi-Paxos well.
🔗
Chapter 8 ended with a question: if no node can trust its own clock, its own liveness, or its own beliefs about its role — how does a group agree on anything? This chapter is the answer. And the answer turns out to be the same answer to four questions that look unrelated.

The Central Result: Four Problems That Are Secretly One Problem

Most people learn consensus as “the algorithm that elects a leader.” That undersells it badly. The deep result in this area — and the thing worth actually understanding — is that the following four problems are formally equivalent. Solve any one and you can build the other three:

1. CONSENSUS Several nodes agree on one value, and never disagree afterwards. 2. TOTAL ORDER BROADCAST (a.k.a. atomic broadcast) Deliver messages to every node, in the same order, losing none. 3. LINEARIZABLE COMPARE-AND-SET One register supporting atomic "set to X only if currently Y". 4. LEADER ELECTION Exactly one node holds the role, and everyone agrees who. ⇩ ALL FOUR ARE THE SAME PROBLEM ⇩ This is not an analogy. It is a proved reduction: each can be mechanically transformed into a solution for the others.
If you can do any one of these, you can do all of them. If you cannot do one, you cannot do any.
💡 Why this equivalence is the most useful thing in the chapter

It converts a vague design question — “do we need consensus here?” — into a concrete, answerable one:

“Does my system need a total order over some set of operations?”

If yes, you need consensus, and there is no cheaper way — not timestamps, not clever hashing, not “we'll just use a lock in Redis.” If no, you can very likely avoid it and keep your availability and your latency.

Seeing the equivalence: building a uniqueness constraint from a log

Suppose you must guarantee that a username is claimed by exactly one user, with no two nodes ever disagreeing. Here is how total order broadcast gives you that — and notice that nothing in it involves clocks or locks:

Two users try to claim "martin" at the same instant, on different nodes. STEP 1 Both append a tentative claim to the shared log. STEP 2 Both wait for their own message to be delivered back to them. STEP 3 Both read the log and look for the FIRST claim for "martin". LOG (every node sees this identical order) ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ 1041 claim "martin" by user A │ ← first │ 1042 claim "martin" by user B │ └────────────────────────────────────────────┘ User A: "the first claim is mine" → COMMIT User B: "the first claim is not mine" → ABORT Every node reaches the same verdict, because every node saw the same order. No locks. No clocks. No coordination beyond the ordering itself.
⚠ A subtlety worth catching

The procedure above gives linearizable writes but not automatically linearizable reads. If you read from a store that is asynchronously updated from the log, you can read stale data — what you actually have is sequential consistency.

Three ways to close it: sequence the read through the log too (etcd quorum reads); ask for the log's latest position and wait until you have applied up to it (this is exactly what ZooKeeper's sync() does); or read from a synchronously-updated replica (chain replication). Whenever someone says “we use etcd so it's linearizable,” ask about the read path.

And the reverse: building a log from a linearizable counter

The equivalence runs both ways. Given a linearizable register with atomic increment-and-get, total order broadcast is nearly trivial: take a number, attach it to your message, broadcast, and have receivers deliver strictly in number order.

The crucial detail is that these numbers form a sequence with no gaps. A node that has delivered message 4 and receives message 6 knows it must wait for 5. That is precisely what timestamp ordering cannot give you — and it is the difference between total order broadcast and Lamport timestamps.

🔍 Why Lamport timestamps are not enough for a uniqueness constraint

Lamport timestamps do produce a total order consistent with causality, so it is tempting to think they solve uniqueness: two nodes claim a username, whoever has the lower timestamp wins.

The problem is when you can declare the winner. To know that your claim has the lowest timestamp, you must be certain no other node is about to produce a lower one — which means checking with every other node. If any node is unreachable, you cannot decide. The scheme cannot tolerate a single fault.

Total order broadcast is stronger because the order is fixed at delivery time: once message 1042 is delivered, nobody may retroactively insert 1041.5 before it. That finality is what makes a decision possible while nodes are down — and it is exactly the property that requires consensus to provide.

Why Leader Election Is a Consensus Problem

This trips people up: if we already have a leader, why do we need consensus? Isn't the leader just... in charge?

The circularity is the point. Consensus is easy once you have a leader — the leader decides. The hard part is agreeing on who the leader is, which is itself a consensus problem. Every consensus algorithm resolves this the same way:

THE PATTERN INSIDE EVERY CONSENSUS ALGORITHM 1. Define an epoch (Raft: term │ Paxos: ballot │ ZAB: epoch) A monotonically increasing number. A fencing token by another name. 2. Within one epoch, there is at most one leader. Not "exactly one" — an epoch may elect nobody. That is fine. 3. To become leader in epoch N, win a quorum vote. 4. To commit a value, win a second quorum vote. ⇩ THE KEY INSIGHT ⇩ These two quorums must overlap in at least one node. That node is the one that says: "I already voted in epoch N+1; your epoch N is stale." So a leader that lost its majority discovers this the moment it tries to commit anything. It cannot do damage.
Two overlapping quorums is the entire safety mechanism. Everything else is engineering.

Notice what this gives you that a lease alone does not: a leader does not decide on its own that it is still leader. It finds out by attempting to commit and being told. That is why consensus-based leadership is safe against the process pauses of Chapter 8, and why a Redis lock is not.

The Cost of Consensus — and How to Buy Less of It

Consensus is not free, and a Staff-level design is largely about minimising how much of your system touches it.

CostWhat it means in practice
Latency floorEvery decision needs a round trip to a majority. Same-zone: 1–2ms. Cross-region: 60–150ms, set by the speed of light and unfixable.
Throughput ceilingAll writes funnel through one leader. Tens of thousands of ops/sec, not millions. etcd is explicitly not a database.
Availability during partitionsThe minority side stops accepting writes entirely. This is deliberate — it is what prevents split brain — but it is real downtime for those clients.
Sensitivity to networkAn unstable network causes repeated elections. The cluster spends its time electing rather than committing. Frequent leader churn is a known failure mode.
Fixed membershipAdding or removing nodes requires a careful reconfiguration protocol (joint consensus), not just editing a config file.
Odd sizes only3, 5, 7. A 4-node cluster tolerates the same single failure as a 3-node one but is slower — you added cost and no fault tolerance.
💡 The architectural move that matters most

Put the metadata through consensus and keep the data out of it.

Kafka does not run consensus on your messages — it runs consensus on which broker leads which partition, then the data flows over ordinary replication. Kubernetes runs consensus on cluster state in etcd, not on your pods' traffic. Spanner shards data into many independent Paxos groups so most transactions touch exactly one group.

The pattern: a small, low-throughput, strongly-consistent control plane governing a large, high-throughput, weakly-coordinated data plane. When you see a design that routes all traffic through a consensus cluster, that is the mistake to point at.

⚠ Common misconception
“We need strong consistency, so we'll put everything in etcd/ZooKeeper.”

These are coordination services, not databases. ZooKeeper holds its entire dataset in memory; etcd recommends staying within a few gigabytes. Both do tens of thousands of writes per second at best.

They are designed for data that is small, slowly-changing, and must be correct: which node is leader, what the partition map is, what the current config is, which workers are alive. That data is measured in kilobytes and changes a few times a minute.

Putting high-churn application data in etcd is a documented way to take down a Kubernetes cluster. If your write rate has four or more digits, consensus is the wrong layer.

✎ Mini exercise 6

For each requirement, decide whether it genuinely needs consensus. Justify by asking: does this need a total order?

  1. Every user gets a globally unique username at signup.
  2. Generate unique IDs for 500k new records/second across 50 servers.
  3. A cron job must run exactly once per hour across 20 replicas.
  4. A feed shows posts roughly in reverse-chronological order.
  5. An account balance must never go negative.
Show the worked answer

1. Unique username — YES, consensus. Two nodes must never both accept “martin”. That is a decision requiring agreement, and it is exactly the linearizable compare-and-set problem. In practice you get it for free: a unique constraint in a single-leader database already runs the total order through that leader. You need explicit consensus only if the usernames are sharded across independent databases.

2. Unique IDs — NO. This is the most instructive one. Uniqueness does not require ordering. Give each server a disjoint slice of the ID space (Snowflake: timestamp + machine ID + sequence) and uniqueness is guaranteed by construction, with zero coordination, at any throughput. The trap is thinking “unique” implies “coordinated.” Note the price: Snowflake IDs are only approximately time-ordered, because the clocks differ — you gave up total order to get scale, and that is the right trade here.

3. Cron exactly once — YES for the election, but that is not the whole answer. Choosing the one runner is leader election, so use etcd/ZooKeeper rather than Redis. But as Chapter 8 showed, the winner can pause past its lease and a second replica can start. So: consensus for the election, plus fencing tokens, plus an idempotent job. Consensus alone does not give you exactly-once execution.

4. Roughly-ordered feed — NO. “Roughly” is the whole answer. Timestamps are fine, out-of-order arrivals are invisible to users, and paying consensus latency on every post would be absurd. Recognising that a requirement is approximate is often worth more than any optimisation.

5. Never negative — DEPENDS, and this is the interesting case. If the balance is one row in one database, a local transaction handles it — no distributed consensus. If the balance is sharded or spread across services, you need either a distributed transaction or consensus. The design move is to make it the first case: keep an account's balance on one shard so the invariant is local. Same instinct as Chapters 4, 5 and 7 — make the constraint local and the hard problem disappears.

The pattern across all five: ask “total order, or just uniqueness? exact, or approximate? global, or can I make it local?” Most requirements that look like they need consensus do not, once you ask.

🎓 Understanding Check — Consensus

Teaching questions with answers supplied.
Why does consensus require a majority rather than, say, any two nodes?

Because two quorums must be guaranteed to overlap. Any two majorities of the same set share at least one member, and that member remembers the earlier decision and can veto a conflicting one.

If quorums could be disjoint — “any two of five” — then {A,B} could decide X while {C,D} decides Y, with nothing connecting them. Majority is not an arbitrary convention; it is the minimum size that guarantees intersection.

Why isn't single-leader replication already consensus?

While the leader is alive it does provide a total order — that is exactly why single-leader replication is so useful and why it gives you linearizability almost for free.

The gap is choosing the next leader. If a human does it, you have consensus with a human in the loop (slow, but safe). If the nodes do it automatically, they must agree — and that is consensus. Single-leader replication is consensus with the hard part deferred, not avoided.

Why does a network partition force a consensus system to become unavailable for some clients?

Because progress requires a majority, and a partition leaves at most one side with a majority. The minority side must refuse writes — not because it is broken, but because accepting them could contradict a decision the majority is making.

This is CAP in its most concrete form. The unavailability is the feature: the alternative is split brain, and an error is recoverable in seconds where divergent histories may not be recoverable at all.

If FLP proves consensus can't be guaranteed, how does etcd work every day?

FLP says no deterministic algorithm can guarantee termination in a fully asynchronous network with even one possible crash. It does not say consensus usually fails.

Real algorithms keep safety unconditionally (never two conflicting decisions, ever) and provide liveness only during periods of synchrony. The timeout is the escape hatch: Raft's randomised election timeout is literally the assumption of partial synchrony made concrete. Under a pathological network, Raft does not decide wrongly — it simply makes no progress. That is FLP in production: not an error, an absence.

Why do consensus clusters stay at 3, 5 or 7 nodes?

Fault tolerance goes up with size, but so does commit latency — you wait for a larger majority across a wider spread of network paths. And even numbers add nothing: 4 nodes need 3 for a majority and so tolerate 1 failure, exactly like 3 nodes, while being slower.

5 is the usual sweet spot: tolerates 2 failures, so you survive one node down during a planned upgrade of another. Beyond 7, latency dominates. If you want more read capacity, add learners/observers that receive the log but do not vote — capacity without slowing the quorum.

What does it actually mean that total order broadcast and consensus are equivalent?

It means each can be mechanically built from the other, so they have identical difficulty and identical impossibility results. Consensus services like ZooKeeper and etcd are total order broadcast implementations — that is not a coincidence, it is the same artefact viewed from a different angle.

Practically: whenever you find yourself needing “everyone must see these events in the same order,” you have discovered a consensus requirement, and you should reach for an existing implementation rather than inventing a protocol. Distributed consensus is a solved problem you should never re-solve.

🎯 Consensus in real architectures — note how little it carries
Kafka
KRaft agrees on partition leadership and metadata. Your messages never touch consensus.
Kubernetes
etcd holds cluster state. Pod-to-pod traffic is entirely outside it.
Spanner
Data split into many Paxos groups so most transactions stay inside one group.
HDFS / HBase
ZooKeeper for master election and fencing. Block data streams directly between nodes.
Service discovery
Consul/etcd hold the registry — small, slowly-changing, must be correct.
Distributed lock / cron
Election via etcd, plus fencing tokens, plus an idempotent job. All three.
Feature flags / config
A textbook fit: kilobytes, rarely written, everyone must agree.
🌱 Takeaway — Consensus

Consensus, total order broadcast, linearizable compare-and-set and leader election are one problem wearing four hats. That single fact reorganises the whole subject.

  • The design question is “do I need a total order?” not “do I need consensus?”. Most requirements that sound like they need it do not.
  • Two overlapping quorums — one to elect, one to commit — is the entire safety mechanism.
  • Epochs are fencing tokens. Raft's term number is the same idea as Chapter 8's lock token.
  • Buy as little as you can. Small strongly-consistent control plane; large weakly-coordinated data plane.
  • Uniqueness ≠ ordering. Disjoint ID ranges give uniqueness at any scale with zero coordination.
  • Never implement it yourself. Use etcd, ZooKeeper, or a database that embeds Raft.

📝 Interview Q&A

In a 5-node Raft cluster, how many node failures can the system tolerate while still making progress?

2 node failures. Raft requires a majority (⌊N/2⌋ + 1 = 3 nodes) for any decision. With 5 nodes and 2 failures, 3 remain — exactly the required majority. A third failure would leave only 2 nodes, less than the required 3, so no new log entries could be committed and no new leader could be elected.

Important nuance: the system can tolerate 2 simultaneous failures. During recovery from 1 failure (adding back a node), the system is vulnerable to a second failure — it's operating at minimum quorum.

A Raft leader crashes immediately after committing an entry (the majority ACKed, but followers haven't been told to apply it yet). What happens?

The committed entry is safe. Here's why: a majority of nodes have the entry in their logs. When a new election happens, any node without this entry will not be able to collect votes from a majority — because the nodes that do have it will reject votes from candidates whose log is behind. Therefore, only a node that already has the committed entry can win the election. The new leader will then send the entry to all followers in its first AppendEntries and tell them to commit it. No data loss.

This is Raft's key safety property: the Log Matching Property. Two logs agree on entries up to the committed index. The Election Restriction ensures this invariant is preserved across leader changes.

Your team is debating whether to use Raft or a database-level lock for distributed coordination. How do you advise?

Use a dedicated consensus service (etcd or ZooKeeper, which use Raft/Paxos internally) rather than rolling your own.

Why not a database lock: Database locks depend on network connectivity to the database. If your service thinks it holds the lock but can't reach the database (partition), it might still proceed. You need fencing tokens (monotonically increasing numbers from the lock service) to prevent this. Database locks also don't survive database failovers cleanly.

Why not roll your own Raft: Consensus is correctness-critical. A subtle bug in your implementation can lead to data loss or two leaders. etcd is battle-tested across millions of Kubernetes clusters. Unless you have very specific needs (e.g., embedded, no external dependency), use the existing tool.

Chapter 7
Distributed Transactions
Making multiple things happen atomically — across machines.
⚡ Quick reference
Most “we need distributed transactions” problems are better solved by not being distributed.
If you need…Reach forBecauseUsed in
Atomicity within one databaseA local transactionFree, fast, and correct. Restructure to reach this whenever you can.Any single-shard write
Atomicity across servicesSaga + compensationsEach step commits locally; failures run compensating actions. No global lock, no blocking coordinator.Order fulfilment, travel booking D19
A message and a DB write to be atomicTransactional outboxBoth are writes to your database, so one transaction covers them. The relay publishes afterwards.Debezium/CDC, Ch 11
Safe retries across an unreliable boundaryIdempotency keyA timeout tells you nothing; the key lets the receiver decide whether it already happened.Stripe, payment APIs, D19
Strict atomicity across shards2PCIt genuinely works, and the coordinator is a blocking single point of failure. Use knowingly.XA, Spanner internally, distributed DBs
To avoid lost updates under concurrencyCompare-and-set / SELECT FOR UPDATETurns a read-modify-write race into an atomic conditional write.D19, D6, optimistic concurrency
Two-phase commit — and the window where the coordinator owns everyone
preparevotecommit
What is moving: the coordinator asks every participant to prepare — do the work, take the locks, promise you can commit — collects the votes, and only then broadcasts the decision. Between the vote and the decision, each participant is holding locks and has given up its right to decide alone.
What goes wrong: the coordinator dies after collecting votes. Every participant has promised to commit and none of them knows the outcome — they cannot commit (the decision may have been abort) and cannot abort (they promised). They hold their locks and block, and any transaction touching those rows blocks behind them. This is why 2PC is a blocking protocol and why the coordinator is a genuine single point of failure, not a theoretical one.

A transaction is a set of operations that either all succeed or all fail together. In a single database, this is straightforward — the database manages it. But what happens when your "transaction" involves multiple services, multiple databases, or multiple rows on different machines?

⚠
Do not skip to 2PC. “In a single database this is straightforward” is the most expensive sentence in system design. It is not straightforward — a single-node database gives you a menu of guarantees, most engineers run on a weak default, and the anomalies that leak through are the direct cause of double bookings, oversold inventory and vanishing money. The distributed problem is the second half of this chapter. This is the first half.

What ACID Actually Promises (and the One Letter That Is Marketing)

ACID is quoted constantly and understood rarely. Three of the letters are real guarantees provided by the database. One is not.

LetterWhat it actually meansWho is responsible
Atomicity Not “concurrent” — it means abortability. If a transaction fails partway, everything it did is discarded. There is no half-applied state to clean up. The database
Consistency Your application's invariants hold (accounts balance, no negative stock). The database cannot know your invariants — it only enforces what you declared as constraints. You. This letter is in ACID mostly because the acronym needed a vowel.
Isolation Concurrent transactions do not step on each other. This is the letter with a dial on it, and the dial is usually set weak. The database — at the level you selected
Durability Once committed, the write survives a crash. In practice: written to a WAL and fsynced, and on a replicated system, present on other nodes. The database + your replication config
⚠ Common misconception
“Our database is ACID, so we don't have concurrency bugs.”

ACID says nothing until you name the isolation level. “Isolation” in the acronym implies transactions behave as if they ran one at a time — but almost nobody runs at that level, because it is expensive.

Real defaults: PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server default to Read Committed. MySQL/InnoDB defaults to Repeatable Read. Neither prevents write skew. Oracle has never had true serializability at all — what Oracle calls SERIALIZABLE is snapshot isolation.

So the accurate sentence is: “We use Postgres at Read Committed, which permits lost updates and write skew, and here is how we handle the two places that matters.” That is an engineering statement. “We're ACID” is not.

The Isolation Ladder — Four Anomalies, Climbing

Isolation levels are best learned as a list of anomalies and which level stops each one. Every level is defined by what it still lets through.

WEAKEST STRONGEST │ │ READ UNCOMMITTED → READ COMMITTED → SNAPSHOT ISOLATION → SERIALIZABLE (a.k.a. Repeatable Read) ANOMALY RU RC SI SER ───────────────────────────────────────────────────── Dirty read YES no no no Dirty write YES no no no Read skew YES YES no no Lost update YES YES some no Write skew YES YES YES no ← the one that surprises people Phantoms YES YES YES* no * SI avoids phantoms for read-only queries, not for read-write transactions
The whole chapter in one table. Note the two rows that only Serializable closes — those are where real production bugs live.

Read Committed — The Common Default

Read committed makes two promises, and they are weaker than they sound.

No dirty reads: you only see data that has been committed. Without this, you could read a value from a transaction that later aborts — acting on data that never officially existed.

WITHOUT no-dirty-reads: T1: BEGIN SET balance = 900 (uncommitted) ROLLBACK │ T2: ▼ READ balance → 900 emails user "your balance is 900" ↑ a balance that never existed

No dirty writes: you only overwrite data that has been committed. This one is subtler and more important than it looks — it is what stops two transactions from interleaving their writes across multiple rows.

WITHOUT no-dirty-writes — a car sale with two buyers: Alice: BEGIN set listing.buyer = Alice ─────┦ Bob: BEGIN set listing.buyer = Bob ─────┦ overwrites Alice Bob: set invoice.to = Bob ─────┦ Alice: set invoice.to = Alice ─────┦ overwrites Bob RESULT: listing sold to Bob, invoice sent to Alice Neither transaction produced this. It is a Frankenstein of both.
Read committed prevents this by making the second writer wait for the first to commit — implemented with row-level write locks held until commit.

How it is implemented: write locks are held until commit (preventing dirty writes), but reads do not take locks. Instead the database keeps both the old committed value and the new uncommitted one, and readers get the old one. That is MVCC in embryo — and it is why readers never block writers.

Snapshot Isolation — Read Skew and the MVCC Machine

Read committed still permits an ugly anomaly: read skew (also called a non-repeatable read). Two reads inside one transaction can see the database in two different states.

Alice has £1000, split across two accounts of £500 each. She checks her balances while a transfer of £100 from Account 2 to Account 1 is in flight. Alice reads Account 1 → £500 (before the transfer commits) │ Transfer commits: acct2 −100, acct1 +100 │ Alice reads Account 2 → £400 (after the transfer commits) Alice's total: 500 + 400 = £900. £100 has apparently vanished. Nothing is actually wrong in the database. She observed a torn view of it.

For a balance screen this is merely alarming. For two other cases it is disqualifying, and these are the reasons snapshot isolation exists:

  • Backups. A backup takes hours. If it reads a torn view, the backup itself contains the inconsistency — permanently.
  • Analytics and integrity checks. A query that scans a large fraction of the database and returns nonsense because rows shifted underneath it is worse than useless.
💡 The idea behind snapshot isolation

Each transaction reads from a consistent snapshot of the database, taken at the moment the transaction began. Even if the data changes afterwards, the transaction sees the frozen state. The slogan — and it is worth memorising because it explains most modern database behaviour — is: readers never block writers, and writers never block readers.

The mechanism is MVCC. The database keeps multiple versions of every row simultaneously. Each row version is tagged with the transaction that created it and, once superseded, the transaction that deleted it:

Row: account_2.balance created_by deleted_by ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── version A: balance = 500 txn 12 txn 78 version B: balance = 400 txn 78 — A transaction with snapshot at txn 75 asks: which version can I see? • created_by 12 → committed before my snapshot ✓ visible • deleted_by 78 → NOT committed at my snapshot ✓ not yet deleted, for me → it sees 500 A transaction with snapshot at txn 90 sees version B → 400 Same row. Two truths. Both correct, for their respective observers.
Visibility rules: a version is visible if the transaction that created it committed before your snapshot, and the transaction that deleted it had not.
⚠ The operational cost nobody plans for

Old versions can only be garbage collected once no running transaction could still need them. One long-running analytics query pins every version created since it started. In PostgreSQL this is the classic bloat incident: an analyst's forgotten 8-hour query prevents VACUUM from reclaiming anything, tables swell by tens of gigabytes, query plans degrade, and in the extreme the database refuses writes to avoid transaction-ID wraparound. Monitor the age of your oldest transaction, not just query latency.

⚠ Common misconception
“MVCC means there are no concurrency problems.”

MVCC eliminates read–write conflicts. It does nothing about write–write conflicts, and nothing at all about a transaction making a decision based on what it read.

That second gap is the entire subject of the next section, and it is where the expensive bugs are.

Lost Updates — The Read-Modify-Write Race

Two transactions read a value, modify it in application code, and write it back. One update silently disappears.

Two users like the same post at the same moment. T1: READ likes = 42 T2: READ likes = 42 both saw 42 T1: WRITE likes = 43 T2: WRITE likes = 43 ← T1's increment is gone Two likes happened. The counter says one. Nothing errored.

Four ways to fix it, in rough order of preference:

  1. Atomic write operation — UPDATE posts SET likes = likes + 1 WHERE id = 42. The read-modify-write happens inside the database under an exclusive lock. Best answer whenever the operation is expressible in SQL.
  2. Explicit locking — SELECT ... FOR UPDATE. Necessary when the modification requires application logic the database cannot express.
  3. Compare-and-set — UPDATE ... SET likes = 43 WHERE id = 42 AND likes = 42. Zero rows affected means you lost the race; re-read and retry. This is optimistic concurrency control, and it is the only option on many distributed stores.
  4. Automatic detection — PostgreSQL repeatable read and Oracle serializable detect lost updates and abort the loser. MySQL/InnoDB repeatable read does not. Know which engine you are on.
⚠ The trap in option 2

SELECT FOR UPDATE only locks rows that exist. If your check is for the absence of rows — “is this username free?”, “is this room unbooked?” — there is nothing to lock, and the fix silently does not work. That is the phantom problem, and it is next.

Write Skew — The Anomaly That Snapshot Isolation Cannot Stop

This is the most important section in the chapter. Write skew is the bug that gets through every isolation level except true serializability, it is invisible in code review, and it is the cause of a large share of real double-booking and oversell incidents.

🎯 The on-call doctors

A hospital scheduling system. The rule: at least one doctor must be on call at all times. A doctor may go off call provided at least one colleague remains.

Alice and Bob are the two doctors on call. Both feel ill. Both click “go off call” at the same instant.

Both transactions run under SNAPSHOT ISOLATION. Both commit successfully. ALICE'S TRANSACTION BOB'S TRANSACTION BEGIN BEGIN SELECT COUNT(*) WHERE on_call SELECT COUNT(*) WHERE on_call → 2 "safe, 2 >= 2" → 2 "safe, 2 >= 2" UPDATE doctors SET on_call=false UPDATE doctors SET on_call=false WHERE name = 'Alice' WHERE name = 'Bob' ↑ DIFFERENT ROW — no write conflict! COMMIT ✓ COMMIT ✓ RESULT: zero doctors on call. The invariant is violated. Each transaction was individually correct. Together they are not.
The database sees no conflict because the two transactions wrote different rows. First-committer-wins never fires.

Why the usual fixes all fail here

  • Atomic operations? No — two different objects are involved.
  • Lost-update detection? No — this is not a lost update. Postgres repeatable read, MySQL repeatable read, Oracle serializable and SQL Server snapshot all fail to catch it.
  • A database constraint? You would need a constraint spanning multiple rows. Most databases cannot express that.
  • SELECT FOR UPDATE? This one works here, because the rows being checked are the rows being written. Lock the on-call doctors for that shift and the second transaction blocks.
🔍 The pattern — learn to recognise this shape anywhere

Every write skew has the same three steps:

  1. A SELECT checks whether some condition holds (“two doctors on call”, “no booking for that room”, “username free”, “enough balance”).
  2. Application code decides based on the result.
  3. A write is made — and that write changes the answer to the query in step 1.

The transaction acted on a premise that is no longer true by the time it commits. If you see read → decide → write in one transaction, you are looking at a potential write skew. Ask immediately: what happens if two of these run at once?

Phantoms — when there is nothing to lock

The doctors case was fixable with FOR UPDATE because the rows existed. Now consider booking a meeting room:

T1: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM bookings WHERE room=123 AND end > 12:00 AND start < 13:00 → 0 T2: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM bookings WHERE room=123 AND end > 12:00 AND start < 13:00 → 0 T1: INSERT booking(room=123, 12:00–13:00, user=Alice) COMMIT ✓ T2: INSERT booking(room=123, 12:00–13:00, user=Bob) COMMIT ✓ Room 123 is double-booked. SELECT FOR UPDATE cannot help: the query returned ZERO rows. You cannot lock a row that does not exist yet.
A phantom: a write in one transaction changes the result of a search query in another. This is what makes absence-checks so dangerous.

The same shape appears in: claiming a username, taking a seat in a booking system, moving to a square in a multiplayer game, and spending the last of an account balance. All are “check that nothing matches, then insert something that matches.”

Two ways out. The first is a hack, the second is the real answer:

Materializing conflicts (last resort)

Invent rows to lock. Pre-create a time_slots table with a row per room per 15 minutes for the next six months. A booking transaction locks the relevant slot rows with FOR UPDATE, then checks and inserts.

  • It works — the phantom becomes a real lock conflict
  • Ugly: concurrency control has leaked into your data model
  • Error-prone: easy to get the slot granularity wrong

True serializable isolation (preferred)

Set the isolation level to SERIALIZABLE and let the database detect the conflict. Handle serialization failures by retrying the transaction.

  • Correct by construction, no schema contortions
  • Costs throughput and requires retry logic
  • Only viable if your engine actually implements it

Serializability — Three Ways to Actually Get It

Serializable isolation guarantees the outcome is the same as if transactions had run one at a time. There are exactly three implementation strategies in production databases, and they make opposite trade-offs.

1. Actual Serial Execution

Literally run one transaction at a time, on a single thread. Sounds absurd; became viable around 2007 because RAM got cheap enough to hold whole datasets, and because OLTP transactions are short.

  • Requires transactions to be small and fast — so they are submitted as stored procedures rather than interactive multi-round-trip sessions. A transaction that waits on network I/O would stall the entire database.
  • Throughput is capped by one CPU core. You scale by partitioning, and a transaction touching multiple partitions becomes dramatically slower.
  • Used by VoltDB and Redis (single-threaded command execution is exactly this idea).

2. Two-Phase Locking (2PL) — Pessimistic

The classic answer for ~30 years. Readers block writers and writers block readers — the opposite of snapshot isolation.

  • Shared locks for reads, exclusive locks for writes; all held until commit.
  • Phantoms are handled with predicate locks — conceptually locking all rows matching a condition, including ones that do not exist yet. Because true predicate locks are slow, real databases approximate them with index-range locks (lock the index entries for room 123 across the whole day rather than exactly 12:00–13:00). Coarser, and therefore safe.
  • Cost: unpredictable latency and deadlocks. A deadlock aborts a transaction, which must be retried. Throughput collapses under contention.

3. Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI) — Optimistic

The modern answer (PostgreSQL 9.1+, FoundationDB). Transactions proceed without blocking, and the database checks at commit time whether serializability was actually violated.

SSI's insight: detect transactions that acted on an outdated premise. Two things to watch for: A. Stale MVCC read (the write was uncommitted when we read) T43 reads a snapshot that ignored T42's uncommitted write. At T43's commit, T42 has since committed. → T43's premise is stale → ABORT T43 Why check at commit and not at read time? Because T43 might be read-only (harmless), or T42 might still abort. Deferring avoids needless aborts and preserves long-running consistent reads. B. Write affecting a prior read (the write came after our read) The DB records "T42 and T43 both read index entry shift_id=1234". When either writes there, it acts as a tripwire — not a lock: it notifies rather than blocks. First to commit wins; the second aborts.
SSI = snapshot isolation + tracking of read–write dependencies, with the losing transaction aborted at commit.
💡 Why SSI is usually the right default now

Compared with 2PL, no transaction ever blocks waiting for a lock, so latency is far more predictable — and read-only queries run on a snapshot with no locks at all. Compared with serial execution, it is not limited to one CPU core; FoundationDB even distributes conflict detection across machines.

The cost is the abort rate. SSI needs read-write transactions to be short: a transaction that reads and writes over a long window is very likely to hit a conflict and abort. Long read-only transactions remain fine.

Serial execution2PL (pessimistic)SSI (optimistic)
ApproachAvoid concurrency entirelyBlock conflicts before they happenAllow, detect, abort
Readers block writers?n/aYesNo
Latency profileVery predictableUnpredictable (lock waits, deadlocks)Predictable
Fails underAny long transaction; multi-partitionHigh contention (deadlocks)High contention (abort storms)
Scales past 1 core?NoYesYes
Used byVoltDB, RedisMySQL, SQL ServerPostgreSQL, FoundationDB
✎ Mini exercise 3

You run a ticketing system. Each event has a fixed number of seats. Your booking code, running on PostgreSQL at the default isolation level, does:

  1. SELECT COUNT(*) FROM tickets WHERE event_id = 99 → if < capacity, continue
  2. INSERT INTO tickets (event_id, user_id) VALUES (99, ...)

An event with 500 seats sells 517 tickets during an on-sale rush.

Work out: name the anomaly precisely, explain why SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on step 1 would not fix it, and give two fixes that would.

Show the worked answer

This is write skew caused by a phantom. Many transactions concurrently read a count of 499, each independently concludes there is room, and each inserts. The inserts are all different rows, so there is no write–write conflict for the database to catch. PostgreSQL's default Read Committed does nothing to prevent it.

Why FOR UPDATE fails: it locks rows returned by the query. The precondition here concerns rows that do not exist yet — the tickets about to be inserted. There is nothing to attach a lock to. This is the defining property of a phantom.

Fix 1 — materialize the conflict. Put a seats_remaining counter on the events row and do UPDATE events SET seats_remaining = seats_remaining - 1 WHERE id = 99 AND seats_remaining > 0. Now every booking contends on one real row, the database serialises them with a row lock, and zero rows affected means sold out. Simple, correct, and it converts a phantom into an ordinary atomic write.

Fix 2 — SERIALIZABLE isolation. Set the transaction to SERIALIZABLE; PostgreSQL's SSI detects that these transactions read a range that another transaction wrote, and aborts the losers with a serialization failure. Your application must catch 40001 and retry.

Which would I ship? Fix 1, and it is worth being clear why: the counter row is also the natural place to model the business concept (“inventory”), and it gives you a single hot row you can shard later if needed. Fix 2 is more general but under an on-sale rush the abort rate on a single hot event would be brutal — optimistic concurrency control is the wrong tool for a known, extreme hotspot.

The bigger lesson: notice that Fix 1 works by changing the data model so the invariant lives on one row. That is the same move as co-locating causally related data in Chapter 4 — making a distributed or multi-row constraint into a local one.

⚠ Common misconception
“We'll just wrap it in a transaction and it'll be fine.”

A transaction gives you atomicity (all-or-nothing) for free. It gives you isolation only at the level you configured, and the default level permits write skew.

“Wrap it in a transaction” protects you against crashes. It does not protect you against concurrency unless you also chose the isolation level deliberately — or restructured the data so the invariant sits on a single row.

🌱 Checkpoint before we go distributed

Everything above happened on one machine, one database. Hold onto these, because the distributed half of the chapter is what happens when you lose even these guarantees:

  • Atomicity means abortability, not concurrency. The C in ACID is your job.
  • Isolation is a dial, and it defaults to weak. Name your level or you have not made a decision.
  • Write skew — read, decide, write — is the shape to recognise. Only true serializability stops it automatically.
  • Phantoms defeat FOR UPDATE, because you cannot lock rows that do not exist.
  • Moving an invariant onto a single row converts a hard concurrency problem into an ordinary atomic write. Reach for this before reaching for stronger isolation.

Now: everything above assumed one database that can see all the data and take all the locks. What happens when the accounts live on different machines?

The Classic Problem: Bank Transfer

🎯 Scenario — The $1000 Transfer

User wants to transfer $1000 from Account A (on Database Shard 1) to Account B (on Database Shard 2).

You need both of these to happen atomically:

  1. Debit $1000 from Account A
  2. Credit $1000 to Account B

What can go wrong?

  • Debit succeeds, then the service crashes before crediting → $1000 vanishes into thin air
  • Credit succeeds, then the service crashes before debiting → $1000 appears from nowhere
  • Network partition between debit and credit → who knows which happened

Two-Phase Commit (2PC)

2PC is the classic solution. It involves a coordinator node and multiple participant nodes.

Two-Phase Commit: Phase 1 checks if everyone can commit. Phase 2 commits or aborts based on all votes.

Phase 1 (Prepare): Coordinator asks each participant "can you commit?" Participants lock the relevant data, write a prepare log entry, and reply "yes" or "no." Saying "yes" is a promise — the participant must be able to commit if asked.

Phase 2 (Commit/Abort): If all said yes → coordinator sends COMMIT. If any said no → coordinator sends ABORT. Participants execute accordingly and release locks.

⚠ Common Mistake

2PC has a critical flaw: if the coordinator crashes after Phase 1 (after participants said YES) but before Phase 2, the participants are stuck. They've promised to commit, locked their data, but don't know whether to commit or abort. They cannot proceed without the coordinator. This is called the 'blocking' problem.

In practice, 2PC coordinators write to a durable log (WAL) before sending Phase 2. On recovery, they read the log and complete the transaction. But during the window between coordinator crash and recovery, participants are blocked holding locks.

Sagas — The Microservices Answer

Sagas are the dominant pattern for distributed transactions in microservices. Instead of a two-phase commit, each step is an individual local transaction. If a step fails, you undo previous steps with compensating transactions.

🎯 Scenario — E-commerce Order Saga
  1. Order Service: Create order (status: PENDING)
  2. Payment Service: Charge credit card → $99.99 charged
  3. Inventory Service: Reserve item → item reserved
  4. Shipping Service: Schedule delivery → delivery scheduled
  5. Order Service: Update order (status: CONFIRMED)

If step 3 fails (item out of stock):

  • Compensate step 2: Refund the $99.99 charge
  • Compensate step 1: Cancel the order
Saga pattern: forward progress or compensate. Each step is an independent local transaction.

The Critical Difference: Sagas Have No Isolation

While steps 1 and 2 have succeeded but step 3 is running, the order exists in the database in a "PENDING" state. Other parts of your system can see this pending order. They might try to read it, reason about it, or react to it. If the saga then fails and compensates, those other parts saw an order that was later cancelled — a phantom.

This is called a dirty read — and it's the price you pay for using sagas instead of ACID transactions. You need to design around it: using status fields, making compensations idempotent, and ensuring consumers handle the "cancelled" state gracefully.

📝 Interview Q&A

When would you choose 2PC over a Saga pattern?

Choose 2PC when: (1) You need true atomicity with isolation — no intermediate states visible to others. (2) You're within a single organization's infrastructure (you control all participants). (3) The transaction is short-lived (seconds, not minutes). (4) You're using databases that support distributed transactions natively (e.g., MySQL with XA transactions, CockroachDB).

Choose Sagas when: (1) You span services owned by different teams (2PC across organizational boundaries is operationally nightmarish). (2) Steps may take minutes or hours (holding locks for minutes kills throughput). (3) Services use different databases or technologies. (4) You can tolerate eventual consistency and design compensating transactions.

A compensation transaction also fails. What do you do in a Saga?

This is a real production challenge. Your options:

(1) Retry the compensation (most common). Compensations must be idempotent — safe to apply multiple times. A refund that's been retried 3 times should still result in exactly one refund. Use an idempotency key.

(2) Dead letter queue. After N retries, move the failed compensation to a DLQ. Alert operations. Human intervention resolves it manually (refund via customer service, etc.).

(3) Pivot transaction. Design the saga to try an alternative action when a compensation fails — e.g., 'if refund fails, issue store credit instead.'

Staff-level insight: compensation failure is often treated as an afterthought, but it should be a first-class concern in your saga design. Every step's compensation should be idempotent, retriable, and tested explicitly.

🎓 Understanding Check — Transactions

Work through these before reading the answers. The first four are about single-node isolation; the last three connect it to the distributed case.
Why is write skew possible under snapshot isolation when lost update is not?

Snapshot isolation's conflict detection is per object: first-committer-wins fires when two transactions write the same row. A lost update is exactly that case, so it can be caught.

Write skew involves two transactions that read an overlapping set of rows but write different rows. There is no object on which the conflict manifests, so nothing triggers. The conflict is between one transaction's write and another's read — and tracking read–write dependencies is precisely the extra machinery SSI adds.

Why can't SELECT ... FOR UPDATE prevent a phantom?

Because it locks the rows the query returned. A phantom arises when your precondition is about the absence of rows — the query returns zero rows, so there is nothing to lock, and both transactions proceed.

To lock absence you need a lock on the predicate rather than on rows. That is what predicate locks and index-range locks do in 2PL, and what SSI's read-tracking approximates.

Both PostgreSQL and Oracle offer “SERIALIZABLE”. Why is that not the same guarantee?

Oracle's SERIALIZABLE is snapshot isolation — it permits write skew. PostgreSQL's (since 9.1) is genuine serializable snapshot isolation and prevents it.

The practical lesson is that isolation-level names are not portable. MySQL's REPEATABLE READ is not PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ either. Never reason about correctness from the keyword — reason about which anomalies your specific engine at your specific setting permits, and verify it.

SSI aborts transactions instead of blocking them. When does that become the wrong trade?

Under high contention on the same data. Optimistic control assumes conflicts are rare; when they are common, transactions do their work, reach commit, discover a conflict and throw the work away — then retry and often lose again. Throughput can collapse toward zero while CPU stays pinned.

Two signals that you are in that regime: a single very hot row or range (a flash-sale item, one popular event), or long read-write transactions that accumulate a large read set. Fixes: shorten the transaction, move the invariant onto one row so an atomic write handles it, or serialise deliberately through a queue.

Why does 2PC multiply your failure probability rather than reduce it?

Because it requires every participant to be available for the transaction to complete. With five participants each at 99.9% availability, the transaction's availability is 0.999⁵ ≈ 99.5% — worse than any individual component.

This is the opposite of how replication works, and it is why 2PC does not compose well in a microservices architecture. Each new participant makes the whole worse. Replication adds redundancy; 2PC adds dependency.

A participant voted YES in 2PC and then lost contact with the coordinator. Why can't it just decide for itself?

Because voting YES was a promise. It cannot abort, since the coordinator may already have collected all the YES votes and told other participants to commit — aborting would break atomicity. It cannot commit either, since some other participant may have voted NO.

It is genuinely stuck, holding its locks, until the coordinator returns. This is the blocking problem, and it is not fixable by a cleverer protocol — it is the Two Generals problem wearing a suit. It is why the coordinator's log must be durable and why production systems replicate the coordinator (as Spanner does over Paxos).

If sagas expose intermediate states, how is that ever acceptable for money?

Because that is how finance has always worked. A card authorisation, a settlement and a refund are separate events, hours or days apart, and the intermediate state is visible — a “pending” charge is a real thing users understand.

The mistake is not exposing intermediate state; it is failing to model it. If your schema has only PAID and UNPAID, a saga will corrupt it. If it has PENDING, AUTHORISED, CAPTURED, REFUNDING, then the intermediate states are legitimate and the UI can show them honestly.

The general principle: sagas require your domain model to have the in-between states as first-class values.

🎯 Choosing a concurrency strategy by workload
Seat / room booking
Phantom-prone. Materialize the conflict onto an inventory row, or use SERIALIZABLE with retries.
Flash sale, one hot SKU
Optimistic control collapses here. Use an atomic decrement on a counter, sharded if needed, or a queue.
Bank ledger
Append-only entries rather than mutable balances — turns a read-modify-write into an insert with no contention.
Analytics on live data
Long read-only transactions on an MVCC snapshot. Watch vacuum/bloat — run on a replica, not the primary.
Order across microservices
Saga with compensations and an outbox. Never 2PC across service boundaries.
Cross-shard transfer, one company
A database that does it for you (Spanner, CockroachDB) beats hand-rolled 2PC every time.
Username registration
Phantom on absence. A unique constraint is the correct, cheap answer — let the database enforce it.
🌱 Takeaway — the arc of this chapter

The chapter moves through three levels of losing guarantees, and the techniques at each level are responses to what was lost:

  • One node, weak isolation: anomalies leak through. Fix by naming your isolation level, or by moving the invariant onto one row.
  • One node, serializable: correctness restored, paid for in throughput (2PL) or aborts (SSI).
  • Many nodes: even serializability is not enough, because no single node can see all the data or hold all the locks. 2PC buys atomicity by making availability worse; sagas buy availability by giving up isolation.

The single most useful instinct: before reaching for a distributed transaction, try to make the transaction local. Redraw the service boundary, co-locate the data, or move the invariant onto one row. Two things that always change together probably should not be two services.

Chapter 8 explains why the distributed case is so much harder than it looks — not because of clever adversaries, but because clocks lie and processes pause.

Chapter 8
Distributed Time — Why You Can't Trust the Clock
Clocks lie in distributed systems. Here's what to do about it.
⚡ Quick reference
Clocks lie. Pick the kind of time that matches the question you are asking.
If you need…Reach forBecauseUsed in
To order events in one processA monotonic clockNever jumps backwards, unlike wall-clock time under NTP correction. Use it for every duration measurement.CLOCK_MONOTONIC, System.nanoTime
To order events across processesLamport clocksGives a total order consistent with causality — but cannot tell you whether two events were concurrent.Kafka offsets, many replicated logs
To detect concurrent writesVector clocks / version vectorsThe only mechanism that distinguishes “happened before” from “concurrent”, which is what conflict detection needs.Dynamo, Riak, D3
Externally consistent transactionsBounded uncertainty + commit-waitWait out the clock error so no transaction can commit before one that preceded it in real time.Spanner TrueTime — atomic clocks and GPS
Roughly-ordered IDs, cheaplySnowflake-style IDsTimestamp + machine + sequence, sortable and generated without coordination.Twitter, Instagram, most ID services
To never trust a timestamp for safetyFencing tokens insteadA lease can expire during a GC pause, so use a monotonic counter, not a clock reading.Ch 6, D6

In a single-machine system, time is simple: System.currentTimeMillis() gives you a number that increases monotonically. Call it twice — the second call is always larger than the first. You can use timestamps to order events.

In a distributed system, you cannot do this.

Why Clocks Lie

Every computer has a hardware clock (quartz crystal oscillator). Quartz crystals are not perfect. They drift at ~10-100 parts per million. That's up to 8.6 seconds per day. Over a week, two servers' clocks can diverge by minutes.

NTP (Network Time Protocol) synchronizes clocks over the network. But NTP has issues:

  • Synchronization accuracy: ±1ms on a LAN, ±10-100ms over the internet.
  • A jump sync can make the clock go backward. Code that assumes now() > prev_now() will break.
  • NTP can be blocked, slow, or wrong.
  • A server recently resumed from a VM snapshot might think it's still in 2024.
⚠ Common Mistake

Never use wall-clock timestamps (System.currentTimeMillis()) to order events across different machines. You will be wrong. Sometimes subtly, sometimes catastrophically.

Clock drift causes LWW to silently lose data. B's clock is fast, so B's earlier write gets a higher timestamp and 'wins.'

Logical Clocks — Ordering Without Wall Clocks

Lamport Clocks

Leslie Lamport's 1978 insight: we don't need wall-clock time to order events. We just need to capture the happened-before relationship.

Rules: Each process has a counter. Before sending a message, increment your counter. When receiving a message, set your counter to max(your counter, message counter) + 1.

Lamport clocks: messages carry timestamps. Receivers take max(local, received)+1. Causality creates order.

Limitation: Lamport clocks give a total order, but can't detect concurrent events. If A has timestamp 5 and B has timestamp 5, you don't know if they're concurrent or one happened before the other.

Vector Clocks

Vector clocks solve the concurrency detection problem. Each process keeps a vector (array) of counters, one per process. When you update something, you increment your own counter. When you send a message, you send the whole vector. The recipient takes a per-component max.

💡 Key Insight

Comparing two vector clocks VC1 and VC2: if VC1[i] ≤ VC2[i] for all i, then VC1 happened before VC2. If neither is ≤ the other, they're concurrent. This is exactly what Amazon Dynamo uses to detect conflicting writes that need application-level resolution.

TrueTime — Google's Engineering Solution

Google took a completely different approach in Spanner: instead of logical clocks, they invested in making physical clocks extremely accurate using GPS receivers and atomic clocks in every data center. The TrueTime API returns an interval [earliest, latest] rather than a single timestamp.

The uncertainty is typically 1-7ms. Spanner uses this to implement commit wait: after committing a transaction with timestamp T, the system waits until TrueTime guarantees T is in the past (until TT.now().earliest > T). This ensures the global ordering property without a global lock.

Two Clocks, Not One — And Using the Wrong One Is a Real Bug

Before going further: every machine has two different clocks, they answer different questions, and mixing them up produces bugs that only appear during an NTP correction — which is to say, rarely and unreproducibly.

Time-of-day clock (wall clock)

System.currentTimeMillis(), CLOCK_REALTIME, time.time()

  • Returns a real calendar date — comparable across machines
  • Can jump backwards when NTP steps it
  • Historically coarse resolution; ignores leap seconds
  • Use for: timestamps a human will read, expiry dates, log lines
  • Never use for: measuring elapsed time

Monotonic clock (duration clock)

System.nanoTime(), CLOCK_MONOTONIC, time.monotonic()

  • Only ever moves forward — never jumps back
  • Its absolute value is meaningless; comparing it across machines is nonsense
  • NTP may slew its rate (±0.05%) but cannot jump it
  • Use for: timeouts, latency measurement, rate limiters, retry backoff
⚠ Common misconception
“Measuring how long something took with two currentTimeMillis() calls is fine.”

It is fine until NTP steps the clock backwards mid-measurement — and then your duration is negative.

What happens next depends on your code. A negative duration in a retry backoff can produce an immediate infinite retry loop. In a rate limiter it can hand out unlimited tokens. In a lease check it can make an expired lease look valid. The bug lives for months and fires once, during a clock correction, with no way to reproduce it.

Rule: if you are subtracting two timestamps, you want the monotonic clock. Always.

Process Pauses — The Assumption That Breaks Everything

Here is the deepest idea in this chapter, and it is the one that separates people who have read about distributed systems from people who have debugged them.

Consider a leader holding a lease — a lock with a timeout. To stay leader it must renew before expiry. The natural implementation looks obviously correct:

// This code is WRONG. Two separate bugs. while (true) { request = getIncomingRequest(); // keep at least 10s of lease remaining if (lease.expiryTimeMillis - System.currentTimeMillis() < 10000) { lease = lease.renew(); } if (lease.isValid()) { process(request); // <-- what if we pause HERE? } }

Bug one: the expiry time was set by a different machine, and is being compared against this machine's wall clock. If those clocks differ by a few seconds, the logic is already wrong.

Bug two is worse, and no clock fixes it. The code assumes almost no time passes between checking lease.isValid() and running process(request). Normally that is microseconds. But if the thread is paused for 15 seconds right there, the lease expires, another node becomes leader — and this thread has no idea. It wakes up and processes the request as though it were still leader.

WHY A THREAD CAN PAUSE FOR SECONDS OR MINUTES ● Stop-the-world GC. JVM full GC pauses have been observed lasting minutes. Even "concurrent" collectors stop the world sometimes. ● VM suspension. A hypervisor can suspend a VM at any instruction and resume it later — live migration does exactly this. ● Laptop lid. On end-user devices, execution simply stops. ● Context switch / hypervisor steal. A noisy neighbour can starve your vCPU for an unbounded time. ● Swap / page fault. One memory access becomes a disk read. Thrashing turns microseconds into seconds. ● Synchronous disk I/O you did not know was there — classloading, a log write to a full disk, an fsync behind a lock. ● SIGSTOP from an operator, resumed much later with SIGCONT. A node cannot detect its own pause. From inside, no time passed. Only the outside world knows, and it has already moved on.
This is why “check the condition, then act” is unsafe in a distributed system: the gap between the check and the act is unbounded.
💡 The mental model to keep

On a single machine with threads, you protect a critical section with a mutex and the OS guarantees exclusion. In a distributed system there is no such guarantee — a node can be arbitrarily delayed while believing it holds exclusive access, and no amount of checking helps, because the check itself can be stale by the time you act on it.

So the safe pattern is never “check that I still hold the lock.” It is “make it impossible for my write to land if I no longer hold the lock” — enforced by the thing being written to.

Fencing Tokens — The Fix, and It Must Live in the Storage Layer

Here is the corruption in full, and it is not hypothetical — HBase shipped this bug:

WITHOUT FENCING — two clients write, file is corrupted Client 1 acquires lease ────────┦ ├─ GC PAUSE (long) ──────────────┦ │ lease expires... │ Client 2 └─ acquires lease ── writes ─┦ │ Client 1 resumes, still believes it holds the lease, WRITES ↓ FILE CORRUPTED WITH FENCING — the storage layer rejects the stale writer Client 1 acquires lease, token = 33 ──┦ ├─ GC PAUSE ──────────┦ Client 2 acquires lease, token = 34 ── write(token=34) → ACCEPTED storage remembers: max seen = 34 Client 1 resumes ─────────┦ write(token=33) → REJECTED 33 < 34 → stale writer ↓ DATA INTACT. Client 1 learns it lost the lock.
A fencing token is a monotonically increasing number issued with every lock grant. The resource tracks the highest token it has seen and rejects anything lower.
⚠ The part that is most often got wrong

The check must happen at the resource, not at the client. A client verifying its own lock status is worthless — the stale client is the thing that is wrong, and it sincerely believes it is fine.

If your storage does not support fencing natively, you can often smuggle it in: put the token in the filename, in a conditional-write predicate, or in a version column (WHERE epoch <= 34). What you cannot do is skip it and rely on the lock alone.

Where do tokens come from? Any monotonic counter from the coordination service: ZooKeeper's zxid or node cversion, etcd's revision, or Raft's term number — Raft's term is a fencing token by another name.

⚠ Common misconception
“We use a distributed lock, so exactly one process is doing the work.”

A distributed lock guarantees that at most one process believes it holds the lock at any moment. It does not guarantee that at most one process is acting on that belief — because a paused process cannot know its belief expired.

This distinction matters enormously in practice. It is why a lock is fine for efficiency (avoid duplicate work; a duplicate is merely wasteful) and unsafe for correctness (duplicates corrupt data) unless fenced.

Ask yourself this before every distributed lock: if two processes ran this simultaneously, would I lose money or corrupt data, or just waste CPU? If the former, a lock is not enough — you need fencing enforced at the resource.

Clock Readings Have a Confidence Interval

The most useful reframing in this chapter: a timestamp is not a point, it is a range. Your clock reads 10:00:00.123, but given drift since the last NTP sync and the network delay in that sync, the true time is somewhere in a window — perhaps 100ms wide on a normal server.

Most APIs hide this and hand you a single number, which invites you to compare timestamps as though they were exact. Google's TrueTime does the opposite — it returns [earliest, latest] and forces you to confront the uncertainty. That honesty is what makes Spanner's ordering guarantee possible:

TWO TIMESTAMPS, ORDER UNKNOWN A: [──────────] confidence interval of A B: [──────────] confidence interval of B ↑ OVERLAP → you CANNOT say A happened before B SPANNER'S ANSWER: make the overlap impossible by WAITING commit at timestamp T A: [──────────] ├─ commit-wait (~2ε, about 7–14ms) ─┦ B: [──────────] ↑ no overlap → B is definitely after A Spanner does not eliminate clock uncertainty. It bounds it, then waits it out. That deliberate wait is a real part of Spanner's write latency.
✎ Mini exercise 5

A nightly billing job must run exactly once. It runs on 5 replicas for availability. You implement it with Redis: SET billing:lock <uuid> NX PX 600000 (10-minute TTL). Whichever replica wins runs the job.

One night, two customers are charged twice. Redis never went down and the logs show only one SET succeeded.

Work out: how this happened despite the lock, and what you would change.

Show the worked answer

What happened: replica A won the lock and started the job. Partway through, it experienced a pause longer than 10 minutes — a stop-the-world GC on a large heap, a VM live-migration, or swap thrashing. Its lock expired. Replica B acquired the lock legitimately and ran the job. Replica A then resumed, unaware that any time had passed, and continued charging customers from where it left off.

Only one SET succeeded at a time — the logs are telling the truth. The lock was never violated. The lock did its job; the lock was simply never sufficient.

What I would change, in order of importance:

  • Make the charge idempotent. Every charge carries an idempotency key like charge:{customer_id}:{billing_period}, enforced by a unique constraint in the ledger. Now a duplicate attempt is rejected by the database regardless of what the lock did. This alone fixes the incident.
  • Add a fencing token. Move the lock to etcd or ZooKeeper, take the revision/zxid as a token, and have the ledger reject writes carrying a token below the highest it has seen. This closes the general case, not just charges.
  • Do not raise the TTL. The instinct is to change 10 minutes to 60. That does not fix anything — it just makes the failure rarer and the recovery slower. There is no TTL that is provably longer than the longest possible pause.

The transferable lesson — and it is the single most valuable one in this chapter: do not try to prevent the stale actor from acting. You cannot. Make its action harmless when it arrives. Idempotency and fencing are both instances of that principle.

🎓 Understanding Check — Time, Pauses and Truth

Teaching questions with answers supplied.
Why does a timeout not tell you whether the server processed your request?

Because a timeout is the absence of a response, and there are at least four ways to get that: the request never arrived; it arrived and is still executing; it executed and the response was lost; or the server crashed midway. All four look identical from the client.

This is why the correct response to a timeout is never simply “retry.” It is “retry an operation I have made safe to repeat” — or query by idempotency key to discover what actually happened.

Why can't a node detect its own pause and refuse to act?

Because from inside the process, no time passed — the pause happens between two instructions and leaves no trace in the program's own state. The thread resumes exactly where it left off with all its assumptions intact.

It could re-read the clock after resuming and notice a large jump — and defensive code sometimes does this. But it is fundamentally a race: the check happens after resuming, and the unsafe action may already be in flight. The reliable fix is external enforcement (fencing), not internal detection.

Why is “the truth is defined by the majority” the only workable rule?

Because no individual node's view can be trusted — a node may be partitioned, paused, or simply wrong about its own status, and it cannot tell the difference. If any single node's belief counted, a partitioned node would keep acting as leader.

A quorum works because two majorities of the same set must overlap in at least one member, and that member carries the memory of the earlier decision. So a node that lost its majority genuinely has lost its authority, whatever it believes.

When are synchronized clocks actually safe to rely on?

When you either (a) only need approximate answers — log timestamps, metric buckets, cache TTLs where a few seconds of error is harmless; or (b) explicitly account for the uncertainty, as Spanner does with confidence intervals and commit-wait.

They are not safe for ordering events across machines when correctness depends on the order. Last-write-wins conflict resolution is the canonical misuse: a node with a fast clock can silently suppress every correct write from its peers for the duration of the skew.

What is the practical difference between a lock used for efficiency and one used for correctness?

An efficiency lock prevents duplicate work; if it occasionally fails, you waste CPU. Redis SET NX PX is entirely adequate here.

A correctness lock prevents data corruption; if it fails, you lose money or destroy data. This needs a consensus-backed lock service plus fencing enforced at the resource — and ideally an idempotent operation underneath so the lock is a performance optimisation rather than the safety mechanism.

Asking which kind you have, out loud, before writing the code, prevents a whole class of production incident.

🌱 Takeaway — Time and Truth

This chapter is about a single uncomfortable fact: you cannot trust your own clock, your own liveness, or your own beliefs about your role.

  • Two clocks. Monotonic for durations, wall clock for calendar times. Subtracting wall-clock timestamps is a bug waiting for an NTP correction.
  • Processes pause arbitrarily — GC, VM migration, swap, hypervisor steal. There is no safe upper bound, so no TTL is provably long enough.
  • A node cannot detect its own pause. Any “check then act” has an unbounded gap between the check and the act.
  • Fencing tokens are the fix, and they must be enforced at the resource. Client-side checking is worthless.
  • Timestamps are intervals, not points. If the intervals overlap, the order is unknown — and pretending otherwise is how LWW loses data.
  • Truth is whatever a quorum agrees on, never what one node believes.

Which raises the question the next chapters answer: how does a group of nodes agree on anything at all, when none of them can be trusted individually? That is consensus.

📝 Interview Q&A

Your team is debating whether to use timestamps or version numbers for conflict detection. How do you advise?

Version numbers (monotonic integers) for conflict detection; timestamps for human-readable ordering.

Timestamps fail for conflict detection because of clock skew. If Server A updates with ts=1000 and Server B updates with ts=999 (B's clock is slightly behind), LWW would choose A's write even if B's write came later in real time. You've silently lost data.

Version numbers (also called sequence numbers or ETags in HTTP) are safe: compare expected_version with current_version. If they match, proceed. If not, conflict detected. No clock dependence.

In practice: use optimistic locking with version numbers for conflict detection. Use timestamps only for things like 'when was this created' (human display), not for deciding which write wins.

Explain why vector clocks are better than Lamport clocks for detecting write conflicts in a distributed database.

Lamport clocks provide a total order — every event gets a number and A < B means A happened before B. But if A has Lamport clock 5 and B has clock 8, you cannot tell if A caused B or if they're concurrent. 8 > 5 just means B happened after A OR at the same time with a different process sequence.

Vector clocks provide partial order with concurrency detection. If VC_A = [2, 0, 0] and VC_B = [0, 2, 0], neither dominates the other — they're concurrent writes. Both happened without knowledge of the other. This is exactly when you have a conflict to resolve.

For a database, concurrent writes to the same key need to be resolved (LWW, app merge, or surfaced to user). Lamport clocks would silently discard one. Vector clocks let you detect and handle the conflict correctly.
