Part 2
26 End-to-End System Designs
Every design answers a question reported from a real Google loop, and every one runs the same nine steps in the same order — so once you have read one, you know where to find anything in all twenty-six. The method below is the point; the systems are how it is practised.

How to read a design — the nine steps, and why in this order

All twenty-six designs run these steps identically. The order is not arbitrary: each step constrains the next, so working them out of order is how people end up designing a system that answers a question nobody asked.

1
📋Requirements
Pin down what you are actually building before building it. Opens with the clarifying questions to ask, each paired with what the answer changes — then functional and non-functional requirements.
2
📊Capacity estimation
Get to the one number that decides the architecture. Opens with the assumptions and what breaks if each is wrong, because an unstated assumption is a bug waiting for traffic.
3
🔌API design
Fix the contract. This is where idempotency keys, cursors and error semantics get decided, and those choices constrain everything downstream.
4
🗂Schema design
Decide where state lives and how it is keyed. The partition key is chosen here, and it is the hardest thing to change later.
5
🏗High-level architecture
The boxes and arrows, plus an animated version showing what data moves — with a toggle for what happens when it breaks.
6
🔍Component deep dives
Two or three components examined properly. This is where an interview is won: depth on the part that actually matters, not breadth on all of them.
7
⚖Trade-off analysis
What was chosen, what was rejected, and why — stated as a decision with an alternative, never as a fact.
8
🛡Fault tolerance
What fails, and what happens when it does. Includes the failures that produce no error at all, which are the dangerous ones.
9
🏁Conclusion
What you say in the last three minutes: the dominant constraint, what you would build first, what you deliberately did not build, and the biggest risk.

How to actually use one of these. Read step 1, then close the page and draw the design yourself before reading on. Comparing your answer with the one here is worth several times what reading it straight through is worth — and the gap between the two is the only part you need to study.

The order matters more than any individual answer. An interviewer watching you go straight from the prompt to a box diagram has already learned something about you. The first two steps are where the L6 signal lives — naming the dominant constraint before anyone steers you there. T6 has the rubric.

Design a URL Shortener (TinyURL / bit.ly)

Difficulty: Medium  .  Target: 45 min
💬 The question, as asked

“Design a URL shortener like TinyURL or bit.ly. Users paste a long URL and get a short one back; anyone who visits the short link is redirected. Some customers want custom aliases and click analytics.”

⚡ What makes it hard

It looks trivial and is really a read-amplification problem — roughly 100 reads per write. The interesting decisions are how short codes are generated without coordination, and whether you can afford a 301 (fast, cacheable, invisible to analytics) or need a 302 (every hit reaches you).

📋1. Understanding the question

The prompt is usually one line: “Design a URL shortener like bit.ly.” Paste a long link, get a short one, and anyone who visits the short one ends up at the long one.

It is the classic opener, and it is deceptive. The functionality takes about five minutes to describe. What the interviewer is actually watching is whether you notice the shape of the traffic.

Because here is the thing about a link shortener: nobody shortens a link a hundred times. They shorten it once and it gets clicked a hundred thousand times. Writes are rare and reads are enormous, and that ratio decides every interesting choice in the design.

🎯 The shape of the problem

Roughly 100 reads for every write. This is not a database problem; it is a caching and redirect problem with a small database attached.

What they are looking for

Do you see the read:write ratio and act on it? If you spend the whole session on the write path, you have designed for 1% of the traffic.

How do you generate the short code? This is the one genuinely interesting technical choice, and there are three reasonable answers with different trade-offs. Having an opinion here, and knowing why, is most of the signal.

Do you know what a 301 costs you? Most people reach for a permanent redirect because it is faster. It is, and it also means you never see the click. If the customer wants analytics, you cannot have both.

❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
What is the read-to-write ratio?
At 100:1 or higher this stops being a database problem and becomes a caching and CDN problem — which changes the entire design.
Are custom aliases allowed?
A yes introduces a global uniqueness constraint and a collision path that a pure counter design does not have.
Do links expire?
Decides whether you need TTL, garbage collection, and whether short codes can be safely reused.
Do we need per-click analytics?
This is what forces 302 over 301. A 301 lets browsers and the CDN absorb the redirect and you never see the hit.
Is it acceptable for codes to be guessable?
A sequential counter in base62 leaks your creation volume and lets anyone enumerate every link ever made.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.
📝2. Functional requirements

Small list. That is fine, and worth saying so rather than padding it.

  • Shorten. Give me a long URL, get back a short one.
  • Redirect. Visit the short one, land on the long one.
  • Custom aliases, optionally. A customer wants /black-friday rather than /a7Kd2p.
  • Expiry, optionally. Some links should stop working after a date.
  • Click analytics, optionally. How many clicks, from where.

The three optional ones each pull the design in a different direction, which is why they are worth surfacing early rather than discovering at minute thirty. Custom aliases introduce a uniqueness problem the generated codes do not have. Analytics rules out the fastest redirect.

⏱3. Non-functional requirements

These matter much more than the feature list.

RequirementTargetWhy
Redirect latency< 50 msThis sits between a click and a page load. Every millisecond here is added to somebody else's site being slow.
AvailabilityVery highA broken shortener does not degrade gracefully. Every link anyone ever shared is dead at once, including in printed material.
Shorten latency< 500 msNobody minds waiting half a second once. Compare that to the redirect budget.
DurabilityAbsoluteLosing a mapping means a link on a billboard now goes nowhere and there is no way to recover it.
Codes not guessableDependsIf links are public that is fine. If they are shared privately, a sequential counter lets anyone walk the whole space.

Notice availability is the unusual one. Most systems degrade: slower, staler, fewer features. A shortener does not. It works or every link in the world that points through you is broken.

🗂4. Data model and API

The data model is almost trivially small, and that is worth noticing. One row per link, keyed by the short code.

-- Primary store (DynamoDB -- key-value, high read throughput) TABLE urls { short_code VARCHAR(10) PARTITION KEY, long_url TEXT, -- up to 2KB owner_id BIGINT, -- NULL = anonymous created_at TIMESTAMP, expires_at TIMESTAMP, -- NULL = never is_active BOOLEAN DEFAULT true } -- Click analytics (Cassandra -- time-series, append-only) TABLE clicks { short_code VARCHAR(10) PARTITION KEY, clicked_at TIMESTAMP CLUSTERING KEY DESC, country VARCHAR(2), referrer TEXT, ip_hash VARCHAR(64) -- hashed for privacy } -- Click counter (Redis, async flush to DynamoDB every 60s) KEY click_count:{short_code} -> INTEGER

There is no relational structure here at all. We look up by short code and nothing else, which is why a key-value store fits so naturally: no joins, no secondary access patterns, and a workload that is 99% point reads.

The API

POST /api/v1/urls Body: { long_url, alias?, ttl_days? } Response: 201 { short_code, short_url, expires_at? } Errors: 400 (bad URL), 409 (alias taken) GET /{short_code} Response: 301 Location: {long_url} (permanent, CDN-cacheable) 302 Location: {long_url} (if analytics tracking needed) Errors: 404 (not found), 410 (expired) GET /api/v1/urls/{short_code}/stats Response: { clicks, top_countries, referrers, created_at } DELETE /api/v1/urls/{short_code} Response: 204 (idempotent -- safe to retry)

The 301 versus 302 line is the whole design in miniature. A 301 says “this is permanent”, so browsers and CDNs cache it and stop asking us. Our traffic drops enormously. We also stop seeing the clicks.

So the answer is per link, not per system. Links that need analytics get a 302 and cost us a request every time. Everything else gets a 301 and costs us nothing after the first visit.

📊5. Capacity estimation

Rough numbers, to show which parts are actually under pressure.

⚖ Assumptions — and what breaks if each is wrong
100M new URLs/day, 10B redirects/day
If the ratio were closer to 1:1 the CDN and cache tier stop paying for themselves and this becomes a write-throughput design.
Short codes are 7 characters, base62
62^7 is ~3.5 trillion. At 100M/day that is ~95 years of headroom; at 10B/day it is under a year and the code length must grow.
Links are effectively permanent
If most links expired in 30 days, storage would plateau and a TTL sweep becomes a required component rather than an optional one.
~1,200
write QPS avg
~3,600
write QPS peak (3x)
~116K
read QPS avg
~350K
read QPS peak
~50 GB
storage/day
~18 TB
storage/year

Look at the two QPS figures. Writes are about a thousand a second, which one modest database handles without thinking. Reads are a hundred times that.

Then notice that most of those reads never reach us at all, because 301s are cached at the edge. The system we are designing mostly exists to handle the small fraction of traffic that gets past the CDN. Storage is similarly undramatic: a few hundred bytes per link, tens of terabytes over years, which is large but not interesting.

⚖6. The key trade-offs

Four choices carry the design.

DecisionChosen vAlternative xReasoning
DB choiceDynamoDBPostgreSQLPure key-value access. No joins. Auto-scales. Managed. 100:1 read ratio means caching dominates -- DB is rarely hit.
ID generationCounter + Base62Random/HashNo collision handling. Predictable length. Pre-allocated ranges eliminate hot path to counter service.
Redirect code301 (popular URLs)302 always301 = CDN/browser cache = massive origin load reduction. 302 required for analytics. Use 301 for non-tracked, 302 for tracked.
AnalyticsAsync Kafka pipelineSync DB write on redirectZero added latency to redirect critical path. Analytics are eventually consistent -- acceptable.

The first row is the one to be able to defend. Hashing the long URL is the instinctive answer and it sounds elegant: same URL, same code, no state. But hashes collide, so now you need collision detection and a retry loop, and you have to decide whether two people shortening the same URL should get the same code (which leaks that somebody else shortened it).

A counter has none of those problems. It cannot collide, the code length is predictable, and handing each server a block of a million ids means the counter is not on the hot path.

🏗7. High-level design
Redirect path — and the viral link that goes cold
request301 redirectlookupmiss
What is moving: a short code out, a 301 back. Because a 301 is permanent, browsers and the CDN cache it, so a popular link is served almost entirely at the edge and the origin never sees most of its traffic.
What goes wrong: a purge or a TTL expiry empties the edge just as a link goes viral. Every request now misses through to the service and the KV store, which was sized on the assumption that the edge absorbs ~95% of reads. The fix is not a bigger database — it is request coalescing so N simultaneous misses become one lookup (Ch 9), plus 301 rather than 302 wherever analytics permits.

Two paths, and they look nothing like each other.

WRITING A LINK rare, ~1,200/s client → API → grab an id from this server's pre-allocated block → base62 encode it → write one row no coordination: the block was handed out in advance READING A LINK constant, ~350,000/s at peak click | v CDN / browser cache most 301s never get past here | miss v REDIRECT SERVICE | v CACHE hot links, ~99% hit | miss v KEY-VALUE STORE one point read
Three layers of caching in front of a very small database. That is the design: the store is almost an implementation detail, and the interesting engineering is in how little traffic ever reaches it.
🔄8. Workflows — what actually happens

Let us walk through it with a real link.

Priya shortens a link
The write path. Happens once.
  1. Priya pastes a long article URL into the box and hits Shorten.
  2. The request lands on server 7. That server was handed ids 4,000,000–4,999,999 when it started, and it is currently on 4,213,887. It takes the next one. No other server can hand out that id, so there is nothing to coordinate.
  3. 4,213,888 in base62 is Ru1M. Four characters, because the number is still small.
  4. One row is written: Ru1M maps to her long URL.
  5. She gets back short.ly/Ru1M and posts it.
One database write, no locks, no collision check, no coordination between servers. The id block is what buys all of that.
200,000 people click it
The read path, and where the traffic actually goes.
  1. First click. The CDN has never seen Ru1M. It asks our redirect service, which checks the cache, misses, reads one row, and returns 301 to the article.
  2. The CDN stores that redirect. So does the visitor's browser.
  3. Second click, different person, same city. The CDN answers it. We never hear about it.
  4. Clicks 3 through 200,000. Handled at the edge, or by browsers that already have it. A few thousand reach us as each new CDN region warms up.
  5. Of 200,000 clicks, we serve maybe a few hundred.
This is why the database being small is not a problem. The design's job is to make sure almost every click is answered by somebody else.
Two customers want /black-friday
Custom aliases, where the generated-code guarantees do not apply.
  1. Both submit the alias black-friday within the same second.
  2. A naive implementation checks “is it taken?”, sees no for both, and then writes for both. One silently overwrites the other.
  3. Instead we do a conditional insert: write this alias only if it does not already exist. The first one succeeds.
  4. The second violates the uniqueness constraint. The database rejects it and we return 409.
  5. That customer is told the alias is taken and offered another.
Generated codes can never collide because the counter guarantees it. Chosen codes can, which is why the two paths need different write logic.
The link goes viral right after a cache purge
The one case that actually hurts.
  1. A deploy purges the CDN. Every cached redirect is gone.
  2. At that moment the link is being shared heavily. 40,000 requests a second arrive, and every one is a miss.
  3. They pass through to the redirect service, which finds nothing in its cache either, and all of them go to the database for the same row.
  4. With request coalescing, the first miss does the read and the other 39,999 wait for that one result.
  5. One database read instead of 40,000. The answer is cached and the next second is served from memory.
Note what coalescing traded: 40,000 requests now depend on one read finishing. That is fine here, because the read is sub-millisecond. It still needs a timeout.
🔍9. Deep dives, and what breaks

Choosing how to make the short code

Three options, and the reasoning matters more than the answer.

Hash the long URL. Take an MD5, keep the first seven characters. It is stateless and the same URL always produces the same code. But hashes collide, so you need to detect the collision and try again, which means a read before every write. And identical URLs producing identical codes leaks information: I can find out whether somebody else has already shortened a link.

Random. Generate seven random characters. No information leak. But with enough links you start colliding, so you are back to checking before writing.

A counter. Keep a global number, encode it in base62. It cannot collide, ever. Code length grows naturally as the number does. The obvious objection is that a global counter is a bottleneck, and the fix is to hand each server a block of a million ids at startup. Now the counter is touched once per million links rather than once per link.

That last design has a downside worth admitting: codes are sequential, so anyone can walk them. If that matters, encrypt the counter before encoding it. You keep uniqueness and lose the predictability.

The 301 decision

A permanent redirect is cached by browsers and CDNs, often for a very long time. That is wonderful for load and terrible for two things.

You cannot count clicks, because you never see them. And you cannot really change where a link points, because copies of the old answer are sitting in caches you do not control.

So this is a per-link decision driven by what the customer bought. Analytics customers get 302s and we absorb their traffic. Everyone else gets 301s, and their links cost us almost nothing after the first visit in each region.

Why a key-value store

There are no joins here. There is one access pattern, by primary key, and it is 99% reads. A relational database would work perfectly well and you would use almost none of what it offers.

The reason to prefer a key-value store is not speed at small scale, where they are comparable. It is that the workload is a natural fit for horizontal partitioning by key, and short codes are uniformly distributed by construction, so the shards stay balanced without any effort.

What breaks

DynamoDB node failure
Managed multi-AZ DynamoDB: automatic failover. Read from Redis during DB degradation -- cache continues serving popular URLs. On cache miss during outage: return 503 with Retry-After header.
Redis failure
Redis Cluster with replicas. On failure: read API falls through to DynamoDB directly (5ms vs 0.1ms, but correct). CDN cache continues serving popular URLs without any origin hit.
ID generator crash
Pre-allocated ranges stored per server. On crash: ID range is abandoned (some IDs wasted, no duplicates). New instance gets new range. No coordination needed on hot path.
CDN outage
DNS failover to origin. Higher latency (CDN miss -> origin). Multi-CDN strategy (CloudFront + Fastly) as mitigation for critical SLAs.
Analytics pipeline lag
Kafka durable (7-day retention). Consumer lag = analytics delayed, not lost. Zero impact on redirect service -- analytics consumer entirely decoupled.
The dominant constraint

The 100:1 read-to-write ratio. Everything follows from it: a counter-based ID so writes never coordinate, and a CDN plus cache tier that absorbs almost all reads before they reach storage.

What I would build first

The KGS counter with pre-allocated ranges and the cache-in-front-of-KV read path. Analytics can be added later without touching either.

What I deliberately did not build

Real-time analytics, custom domains, and link previews. I would use 302 only for the small subset of links that need per-click tracking, and 301 for the rest so the CDN keeps absorbing them.

The biggest risk

The cache tier. At a 99% hit rate the origin sees 1% of 350K QPS; at 95% it sees five times that. I would alert on hit rate, not just on origin latency.

💬 If you get this far, here is what they will push on
Follow-ups an interviewer is likely to ask once the design is on the board. Answers supplied — read the question, answer it out loud, then open it.
“What if a single short link goes viral and gets 50,000 requests a second?”Answer

Almost all of that never reaches us. The redirect is a 301, so browsers and the CDN cache it, and a hot link is served at the edge. That is the main reason to prefer 301 over 302 wherever you can.

The case that hurts is a viral link right after a cache purge, when everything misses through at once. The fix is request coalescing: the first miss does the lookup and everyone else waits for that one result, rather than 50,000 identical queries hitting the database.

If the customer needs per-click analytics we cannot use 301, because we never see the hit. Then the link genuinely is hot on our side, and it wants its own cache entry with a short TTL.

“How do you stop someone scraping every short link you have ever made?”Answer

A sequential counter in base62 makes this trivial for an attacker: abc123 is next to abc124. They can walk the whole space, and along the way they learn exactly how many links you create per day.

The usual fix is to keep the counter (it is what gives you collision-free ids) but obscure the output, either by encrypting the counter with a block cipher before encoding, or by allocating ranges to servers out of order. Either way you keep uniqueness without publishing your growth rate.

Rate limiting per IP helps a little but does not solve it, because the space is enumerable by anybody patient.

“What happens when you run out of 7-character codes?”Answer

Base62 with 7 characters is about 3.5 trillion combinations. At 100 million new links a day that is roughly 95 years, so in practice you do not run out.

What you should say is what happens if the assumption is wrong. Because ids come from a counter, the length grows naturally: when the counter passes 627 the encoding produces 8 characters and nothing else changes. No migration, no reshuffle. That is a nice property of counter-based ids that hash-based ones do not have.

“Can you support custom aliases like /black-friday?”Answer

Yes, but it changes the shape of the problem. Generated codes never collide because the counter guarantees it. Custom aliases are chosen by users, so two people can want the same one, and now you need a uniqueness check at write time.

That is a conditional insert on the alias, not a read-then-write, or two people racing both see it free and both think they won. It also needs a reserved list, because you do not want somebody claiming /login or /api.

“How do you delete a link, given it is cached everywhere?”Answer

You cannot pull it out of every browser cache, which is the honest answer and worth saying. A 301 you have handed out may be cached for a year.

So deletion is best-effort: remove it from the database, purge the CDN, and accept that clients who already cached it will keep redirecting for a while. If a customer genuinely needs revocation to be immediate, they cannot have 301s at all, and the cost is that every hit now reaches your origin.

Design Twitter / Social Media Feed

Difficulty: Hard  .  Target: 45 min
💬 The question, as asked

“Design the home timeline for a social network. A user posts; their followers should see it. Timelines must load fast for hundreds of millions of users.”

⚡ What makes it hard

Follower-count skew. Most accounts have a few hundred followers and a handful have tens of millions, so no single strategy works for both. Precomputing timelines is fast to read and impossible for celebrities; computing on read is the reverse.

📋1. Understanding the question

The prompt: “Design the home timeline for a social network. Someone posts; their followers see it.”

Two sentences, and almost all of the difficulty is hidden in the word followers.

If everyone had roughly the same number of followers, this would be easy. Pick either strategy and it works. But follower counts are wildly uneven: most accounts have a few hundred, and a handful have forty million. No single strategy serves both ends of that distribution, and recognising that is the entire question.

🎯 The tension

You can do the work when someone posts (fast reads, impossible for celebrities) or when someone reads (cheap writes, slow feeds). Neither works alone. The answer is both, with a threshold.

What they are looking for

Do you reach for fan-out and then notice it breaks? Precomputing every follower's timeline is the natural first answer and it is right for 99.9% of accounts. The signal is whether you catch the case where it is catastrophically wrong before being prompted.

Do you know which way the traffic runs? Reads outnumber writes by orders of magnitude. That is what justifies doing expensive work at write time at all.

Can you name the cost of your choice? Fan-out-on-write makes deletes expensive and ranking awkward. Saying so unprompted is worth more than the design itself.

❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
What is the follower count at the 99th percentile?
This is the dominant constraint. A few accounts with tens of millions of followers is what breaks fan-out-on-write and forces a hybrid.
Is the timeline chronological or ranked?
Ranked puts a scoring service on the read path, which changes the latency budget and makes precomputation much harder.
How stale may a new post be before it appears?
Seconds allows fan-out-on-write; instant forces pull. This single number decides push versus pull.
Do we support edits and deletes?
Fan-out-on-write copies a post into millions of timelines, so retraction becomes an expensive distributed cleanup.
What is the read-to-write ratio?
Fan-out-on-write only pays off when reads dominate. If they do not, you have pre-computed work nobody reads.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.
📝2. Functional requirements
  • Post. Write something; it becomes visible to followers.
  • Home timeline. A reverse-chronological list of posts from people you follow, paginated.
  • User timeline. Everything one account posted.
  • Follow and unfollow.
  • Delete. A post disappears from everywhere it was shown.

Delete is the one people skip, and it is worth keeping on the list because it is the requirement that punishes the design we are about to choose. If a post has been copied into half a million timelines, removing it is half a million writes unless you plan for it.

⏱3. Non-functional requirements
RequirementTargetWhy
Timeline load< 200 msThis is the app's home screen. It is the most-run query in the entire system, by a wide margin.
Post visibilityA few secondsNobody can tell whether their post reached followers instantly or three seconds later. This tolerance is what makes asynchronous fan-out possible.
Read:write ratio~1000:1People scroll far more than they post. Spending effort at write time to make reads cheap is therefore a good trade.
AvailabilityReads > writesA feed that will not load is a dead app. A post that fails can be retried by the user.
OrderingRoughly chronological“Roughly” matters. Strict global ordering across millions of writers would need coordination nobody needs.

That third row is the one that licenses the whole design. When reads outnumber writes a thousand to one, doing a thousand units of work at write time to save one unit at read time is still a win.

🗂4. Data model and API

Two things to store: the posts themselves, and each person's precomputed timeline.

-- Tweets (Cassandra -- write-heavy, time-series, no joins) TABLE tweets { tweet_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, -- Snowflake: time-sortable user_id BIGINT, content TEXT, media_ids LIST<UUID>, reply_to BIGINT, -- NULL for original tweets like_count BIGINT, -- eventually consistent Redis counter created_at TIMESTAMP } -- User timelines (Redis sorted set -- fast, ephemeral) KEY timeline:{user_id} -> ZSET { tweet_id: score=tweet_id } -- Capped at 800 entries. tweet_id = Snowflake = time-sorted. -- Social graph (separate service -- high read throughput) TABLE follows { follower_id BIGINT PARTITION KEY, followee_id BIGINT CLUSTERING KEY, created_at TIMESTAMP } TABLE followers { -- reverse: who follows a given user? followee_id BIGINT PARTITION KEY, follower_id BIGINT CLUSTERING KEY } -- Users (MySQL -- low write rate, strong consistency needed for uniqueness) TABLE users { user_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, username VARCHAR(50) UNIQUE, is_celebrity BOOLEAN, -- follower_count > 1M follower_countBIGINT }

Storing ids rather than posts in the timeline is the decision that makes this affordable. A post appearing in a million timelines is stored once and referenced a million times. It also makes deletion cheap, which we will come back to.

Post ids are time-sortable, so a timeline is already in order without storing timestamps alongside, and pagination is a cursor rather than an offset. Offsets break badly on a feed that mutates while you read it.

The API

POST /v1/tweets Body: { text, media_ids?, reply_to? } Response: 201 { tweet_id, created_at } // returns as soon as the tweet is durable; fan-out is async GET /v1/timeline/home?cursor=&limit=50 Response: { items:[{tweet_id, author, text, ts}], next_cursor } // cursor is (ts, tweet_id), never an offset -- offsets skip // or repeat items when the feed mutates under the reader GET /v1/timeline/user/{user_id}?cursor=&limit=50 POST /v1/follow Body: { target_id } -> 202 // 202: following a celebrity may enqueue backfill work DELETE /v1/tweets/{id} -> 204 (idempotent)
📊5. Capacity estimation

The numbers that decide things.

⚖ Assumptions — and what breaks if each is wrong
Median user follows a few hundred accounts
If the median were tens of thousands, fan-out-on-write stops being affordable for everyone, not just celebrities.
Timeline is chronological
Ranking would put a scoring service on the read path and largely invalidate precomputed timelines.
A few seconds of delay before a post appears is acceptable
Instant visibility rules out fan-out-on-write entirely and forces a pull-and-merge design.
~12K
tweet write QPS avg
~36K
write QPS peak
~1.2M
read QPS avg
~3.6M
read QPS peak
~500 GB
tweet storage/day
2.4M
fan-out ops/sec avg

The important one is not in the table: the follower distribution. Median around a few hundred, ninety-ninth percentile in the tens of thousands, and a long tail running to tens of millions.

Fan-out cost is the sum of follower counts across all posts. At the median that is a few hundred writes per post, which is nothing. For one account with forty million followers it is forty million writes for a single post, which is more work than the entire rest of the platform does in that second.

⚖6. The key trade-offs

The choices, and what each costs.

DecisionChosen vAlternative xReasoning
Fan-out strategyHybrid (write for regular, read for celebs)Pure write OR pure readPure write: 100M ops for one celebrity tweet impossible. Pure read: 1,000 Cassandra reads per timeline load for heavy followers. Hybrid balances both.
Tweet storageCassandraMySQLWrite-heavy, time-series access, no joins. Cassandra's LSM-tree excellent for append-heavy workloads. MySQL's B-tree would be slower for writes.
Timeline storageRedis sorted setCassandraSub-ms sorted reads. Volatile OK (rebuild from Cassandra on miss). ZRANGE is ideal for time-ordered tweet IDs.
ConsistencyEventual (seconds lag OK)StrongStrong consistency requires synchronous fan-out to millions of Redis nodes. Not feasible. 2-5 second timeline lag is invisible to users.

The first row is the design. Everything after it follows.

Fan-out-on-write means a read is a single sequential fetch of a list somebody already built for you. That is why feeds load fast. You pay for it at write time, and you pay again on delete, and you pay a third time if ranking ever arrives.

🏗7. High-level design
Fan-out on write — and the celebrity that stalls it for everybody
the posttimeline copies40M copies
What is moving: the post is written once and made durable, then — asynchronously — copied into every follower’s timeline. Reads afterwards are a single sequential fetch of a precomputed list, which is why this shape wins when reads vastly outnumber writes.
What goes wrong: an account with 40 million followers posts. The same loop now enqueues 40 million copies, saturating the fan-out workers, and every ordinary user’s post sits behind it — a queue delay that has nothing to do with those users. This is why production systems are hybrid: above a follower threshold, stop fanning out and merge the celebrity’s posts at read time instead.

The two halves.

WRITE someone posts author → write post (durable) → return 201 immediately | v FAN-OUT QUEUE asynchronous: the author is not waiting | +-----------+-----------+ v v ORDINARY AUTHOR CELEBRITY push post_id into do nothing. each follower's list leave it in their own timeline. a few hundred writes zero writes READ someone opens the app precomputed timeline (one sequential read) + recent posts from the celebrities they follow (a few reads) | v merge by time, return 50
Most users follow nobody above the threshold, so the merge is usually a no-op and the read is a single fetch. The hybrid only costs something for the people it exists to serve.
🔄8. Workflows — what actually happens
Sam posts, and his 400 followers see it
The ordinary case, which is 99.9% of posts.
  1. Sam posts. We write one row and return 201 straight away. He is not waiting for anything else.
  2. A job picks it up from the fan-out queue and looks up who follows Sam. 400 people.
  3. It pushes Sam's post id onto the front of each of those 400 timeline lists. Ids only, about 8 bytes each.
  4. Each list is trimmed to its most recent few hundred entries, so it cannot grow forever.
  5. Total time from post to visible: under two seconds.
  6. When Dana opens the app, we fetch her list, take the first 50 ids, and load those 50 posts. One sequential read plus a batch get.
Dana's feed loaded without touching the follow graph at all. The work was done two seconds earlier, once, by Sam's post.
An account with 40 million followers posts
Where the strategy above falls apart.
  1. Same first step: write the post, return 201.
  2. The fan-out job looks up the follower count and sees 40,000,000.
  3. If we fanned out, that is 40 million list writes for one post. At any realistic throughput this takes minutes, and every other post queued behind it waits.
  4. That is the real damage. It is not that the celebrity's post is slow; it is that Sam's post, sitting behind it in the queue, is now also slow.
  5. So we stop. The post stays in the celebrity's own timeline and nothing is pushed anywhere.
  6. When Dana opens the app, we fetch her precomputed list and the recent posts of the three celebrities she follows, and merge by time.
Three extra reads on Dana's feed load. Compare that to 40 million writes, most of which would land in timelines nobody opens today.
Sam deletes a post that reached 500,000 timelines
The bill for fan-out-on-write.
  1. The post id is sitting in half a million lists.
  2. Deleting it properly means half a million list edits, which is as expensive as the original fan-out.
  3. Instead we do one write: mark the post deleted, and put its id in a small set of deleted ids held in cache.
  4. When Dana loads her feed, we fetch 50 ids and drop any that are in that set before loading the posts.
  5. The stale ids are cleaned out of the lists lazily, in the background, whenever a list is next trimmed.
Reads do a tiny bit more work; the delete is one write instead of 500,000. That is the right side to pay on, because deletes are rare and reads never stop.
🔍9. Deep dives, and what breaks

Why precompute at all

The alternative is to build the feed when it is asked for: look up who you follow, fetch their recent posts, merge, return. It is simple and it stores nothing extra.

It is also the same work repeated on every single feed load. If you follow 500 accounts, that is 500 lookups every time you pull to refresh, and you refresh far more often than the people you follow post. Doing it once at write time and reusing the result is strictly less work when reads outnumber writes a thousand to one.

Where the threshold should sit

There is no correct number, and saying so is better than inventing one. What matters is what you watch.

The metric is fan-out lag: how long between a post being accepted and it reaching the last follower's timeline. Set the threshold too high and one large account stalls the queue for everybody, which shows up as ordinary users' posts taking minutes to appear. Set it too low and you push lots of accounts onto the read-time merge path, which makes feeds slower for the people who follow them.

Start somewhere in the tens of thousands, watch lag broken down by author tier, and move it. The point is that it is a dial with an observable consequence, not a constant.

What ranking would cost

Everything here assumes reverse-chronological order, and that assumption is load-bearing. A timeline is a sorted list, so appending to it is cheap and reading it is a sequential scan.

Ranking breaks that. If the order depends on a score computed from recency, engagement and your own history, then the list is no longer stable and precomputing it means recomputing it constantly.

The usual compromise keeps fan-out for the candidate set and ranks at read time over a few hundred candidates rather than the whole corpus. You keep the cheap write path and accept a scoring service on the read path, which is a real latency cost you should name rather than gloss over.

What breaks

Redis timeline lost
Redis Cluster. On node loss: rebuild affected timelines from Cassandra on next request. Slow first load (~500ms), fast thereafter. Alert if rebuild rate is high (many nodes lost).
Fan-out service overwhelmed
Kafka back-pressure: fan-out workers pull at their own rate. Scale worker pods horizontally. Kafka retains messages for 7 days -- no loss during overload. Users see timeline lag, not errors.
Cassandra node failure
RF=3, quorum reads/writes. Node failure -> automatic reroute to replicas. Cassandra's gossip protocol detects failure in ~3s. No manual intervention.
Celebrity posts viral tweet (traffic spike)
Celebrity tweets use read fan-out -- no write spike. CDN caches user profile pages. Rate limit profile page fetches. Auto-scale read API pods on CPU metric.
The dominant constraint

Follower-count skew. A handful of accounts with tens of millions of followers is what makes a single fan-out strategy impossible, so the design is a hybrid rather than a choice between push and pull.

What I would build first

Fan-out-on-write for the ordinary case, with a celebrity threshold above which posts are pulled and merged at read time.

What I deliberately did not build

Ranking, ads and notifications. A chronological timeline is a legitimate v1 and it keeps the read path free of a scoring service.

The biggest risk

Getting the celebrity threshold wrong. Too high and one account can stall the fan-out queue for everyone; I would make it a tunable and monitor fan-out lag per tier.

💬 If you get this far, here is what they will push on
Follow-ups an interviewer is likely to ask once the design is on the board. Answers supplied — read the question, answer it out loud, then open it.
“A user with 40 million followers posts. What actually happens?”Answer

If we fanned out, we would be writing 40 million rows for one tweet, and every ordinary user's post would queue behind it. So above a follower threshold we stop fanning out entirely.

Their posts stay in their own timeline only. When you load your feed, we fetch your precomputed timeline and then separately fetch recent posts from the handful of celebrities you follow, and merge the two at read time.

Most users follow few or no celebrities, so most reads stay cheap. The merge is bounded because it only touches accounts above the threshold.

“What is the right follower threshold, and how did you pick it?”Answer

I would not pick it in the interview; I would make it a tunable and say what I would watch. The number that matters is fan-out lag: how long between a post being accepted and it appearing in the last follower's timeline.

Set it too high and one account can stall the queue for everybody. Too low and you push lots of accounts onto the read-time merge path, which makes feed loads slower for the users who follow them.

Start somewhere around tens of thousands, watch lag per tier, and move it. The important part is that it is observable and adjustable, not that it is right on day one.

“How do you handle a deleted tweet that has already been fanned out to 500,000 timelines?”Answer

This is the real cost of fan-out-on-write, and it is worth naming. The post now exists in half a million places.

Rather than deleting half a million rows synchronously, keep timelines as lists of post ids and filter at read time against a small set of deleted ids. The delete is then one write plus a cache entry, and cleanup of the timeline rows happens lazily in the background.

The trade is that reads do slightly more work. That is the right side to pay on, because deletes are rare and reads are constant.

“Would this design work for a chronological feed or a ranked one?”Answer

As described it is chronological, and that is what makes precomputation worth it: the timeline is a sorted list you can append to.

Ranking breaks that. If the order depends on a model score computed from recency, engagement and your own history, the timeline is no longer a stable list, and precomputing it means recomputing it constantly.

The usual compromise is to precompute the candidate set and rank at read time over a few hundred candidates rather than the whole corpus. You keep the cheap fan-out and accept a scoring service on the read path.

“What if a user follows 50,000 accounts?”Answer

The mirror image of the celebrity problem, and much rarer. Fan-out-on-write is fine for them, because it costs the writers, not the reader. Their timeline is just a longer list.

Where it hurts is the read-time merge for any celebrities in that set. If someone follows 5,000 accounts that are all above the threshold, their feed load is 5,000 fetches.

In practice you cap it: merge only the most recent N celebrity posts, and accept that a user following thousands of large accounts sees an approximate feed.

Design a Distributed Key-Value Store (like Redis / Amazon Dynamo)

Difficulty: Hard  .  Target: 45 min
💬 The question, as asked

“Design a distributed key-value store like Dynamo. It must stay available for writes even when nodes fail or the network partitions.”

⚡ What makes it hard

The requirement is availability during a partition, which forces you off strong consistency by definition. Everything then becomes: how do you detect that replicas have diverged, and who resolves it?

📋1. Understanding the question

The prompt: “Design a distributed key-value store like Dynamo. It must stay available for writes even when nodes fail or the network partitions.”

Read that second sentence slowly, because it has already decided the design.

“Available for writes during a partition” is one half of a choice you are not allowed to have both halves of. If two groups of nodes cannot talk to each other and both keep accepting writes for the same key, they will end up holding different values. There is no clever engineering that avoids this. It is a theorem, not a limitation.

🎯 What the question is really asking

The interviewer has chosen availability for you. So the design work is not “how do I keep replicas identical” — you cannot. It is “how do I notice they diverged, and who decides which value wins?”

A concrete version of the problem

Alice's shopping cart is stored under one key, replicated on three nodes. A network fault splits the cluster. Alice adds a book on her laptop; that write lands on node A. She adds a lamp on her phone; that write lands on node C, which cannot see A. Both writes succeed — that is what “available” means.

The partition heals. Node A says the cart is {book}. Node C says it is {lamp}. Neither is wrong, neither is newer in any meaningful sense, and if you pick one by wall-clock timestamp you have just silently deleted something a customer put in their cart.

Everything in this design — version vectors, read repair, Merkle trees, sibling values — exists to handle that moment well.

What they are looking for

Do you know you have been pushed off strong consistency? Candidates who sketch a quorum system and then describe reads as always returning the latest write have not noticed.

Do you have an answer for conflicts beyond “last write wins”? LWW is a legitimate choice, but only if you say what it costs.

Do you handle the cold data? Read repair only fixes keys somebody reads. A key written once and read in a year will stay diverged unless something sweeps for it.

❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
Strong or eventual consistency?
The single biggest fork in the design. Strong means consensus on the write path and cross-region latency; eventual means quorums and conflict resolution.
Point lookups only, or range scans?
Decides hash versus range partitioning, and range partitioning brings hot-shard problems that hashing does not.
What is the value size distribution?
Multi-megabyte values need a different storage path from 200-byte ones, and change the memory overhead arithmetic entirely.
Single region or multi-region?
Determines whether an acknowledged write has to cross an ocean, which is a floor on write latency you cannot engineer away.
What must be durable when we acknowledge?
fsync-before-ack versus page-cache-and-hope is a correctness decision, not a tuning knob.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.
📝2. Functional requirements
  • get(key) → value, or nothing.
  • put(key, value) → acknowledged once enough replicas have it.
  • delete(key) → and this is harder than it looks; see below.
  • Tunable durability per call. The caller says how many replicas must confirm before we acknowledge (W) and how many we consult on a read (R).
  • Add and remove nodes without downtime. Capacity changes should move a fraction of the data, not all of it.
  • Survive node loss automatically. No operator in the failure path.

Delete deserves a sentence. You cannot actually remove the row, because a replica that was offline during the delete still has the old value, and when it comes back it will happily hand that value to the next reader — the data resurrects. So a delete writes a tombstone: a marker that says “this key is gone as of this version”, which wins over the old value and is itself garbage-collected much later.

⏱3. Non-functional requirements
RequirementTargetWhy it matters here
Write availabilitySurvives a partitionStated in the question. This is the constraint everything else bends around.
Read latencyp99 < 1 msThis sits behind other services. It has to be faster than the thing calling it, or people stop using it.
Write latencyp99 < 5 msBounded by the slowest of the W replicas we wait on. Raising W raises this directly.
Throughput10M ops/secCluster-wide. Divided by per-node capacity, this is what sets the node count.
DurabilitySurvives N/2 lossesThree replicas, spread across failure domains. Three copies in one rack is one copy.
ConsistencyEventual, by defaultCallers that need more can raise R and W. Callers that need linearizability need a different system.

The R + W > N rule, and what it actually promises

With three replicas, if every write waits for 2 of them and every read consults 2 of them, then any read set and any write set must share at least one node. That shared node has the latest value. So the read sees it — provided it knows to prefer it, which is what versions are for.

It is a pigeonhole argument, not a consistency protocol, and the distinction matters. It says the new value is present in what you fetched. It does not say the replicas agree, it does not survive a sloppy quorum, and it says nothing about two writes that happened concurrently.

🗂4. Data model and API

There are two very different kinds of state here: the data, and the map that says where data lives.

-- On each node (RocksDB or custom LSM-tree store) KEY -> { value: bytes, version: VectorClock | Timestamp, tombstone: bool } -- Metadata (gossip-distributed to all nodes) RING -> sorted([(hash_position, node_id, address)]) NODE_STATUS -> { node_id: { status, last_heartbeat, token_count } } -- Hint store (per node, for hinted handoff) HINTS -> { target_node: [(key, value, timestamp)] }

The ring is the interesting one. Rather than a coordinator that assigns keys to nodes, every node holds the same small map of token positions, kept in sync by gossip. Any node can therefore route any request, and there is no lookup service to be a single point of failure.

The version field on each value is what makes conflict detection possible. A plain timestamp gives you last-write-wins. A version vector — a small map of node → counter — lets you tell apart two genuinely different cases:

  • One version descends from the other. Alice read the cart, added a book, wrote it back. The new version knows about the old one. Keep the new one; this is not a conflict.
  • Neither descends from the other. Alice's laptop and phone wrote without seeing each other. This is a real conflict and something has to decide.

A timestamp cannot distinguish those. That is the whole argument for version vectors, and also the whole cost: they are bigger, they need pruning, and the client has to carry one around.

The API

GET /v1/keys/{key}?consistency=one|quorum Response: 200 { value, version_vector, coordinator } 404 not found // may return SIBLINGS when concurrent writes diverged -- // the client resolves and writes back PUT /v1/keys/{key}?w=2 Body: { value, context } // context = version vector from a prior read Response: 200 { version_vector } 503 insufficient replicas (when sloppy quorum is disabled) DELETE /v1/keys/{key} // writes a TOMBSTONE, not a removal -- // deleting outright lets a stale replica resurrect it // Admin: GET /v1/ring -- the token map, polled by smart clients

Two things there are not decoration. The context on a write is the version the client last read — it is how the server knows whether this write descends from what it has. And a read can return siblings: more than one value, because the store genuinely does not know which is right. Handing that to the caller feels like a cop-out and is in fact the honest answer, because only the caller knows that two carts should be merged by union.

📊5. Capacity estimation

The arithmetic that sets the cluster size.

⚖ Assumptions — and what breaks if each is wrong
Callers tolerate eventual consistency
If any caller needs linearizability, quorums are not enough and the write path needs consensus, roughly tripling write latency.
Access is by key, no range scans
Range queries would force range partitioning, which reintroduces hot shards that hashing avoids.
Values are small, order of kilobytes
Multi-megabyte values need a separate blob path; storing them inline destroys the memory model.
10M
cluster QPS
~1 KB
avg value size
~10 GB/s
read bandwidth
~100 TB
data total
3
replication factor
~33 nodes
at 300K QPS/node

Read the chain: 100 TB of data, times 3 for replication, is 300 TB to place. At roughly 3 TB per node that is about a hundred nodes on storage grounds. Ten million operations per second across those nodes is around 300K per node, which an SSD-backed store with a hot set in page cache can serve. The two numbers land in the same place, which is the sign of a balanced cluster.

If they had not, that would itself be the finding: storage-bound means you buy disk and waste CPU; throughput-bound means you buy nodes and waste disk. Saying which one you are is worth more than the node count.

⚖6. The key trade-offs

The choices, and their bills.

DecisionChosen vAlternative xReasoning
Consistency modelTunable quorum (R+W>N=strong, else eventual)Always strongTunable gives flexibility: low-latency apps use W=1,R=1; financial use W=3,R=2. One size doesn't fit all.
Conflict resolutionLWW (default) + vector clocks (opt-in)Reject conflicts (require re-read)Rejecting conflicts kills availability. LWW is simple. Vector clocks enable app-level merge for complex data types.
PartitioningConsistent hashing + vnodesRange partitioningConsistent hashing: smooth rebalancing. Vnodes: even distribution. Range: good for scans but creates hot partitions for sequential writes.

The one worth dwelling on: how conflicts get resolved

Last-write-wins is one timestamp per value, trivial to implement, and silently loses data. When Alice's laptop and phone both wrote, LWW picks whichever had the later clock reading — and clocks on different machines disagree by milliseconds, so “later” may not mean later at all. The lamp vanishes and nobody gets an error. Cassandra ships this as its default and it is fine for values that are replaced rather than edited: a cached render, a session blob, a last-known-location.

Version vectors plus sibling values never lose a write, because the store refuses to choose and hands both back. Alice's client merges the carts by union and writes the result. The cost is real: bigger metadata, a client that must understand merging, and a failure mode where siblings accumulate if nobody ever reads and resolves them.

The rule of thumb worth stating out loud: if losing a concurrent write is invisible to a user, use LWW; if it is a missing item in their cart, do not.

🏗7. High-level design
Quorum write — and the sloppy quorum that trades consistency for uptime
client writereplica writeackhinted handoff
What is moving: the write goes to any node, which forwards it to all replicas and acknowledges as soon as W = 2 of them confirm. With R + W > N, any later read of 2 replicas is guaranteed to overlap this write.
What goes wrong: replica 3 is unreachable. A sloppy quorum accepts the write anyway and parks a hint on a healthy node to be handed off later — so the system stays available, but the R + W > N overlap guarantee no longer holds and a read can miss this value. Availability was bought with consistency, exactly as Ch 3 says it must be.

The shape of it.

THE RING every node knows it; gossip keeps it current key → hash → a position on the ring the next 3 nodes clockwise are its replicas A ---- B ---- C ---- D ---- E ---- F ---- (back to A) ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ replicas for this key WRITE put(k, v) with W=2 client → any node it becomes the coordinator; no special node exists | +--> B ack +--> C ack 2 acks → return OK to the client +--> D ... still in flight; it will catch up READ get(k) with R=2 coordinator asks 2 replicas both agree → return it one is stale → return the newer, write it back read repair neither descends → return both the client merges
No leader, no lookup tier, no special node. Every node can coordinate, which is why losing any one of them costs you capacity rather than a function.

Why the ring, rather than hash(key) % N

Modulo hashing is simpler and completely unusable here. Go from 100 nodes to 101 and the modulus changes, so nearly every key maps somewhere new: you have to move essentially the entire dataset to add one machine.

On a ring, each node owns the arc between it and its predecessor. Insert a new node and it takes over part of one arc. Everything else stays exactly where it was. Adding 1% capacity moves about 1% of the data, which is the property that makes the cluster growable at all.

One wrinkle: placing each node at a single ring position gives wildly uneven arcs, so real systems give each node a few hundred virtual positions. The arcs average out, and a departing node's load spreads across many neighbours instead of landing entirely on the next one.

🔄8. Workflows — what actually happens
A normal write, and then a normal read
Nothing is broken. This is the 99.9% case.
  1. A client calls put("cart:alice", {book}). It connects to node B, which happens to be nearest; B is now the coordinator for this request.
  2. B hashes the key, finds the three replicas — say C, D and E — and sends the write to all three at once.
  3. C and D confirm within a millisecond. That is W=2, so B returns OK to the client. E's write is still in flight and nobody is waiting for it.
  4. E confirms 4 ms later. All three now hold the value. Total client-visible latency: the second-fastest replica, not the slowest.
  5. A read arrives at node F. F asks two replicas, both return the same version, F returns the value.
Waiting for 2 of 3 rather than 3 of 3 is what keeps p99 low: you are immune to one slow replica, and at any moment one of them is always garbage-collecting or flushing.
Replica E is down when a write arrives
Hinted handoff, and the guarantee it quietly cancels.
  1. Coordinator B sends the write to C, D and E. C and D ack; E does not respond.
  2. W=2 is satisfied, so the client already has its OK. Nothing is wrong yet.
  3. B writes a hint to a healthy node: “this value belongs to E, hand it over when E returns.”
  4. E comes back an hour later. The hint holder notices and replays the write. E is now current.
  5. The catch: while E was away, if the coordinator had counted the hint holder toward the quorum — a sloppy quorum — then the write set and a later read set need not overlap at all. R + W > N no longer holds.
This is the availability purchase made explicit. You kept accepting writes through a failure and paid for it with a guarantee. Worth saying out loud in the interview — most candidates describe hinted handoff as free.
Alice's cart diverges, and comes back together
The scenario from step 1, all the way through.
  1. A partition splits the replicas. Alice's laptop writes {book} to one side; her phone writes {lamp} to the other. Both get an OK.
  2. Neither version vector descends from the other, so both survive as siblings rather than one overwriting the other.
  3. The partition heals. Nothing happens yet — nodes do not proactively compare every key.
  4. Alice opens her cart. The coordinator reads 2 replicas, sees two unrelated versions, and returns both.
  5. The client merges them the only way that makes sense for a cart — union — and writes back {book, lamp} with a version that descends from both.
  6. That write supersedes both siblings. The conflict is gone.
The store never guessed. It detected the conflict and handed it to the only layer that knew carts merge by union. Under last-write-wins, Alice would simply have found one item missing.
A key nobody reads, diverged for six months
Why read repair is not enough on its own.
  1. Read repair only fixes keys that somebody reads. A key written once and never read again stays diverged forever.
  2. So each pair of replicas periodically compares a Merkle tree: a tree of hashes where each leaf covers a range of keys and each parent hashes its children.
  3. They exchange root hashes first. Equal roots mean the entire range matches — two hashes exchanged, terabytes verified.
  4. Different roots mean they walk down, comparing children, until they reach the leaves that actually differ.
  5. Only those keys are shipped across. A cluster with one stale key transfers one key, not a replica.
Comparing two large datasets over a network is a general problem, and hashing the structure rather than the contents is the general answer. The same trick is how Git tells whether two trees differ.
🔍9. Deep dives, and what breaks

Choosing R and W

These are per-call knobs, and different callers should use different ones.

  • W=1, R=1 — fastest, no overlap guarantee. Fine for metrics, view counters, anything where a lost write is a rounding error.
  • W=2, R=2 with N=3 — the default. Overlap holds, and you tolerate one node being slow or dead on either path.
  • W=3, R=1 — reads are as cheap as possible, writes wait for everyone. Good for config data: written rarely, read constantly.
  • W=1, R=3 — the mirror image. Good for an ingest path that must never block, where readers can afford the extra fan-out.

The useful framing is that R and W move latency between the read path and the write path. They do not create consistency; they only decide where you pay.

Why not just run consensus

A perfectly good answer to “replicas disagree” is to not let them: put every write through Raft and there is one log, one order, no conflicts. Spanner does this.

It costs you the thing the question asked for. Consensus needs a majority to be reachable, so a minority partition cannot accept writes — it returns errors instead. Every write also pays a round trip to the leader, which across regions is tens of milliseconds rather than one.

The honest summary: consensus gives you one truth and refuses service when it cannot; quorums give you continuous service and several truths to reconcile. The question asked for the second. If it had asked for account balances, the answer would be the first.

Tombstones, and when they can be dropped

A tombstone has to outlive any replica that might still hold the deleted value. Drop it too early and a node returning from a long outage re-introduces data a user deleted — a bug that looks like a ghost and is nearly impossible to reproduce.

The standard rule is to keep tombstones for longer than the maximum time a node is allowed to be down before it is rebuilt from scratch rather than repaired. Ten days is a common setting. The corollary is that a workload of constant writes and deletes accumulates tombstones and reads slow down, which is why queue-like workloads on this kind of store are a known trap.

What breaks

Node failure (permanent)
Detect via gossip heartbeat timeout (phi = 8 threshold). Remove from ring. Adjacent nodes inherit its key range. Replica count temporarily drops to 2; auto-repair brings it back to 3 via anti-entropy within minutes.
Network partition (split-ring)
Both halves continue serving with their available replicas. Writes with W=2 succeed on majority side, fail on minority (if only 1 replica there). On heal: anti-entropy detects divergence, repairs. LWW resolves conflicts.
Hot key (one key getting 1M QPS)
Detect via coordinator: if key appears in >10% of requests -> replicate to local cache. Or: key sharding -- append suffix (0-9), fan-out writes to 10 keys, fan-in reads with merge.
The dominant constraint

Whether the caller needs strong or eventual consistency. I designed for eventual with tunable quorums, because that is what buys availability during a partition; strong consistency would mean consensus on the write path and a different system.

What I would build first

Consistent hashing with virtual nodes, plus R + W > N quorums. Anti-entropy and hinted handoff come next, because without them eventual never actually converges.

What I deliberately did not build

Secondary indexes, transactions and range scans. Each of those pulls the design back toward a database.

The biggest risk

Silent divergence. Without Merkle-tree anti-entropy running and being monitored, replicas drift and nobody finds out until a read repair surfaces it years later.

💬 If you get this far, here is what they will push on
Follow-ups an interviewer is likely to ask once the design is on the board. Answers supplied — read the question, answer it out loud, then open it.
“Two clients write the same key at the same time on different nodes. What does a later read see?”Answer

It can see both values. That is the honest answer with leaderless replication, and pretending otherwise is the mistake.

Each write carries a version vector describing what it saw. When the two versions are concurrent, neither descends from the other, so the system cannot pick a winner without guessing. It returns both to the client as siblings.

The application resolves them, and how depends on the data. A shopping cart merges by union. A counter merges by addition. A profile name probably takes the later timestamp and accepts occasional loss. The key point is that resolution is a business decision, not a storage one.

“Why not just use last-write-wins and avoid all that?”Answer

You can, and plenty of systems do. But understand what you are buying: last-write-wins silently discards data, and the “last” is decided by clocks on different machines which disagree.

So a write that genuinely happened later can be thrown away because that node's clock was slow. Nothing errors and nobody notices until a customer complains that their change vanished.

It is the right choice when losing the occasional write is acceptable and simplicity matters more. It is the wrong choice for anything a user would be upset to lose.

“What does R + W > N actually guarantee, and when does it stop holding?”Answer

With N replicas, writing to W and reading from R where R + W > N means the read set and write set must overlap by at least one node. So a read is guaranteed to see at least one replica that has the latest write.

It stops holding the moment you allow sloppy quorums. If a replica is unreachable and you accept the write on some other node with a hint to hand off later, you kept availability but the overlap guarantee is gone. A subsequent read of R nodes can miss the value entirely.

That is a deliberate trade, not a bug, but you should be able to say which one you have chosen.

“How do replicas that missed writes ever catch up?”Answer

Three mechanisms, and you want all of them. Read repair fixes divergence opportunistically: when a read notices replicas disagree, it writes the newer value back. Hinted handoff covers short outages, replaying writes that were parked elsewhere.

Neither is sufficient, because a key nobody reads is never repaired. So there is anti-entropy: replicas periodically compare Merkle trees and exchange only the subtrees that differ, which lets you compare huge datasets cheaply.

Without anti-entropy running and being monitored, “eventual” consistency quietly means “never” for cold data.

“What if I need a range scan, like all keys between two values?”Answer

You cannot, and that is by design. Keys are hashed onto the ring, so adjacent keys land on unrelated nodes and a range query becomes a scatter-gather over every partition.

If range queries are a real requirement, hash partitioning is the wrong choice and you want range partitioning instead. But that reintroduces hot spots, because sequential keys like timestamps all land on one node.

The usual answer is to keep the KV store for point lookups and maintain a separate index for range access.

Design WhatsApp / Messaging System

Difficulty: Hard  .  Target: 45 min
💬 The question, as asked

“Design a messaging system like WhatsApp. One-to-one and group chats, delivery and read receipts, and messages must arrive even if the recipient is offline.”

⚡ What makes it hard

Millions of long-lived connections rather than short requests, which inverts the usual scaling model. Ordering must hold per conversation, and end-to-end encryption rules out most server-side features you would otherwise reach for.

📋1. Understanding the question

The prompt: “Design a messaging system like WhatsApp. One-to-one and group chats, delivery and read receipts, and messages must arrive even if the recipient is offline.”

Most systems you design are request-response: a client asks, a server answers, the connection closes, and the server remembers nothing. This one is not, and that single difference generates most of the work.

Here the server has to push. When Priya sends a message to Dev, nothing on Dev's phone asked for it. So Dev's phone must already be holding an open connection, and the server must know which of its thousands of machines is holding it.

🎯 The shift in model

A stateless web tier can route any request to any server, because no server holds anything. Here a message for Dev can only be delivered by the one machine holding Dev's socket. You have gone from “any server will do” to “find the right server”, and that lookup is the core of the design.

Two more things the prompt smuggles in

“Even if the recipient is offline.” Phones lose signal constantly — tunnels, lifts, flights, flat batteries. So delivery is never a synchronous handoff. The message has to become durable the moment we accept it, and be replayable whenever Dev's phone comes back, which might be next week.

Receipts. Two grey ticks, then two blue ones. These look like decoration and are actually a second delivery problem running backwards, at roughly the same volume as the messages themselves — and one that is far more forgiving, which is worth exploiting.

What they are looking for

Do you reach for a persistent connection and then handle the registry? Everyone says “WebSocket”. Fewer immediately ask how server A finds out that Dev is on server C.

Do you design for reconnection rather than connection? On mobile, disconnection is the normal state of affairs, not the failure case.

Do you notice what end-to-end encryption takes away? If the server cannot read the message, it cannot index it, filter it, or generate a useful notification preview. That constrains features, and saying so unprompted is a strong signal.

❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
1:1 only, or groups — and how large?
Group size drives fan-out cost. A 100,000-member group is a completely different write amplification problem from a 1:1 chat.
Is ordering required per conversation or globally?
Per-conversation ordering lets you partition by conversation and avoid coordination. Global ordering does not.
Do we store history server-side?
Decides whether end-to-end encryption is possible, and whether server-side search can exist at all.
Is presence (online / typing) in scope?
Presence has a far higher write rate than messaging and is usually a separate system. Saying so is a scoping signal.
Multi-device per account?
Changes key management, read-state synchronisation and delivery semantics all at once.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.
📝2. Functional requirements
  • 1:1 and group messaging, with groups bounded at a few hundred members.
  • Ordered delivery within a conversation. If Priya sends three messages, Dev sees them in that order. Across different conversations, order does not matter and should not be enforced.
  • Receipts: sent → delivered → read.
  • Offline delivery. Messages are held until acknowledged, then replayed on reconnect.
  • Push notifications when the app is not running.
  • End-to-end encryption, so the server stores ciphertext it cannot read.
  • Media — images, video, documents — which do not travel over the message path at all.

Two of these are worth a sentence each because they shape everything downstream.

Per-conversation ordering, not global. This is the most valuable requirement in the list, because of what it lets you not build. Ordering messages within one conversation means one writer's worth of sequence numbers, which one partition can assign by itself. Ordering messages globally across two billion users would require every message in the system to agree on a position, which is a coordination problem with no good answer at this scale.

Media is not a message. A 40 MB video does not go through the chat pipeline. The sender uploads it to blob storage and sends a message containing a reference. The chat path stays small-message and low-latency, and the upload can retry and resume without touching it.

⏱3. Non-functional requirements
RequirementTargetWhat it forces
Delivery latencyp99 < 500 msRecipient online. This is a chat, and anything slower feels broken.
Concurrent connections~600MThe defining number. Not requests per second — simultaneously open sockets, each costing memory whether or not it is carrying anything.
DurabilityWeeks offlineAn undelivered message must survive the recipient being unreachable for a very long time.
Availability99.99%Roughly an hour a year. And an outage means reconnecting hundreds of millions of clients at once, which is its own problem.
OrderingPer conversationDeliberately not global. This is what permits partitioning by conversation with no coordination.
Delivery semanticsAt least onceExactly-once over a lossy mobile link is not achievable. Duplicates are handled by the client instead.

Why at-least-once, and why that is fine

Dev's phone receives a message and sends an acknowledgement. The signal drops before the ack lands. The server, having no way to tell “delivered but unacked” from “never delivered”, does the only safe thing and sends it again.

You cannot engineer this away; you can only choose which way to fail. Retry and you risk duplicates. Do not retry and you risk lost messages. A duplicate message is a visual annoyance; a lost message is a broken product.

So we retry, and we give every message an id chosen by the sending client. The receiving client keeps a small set of ids it has already displayed and drops repeats. The duplicate never reaches the user, and the server never has to solve an unsolvable problem.

🗂4. Data model and API

Four kinds of state, with genuinely different access patterns — which is why they live in different places.

-- Messages (Cassandra -- write-heavy, time-series) TABLE messages { conversation_id UUID PARTITION KEY, message_id BIGINT CLUSTERING KEY DESC, -- Snowflake sender_id BIGINT, content BLOB, -- encrypted ciphertext media_id UUID, -- reference to media service message_type ENUM(text, image, video, doc), created_at TIMESTAMP } -- Delivery receipts (separate table for performance) TABLE receipts { message_id BIGINT PARTITION KEY, user_id BIGINT CLUSTERING KEY, status ENUM(sent, delivered, read), updated_at TIMESTAMP } -- User presence (Redis -- ephemeral, frequently updated) KEY presence:{user_id} -> { status: online|offline, last_seen: timestamp } -- TTL: 30 seconds. Refreshed every 20s by client heartbeat. -- Message queue for offline delivery (Redis List per user) KEY inbox:{user_id} -> LIST [ message_ids... ] (max 1000)

Messages are partitioned by conversation id and clustered by message id descending. That layout is chosen to match the only query that matters: give me the last fifty messages in this chat. It is a single sequential read of one partition, with no sorting and no cross-partition fan-in.

Presence lives in a cache with a 30-second expiry rather than in a database, and the reasoning is worth stating. Presence changes far more often than messages are sent — every client refreshes it every 20 seconds whether or not anything happened. Writing that to durable storage would mean a write rate several times the message rate, for data that is worthless the moment it is stale. So it is a key with a TTL, and when a client stops refreshing, the key expires and the user is offline. No logout event needed; disappearing is the signal.

Receipts are stored apart from messages. A message is written once and read many times; a receipt is written twice per recipient and read rarely. Putting them in the same row would mean updating a message row on every receipt, turning an append-only table into an update-heavy one.

The API

// Long-lived WebSocket. HTTP is used only for auth and media. WS /v1/connect Header: Bearer <token> <- { type:"ack", client_msg_id, server_msg_id, seq } <- { type:"message", conversation_id, seq, from, ciphertext, ts } <- { type:"receipt", message_id, state:"delivered"|"read" } -> { type:"send", conversation_id, client_msg_id, ciphertext } // client_msg_id makes the send idempotent across reconnects POST /v1/media -> { media_id, upload_url } GET /v1/sync?since_seq= -> missed messages after reconnect POST /v1/keys/prekeys -> replenish the one-time prekey pool

Note what is not a WebSocket frame: auth and media upload are plain HTTP. The socket carries small, ordered, latency-sensitive traffic and nothing else.

The /sync?since_seq= endpoint is how reconnection works, and it is the most important call in the API. The client says what it last saw; the server sends everything after it. That single idea replaces any attempt to track delivery state per connection — the client is the source of truth about what it has, which is the only arrangement that survives a phone that vanished mid-stream.

📊5. Capacity estimation

The numbers, and the one that actually sizes the fleet.

⚖ Assumptions — and what breaks if each is wrong
Groups are bounded, order of hundreds
A 100,000-member group changes fan-out from a loop into its own subsystem.
Ordering is required per conversation only
Global ordering across conversations would force coordination and remove the partitioning that makes this scale.
Messages are not stored after delivery
If history must be retained server-side, end-to-end encryption becomes far harder and search becomes possible.
~1.16M
messages/sec avg
~3.5M
