concurrent WS conns/server

The headline is not messages per second. At around 3.5M messages/sec peak, each a few hundred bytes of ciphertext, the write path is large but ordinary — comparable to a busy analytics pipeline.

The number that shapes the system is 600 million simultaneously open connections. Those sockets cost memory even at three in the morning when nobody is typing. At roughly 50,000 connections per machine — which needs tuned file-descriptor limits, small socket buffers and an event loop rather than a thread per connection — that is about 12,000 gateway machines whose job is mostly to hold sockets open.

That is the insight worth stating: this fleet is sized by idle connections, not by traffic. Which in turn means a mass reconnection event — a deploy, a regional network blip — is the worst load this system ever sees, because every one of those clients tries to re-establish and re-sync at the same moment.

⚖6. The key trade-offs

The choices, and their costs.

DecisionChosen vAlternative xReasoning
TransportWebSocket (persistent)HTTP pollingPersistent connection = instant delivery, no polling overhead. Critical for sub-500ms delivery. Poll would require 1-5 req/sec x 2B users = billions of wasted requests.
Message storeCassandraPostgreSQLTime-series append workload. 100B msgs/day = 1.16M writes/sec. Cassandra's LSM-tree handles this. PostgreSQL B-tree would require enormous infrastructure for this write rate.
Group messagingFan-out on send (for small groups)Fan-out on receiveFor 256-member groups: fan-out on send = 256 DB writes + 256 WS pushes. Manageable. On receive = one write but N reads on timeline load. Fan-out on send is better for groups this size.

The one that decides the fleet: persistent sockets vs polling

The alternative to holding 600 million connections is to have clients ask periodically: anything for me? No connection state, no registry, ordinary stateless servers behind an ordinary load balancer.

It fails on both ends at once. Poll every 30 seconds and messages arrive up to 30 seconds late, which is not a chat app. Poll every second and you are serving two billion requests per second, almost all of which answer “nothing” — and every one of those wakes the phone's radio, which is the single largest battery cost on a mobile device.

So we hold the connection. The bill is 12,000 stateful machines, a registry to find them, and reconnection logic that has to be correct because it runs constantly.

The other one: what encryption costs the product

End-to-end encryption means the server stores bytes it cannot read. Everything that would have been a server-side feature now has to be a client-side feature or not exist:

  • Search runs on the device, over messages that device has. Search a chat from three years ago on a phone you bought last month and there is nothing to find.
  • Notification previews cannot be generated by the server, because the server cannot read the message. The push carries a wake-up; the client decrypts and renders the text.
  • Multi-device stops being a display problem and becomes a key-management problem: every device needs its own identity and its own copy of each message, encrypted to it.
  • Server-side moderation of content is off the table entirely. Abuse handling has to work from metadata and user reports.

Naming these unprompted is the point. Encryption is not a checkbox in the requirements; it deletes several features you would otherwise have assumed.

🏗7. High-level design
Message delivery — and the reconnect that can deliver twice
sendordered deliveryreceiptqueued while offline
What is moving: a message travels to the gateway holding the sender’s socket, is appended to the conversation’s ordered log with a sequence number, then pushed to the recipient. Ordering is guaranteed per conversation, which is what lets the system partition by conversation ID and coordinate nowhere.
What goes wrong: the recipient goes offline mid-delivery. Messages queue, and on reconnect the client asks for everything after its last acknowledged sequence. If the client acknowledged but the ack was lost, the server replays messages it already delivered — a duplicate. The fix is the client-supplied message ID: delivery is at-least-once and the client deduplicates on it (Ch 11).

Three tiers, with the middle one doing the interesting work.

Priya's phone Dev's phone | ^ | persistent socket | persistent socket v | GATEWAY A GATEWAY C holds Priya's socket holds Dev's socket | ^ | 1. append to conversation log | v | 4. push MESSAGE STORE partitioned by conversation_id | assigns seq 41, durable before we ack | | | | 2. who has Dev? | v | CONNECTION REGISTRY Dev -> Gateway C, TTL 30s | | | +--- 3. forward to C ----------------------------------+ Dev is offline — registry has no entry message stays durable in the log a push notification wakes the app wake-up only; no readable text on reconnect: GET /sync?since_seq=40 → everything after 40
Gateways are stateful only in the sense that they hold sockets — they store no messages. Lose a gateway and its clients reconnect elsewhere and re-sync. Nothing is lost, because durability lives in the log, not in the connection.

Why the registry is a cache with a TTL

The registry maps each online user to the gateway holding their socket. It is written on every connect, which at this scale is a very high write rate, and read on every message.

It is also allowed to be wrong. If it says Dev is on gateway C and Dev has actually just reconnected to gateway F, C receives a message for a socket it no longer has, replies “not mine”, and the message falls back to the offline path — where Dev picks it up on sync anyway. A stale entry costs one wasted hop, not a lost message.

That tolerance is why it can be an in-memory cache with a short TTL rather than a replicated consistent store, and the difference in cost between those two is enormous.

🔄8. Workflows — what actually happens
Priya messages Dev, and Dev is online
The happy path, end to end.
  1. Priya's client encrypts the text for Dev, attaches a client message id it generated itself, and sends it over its open socket to gateway A.
  2. A appends it to the conversation's log, which assigns seq 41 and makes it durable. Only now does A send Priya an ack — her first tick.
  3. A asks the registry where Dev is. Answer: gateway C.
  4. A forwards the message to C, which writes it down Dev's socket. Total elapsed: a few tens of milliseconds.
  5. Dev's phone displays it and sends a delivered receipt back along the same path. Priya's second tick appears.
  6. Dev opens the chat. A read receipt follows, and the ticks turn blue.
The message was durable before Priya saw a single tick. That ordering is deliberate: a tick is a promise, and promising delivery for something held only in memory is how messages disappear.
Dev is in the London Underground
Offline delivery, which is the normal case on mobile.
  1. Priya sends four messages over twenty minutes. Each is appended to the log with seq 42 through 45 and each is durable.
  2. The registry has no entry for Dev — his socket died when the signal did, and the TTL expired thirty seconds later.
  3. For the first message we send a push notification through the platform's service. It carries no text, because the server cannot read the text. It is a wake-up.
  4. We do not send a push for the next three. Priya's client shows a single tick on all four: sent, not delivered.
  5. Dev surfaces. The client reconnects, lands on gateway F this time, and calls /sync?since_seq=41.
  6. The server returns 42 through 45 in order. Dev's phone renders them, sends delivered receipts, and Priya's four single ticks become doubles at once.
Nothing tracked Dev's state while he was away. The client said what it last saw and the server answered from the log — which is the only approach that survives a phone that disappears for a week.
The ack is lost and the message arrives twice
At-least-once, and where the duplicate actually dies.
  1. Gateway C delivers seq 43 to Dev's phone. The phone displays it and sends the ack.
  2. The train enters a tunnel. The ack never arrives.
  3. The server sees an unacked message and, on Dev's next connection, sends 43 again. It cannot distinguish delivered but unacked from never delivered.
  4. Dev's client looks at the message id, finds it in the set of ids it has already displayed, and drops it silently.
  5. It re-sends the ack. This time it lands, and the server stops retrying.
Deduplication happens on the client because that is the only place with enough information to do it. The server chose the safe failure — send twice rather than risk zero — and the client cleaned up after it.
A 200-member group chat
Fan-out at a bounded size, which is what makes this tractable.
  1. Priya sends to the group. Because of end-to-end encryption she does not send one message — her client encrypts the same content once per recipient device, since each has a different key.
  2. All of those go up the one socket in a single batch. The upload is one round trip, not two hundred.
  3. The server appends them to the group's conversation log with one sequence number shared across the batch, so every member sees group messages in the same order.
  4. It looks up all 200 members in the registry: perhaps 60 are online. Those get an immediate push to their gateways.
  5. The other 140 get a notification wake-up and their copies wait in the log until they sync.
  6. Receipts come back from 200 devices. We aggregate them — Priya sees “delivered to 200”, not two hundred separate events.
This works because groups are bounded at a few hundred. At a hundred thousand members, per-recipient encryption stops being viable and the design changes shape entirely — which is exactly why group size was the first thing to clarify.
🔍9. Deep dives, and what breaks

Holding 600 million sockets

A gateway's job is nearly all waiting. The engineering is about making idle connections cheap.

A thread per connection is immediately out — 50,000 threads on one machine spend their lives context-switching. It is an event loop with non-blocking I/O, where one thread manages tens of thousands of sockets and only does work when one of them actually has bytes.

Then the per-connection memory. Default socket buffers are sized for throughput; here they should be small, because the traffic is tiny messages, and 50,000 × a few hundred kilobytes of buffer is the whole machine. File descriptor limits and ephemeral port ranges both need raising past their defaults, which are set for servers holding hundreds of connections, not tens of thousands.

And keepalives. The connection must survive carrier NAT timeouts, which on mobile networks can be as short as a couple of minutes, so something has to send a byte periodically. Too frequent and you drain batteries across the entire user base; too infrequent and connections die silently and messages take a push notification to arrive. It is a tuned number, usually a few minutes, and it is one of the higher-leverage constants in the whole system.

Sequence numbers, and why they are per conversation

Each conversation has its own counter. Messages in it are 1, 2, 3, and a client that has seen 41 knows immediately whether it is missing anything.

Because the counter is scoped to one conversation, one partition owns it and can hand out numbers without asking anybody. Two billion conversations therefore assign sequence numbers entirely in parallel. A global counter would mean every message in the world queueing behind one assignment point.

Within a single conversation the ordering does have to be decided somewhere — two members sending simultaneously is a genuine race — but that is one partition serialising two writes, which is cheap and local. This is the same move that appears throughout the guide: make the constraint local instead of coordinating.

Receipts, and why they get a cheaper pipeline

Receipts roughly double the system's event count, but they have much weaker requirements: a delayed tick is unnoticeable, and a lost one is nearly so.

So they are not treated like messages. They are batched — a client that has been offline sends one aggregate rather than forty individual receipts — they are not retried indefinitely, and in groups they are collapsed to a count before the sender ever sees them.

Recognising that two flows of similar volume can have very different guarantees, and building the cheaper pipeline for the cheaper one, is the kind of thing that separates a design that scales from one that is merely correct.

What breaks

WebSocket server crashes
All connections on that server disconnect. Clients auto-reconnect to any WS server (load balancer with sticky session NOT required -- connection registry handles routing). Reconnect within 1-2 seconds. Messages in flight are re-delivered from Cassandra.
Connection registry (Redis) down
Short outage: WS servers cache recent {user->server} mappings locally (LRU, 5 min TTL). On cache miss: fan-out to all WS servers (expensive but rare). Redis Cluster + sentinels for HA.
Cassandra node failure
RF=3, W=2, R=1. Node failure -> writes still succeed (2 of remaining 4 nodes). Read: if returning stale data, read-repair brings it up to date. Hinted handoff for writes during node unavailability.
Message lost in transit
Message ID is Snowflake (globally unique). ACK from WS server means it received the message. If sender doesn't get ACK in 5s -> retry (idempotent: same message_id = same Cassandra row). Three retries, then store in outbox for async retry.
The dominant constraint

Delivery ordering is required per conversation, not globally. That single relaxation is what lets me partition by conversation ID and avoid any cross-shard coordination on the hot path.

What I would build first

The WebSocket gateway plus per-conversation sequencing and the offline queue. Presence is deliberately a separate service.

What I deliberately did not build

Server-side search, which end-to-end encryption largely rules out, and global message ordering, which nobody needs.

The biggest risk

Presence. It has a far higher write rate than messaging and, if co-located, its load will take the messaging path down with it.

💬 If you get this far, here is what they will push on
Follow-ups an interviewer is likely to ask once the design is on the board. Answers supplied — read the question, answer it out loud, then open it.
“A group has 100,000 members. Someone sends a message. What happens?”Answer

The naive loop writes 100,000 delivery records for one message, and at any real message rate that saturates the write path.

So above a size threshold, groups stop behaving like fan-out and start behaving like a feed: the message is written once to the conversation log, and members pull from it when they connect. Small groups keep push, because push is what makes a two-person chat feel instant.

The same threshold idea as the celebrity problem in D2, for the same reason: one strategy cannot serve both ends of a skewed distribution.

“A user has been offline for two weeks. What do they get on reconnect?”Answer

Their client says “I have everything up to sequence 4,812” and we send what came after. That is the whole protocol, and it is why per-conversation sequence numbers matter more than timestamps.

The limit is retention. We do not hold undelivered messages forever, so past some window they are gone. That is a product decision and it should be stated: a phone that has been off for a month may miss messages, and the alternative is unbounded per-user storage.

If the client acknowledged but the ack was lost, it will be sent messages it already has — which is why the client deduplicates on message id.

“If it is end-to-end encrypted, how does search work?”Answer

It does not, on the server. That is the cost of E2E and it is worth saying plainly rather than hedging.

Search has to happen on the device, over the messages that device holds. That means each client maintains its own local index, search results differ between your phone and your laptop depending on what each has, and a newly installed device can search nothing until it syncs history.

If the product needs server-side search across all history, it cannot be end-to-end encrypted. Those two requirements are in direct conflict and someone has to choose.

“How do you show “typing…” without melting the system?”Answer

Presence is a much higher write rate than messaging — a typing indicator changes several times per message sent — so it must not share the messaging path.

Keep it entirely in memory, never persist it, give it a short TTL so a crashed client stops appearing to type, and send it only to people currently looking at that conversation rather than all members.

The reason to separate it is blast radius: if presence falls over, messaging should be completely unaffected. Co-locating them means the noisiest feature can take down the important one.

Design YouTube (Video Upload & Streaming)

Difficulty: Hard  .  Target: 45 min
💬 The question, as asked

“Design a video platform like YouTube. Users upload video; other users stream it worldwide at whatever quality their connection supports.”

⚡ What makes it hard

Upload and playback are two different systems that scale independently — transcoding is throughput-bound, delivery is egress-bound, and they are rarely the same order of magnitude. The transcode rendition matrix is the multiplier on your entire compute bill.

📋1. Understanding the question

The prompt: “Design a video platform like YouTube. Users upload video; other users stream it worldwide at whatever quality their connection supports.”

The mistake is to treat that as one system. It is two, and they have almost nothing in common.

Upload is a batch pipeline. Someone hands you a large file, you spend a lot of CPU turning it into many smaller files, and nobody is waiting in real time. It is measured in machine-hours, it can queue, and a five-minute delay is completely acceptable.

Playback is the opposite. It is latency-sensitive, enormous in volume, and mostly a question of moving bytes as close to the viewer as possible. There is barely any computation in it at all.

🎯 The framing that unlocks it

Upload is compute-bound. Playback is egress-bound. They scale on different axes, fail in different ways, and should be sized and operated separately. Say that in the first two minutes and the rest of the design has somewhere to go.

Where the money actually goes

Two numbers dominate the bill, and neither is storage.

Transcoding. An uploaded video is useless as-is — it is one file, in whatever the uploader's phone produced. To serve it to a 4K television and to someone on a train, you need several versions at different resolutions and bitrates. Every extra version you produce multiplies your CPU cost across every video ever uploaded. Going from six renditions to eight is not a 2-unit change; it is a 33% increase in the entire transcode fleet, forever.

Egress. The vast majority of bytes leaving this system are video segments going to viewers. If those come from your origin servers, you pay for the bandwidth and the viewer waits for a long round trip. If they come from a cache near the viewer, both problems go away. This is why a CDN is not an optimisation here; it is the delivery architecture.

What they are looking for

Do you separate the two pipelines? Candidates who draw one box labelled “video service” have not started.

Do you know why video is chopped into segments? It is what makes adaptive quality possible, and it is what makes CDN caching work. One idea, two payoffs.

Do you treat uploads as unreliable? A 10 GB file over a phone connection will fail partway through. If that means starting again, your product is unusable.

❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
Upload rate versus watch rate?
These size two completely different systems: transcoding capacity and CDN egress. They are rarely the same order of magnitude.
Live streaming, or video-on-demand only?
Live removes the batch transcode window and turns this into a latency problem instead of a throughput problem.
How many output renditions per video?
The transcode matrix — resolutions × codecs × bitrates — is the multiplier on your entire compute bill.
Must view counts be real-time and exact?
Counting at this scale is its own distributed problem. Approximate-and-eventually-correct is dramatically cheaper.
Is DRM or geo-restriction required?
Changes the delivery path and rules out simple CDN caching of a single artefact.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.
📝2. Functional requirements
  • Upload a video, up to around 10 GB, resumably.
  • Transcode it into a set of renditions — 360p through 4K, in a couple of codecs.
  • Stream with adaptive quality, so the picture degrades instead of stalling when the connection gets worse.
  • Metadata: title, description, duration, channel, publish state.
  • View counts, likes, comments, subscriptions.
  • Search and recommendations, which are their own systems and worth scoping out loud rather than hand-waving.

One requirement is doing more work than it appears to. “Adaptive quality” is why every rendition is cut into short segments — a few seconds each — rather than stored as one long file. The player fetches segment by segment and re-picks the quality each time. A viewer on a train can be watching 1080p, drop to 480p when the signal degrades, and climb back up, all without a rebuffer, because each decision only commits four seconds.

That same segmentation is what makes the CDN work: a few thousand small immutable files cache beautifully, where one multi-gigabyte file does not.

⏱3. Non-functional requirements
RequirementTargetWhat it drives
Playback start< 2 sThe number viewers actually feel. It is dominated by distance to the first segment, which is why edge caching is the design.
Rebuffer rateNear zeroA stall is far worse than lower quality. This is the requirement adaptive bitrate exists to satisfy.
Upload → watchable< 5 minGenerous, and deliberately so. It is what lets transcoding be a queue rather than a synchronous path.
EgressTens of GB/sThe dominant operating cost. Cache hit ratio at the edge is therefore a first-class metric, not an ops detail.
Durability11 ninesThe uploader may have deleted their only copy. Losing it is unrecoverable in a way losing a cache entry is not.
View countsEventually correctNobody can tell if a count is thirty seconds stale. Making it exact and real-time would cost more than everything else on this list.

That last row is worth arguing for explicitly, because it is a real design decision dressed up as a detail. Exact real-time counts mean a synchronous increment on the hottest rows in the system — a video with ten million concurrent viewers becomes ten million contending writes to one row. Accepting “correct within a minute” turns that into an append to a stream and a periodic aggregate, which is trivially scalable.

🗂4. Data model and API

The single most important decision here is what you do not put in the database: the video bytes. Metadata goes in a relational store, bytes go in object storage, and the database holds keys pointing at them.

-- Metadata in a relational store; bytes in object storage. TABLE videos { video_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, channel_id UUID, title, description TEXT, state ENUM(uploading, transcoding, ready, failed), duration_s INT, published_at TIMESTAMP } -- INDEX: (channel_id, published_at DESC) for a channel page TABLE renditions { -- one row per output of the transcode DAG video_id UUID, height INT, codec VARCHAR, bitrate_kbps INT, object_key TEXT, state ENUM(pending, ready), PRIMARY KEY (video_id, height, codec) } TABLE view_counts { -- eventually correct, written from a stream video_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, count BIGINT, updated_at TIMESTAMP } -- Never incremented synchronously on the playback path.

The renditions table is one row per output. A video is not ready when its upload finishes; it is ready when enough renditions exist to serve a manifest. Modelling them as separate rows with their own states means a 4K transcode failing does not block the video from going live in 1080p — the manifest simply lists what exists.

The state column on the video is a small state machine: uploading → transcoding → ready, with failed as a terminal. It is the only thing the player-facing API needs to consult before serving a manifest, and making it explicit avoids the classic bug where a video is discoverable before it is playable.

The API

POST /v1/uploads Body: { filename, size_bytes, content_type } Response: 201 { upload_id, chunk_size, upload_urls[] } // resumable: the client PUTs chunks directly to object storage PUT {upload_url}/chunk/{n} -> 200 { etag } POST /v1/uploads/{id}/complete -> 202 { video_id, state:"transcoding" } GET /v1/videos/{id}/manifest?profile=hls|dash Response: 200 HLS/DASH manifest of the available renditions // the player picks a rendition per segment; the server never decides POST /v1/videos/{id}/view -> 202 // fire-and-forget into a stream; counts are eventually correct

Three things there are load-bearing.

The client uploads chunks directly to object storage. The API hands out pre-signed URLs; the bytes never pass through the application tier. A service that proxied 8 GB/s of uploads would be a fleet of machines doing nothing but copying.

Chunked and resumable. A 10 GB upload over a home connection takes hours and will be interrupted. Chunks let it resume from where it stopped, and let chunks upload in parallel.

The manifest describes; it does not decide. The server returns the list of available renditions and their segment URLs. Which one to fetch is entirely the player's call, because only the player knows how fast the last segment arrived.

📊5. Capacity estimation

The arithmetic, and what it tells you to build first.

⚖ Assumptions — and what breaks if each is wrong
Watch volume is orders of magnitude above upload volume
If uploads dominated, transcode capacity rather than CDN egress would be the binding cost.
Video-on-demand only
Live removes the batch transcode window and changes this into a latency-bound design.
A handful of renditions per video
Every extra rendition multiplies the transcode bill across the entire catalogue.
500 hrs
uploaded/min
~8.3 GB/s
upload bandwidth raw
~100x

~50 GB/s

~10 PB

~4 EB
stored video total

The transcode fleet, worked through

500 hours of video arrive every minute. Each needs several renditions, and high-resolution encoding runs slower than real time — call it a few times slower for 4K on a general-purpose core.

Multiply it out and you need thousands of machine-hours of encoding per minute of wall-clock time, which means thousands of machines doing nothing but transcode. That is a bigger fleet than everything else in the design put together.

Two consequences follow immediately. First, transcoding should be parallelised within a video, not just across videos: split the source into chunks, encode them on different machines, concatenate. A one-hour video then takes a minute rather than an hour, and a long upload does not occupy one machine for an hour. Second, this fleet is a natural fit for preemptible capacity — the work is retryable, nothing is waiting on it, and losing a machine mid-chunk costs you one chunk.

The egress side

Views outnumber uploads by roughly a hundred to one, and each view streams megabytes. Playback bandwidth is therefore an order of magnitude above upload bandwidth, and essentially all of it is repeated reads of the same popular segments.

Which is the argument for the CDN in one line: the traffic is enormous, and almost all of it is duplicate. A cache hit at the edge saves both the origin bandwidth and the round trip, and at a 95% hit ratio the origin only ever sees 5% of the load.

⚖6. The key trade-offs

The choices, and what each one costs.

DecisionChosen vAlternative xReasoning
TranscodingAsync Kafka pipeline (eventual availability)Sync (block upload until done)Sync transcode = wait 5-60 min for every upload. Terrible UX. Async = upload acknowledged immediately, video available in ~5 min. Acceptable.
Streaming formatHLS (HTTP Live Streaming)RTMP / WebRTCHLS works over standard CDN HTTP. RTMP requires special servers. WebRTC good for sub-second latency (live streaming) but overkill for pre-recorded video. HLS adaptive bitrate = optimal for variable bandwidth.
StorageGCS object storageHDFS / customGCS: 11-nine durability, petabyte scale, CDN integration, managed. HDFS: operational burden, no CDN, doesn't scale to exabytes easily.

How many renditions — the multiplier nobody prices

This looks like a product question and is actually the largest line item in the compute budget. Every rendition is another full encode of every video.

The naive answer is to encode everything into every rendition. The better answer is that the catalogue is extremely skewed: most videos get almost no views, and a small fraction get nearly all of them.

So encode a safe baseline for everything on upload — enough to be watchable on a phone and a laptop — and generate the expensive renditions on demand, when a video first gets traffic, caching the result. A video that never gets watched never costs you a 4K encode. The first viewer of a newly popular video may briefly get a lower quality, which is a price nobody notices.

Adaptive bitrate: why the player decides

The server could pick a quality by looking at the request. It would be wrong constantly, because bandwidth on a mobile connection changes between one segment and the next, and the only entity that knows how fast the last segment actually arrived is the player.

So the server publishes options and the client chooses. This is a general pattern worth naming: put the decision where the information is. It also happens to make the server stateless with respect to playback, which is what lets segments be plain cacheable files.

🏗7. High-level design
Upload and transcode — and the backlog users experience as “processing”
upload chunkstranscode jobrenditionsqueued jobs
What is moving: the client uploads chunks straight into object storage, then a transcode DAG fans each source out into a ladder of renditions, which are pushed to the CDN. Upload and transcode are deliberately decoupled: the upload succeeds long before the video is watchable.
What goes wrong: transcode is throughput-bound and uploads are bursty, so a spike fills the queue and every new video sits in processing. Nothing errors — which is what makes it insidious. The levers are to transcode lazily for the long tail (most uploads are never watched) and eagerly only for the low renditions, and to publish the source rendition immediately so the video is at least playable.

Two pipelines. Note that they only touch at object storage.

UPLOAD compute-bound, asynchronous, nobody is waiting client --> chunks straight into object storage pre-signed URLs; bypasses the app tier | v "upload complete" TRANSCODE QUEUE | +-------------+-------------+-------------+ v v v v chunk 1 chunk 2 chunk 3 chunk 4 parallel across machines | | | | +-------------+------+------+-------------+ v renditions: 360p 480p 720p 1080p 4K each cut into ~4-second segments | v object storage + manifest state = ready PLAYBACK egress-bound, latency-sensitive, enormous player --> manifest what renditions exist, where the segments are | +--> CDN EDGE segment 1 @ 1080p cache hit: never reaches origin +--> CDN EDGE segment 2 @ 1080p +--> CDN EDGE segment 3 @ 480p bandwidth dropped; player stepped down +--> CDN EDGE segment 4 @ 720p recovering
The player re-decides on every segment, so a bad four seconds costs four seconds of quality rather than a stall. Segments are immutable files with long cache lifetimes — the ideal CDN object.
🔄8. Workflows — what actually happens
Marco uploads a 45-minute 4K video from a café
Upload, transcode, publish — and what happens when the wifi drops.
  1. Marco's client asks to start an upload and gets back an upload id, a chunk size, and a set of pre-signed URLs. The bytes will go straight to object storage, not through our servers.
  2. It uploads chunks in parallel. Twenty minutes in, the café wifi dies. Four chunks were in flight and are lost.
  3. Marco reconnects. The client asks which chunks are already stored, re-uploads only those four, and continues. Nothing restarts.
  4. On completion we mark the video transcoding and put a job on the queue. Marco's browser is free; he closes the tab.
  5. The transcode pipeline splits the source into chunks and fans them across many machines. Each produces every rendition for its chunk.
  6. Chunks are concatenated per rendition and cut into ~4-second segments. A manifest is written listing what exists.
  7. Once 720p and 1080p are ready, the video flips to ready — roughly three minutes after upload finished. The 4K encode is still running and will be added to the manifest when it lands.
Marco waited for the upload and nothing else. Publishing did not wait for the most expensive rendition, because the manifest describes what exists rather than what was planned.
Aditi watches it on a train
Adaptive bitrate doing its job, segment by segment.
  1. Her player fetches the manifest and sees five renditions. It starts conservatively at 480p, because starting high and stalling is worse than starting low and climbing.
  2. First segment arrives in 300 ms — far faster than the four seconds of playback it contains. The player has headroom, so it requests the next one at 720p.
  3. That also arrives quickly. It steps up to 1080p and stays there while the buffer fills.
  4. The train enters a cutting and throughput collapses. The next segment is arriving too slowly to keep up with playback.
  5. The player drops to 360p for the following segment. The picture gets soft; the video does not stop.
  6. Signal returns, the buffer refills, and within a few segments it is back at 1080p.
Every one of those segments came from a cache near Aditi — each is an immutable file that thousands of other viewers had already requested. The origin served none of them.
A video goes viral in twenty minutes
Where the edge cache earns its keep, and where it briefly does not.
  1. Views go from a few hundred to two million. Requests land at edge caches all over the world.
  2. The first viewer at each edge misses the cache. That segment is fetched from the origin once and stored.
  3. Every subsequent viewer at that edge is served locally. With a hundred edges and two million viewers, the origin sees on the order of hundreds of requests, not millions.
  4. The early minutes are the dangerous window: many edges missing simultaneously on the same popular segments. Request coalescing at the edge collapses concurrent misses for the same object into a single origin fetch.
  5. View counts are appended to a stream rather than incremented in the database. A background job aggregates and updates the count every few seconds.
  6. The counter is briefly behind reality. Nobody notices, and the alternative — two million writes to one row — would have taken the database down.
This is the entire argument for a CDN in one scenario: the load is enormous and almost entirely duplicate, so caching turns a million-fold problem into a hundred-fold one.
🔍9. Deep dives, and what breaks

What a transcode job actually does

Decode the source into raw frames, then re-encode those frames several times with different resolution and bitrate settings, then cut each output into aligned segments and write a manifest.

Two details matter more than the rest. Segments must be aligned across renditions — segment 12 of the 480p stream must cover exactly the same four seconds as segment 12 of the 1080p stream, or the player cannot switch between them cleanly. That means every segment starts on a keyframe, at the same timestamps in every rendition.

And chunk-level parallelism has a seam. If you split the source and encode chunks independently, the joins between chunks can show artefacts unless the split points are keyframes and the encoder settings are identical. It is the classic parallelism trade: enormous speedup, at the cost of care at the boundaries.

Why the CDN is the architecture, not a layer

It is tempting to draw a CDN as a box in front of the origin. In a video system it is closer to the other way round: almost every byte a user receives comes from an edge, and the origin exists to populate edges.

That reframing changes what you monitor. Cache hit ratio is a top-line metric, because a drop from 95% to 90% doubles origin egress. It also changes how you think about cache keys: segments are immutable and get long lifetimes, while manifests change when a rendition is added and get short ones.

Popularity is extremely skewed, which works in your favour. A small set of segments accounts for most requests and stays resident at every edge. The long tail misses more often, but it is a small fraction of total traffic, so the origin load stays manageable.

Live streaming, if they ask

Worth having an answer ready, because it is the natural follow-up and it breaks the design above in a specific way.

Everything here assumes you have the whole file before you start. Live has no end: segments must be produced continuously, a few seconds behind reality, and published as they are created. The batch queue becomes a streaming pipeline, the manifest becomes something that grows, and the transcode budget per second becomes a hard real-time constraint rather than a throughput target — falling behind is not slow, it is broken.

The delivery half, happily, barely changes. Segments are still segments and the CDN still caches them; they just have very short lifetimes.

What breaks

Transcode worker crashes mid-job
Kafka offset not committed until job complete. Worker crash -> message re-delivered -> new worker picks up from beginning (idempotent: transcode is pure function, same input = same output). Partial segments discarded.
GCS regional outage
Multi-region GCS bucket (US + EU). If primary region down, read from secondary with minimal latency increase. Writes queued and replayed when primary recovers. CDN cache continues serving most traffic during outage.
CDN node failure
CDN routes around failed edge nodes automatically. Traffic shifts to next-nearest edge. Brief latency increase. Popular content likely cached on multiple edges.
The dominant constraint

Upload volume and watch volume are different systems. Transcoding is a throughput problem sized by uploads; delivery is an egress problem sized by watches, and they scale independently.

What I would build first

Chunked resumable upload into object storage, then an asynchronous transcode DAG. Playback can serve the original rendition until the ladder is ready.

What I deliberately did not build

Live streaming, DRM and recommendations. Live in particular removes the batch transcode window and is a different design.

The biggest risk

Transcode cost. The rendition matrix multiplies your entire compute bill, so I would transcode lazily for the long tail rather than eagerly for everything.

💬 If you get this far, here is what they will push on
Follow-ups an interviewer is likely to ask once the design is on the board. Answers supplied — read the question, answer it out loud, then open it.
“A video gets 10 million views in an hour. Where does it hurt?”Answer

Almost nowhere, and that is the point of the design. Playback is served from the CDN, and a popular video is the best possible case for a cache — one object, requested constantly, cached at every edge.

What does hurt is the first few minutes, when the video is not yet on the edges and every request goes to origin. That is a cold-start stampede, and the mitigation is to pre-push popular uploads to edges proactively rather than waiting for demand.

The view counter is the other pressure point, and it is why counts are aggregated from a stream rather than incremented per view.

“Why not transcode every rendition immediately?”Answer

Because most videos are never watched. Transcoding the full ladder for every upload means paying the full compute cost for a catalogue where a small fraction gets any traffic at all.

So transcode the low renditions eagerly, because they are cheap and cover most devices, and generate higher ones lazily on first request. A viewer who wants 4K waits a little the first time; everyone after that gets it from cache.

The trade is a slower first play for rare, high-quality requests, in exchange for not paying for renditions nobody ever asks for.

“How do you make view counts accurate?”Answer

You do not make them exactly accurate, and you should say so. A view event is fired from the client, which means it can be replayed, faked or lost.

Counts go through the same pipeline shape as D26: events into a durable log, deduplicated by a client-generated id, aggregated in batch. The number you show is provisional and the number you use for creator payouts is the batch one, computed after a close window.

Trying to increment a counter synchronously on the playback path would put a hot write on every view and still be wrong.

“What changes if this is live streaming instead?”Answer

Almost everything. Live removes the batch transcode window: you cannot take five minutes to produce renditions when the event is happening now, so transcoding becomes a low-latency pipeline running alongside the broadcast.

Segments are produced continuously and pushed to the CDN as they are made, so the CDN caches a rolling window rather than a complete file. Latency becomes the headline metric instead of throughput.

It is a different design, and the right move in an interview is to scope it out explicitly rather than pretend the same architecture covers both.

Design a Distributed Job Scheduler (like AWS Lambda / Cron)

Difficulty: Medium-Hard  .  Target: 40 min
💬 The question, as asked

“Design a distributed job scheduler. Jobs run at a scheduled time or on a cron expression, across a fleet of workers, and must not run twice.”

⚡ What makes it hard

“Must not run twice” is not achievable as stated — you cannot have exactly-once execution across a network. The real design question is who absorbs the duplicate, and what stops a paused worker acting on an expired lease.

📋1. Understanding the question

The prompt: “Design a distributed job scheduler. Jobs run at a scheduled time or on a cron expression, across a fleet of workers, and must not run twice.”

There is a trap in that last clause, and finding it is most of the interview.

“Must not run twice” cannot be delivered as stated. Not with a better database, not with a cleverer lock. Here is why, concretely.

🎯 The impossibility, in four lines

A worker claims job 7 and starts running it. Its process pauses — a long garbage collection, a hypervisor stall, a network partition. From the outside it is indistinguishable from a dead machine, so the scheduler hands job 7 to another worker. Then the first worker wakes up and carries on, having no idea any time passed.

Two workers are now running job 7. Nothing was misconfigured. This is what a distributed system does.

So what is the real question

Not “how do I prevent duplicates” but “where does the duplicate get absorbed, and what stops the zombie worker doing damage after its claim expired?”

There are two honest answers and you should offer both:

  • Make the handler idempotent. Running it twice has the same effect as running it once. Cheap, robust, and it pushes the problem to people who can actually solve it, because only the handler knows what its own work means.
  • Give each claim a number that only increases, and have the downstream system reject stale ones. The woken-up worker tries to write with an old number and is refused. This is a fencing token, and it is the only thing that genuinely stops a zombie.

What does not work is a lease alone. A lease says “you have this job for 30 seconds”, but the paused worker cannot check its watch, and the resource it is writing to has no idea the lease expired.

What they are looking for

Do you push back on “exactly once”? Politely, with the pause scenario. Candidates who promise it are promising something they cannot build.

Do you know how to poll a database from many workers? The naive version has every worker fighting for the same rows.

Do you have a plan for the backlog after an outage? The scheduler recovering is exactly when it is least able to cope with catch-up work.

❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
Exactly-once, or at-least-once with idempotent handlers?
Exactly-once execution is not achievable across a network, so the honest question is who absorbs the duplicate — you, or the handler.
What scheduling precision is required?
One second versus one minute changes the polling architecture completely, and precision is far more expensive than it sounds.
How long can a job run?
Long jobs need leases and heartbeats, and a lease that expires mid-run is the classic fencing problem.
Do jobs have dependencies on each other?
A DAG scheduler is a different system from a cron scheduler. This is worth scoping out loud.
What happens to a window missed during an outage?
Skip, or catch up? Catch-up creates a thundering backlog exactly when the system is already unhealthy.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.
📝2. Functional requirements
  • One-shot jobs: run this at 14:30 tomorrow.
  • Recurring jobs: a cron expression, evaluated forward to the next run.
  • Each job names a handler — a URL to call or a function to invoke — and a payload.
  • At-least-once execution, with duplicates handled by idempotency or fencing.
  • Retries with backoff, bounded, ending in a dead-letter state rather than looping forever.
  • Status and history: pending, running, succeeded, failed, and what happened last time.
  • Pause, resume, delete — the operational controls, which get forgotten and are the first thing anyone reaches for at 3am.

Worth scoping out loud: job dependencies are not in this. “Run B after A succeeds” is a workflow engine, which is a different system with a different data model — a DAG rather than a schedule. Conflating the two is a common way to end up designing neither well.

⏱3. Non-functional requirements
RequirementTargetWhat it forces
Firing precisionWithin 1 sThe expensive one. Second-level precision means constantly polling for work that is due; minute-level would allow a much lazier design.
Throughput100K fires/sec peakPeak, not average — and the peak is concentrated. Far more jobs are scheduled for the top of the hour than for 14:37.
Duplicate executionRare, and harmlessStated honestly. Not “never” — rare, and absorbed by idempotent handlers or fencing.
Lost executionNeverThis is the one that must actually hold. A missed billing run is a real incident; a duplicated idempotent one is not.
Availability99.99%And critically: an outage must not lose fires, only delay them. Time keeps passing while you are down.

The peak is not uniform, and that matters

Humans write cron expressions, and humans like round numbers. An enormous share of scheduled jobs fire at 0 * * * * — the top of every hour — and a smaller spike at midnight.

So the 100K/sec peak is not spread across the minute; it arrives in a burst in the first second of the hour. Two consequences: the claim path must handle a thundering herd, and it is worth jittering the stored next-run time by a few seconds for jobs that do not care, which flattens the spike at essentially zero cost.

🗂4. Data model and API

One table does most of the work, and one column on it is the entire scheduling algorithm.

-- Jobs table (PostgreSQL -- ACID needed for scheduling locks) TABLE jobs { job_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(255), cron_expr VARCHAR(100), -- NULL for one-shot next_run_at TIMESTAMP, handler_url TEXT, payload JSONB, status ENUM(pending, running, succeeded, failed), retry_count INT DEFAULT 0, max_retries INT DEFAULT 3, last_run_at TIMESTAMP, locked_by VARCHAR(64), -- worker_id holding lock lock_expires TIMESTAMP -- fencing: lock expires if worker crashes } -- INDEX: (next_run_at, status) WHERE status = 'pending' -- This index allows efficient polling: 'give me pending jobs due now'

The important column is next_run_at, with an index on it. Finding work to do is then a single query: rows where next_run_at <= now and status is pending. That is an index range scan over a tiny slice of a large table.

Everything else follows. When a recurring job finishes, you evaluate its cron expression forward and write the next next_run_at. The schedule is not a separate structure; it is a column and an index.

The lease columns — who holds it, until when, and the fencing token — are what make claiming safe. The token is a counter that increments on every claim of that job, so a later claim always has a strictly higher number than an earlier one. That ordering is the whole mechanism.

The claim query, which is the heart of it

BEGIN; SELECT job_id, payload FROM jobs WHERE next_run_at <= now() AND status = 'pending' ORDER BY next_run_at LIMIT 50 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED; -- the load-bearing clause UPDATE jobs SET status = 'running', lease_owner = :worker, lease_expires = now() + '30s', fence = fence + 1 WHERE job_id IN (...); COMMIT;

SKIP LOCKED is the difference between this working and not working. Without it, fifty workers issuing that query all try to lock the same fifty oldest rows; forty-nine of them block, waiting for the first to commit, and your throughput is one worker's worth no matter how many you add.

With it, each worker takes rows nobody else has locked and moves on. Fifty workers claim fifty disjoint batches with no contention at all. It is one clause, and it converts a serialised queue into a parallel one.

The API

POST /v1/jobs Body: { name, cron_expr | run_at, handler_url, payload, max_retries, idempotency_key } Response: 201 { job_id, next_run_at } // idempotency_key makes job creation safe to retry GET /v1/jobs/{id} -> { state, next_run_at, last_run, retry_count } PATCH /v1/jobs/{id} Body: { paused: true } DELETE /v1/jobs/{id} -> 204 (idempotent) GET /v1/jobs/{id}/runs -> execution history with fencing tokens // Worker-facing, not public: POST /internal/claim Body: { worker_id, lease_ms, batch } Response: { jobs:[{ job_id, payload, fencing_token, lease_expires }] } POST /internal/heartbeat // extends the lease mid-run
📊5. Capacity estimation

The numbers, and the one that shapes the claim path.

⚖ Assumptions — and what breaks if each is wrong
10M scheduled jobs, 100K fires/sec at peak
If peak were 1M/sec the single-database claim loop breaks and the scheduler must shard by time bucket.
Jobs fire within 1 second of schedule
Relaxing to a minute allows a far simpler polling design with much lower database pressure.
Handlers are idempotent
Otherwise at-least-once delivery is unsafe and a deduplication store joins the execution path.
10M
scheduled jobs
100K/s
peak fires
~35K/s
claim queries at batch 3
~20 GB
job rows
200 MB/s
payload throughput
<1 s
fire precision

At 100K fires per second, claiming one row per query would mean 100,000 transactions per second against one table — comfortably past what a single primary sustains, and all of it contending on the same hot index range.

Batching is what rescues it. A worker claiming 50 jobs per query turns 100K claims/sec into 2,000 queries/sec, which one Postgres primary handles without noticing. The batch size is a genuine trade: larger batches mean fewer queries but a bigger blast radius when a worker dies mid-batch, since all 50 of those jobs wait for the lease to expire.

The data itself is small. Ten million job rows at a couple of kilobytes each is around 20 GB — it fits in memory on a normal machine. This is not a storage problem, it is a contention problem, and saying which one it is tells the interviewer you sized it rather than guessed.

⚖6. The key trade-offs

The choices, and their bills.

DecisionChosen vAlternative xReasoning
Job claimSELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKEDDistributed lock (Redis)DB-level locking eliminates network round-trip to external lock service. SKIP LOCKED allows concurrent schedulers without contention. Simpler -- no lock service dependency.
Exactly-onceDB lock + idempotent handler contractTransactionsFull exactly-once requires handler to be idempotent (we guarantee at-most-once delivery; handler must handle retries). Telling customers: 'your handler may run twice on failure -- make it idempotent' is standard practice.
DeliveryPull (DB poll every 1s)Push (DB triggers)DB triggers couple scheduler to DB internals. Poll is simple, predictable, scalable. 1-second poll granularity acceptable for most cron use cases. Sub-second scheduling needs a different architecture.

Push or pull

Push: the scheduler tracks which workers exist and dispatches jobs to them. It gives tight control over placement, and it means the scheduler must now do health checking, load tracking, and retry-on-worker-death. It has become a cluster manager.

Pull: workers ask for work when they have capacity. The scheduler stops caring how many workers exist or whether any of them are healthy. A worker that dies simply stops asking, and its lease expires.

Pull wins here, and the reason is worth generalising: it makes worker failure a non-event rather than something to detect. There is no health check to get wrong, because not asking for work is itself the signal. It also load-balances for free, since a busy worker naturally polls less often.

Catch-up or skip after an outage

The scheduler is down for twenty minutes. Forty thousand fires were missed. What happens when it comes back?

“Catch up” sounds obviously right and is dangerous: a system that just recovered immediately gets its worst-ever burst of load, which is a very good way to knock it straight back over. And for many jobs the catch-up is meaningless — running twenty missed copies of “refresh the cache” is nineteen wasted runs.

The answer is per-job policy, defaulted sensibly:

  • Skip for idempotent refresh-style jobs. Run the current one, drop the backlog. This is the right default.
  • Catch up, rate-limited for jobs where each occurrence matters — a billing run per customer per day. Replay them, but drip-fed so recovery does not become a second outage.
🏗7. High-level design
Lease-based claim — and the paused worker that wakes up believing it still owns the job
claim + fencing tokenexecutionstale execution
What is moving: workers claim batches with SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED so they never block each other, each claim carries a monotonically increasing fencing token, and the worker heartbeats to extend its lease while it runs.
What goes wrong: worker 1 hits a long GC pause. Its lease expires, the scheduler hands the job to worker 2 with a higher token, and then worker 1 wakes up still believing it holds the lease — it cannot tell that time passed. Without fencing both would execute. The handler rejects token 41 because it has already seen 42, which makes the stale actor harmless rather than trying to prevent it. Ch 6

Three parts, and the database is the coordination point.

JOBS TABLE index on next_run_at job_id next_run_at status lease_expires fence ------ ----------- ------- ------------- ----- 7 14:30:00 pending - 4 8 14:30:00 running 14:30:31 12 9 15:00:00 pending - 1 WORKERS pull, they are never pushed to worker-A ---> "give me 50 due jobs" SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED worker-B ---> "give me 50 due jobs" gets a disjoint 50; no blocking worker-C ---> "give me 50 due jobs" each claim: status=running, lease=+30s, fence += 1 RUNNING worker invokes the handler, carrying its fence token | +-- heartbeat every 10s ---> extends the lease | +-- success ---> status=succeeded, next_run_at = cron.next() | +-- failure ---> retry_count++, next_run_at = now + backoff | +-- silence ---> lease expires, the row becomes claimable again the old worker may still be alive; its fence is now stale REAPER one query, on a timer UPDATE jobs SET status='pending' WHERE status='running' AND lease_expires < now()
There is no leader election and no membership list. The database is the only shared state, and a worker's liveness is expressed entirely by whether its lease is still fresh.
🔄8. Workflows — what actually happens
An hourly report job fires normally
The path everything else is a deviation from.
  1. Job 7 sits with next_run_at = 14:00:00, status pending. Nothing is watching it; it is just a row.
  2. At 14:00:00, worker A's claim query finds it in the due range and locks it along with 49 others.
  3. In the same transaction: status becomes running, the lease is set 30 seconds out, and the fence token goes from 4 to 5.
  4. Worker A calls the handler URL, passing the payload and fence token 5. The handler takes 90 seconds.
  5. Every 10 seconds A heartbeats, pushing the lease forward. The reaper never sees it as expired.
  6. The handler returns 200. A evaluates the cron expression, writes next_run_at = 15:00:00, sets status back to pending, and clears the lease.
The heartbeat is what makes long jobs possible without long leases. A 30-second lease with heartbeats recovers from a dead worker in 30 seconds; a 2-minute lease sized for the job's runtime would take 2 minutes.
Worker A pauses for 40 seconds and job 7 runs twice
The scenario from step 1, with the fence doing its job.
  1. Worker A is holding job 7 with fence 5. Its process stalls — a long GC pause. It stops heartbeating and, critically, it does not know it has stopped.
  2. At 30 seconds the lease expires. The reaper flips job 7 back to pending.
  3. Worker B claims it, gets fence 6, and runs the handler. The report is written, tagged with fence 6.
  4. Worker A wakes up. As far as it is concerned no time has passed. It finishes its work and tries to write the report with fence 5.
  5. The storage layer sees a write with a fence lower than the 6 it has already accepted and rejects it.
  6. Worker A gets an error, sees the fence rejection, and abandons the job rather than retrying.
The job genuinely ran twice — that part was never preventable. What was preventable was the stale run's effect, and a monotonically increasing token is the mechanism. Note the requirement this pushes downstream: the storage layer must check the fence. A design that mints tokens nobody validates has achieved nothing.
Midnight: 400,000 jobs are due in the same second
The thundering herd that cron expressions create.
  1. Everyone writes 0 0 * * *. At 00:00:00 the due range suddenly contains 400,000 rows.
  2. Every worker's next claim query hits the same hot slice of the index simultaneously.
  3. SKIP LOCKED keeps them from blocking each other — each takes a disjoint batch — but the database is still doing 8,000 claim queries per second against one index range.
  4. Jobs execute for several minutes, so the tail of the backlog fires late. That violates the 1-second precision target for most of those 400,000.
  5. The fix is upstream of all this: at creation time, jitter the first next_run_at by a random offset within a window, for jobs that declare they tolerate it.
  6. The same 400,000 jobs now spread across 60 seconds. Peak claim rate drops by more than an order of magnitude and precision holds for nearly all of them.
The cheapest fix for a synchronised load spike is almost always to desynchronise it. It costs nothing and it prevents the problem rather than absorbing it.
The handler is slow and the retry storm begins
Why backoff has to be capped and jittered.
  1. A downstream service starts returning 500s. Ten thousand jobs fail.
  2. Each schedules a retry. With a fixed 1-minute delay, all ten thousand retry at the same moment — the failure synchronised them.
  3. That burst hits the already-struggling service and keeps it down. The retries have become the outage.
  4. With exponential backoff the delays spread out — 1, 2, 4, 8 minutes — but they are still synchronised, just at coarser intervals.
  5. Adding jitter to each delay breaks the alignment. Retries arrive as a smooth trickle instead of waves.
  6. After the configured maximum, the job stops retrying and moves to a dead-letter state with its error recorded. It waits for a human rather than looping forever.
Retries without backoff turn one failure into a denial-of-service you performed on yourself. The dead-letter state matters just as much: an unbounded retry hides a broken job indefinitely, and a job that needs attention should be visible, not quietly spinning.
🔍9. Deep dives, and what breaks

Cron evaluation, and the two bugs everyone ships

Computing the next fire time from an expression looks like a parsing exercise and has two traps that only appear in production.

Daylight saving. A job scheduled for 02:30 local time in a zone that springs forward has no 02:30 on that day — and in autumn it has two. You must decide what happens, and the only sane answer is to store the timezone with the job, compute in local time, and pick an explicit policy for the missing and doubled hours. Storing everything in UTC and converting is the tempting shortcut and it silently moves people's jobs by an hour twice a year.

Computing the next time from “now” rather than from the scheduled time. If a job was due at 14:00 and actually ran at 14:03, the next run must be 15:00, not 15:03. Otherwise the schedule drifts forward every cycle and an hourly job slowly becomes a job that runs whenever it feels like it.

Choosing the lease duration

It is a direct trade between recovery time and false reclaims, and there is no universally right answer.

Short leases recover from dead workers quickly, but a worker that is merely slow gets its job stolen — producing exactly the duplicate you have been working to make rare. Long leases avoid false reclaims but mean a genuinely dead worker's jobs sit idle for the full duration.

Heartbeats resolve most of the tension. Keep the lease short — tens of seconds — and have the worker extend it while it is alive. Then lease duration is about detecting death, not about job runtime, and the two stop being coupled. A job that runs for an hour still has a 30-second recovery window.

When one database stops being enough

The single-table design holds to a surprisingly high load, and you should say where it stops.

The binding constraint is claim-query throughput against one primary. Past that, shard the jobs table — by time bucket or by a hash of the job id — and have each worker poll a subset of shards. The claim logic is unchanged; there are simply several independent copies of it.

The thing worth resisting is reaching for that early. A sharded scheduler has rebalancing, hot shards and cross-shard visibility problems that the single-table version simply does not have. Name the threshold, and say you would cross it when measured, not when imagined.

What breaks

Scheduler leader crashes
Follower detects via etcd lease expiry (~15s). Takes over leadership. Jobs due during those 15s: lock_expires hasn't passed, so they're safe. After 15s: new leader picks up pending jobs. Max 15-second delay.
Worker crashes mid-execution
lock_expires passes -> sweeper resets job to pending -> re-executed. Handler MUST be idempotent (most are: send email with idempotency key, write to DB with upsert). Document this contract clearly.
DB (PostgreSQL) failure
Primary fails -> replica promoted (RDS Multi-AZ: ~30s). Schedulers lose DB connection, buffer job picks in memory (Kafka), retry DB connection. No jobs lost. Some delayed by up to ~1 min.
The dominant constraint

Nobody can promise exactly-once execution across a network. So the design provides at-least-once delivery with fencing tokens, and requires handlers to be idempotent. Saying that plainly is the honest answer.

What I would build first

The leased-claim loop: SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, a lease with a heartbeat, and a fencing token so a resurrected worker cannot act on stale authority.

What I deliberately did not build

DAG dependencies between jobs. That is a workflow engine, and it is a different system worth scoping out explicitly.

The biggest risk

The catch-up stampede. After an outage, every missed window fires at once against a system that is already unhealthy; the backlog needs rate limiting, not just replay.

💬 If you get this far, here is what they will push on
Follow-ups an interviewer is likely to ask once the design is on the board. Answers supplied — read the question, answer it out loud, then open it.
“A worker claims a job, then its process freezes for 40 seconds. What stops the job running twice?”Answer

Nothing stops it from being attempted twice, and that is the honest framing. The lease expires, the scheduler hands the job to another worker, and then the frozen worker wakes up still believing it owns it. It cannot tell that time passed.

What saves you is the fencing token. Each claim carries a number that only increases. The second worker got a higher one. When the frozen worker finally calls the handler, the handler sees an older token than one it has already accepted and rejects it.

So the stale worker is not prevented, it is made harmless. That distinction is the whole idea.

“What if a job needs to run for six hours?”Answer

Then the lease has to be renewed rather than granted once. The worker heartbeats while it runs, extending its claim, and if the heartbeats stop the lease lapses and someone else picks the job up.

Long jobs also change the failure economics. Losing a six-hour job at hour five is expensive, so you want checkpointing inside the job itself, which means the handler needs to be resumable rather than merely idempotent.

At that point you are close to needing a workflow engine, and it is worth saying that out loud as a scope boundary.

“The system was down for two hours. Ten thousand jobs missed their window. Now what?”Answer

This is the catch-up stampede, and the default behaviour is usually wrong. If every missed job fires the moment the scheduler recovers, you hit an already-fragile system with ten thousand simultaneous executions.

The policy has to be explicit per job. Some jobs should skip entirely — a report for a window that has passed is useless. Some must catch up, but at a controlled rate rather than all at once.

So: a per-job catch-up policy, and a rate limit on the replay. Firing everything immediately is how a recovery becomes a second outage.

“Why SKIP LOCKED rather than just selecting pending jobs?”Answer

Because without it, workers block on each other. Ten workers all run “select the next pending jobs and lock them”, and nine of them wait behind the first transaction rather than getting on with other work.

SKIP LOCKED tells the database to ignore rows another transaction has locked and move on. So each worker picks up a disjoint batch and nobody queues.

It turns what looks like a contention problem into parallel work, using a feature the database already has, which is much better than building a distributed queue on top of it.

Design a Distributed Message Queue (Apache Kafka / Google Cloud PubSub)

Difficulty: Hard (Staff Expectation)  •  Target: 45 min
💬 The question, as asked

“Design a distributed message queue like Kafka. Producers publish, multiple independent consumer groups read, and nothing may be lost.”

⚡ What makes it hard

Ordering and throughput are in direct tension. A global order means one partition and one machine’s worth of throughput. Everything here follows from accepting per-partition ordering instead.

📋1. Understanding the question

The prompt: “Design a distributed message queue like Kafka. Producers publish, multiple independent consumer groups read, and nothing may be lost.”

Start by being precise about what “queue” means here, because the word covers two very different things and the design depends entirely on which one is meant.

A traditional queue hands each message to one consumer and deletes it. Messages are removed as they are processed; the queue's job is to hold work until someone takes it.

What is being asked for is a log. Messages are appended to a file and stay there for a retention period whether or not anyone read them. Each consumer group tracks its own position in that file — a number saying “I have processed up to here”. Reading does not consume; it advances a bookmark.

🎯 Why the log model matters

Because the data stays, five teams can read the same stream independently and a sixth can join next month and start from the beginning. And when a consumer ships a bug, the fix is to rewind its bookmark and reprocess — the data is still there. In a delete-on-read queue it is gone.

The tension the whole design is built around

Ordering and throughput pull in opposite directions, and you cannot have both at full strength.

To guarantee that messages come out in the order they went in, they have to be written to one place, in one sequence, by one machine. One machine's throughput is your ceiling — and no amount of hardware moves it much.

To scale past that you need many machines appending in parallel, and the moment you have that, there is no single order. Two messages written to two machines at the same instant have no defensible “first”.

The resolution is to split the topic into partitions and guarantee order only within each. Messages that need ordering relative to each other — all events for one user, say — are routed to the same partition by a key. Everything else spreads out.

This is the same move that appears throughout the guide: make the constraint local instead of coordinating. You do not need global order. You need order per user, per account, per conversation — and that fits in one partition.

What they are looking for

Do you know why it is fast? The answer is not “it is in memory” — it is on disk. Sequential disk writes plus zero-copy reads, explained below.

Do you understand what a consumer group is for? It is the mechanism for both parallelism and independence, and most candidates can only explain one of the two.

Can you place “nothing may be lost” precisely? There is a specific setting that decides it, and a specific cost to turning it on.

❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
Ordering: per partition, or global?
Global ordering means a single partition, which caps your throughput at one machine. Almost nobody actually needs it.
At-least-once or exactly-once delivery?
Exactly-once needs idempotent producers plus transactions, and costs throughput. Most consumers are cheaper to make idempotent.
Retention: how long, and is replay required?
Replay turns the queue into a durable log and changes storage sizing by orders of magnitude.
How many consumer groups, and what lag is tolerable?
Decides fan-out cost and whether slow consumers can be isolated from fast ones.
What is the maximum message size?
Large payloads need a claim-check pattern — put the blob in object storage and send the pointer.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.
📝2. Functional requirements
  • Publish to a named topic, optionally with a key that decides the partition.
  • Subscribe as part of a consumer group. Each partition goes to exactly one member of the group, so the group's members share the work without overlapping.
  • Strict ordering within a partition. Across partitions, explicitly not guaranteed — and that is a feature, not a gap.
  • Retention by time or size, independent of whether anyone consumed.
  • Replay. A consumer can reset its position and reprocess from any point still retained.
  • Fan-out to independent groups. Five groups reading the same topic each get every message and keep their own position.

What a consumer group actually does

It is worth spelling out, because it is the piece most often misdescribed.

A topic with 12 partitions and a group of 4 consumers gives each consumer 3 partitions. Add two more consumers and the group rebalances to 2 each. Add more consumers than partitions and the extras sit idle — partition count is the hard ceiling on a group's parallelism, which is why it is chosen up front and painful to change.

Meanwhile a second group reading the same topic gets its own complete copy of the assignment and its own offsets. The billing team and the analytics team read the same events, at different speeds, without knowing about each other.

⏱3. Non-functional requirements
RequirementTargetWhat it forces
Write throughput1M msg/secAbout 1 GB/s of ingress. This is what rules out any design that does a random disk write or a synchronous fsync per message.
Read throughput5M msg/secFive consumer groups reading everything. Egress is 5× ingress, which is why the read path gets its own optimisation.
Produce latencyp99 < 10 msWith acks from all in-sync replicas. The floor is the slowest replica's round trip.
DurabilityNo acknowledged lossThe requirement with the clearest price tag. See below.
Leader failover< 5 sA partition without a leader accepts nothing. Detection plus election is the entire write outage for that partition.
Retention7 daysSets the storage bill and bounds how far back a consumer can rewind.

“Nothing may be lost”, made specific

That phrase resolves to one producer setting, and knowing it is a strong signal.

  • acks=0 — fire and forget. Fastest, and a broker restart loses whatever was in flight.
  • acks=1 — the leader has it. Feels safe and is not: if the leader dies before the followers replicate, the message is gone and the producer was told it succeeded.
  • acks=all — every in-sync replica has it. This is the one that satisfies the requirement.

The cost of acks=all is that produce latency becomes the slowest replica's latency, so one struggling follower slows every producer. Which is why the in-sync replica set is dynamic: a replica that falls too far behind is removed from the set, so it stops holding up acknowledgements. That in turn creates the failure mode discussed below, where the set shrinks to one and acks=all quietly stops meaning what you think it means.

🗂4. Data model and API

There is no schema in the database sense. The storage format is the design, and it is a file.

-- Log Segment File Structure on Broker Disk -- File: /data/kafka/topics/{topic_name}-{partition_id}/{base_offset}.log -- Append-Only Binary Record Format: [Offset: 8B][Size: 4B][CRC: 4B][Magic: 1B][Attributes: 1B][Timestamp: 8B] [Key_Length: 4B][Key_Bytes][Value_Length: 4B][Payload_Bytes] -- Sparse Memory-Mapped Index: {base_offset}.index -- Every 4KB of log data, append entry (Relative Offset: 4B, Physical Byte Position: 4B) [Rel_Offset: 0 -> Pos: 0] [Rel_Offset: 120 -> Pos: 4096] [Rel_Offset: 245 -> Pos: 8192] -- Consumer Offset Tracking (__consumer_offsets internal compacted topic) KEY: (consumer_group_id, topic, partition_id) VALUE: (offset: int64, commit_timestamp: int64, metadata: string)

Each partition is a directory of segment files. Writes append to the newest file and nothing else is ever modified. When a segment reaches a size or age limit it is closed and a new one starts; retention deletes whole closed segments rather than individual records.

That choice — append-only, delete by whole file — is what makes the storage layer boring. There is no compaction of live data, no fragmentation, no rewriting. Expiring a day of data is an unlink.

Why this is faster than it sounds

“It writes to disk” sounds slow and is not, for two specific reasons that are worth naming precisely.

Sequential writes are not random writes. The cost people associate with disk is seek time. An append has no seek: the head is already there. Sequential throughput on modern storage is in the hundreds of megabytes to gigabytes per second, comparable to network bandwidth. The broker does not fight the disk, it uses it the one way it is fast.

The reads come from page cache. Consumers are usually near the tail, reading data written seconds ago — which is still in the operating system's page cache. So the common read never touches a physical disk at all, and the broker gets a large cache for free without managing one.

And the bytes are not copied. Normally sending a file over a socket copies it from page cache into the application, then into a socket buffer. sendfile tells the kernel to move it directly from page cache to the network card. The data never enters the broker's address space. At 5 GB/s of egress that is the difference between a fleet and a few machines — and it is only possible because the broker does not need to look at the messages. It ships opaque bytes. Any feature requiring the broker to inspect payloads would destroy this.

The API

// 1. Produce Message (gRPC / TCP Streaming) rpc Produce(ProduceRequest) returns (ProduceResponse); message ProduceRequest { string topic = 1; int32 partition = 2; // -1 for hash(key) auto-routing bytes key = 3; bytes payload = 4; int32 acks = 5; // 0=no ack, 1=leader ack, -1(all)=ISR ack int64 producer_id = 6; // for idempotent deduplication int32 sequence_number = 7; } // 2. Fetch / Consume Messages (Long Polling Batch) rpc Fetch(FetchRequest) returns (FetchResponse); message FetchRequest { string consumer_group = 1; string topic = 2; int32 partition = 3; int64 fetch_offset = 4; int32 max_bytes = 5; // e.g. 1MB batch int32 max_wait_ms = 6; // long-poll timeout (e.g. 500ms) } // 3. Commit Offset rpc CommitOffset(CommitRequest) returns (CommitResponse); message CommitRequest { string consumer_group = 1; string topic = 2; int32 partition = 3; int64 committed_offset = 4; }

Note max_wait_ms on fetch: consumers long-poll. Rather than asking repeatedly and getting “nothing yet”, the request parks at the broker until data arrives or the timeout expires. Low latency when there is data, no busy-polling when there is not.

📊5. Capacity estimation

The numbers that size the cluster.

⚖ Assumptions — and what breaks if each is wrong
Per-partition ordering is sufficient
Global ordering means one partition and caps throughput at a single machine.
Consumers can be made idempotent
Otherwise exactly-once semantics are required, which costs meaningful throughput.
Retention is measured in days, not years
Long retention turns this into a storage design and changes the cost model entirely.
1M msgs/sec
Peak produce rate (~1 KB avg message payload)
1 GB/sec
Network ingress bandwidth into broker cluster
5 GB/sec
Network egress bandwidth (5x fan-out consumption)
86.4 TB/day
Daily raw storage without replication
605 TB / 7 days
Cluster retention with 3x replication factor
100 brokers
Broker nodes assuming 10 Gbps NIC and NVMe storage

A million 1 KB messages per second is 1 GB/s in. With three replicas, every message is written three times, so the cluster absorbs 3 GB/s of writes. Five consumer groups reading everything is 5 GB/s out, plus replication traffic between brokers.

On a 10 Gbps NIC — about 1.25 GB/s — the network, not the disk and not the CPU, is what you run out of first. That is the sizing conclusion: this is a network-bound system, and it is why brokers get fast NICs and why cross-rack replication placement is a real cost rather than a diagram detail.

Storage is the easy half: 86 TB a day raw, times three for replication, times seven days of retention lands in the high hundreds of terabytes. Spread across a hundred brokers that is a few terabytes each, which is unremarkable.

⚖6. The key trade-offs

The choices, and their costs.

DecisionChosen ✓Alternative ✗Reasoning
