Storage EngineAppend-Only Segmented LogB-Tree / Embedded DB (RocksDB)Log gives O(1) disk writes, sequential reads, and instant zero-copy transfer. B-Trees incur random writes, write amplification, and complex locking.
Replication ConsensusISR with Quorum Controller (KRaft)Paxos / Raft per partitionISR allows dynamic quorum based on live replica speed, achieving maximum write throughput. KRaft manages cluster metadata with a single Raft quorum instead of ZooKeeper.
Consumption ModelPull (Long-Polling by Consumers)Push (Broker pushes to clients)Pull lets consumers pace themselves according to their processing capacity (eliminating consumer overload) and simplifies batch fetching and replay.

Choosing the partition count

This is the decision with the longest shadow, because it is set at topic creation and every option for changing it later is unpleasant.

Too few and you have capped consumer parallelism — adding consumers past the partition count does nothing, and you cannot process faster no matter how much hardware you buy.

Too many and every broker holds thousands of open files, leader elections during a failover take much longer because there are more partitions to reassign, and each partition's batching gets worse because the same traffic is split more ways.

Increasing it later is possible but breaks the one guarantee people depend on: keys are mapped to partitions by hash(key) % partition_count, so changing the count re-maps existing keys. A user whose events all went to partition 3 starts going to partition 7, and their old and new events are now in two partitions with no ordering between them. Ordering breaks retroactively, at the moment you scale.

Which is why the practical advice is to over-provision partitions modestly at creation time. It is a rare case where guessing high is genuinely cheaper than being right later.

Where the offset gets committed

A small choice that decides your delivery semantics entirely.

Commit before processing and you get at-most-once: if the consumer dies mid-work, the offset already moved and the message is never reprocessed. Lost.

Commit after processing and you get at-least-once: if the consumer dies after doing the work but before committing, the message is redelivered and processed twice.

Almost everyone picks the second and makes the processing idempotent, for the same reason as everywhere else in this guide: a duplicate is an inconvenience, a loss is a bug. The honest framing is that the queue cannot give you exactly-once on its own — it can give you at-least-once delivery, and exactly-once effects are something you build at the consumer.

🏗7. High-level design
Replication and leader election — why only the in-sync set may be elected
produced recordreplicationacknowledgement
What is moving: a record is appended to the partition leader, replicated to the followers, and acknowledged to the producer only once every replica in the in-sync set has written it. The lagging replica is deliberately excluded from that set — it is allowed to fall behind without slowing anybody down.
What goes wrong: the leader dies. Election must choose only from the in-sync set, because those replicas provably hold every acknowledged record. Electing the lagging replica — which some systems will do to stay available, called unclean election — means records the producer was told were durable simply vanish. That is the availability-versus-durability choice from Ch 3, made concrete in one config flag.

Topics, partitions, replicas, groups.

TOPIC "orders" — 4 partitions, replication factor 3 producer --> partition = hash(key) % 4 all events for user-42 land on the same partition, always P0 [ 0 ][ 1 ][ 2 ][ 3 ][ 4 ]... leader: broker A followers: B, C P1 [ 0 ][ 1 ][ 2 ]... leader: broker B followers: C, D P2 [ 0 ][ 1 ][ 2 ][ 3 ]... leader: broker C followers: D, A P3 [ 0 ][ 1 ]... leader: broker D followers: A, B append-only. offsets never change. nothing is deleted on read. WRITE acks=all producer --> P0 leader --> followers replicate | +-- all in-sync replicas have it --> ack latency = the slowest in-sync replica READ two independent groups, same data group "billing" consumer-1: P0 P1 offsets: P0=1050 P1=880 consumer-2: P2 P3 group "analytics" consumer-1: P0 P1 P2 P3 offsets: P0=40 ← days behind, fine each group has its own offsets. a slow group slows nobody else. RETENTION segments older than 7 days are deleted whole unlink, not compaction a consumer that falls further behind than retention loses data
The last line is the one people miss: retention is a deadline, not a buffer. A consumer group lagging by more than the retention window is silently skipping messages.
🔄8. Workflows — what actually happens
An order event is published and two teams read it
The path that shows why the log model is worth the complexity.
  1. The checkout service publishes {order: 9981, user: 42} with key user-42. The client hashes the key, gets partition P1, and sends it to P1's leader, broker B.
  2. B appends it to the open segment file. That is a sequential write — no seek, no index update, no random I/O. The offset assigned is 1,204.
  3. Followers C and D pull the record and append it to their own copies. Once both have it, B acknowledges the producer. Elapsed: single-digit milliseconds.
  4. The billing group's consumer for P1 is at offset 1,203. Its long-poll fetch returns immediately with the new record. It charges the card, then commits offset 1,204.
  5. The analytics group is 400,000 records behind because it batches into a warehouse hourly. It will reach 1,204 later. Nobody cares, and billing is unaffected.
  6. Seven days later the segment containing offset 1,204 is deleted. Both groups are long past it.
One write, two independent readers, no coordination between them and no copy of the data per consumer. That is what the delete-on-read queue cannot do.
Broker B dies holding two partition leaderships
Failover, and the write outage it costs.
  1. B stops heartbeating to the controller. Detection takes a few seconds — you cannot make this instant without false positives on every GC pause.
  2. During that window, produces to P1 fail. There is no leader to accept them. Producers retry, which is why producer retries are not optional.
  3. The controller picks a new leader for P1 from the in-sync replicas only — C or D, both of which had every acknowledged message.
  4. C becomes leader. Metadata propagates, producers refresh and resume. Total write outage for P1: a few seconds.
  5. Consumers assigned to P1 reconnect to C and continue from their committed offsets. They lose nothing, because C has everything that was acknowledged.
  6. B returns later as a follower, catches up from C, and rejoins the in-sync set once it is current.
Electing only from in-sync replicas is what makes the acks=all promise hold through failover. Allowing an out-of-sync replica to take over — an unclean election — restores availability faster and loses acknowledged messages. That switch exists, and turning it on means the durability requirement no longer holds.
A consumer group falls behind and starts losing data
The quietest failure in the whole system.
  1. The analytics group's processing slows — a downstream database is struggling. Lag grows from minutes to hours.
  2. Nothing is broken. Producers are fine, brokers are fine, the other groups are fine. The only symptom is a lag number nobody has an alert on.
  3. At six days of lag, the group is reading from segments that are one day from deletion.
  4. Retention runs and deletes the segment the consumer was about to read. Its next fetch asks for an offset that no longer exists.
  5. Depending on configuration it either errors or silently jumps to the oldest available offset — and that second option means messages were skipped and nothing reported it.
  6. Recovery means reprocessing from the source, if a source still exists. The queue cannot help; the data is gone.
Consumer lag deserves an alert with a threshold well below the retention window — a quarter of it is a reasonable starting point. It is the metric that tells you a consumer is dying hours before it dies.
A new consumer joins and the group pauses
Rebalancing, which is correct and disruptive.
  1. The billing group has 2 consumers across 4 partitions, 2 each. Traffic rises and a third consumer starts.
  2. The group coordinator notices the membership change and triggers a rebalance.
  3. Under the basic protocol, all consumers stop and give up their partitions — the stop-the-world step. Consumption halts across the entire group for as long as the rebalance takes.
  4. Partitions are reassigned: 2, 1, 1. Each consumer resumes from the committed offset of its new partitions.
  5. Any work done but not committed before the pause is redone. This is the at-least-once path showing up again.
  6. A consumer that merely restarts — a deploy — triggers the same thing, which is why a rolling deploy of 10 consumers can cause 10 rebalances.
The mitigations are worth naming: a session timeout long enough to ride out a quick restart, and incremental rebalancing that moves only the partitions that must move rather than revoking everything. Rebalance frequency is a real operational metric on busy clusters.
🔍9. Deep dives, and what breaks

The in-sync replica set, and how acks=all quietly weakens

This is the subtlest failure mode in the design and a genuinely good thing to raise unprompted.

acks=all means “all replicas in the in-sync set” — and that set shrinks under stress. A follower that falls behind is removed so it stops delaying acknowledgements. Sensible in isolation.

Now suppose both followers are struggling. Both get removed. The in-sync set is just the leader, and acks=all now means acks=1. The producer is still passing the same flag and still getting acknowledgements, and the durability it believes it has is gone.

The guard is a minimum in-sync replica count: if the set drops below it, refuse writes. That converts a silent durability loss into a loud availability loss, which is almost always the right conversion — an error a producer can retry is far better than a lie it cannot detect.

Batching, which is where the throughput actually comes from

Sending a million individual 1 KB messages per second means a million network round trips and a million appends. Nothing survives that.

So producers accumulate messages briefly — a few milliseconds or up to a batch size — and send them as one request. The broker appends the whole batch as a single write. Compression is applied per batch, and batches of similar records compress far better than records individually.

The trade is plain: a larger batch window means better throughput and more latency, because a message may wait for its batch to fill. It is a slider between the two, and it is the main knob anyone tunes.

Compacted topics

Worth mentioning as the variant that answers a different problem. Instead of deleting by age, compaction keeps the most recent value for each key and discards older ones.

The topic then becomes a changelog you can replay to reconstruct current state. A new service reads from the beginning and ends up with the latest value for every key, however old. That is the mechanism behind stream-table duality and behind rebuilding a cache or a search index from a topic rather than from the source database.

What breaks

Leader Broker Crashes
KRaft controller detects heartbeat failure in <3s. Elects new leader from the ISR pool. No committed data is lost because ISR nodes are byte-for-byte in sync up to HW.
Slow / Stalled Follower
Controller evicts the lagging node from ISR so it does not block produce requests when acks=all. Once caught up, it rejoins the ISR.
Consumer Crashes during processing
Consumer group coordinator detects missed heartbeat (session.timeout.ms). Triggers Consumer Group Rebalance, reassigning crashed consumer's partitions to remaining workers from last committed offset.
Split Brain in Controller Quorum
KRaft uses Raft majority quorum (e.g. 3 of 5 nodes). A network partition cannot elect an illegitimate leader in the minority partition.
The dominant constraint

Sequential disk I/O plus the page cache is faster than most people assume. The whole design leans on it: an append-only log, zero-copy sendfile to consumers, and no per-message random access anywhere.

What I would build first

The partitioned append-only log with an ISR replication protocol. Ordering is per partition, which is the trade that makes throughput scale linearly with partitions.

What I deliberately did not build

Exactly-once semantics and global ordering. Both are available and both cost throughput; most consumers are cheaper to make idempotent.

The biggest risk

Partition count. It is effectively permanent once keys are hashed to partitions, and under-provisioning it caps your throughput in a way you cannot fix without a migration.

💬 If you get this far, here is what they will push on
Follow-ups an interviewer is likely to ask once the design is on the board. Answers supplied — read the question, answer it out loud, then open it.
“Why can you not just guarantee global ordering across all messages?”Answer

You can, and it costs you the entire point of the system. Global order means a single partition, and a single partition means one machine's worth of throughput with no way to scale.

So ordering is per partition, and you choose the partition key to make that useful: if everything about one user must be ordered, partition by user id, and that user's events are ordered even though the topic as a whole is not.

The right response to “we need global ordering” is usually to ask what actually needs ordering. It is almost never everything.

“A consumer is 4 hours behind. What do you do?”Answer

First find out which shape it is, because the two have opposite fixes. If lag is spread evenly across partitions, the consumer group is simply too slow, and you add consumers — but only up to the partition count, because a partition is consumed by exactly one member of a group.

If lag is concentrated in one partition, adding consumers does nothing. That is a hot key, and the fix is repartitioning or changing the key.

Also check retention. If the consumer falls behind further than retention holds, data is deleted before it is read, and the lag turns into silent loss.

“How do you add partitions to a topic later?”Answer

Carefully, and ideally never. Messages are routed by hash(key) mod partitions, so changing the partition count sends the same key somewhere new. Its old and new messages now sit in two partitions with no ordering relationship between them.

Any consumer holding per-key state — a running total, a state machine — is now wrong, and nothing tells you.

So the practical advice is to over-provision partitions from the start, because they are cheap and a migration is not. If you must change it, you are doing a dual-write migration into a new topic, not an in-place resize.

“What does acks=all actually cost?”Answer

Latency on every write, in exchange for durability. With acks=all the producer waits for every in-sync replica to have the record, so a slow replica slows every producer.

With acks=1 only the leader confirms, which is faster and means an acknowledged record can be lost if the leader dies before replicating — exactly the failure in the Ch 4 animation.

The right setting depends on what the topic carries. Payments take the latency. Click telemetry does not need to.

Design Google Drive / Dropbox (Distributed File Storage & Delta Sync)

Difficulty: Hard (Staff Expectation)  •  Target: 45 min
💬 The question, as asked

“Design a file sync service like Google Drive or Dropbox. Files sync across a user’s devices, with version history and sharing.”

⚡ What makes it hard

Sync is not collaborative editing, and conflating them ruins the design. The hard part is bandwidth: re-uploading a 2 GB file after a one-line change is unacceptable, which forces content-defined chunking.

📋1. Understanding the question

The prompt: “Design a file sync service like Google Drive or Dropbox. Files sync across a user's devices, with version history and sharing.”

The first thing to do is rule something out, because if you get this wrong nothing after it can be right.

This is not collaborative editing. Two people typing in the same document at the same time, seeing each other's cursors, is a different system with a different data model — character-level operations, CRDTs or operational transformation, no concept of a file version. That is D20.

File sync is coarser and simpler: a file is a blob of bytes, one device edits it, and the change propagates to the others. Version history means whole versions, not merged edits. Saying this out loud in the first minute is worth a lot, because it is the fork most candidates walk past.

What is actually hard here

Bandwidth. Specifically, this scenario:

🎯 The problem in one example

You have a 2 GB video project file. You change one setting and save. If syncing means uploading 2 GB, then a day's work is hundreds of gigabytes of upload and the product is unusable on any normal connection.

So the system must be able to say: only these 4 MB actually changed — send those. Everything interesting in this design follows from that sentence.

Which leads immediately to a second problem that is less obvious. To send only what changed, you have to break the file into pieces and compare them. But if you cut the file at fixed positions — every 4 MB — then inserting a single byte near the beginning shifts every subsequent byte, every boundary lands in a new place, and every chunk after the insertion looks different. You are back to uploading the whole file.

Fixing that properly is the technical core of the design, and it is covered in step 4.

What they are looking for

Do you separate metadata from bytes? They have completely different consistency needs, and the design falls apart if you treat them the same.

Do you notice the fixed-chunk problem? Most candidates say “chunk the file” and stop there.

Do you have a conflict story? Two devices editing offline is not an edge case; it is Tuesday.

❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
Sync only, or real-time collaborative editing?
These are different systems. Collaborative editing needs CRDTs or OT; file sync needs chunking and version vectors. Get this wrong and everything after it is wrong.
What is the largest file we must support?
Decides chunk size, resumable upload design, and whether a single file can exceed one machine.
Must offline edits merge, or is last-writer-wins acceptable?
Merging offline divergence is the hardest requirement in the design, and it is often not actually needed.
What is the sharing granularity — file, folder, or link?
Determines the ACL model and whether permission checks can be cached.
Do we deduplicate across users?
Cross-user dedup is a large storage win and a privacy leak: it lets someone test whether a file already exists.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.
📝2. Functional requirements
  • Upload, download, delete, search across web, desktop and mobile.
  • Automatic sync. A change on one device appears on the others without anyone pressing anything.
  • Delta sync. Only the changed parts of a file cross the network. This is the requirement doing all the work.
  • Version history — roll back to a previous version — and a recycle bin, so deletion is reversible for a while.
  • Sharing with view / comment / edit permissions, at file or folder level.

Two things worth splitting apart

Metadata and file contents are different problems. The metadata — the folder tree, names, which chunks make up which version, who can see what — is small, highly structured, and needs to be strongly consistent. If you move a file and the tree is stale, the user sees their file in two places or neither, and that reads as data loss even though nothing was lost.

The contents are large, immutable, and need eleven nines of durability but no transactional guarantees at all. A chunk is written once and never modified.

So: metadata in a replicated relational store, contents in object storage, and the metadata holds the keys. Nearly every good decision in this design descends from that split.

⏱3. Non-functional requirements
RequirementTargetWhy
Durability11 ninesThis is often the user's only copy. Losing a file here is unrecoverable in a way that no other failure in this design is.
Metadata consistencyStrongA stale folder tree looks exactly like data loss to a user. This is the one place where eventual consistency is not acceptable.
Sync latencySecondsFor a small change on an online device. Nobody expects instant; everybody notices minutes.
Upload volume~1 PB/dayBefore deduplication. After it, substantially less — which is the entire economic argument for content-addressed chunks.
Availability99.99%And a soft failure mode: if the service is unreachable, the desktop client should queue changes locally and sync later, not error.
Offline editingSupportedWhich guarantees conflicts. The question is not whether to handle them but how.

The interesting pairing is the first two rows. Durability is about the bytes; consistency is about the metadata. Trying to get both properties from one storage system would mean either a database holding petabytes of blobs or an object store pretending to be transactional. Splitting them lets each system do the one thing it is good at.

🗂4. Data model and API

First, the chunking problem — because it decides the schema

Recall the difficulty: cut a file every 4 MB and inserting one byte at the start shifts every boundary, so every chunk changes.

The fix is to stop cutting at fixed positions and start cutting at positions determined by the content itself. Slide a small window over the bytes, compute a rolling hash at each position, and declare a boundary wherever that hash has some property — say, its low 22 bits are zero. Boundaries then occur roughly every 4 MB on average, but always at the same byte patterns.

Now insert a byte near the start. The boundary positions after the insertion are decided by the same byte patterns as before, which have simply moved along by one. So the chunks after the insertion are identical to what they were. Only the one chunk containing the insertion changed.

FIXED-SIZE CHUNKS insert 1 byte at the front before: [A][B][C][D][E] after: [A'][B'][C'][D'][E'] every boundary shifted → re-upload everything CONTENT-DEFINED CHUNKS boundaries found by a rolling hash before: [A][B][C][D][E] after: [A'][B][C][D][E] one chunk changed → upload 4 MB, not 2 GB

Each chunk is then named by the hash of its contents. That single choice gives you three things at once: deduplication is automatic (identical content produces an identical name), integrity checking is free (re-hash and compare), and chunks are immutable, so they can be cached anywhere forever.

-- Metadata DB (CockroachDB / Spanner for global ACID consistency) TABLE files { file_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, workspace_id UUID, parent_folder_id UUID, name VARCHAR(255), latest_version INT, is_deleted BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE, created_at TIMESTAMP, updated_at TIMESTAMP } TABLE file_versions { file_id UUID, version_number INT, total_size BIGINT, checksum_sha256 CHAR(64), created_by UUID, created_at TIMESTAMP, PRIMARY KEY (file_id, version_number) } TABLE file_chunks { file_id UUID, version_number INT, chunk_index INT, chunk_hash CHAR(64) REFERENCES chunks(chunk_hash), PRIMARY KEY (file_id, version_number, chunk_index) } TABLE chunks { chunk_hash CHAR(64) PRIMARY KEY, byte_size INT, storage_path VARCHAR(512), -- S3 / GCS object key ref_count BIGINT -- GC: deleted when ref_count == 0 }

A file version, then, is just an ordered list of chunk hashes. Version history costs almost nothing: version 4 and version 5 of a 2 GB file share every chunk except the one that changed, so keeping thirty versions costs thirty lists plus the handful of chunks that actually differ.

The API

// 1. Initiate Resumable Chunked Upload POST /api/v1/files/upload/init Header: Authorization: Bearer {token}, Idempotency-Key: {uuid} Body: { "filename": "annual_report.pdf", "folder_id": "f_98234", "total_bytes": 41943040, "chunk_hashes": ["sha256_chunk1", "sha256_chunk2", ...] } Response: 200 OK { "upload_id": "upl_8723", "missing_chunk_hashes": ["sha256_chunk2", "sha256_chunk5"], // Server deduplicates existing chunks! "presigned_s3_urls": { "sha256_chunk2": "https://s3.../chunk2", ... } } // 2. Commit File Version POST /api/v1/files/upload/commit Body: { "upload_id": "upl_8723", "file_id": "fil_1029", "version": 4, "chunk_hashes": ["sha256_chunk1", "sha256_chunk2", "sha256_chunk3"] } // 3. Real-Time Sync Event Stream (WebSocket / HTTP Long-Polling) GET /api/v1/sync/events?cursor={last_sync_seq_no}

Look at what the upload-init call does. The client sends the hashes of its chunks and the server replies with which ones it does not already have. On a file where one chunk changed, that is one small request and one 4 MB upload — and if someone else already uploaded an identical chunk, even that disappears.

The two-phase shape matters too: chunks go to object storage first, and only then does a commit call write the new version into the metadata. The version becomes visible atomically, when every chunk it references is already durable. There is never a moment where the tree points at bytes that do not exist.

📊5. Capacity estimation

The numbers, and where they come from.

⚖ Assumptions — and what breaks if each is wrong
Files are edited by one user at a time
Concurrent editing of the same file needs CRDTs and is a different system.
Average file is small; large files are rare
If large files were the norm, chunk size and transfer scheduling would dominate the design.
Deduplication is per account
Cross-user dedup saves more storage and leaks the existence of files between users.
100M DAU
Active users uploading/syncing files daily
100M files/day
Daily upload volume (~10 MB avg file size)
1 PB/day
Daily raw incoming data ingestion
100 Gbps
Peak network ingress bandwidth into block servers
4 MB Chunks
Optimal content-defined chunk size with Rabin Fingerprinting
60% Savings
Storage reduction via cross-user content hashing & deduplication

A petabyte a day of raw uploads is the headline, and the useful observation is how much of it is not real. People share the same attachments, keep the same photos, and re-save the same documents with small edits. Content-addressed chunks mean each distinct chunk is stored once no matter how many files or users reference it, and a large fraction of that petabyte turns out to be a chunk that already exists.

The chunk size is a genuine trade-off rather than a constant. Smaller chunks find more duplicates and transfer less on a small edit; they also multiply the number of chunk records, and the metadata for a large file starts to be substantial. Somewhere around a few megabytes is where the two curves cross for mixed real-world content.

The metadata side is small in bytes and demanding in every other way: a few hundred bytes per file version, but strongly consistent, queried on every sync poll from every device. It is a transaction-rate problem, not a storage problem, and sizing it means counting sync checks, not gigabytes.

⚖6. The key trade-offs

The choices, and their costs.

DecisionChosen ✓Alternative ✗Reasoning
Chunk SplittingClient-side Rabin ChunkingServer-side ChunkingClient-side saves huge upload bandwidth (never uploads chunks already in S3) and offloads CPU hashing from server infrastructure.
Metadata StoreSpanner / CockroachDB (NewSQL)Cassandra / DynamoDB (NoSQL)File tree operations (renaming a folder, moving 10,000 files) require atomic multi-row ACID transactions. NoSQL eventual consistency causes phantom or orphaned files.
Sync ProtocolDelta Sync with WebSocket notifyPeriodic Client PollingWebSockets deliver sub-second sync latency to all connected devices without hammering servers with millions of empty poll requests.

Deduplicating across users — a real privacy problem

Within one account, dedup is free and uncontroversial. Across all users it saves dramatically more, because popular files are stored once globally rather than once per person.

It also leaks information, and the attack is simple enough to explain in a sentence. Upload a file and watch whether the server asks for the bytes. If it does not, someone else already has that exact file. That turns the service into an oracle for “does this document exist in the system?”, which for a leaked document, a private photo, or an internal memo is a meaningful disclosure.

The mitigations all cost something. You can dedup per account only, giving up most of the saving. You can always request the upload and discard it server-side, keeping the storage saving while paying the bandwidth. Or you can accept the leak and document it. There is no free version, and being able to state the trade rather than picking a side is the point.

Conflicts: merge, or keep both

Two devices edit the same file offline. Both come back online. Something has to happen.

Last write wins silently destroys one person's work. For a file sync product that is not an acceptable default — the whole promise is that your files are safe.

Merging is impossible in general. You cannot merge two versions of a binary video project or a spreadsheet; the bytes have no structure the system understands.

So the answer is to keep both: one file becomes two, the second named something like “report.docx (Priya's conflicted copy)”. It is inelegant, it is visible to the user, and it is right — it never loses data and it puts the decision with the only party who can make it. This is the same instinct as returning siblings in D3: when the system cannot know the answer, surface the conflict rather than guessing.

🏗7. High-level design
Chunked sync — and the offline edit that has no correct automatic answer
changed chunkschunk / deltametadataconflicting edit
What is moving: only changed chunks. The file is split by content-defined boundaries, each chunk is named by its hash, and the client uploads just the hashes the server has not seen — which is why a one-line change to a large document costs kilobytes.
What goes wrong: both devices edit the same file while offline. Neither version descends from the other, so the version vectors are concurrent — there is no correct automatic merge. Last-writer-wins is simple and silently destroys somebody’s work. The honest answer is to keep both and surface a conflicted copy, which is exactly what production file-sync products do. Ch 4

Two paths, kept apart on purpose.

METADATA small, structured, strongly consistent client --> METADATA SERVICE --> replicated SQL folder tree, file versions, chunk lists, ACLs, sync cursor CONTENT large, immutable, content-addressed client --> OBJECT STORAGE via pre-signed URLs; bypasses our servers chunk_hash -> bytes written once, never modified AN UPLOAD 1. client chunks the file locally, hashes each chunk 2. init: "here are my 500 chunk hashes" server: "I already have 499. send me chunk #37." 3. client PUTs chunk #37 straight to object storage 4. commit: "version 5 = [these 500 hashes]" now the version becomes visible, atomically NOTIFYING OTHER DEVICES laptop <-- long-poll --> NOTIFICATION SERVICE "something changed" phone <-- long-poll --> | v client asks metadata: "what changed since cursor 8812?" the notification carries no data, only a nudge
The notification is deliberately content-free. It says “go ask”, and the client then does a normal incremental sync. That keeps the push path trivial and means a missed notification costs a delay rather than a lost change — the next poll catches it.
🔄8. Workflows — what actually happens
Priya changes one line in a 2 GB project file
Delta sync, which is the whole reason this design exists.
  1. The desktop client notices the file changed and re-chunks it locally using the rolling hash. It gets 500 chunks and hashes each one.
  2. It compares against the 500 hashes from the last synced version. 499 are identical. Only chunk 37 — the one containing her edit — is new.
  3. It calls upload-init with all 500 hashes. The server checks which it already holds and replies: send me chunk 37, with a pre-signed URL.
  4. The client PUTs 4 MB directly to object storage. A few seconds on a normal connection.
  5. It commits: version 5 is this ordered list of 500 hashes. The metadata service writes one row. Now the new version exists.
  6. Total uploaded: 4 MB and two small API calls, for a 2 GB file.
Version 4 and version 5 share 499 chunks. Keeping the old version costs one extra list and one extra chunk, which is why thirty versions of history is affordable rather than thirty times the storage.
Her phone picks up the change
And downloads 4 MB, not 2 GB.
  1. The phone holds a long-poll against the notification service. The commit wakes it with a content-free nudge.
  2. The phone asks the metadata service: what has changed since my cursor? It gets back: this file is now at version 5, here is the chunk list.
  3. It diffs that list against its local version 4. One hash is unfamiliar.
  4. It downloads that one chunk from object storage and reassembles the file locally from 499 chunks it already had plus the new one.
  5. It verifies by re-hashing each chunk. Content addressing means integrity checking is free — a corrupted chunk simply will not hash to its own name.
  6. Cursor advances. Done.
Symmetry is the nice property here: the same chunk list that made the upload small makes the download small, and neither side needed a special diff format.
Two devices edit the same file offline
The conflict, handled honestly.
  1. Priya's laptop is offline on a flight. She edits the file; the client queues version 5 locally.
  2. Meanwhile her desktop at home edits the same file and successfully commits version 5.
  3. The laptop lands and tries to commit. It says: my parent is version 4. The server sees version 5 already exists with parent 4.
  4. This is a genuine fork. Neither version descends from the other, and the server cannot merge two binary files.
  5. So it keeps both. The laptop's work is committed as a new file: report.docx (Priya's laptop conflicted copy), with its own chunk list.
  6. Both appear in the folder on every device. Priya opens them, decides, and deletes one.
Ugly and correct. The alternative — picking a winner by timestamp — would have silently discarded a flight's worth of work, and she would have had no way to know.
A folder is shared with 200 people
Where permission checks become a performance problem.
  1. Priya shares a folder. The permission is stored once, on the folder — not copied onto the thousands of files inside it.
  2. Dev opens a file six levels deep. Checking access means walking up the tree to find an inherited permission, which is several metadata reads.
  3. Doing that on every file access, for every user, would make permission checking a larger workload than the sync itself.
  4. So the effective permission set is cached per user, with a short expiry.
  5. Priya revokes Dev's access. The cache is invalidated for the affected subtree, but there is a window — measured in seconds — where a cached entry still permits access.
  6. For anything genuinely sensitive, the revoke path invalidates immediately rather than waiting for expiry.
A short window of stale permission is usually acceptable and must be a deliberate decision, not an accident. Any answer where the number is “however long the cache happens to live” is the wrong answer.
🔍9. Deep dives, and what breaks

How the client detects a change at all

Easy to skip and genuinely load-bearing: before any of the sync machinery runs, something has to notice that a file changed.

Polling the filesystem by hashing every file is out — on a folder with a hundred thousand files that is minutes of disk I/O per scan. So the client uses operating system change notifications, which tell it exactly which paths were touched.

Those are not entirely reliable. Events get dropped under load, and they are missed entirely while the client is not running. So the design is events for speed, periodic full scan for correctness: react instantly to notifications, and reconcile properly every so often to catch whatever was missed. The scan compares size and modification time first and only hashes files where those changed, which keeps it cheap.

Why the commit is separate from the upload

It would be simpler to upload chunks and have the server figure out the version. The two-phase shape exists because of what must be true at the moment a version becomes visible: every chunk it references must already be durable.

If a version could appear while a chunk was still uploading, another device could fetch its chunk list and find a chunk that does not exist. That is a broken file, and worse, it is broken in the metadata rather than in the bytes — so it looks like corruption rather than a transient error.

Separating them makes the visible transition a single small metadata write, which is atomic, cheap, and easy to reason about. A failed upload leaves orphaned chunks, and a background job collects chunks nothing references — the cheap failure to have.

The sync cursor

Each client keeps a position in a per-user change log, and asks “what happened after this?” rather than “what does my folder look like?”

This is the same idea as the sequence number in D4, and it matters for the same reason: the client is the source of truth about what it has seen, so the server keeps no per-device delivery state. A device that has been off for six months asks with an old cursor and gets everything since. A device that crashed mid-sync asks again from its last durable cursor and repeats a little work.

The bound worth knowing: if the log is trimmed past a client's cursor, that client must fall back to a full listing. Rare, expensive, and the reason the log is retained generously.

What breaks

Upload Aborted Midway (Network drop)
Chunk uploads are idempotent. Client queries /upload/status with upload_id, receives list of already-persisted chunks, and resumes only the remaining chunks without re-uploading.
S3 / Cloud Storage Outage
Blob storage is multi-region replicated (e.g. S3 Cross-Region Replication). Read requests failover to secondary region CDN endpoint.
Metadata DB Primary Failure
Spanner / CockroachDB uses Multi-Paxos / Raft per range. Automatic leader election completes in <2s with zero data loss.
Zombie / Corrupt Chunks
Every downloaded chunk is verified against its expected SHA-256 hash by the client. If corrupted, client requests chunk from alternate replica.
The dominant constraint

Sync is not collaborative editing. I scoped this as file sync with versioning, which makes content-defined chunking and delta transfer the core, rather than CRDTs and operational transform.

What I would build first

Rabin-fingerprint chunking plus a chunk-hash manifest. Deduplication and delta sync both fall out of it for free.

What I deliberately did not build

Real-time co-editing, and cross-user deduplication. The second is a genuine storage win and a privacy leak, so I would keep dedup per-account.

The biggest risk

Conflict handling on offline edits. Last-writer-wins is simple and silently destroys work; the honest answer is to keep both versions and tell the user.

💬 If you get this far, here is what they will push on
Follow-ups an interviewer is likely to ask once the design is on the board. Answers supplied — read the question, answer it out loud, then open it.
“Two devices edit the same file while both are offline. What happens?”Answer

You get two versions where neither descends from the other, and there is no correct automatic merge. Any answer that claims to merge them is either lying or is actually solving a narrower problem.

Last-writer-wins is simple and silently destroys somebody's work, which for a document people care about is the worst possible outcome because nobody finds out.

So keep both. Produce a conflicted copy, tell the user, and let them decide. Every production file-sync product does this, which is a good sign it is the right answer rather than a cop-out.

“Someone changes one line in a 2 GB video file. How much gets uploaded?”Answer

Ideally a few kilobytes. The file is split using content-defined boundaries rather than fixed offsets, so an edit in the middle only changes the chunks it touches — it does not shift every subsequent boundary the way fixed-size chunking would.

The client computes hashes for its chunks, asks the server which it already has, and uploads only the missing ones.

For a video file specifically the answer may be worse than that, because a small logical edit can rewrite container metadata throughout. Worth acknowledging rather than claiming it is always a few kilobytes.

“Should you deduplicate identical chunks across different users?”Answer

It is a large storage win and a genuine privacy leak, so this is a policy question rather than a technical one.

If chunks are shared globally, I can test whether a file already exists by uploading it and watching whether the upload is instant. That tells me somebody else has that file, which for some files is information you have no right to reveal.

The usual compromise is to deduplicate within an account or within an organisation, where the members already share a trust boundary, and not across the whole population.

“How does a new device get 100 GB of files without a thundering herd?”Answer

It pulls the manifest first — the list of files and chunk hashes — which is small, then fetches chunks it lacks. Because chunks are content-addressed, they come from object storage or a CDN rather than from a service, so this is bandwidth rather than load on the metadata tier.

Prioritise by what the user is likely to open: recently modified files first, everything else in the background. Cold-syncing alphabetically is how you make a user wait an hour to see the document they just edited.

Design Uber / Lyft (Real-Time Geospatial Indexing & Ride Matching)

Difficulty: Hard (Staff Expectation)  •  Target: 45 min
💬 The question, as asked

“Design a ride-hailing dispatch system. Riders request a ride, nearby drivers are found and one is matched, and both track the trip live.”

⚡ What makes it hard

Continuous geospatial writes at enormous volume — every driver reporting position every few seconds is the largest stream in the system — combined with a matching decision that must complete in seconds.

📋1. Understanding the question

The prompt: “Design a ride-hailing dispatch system. Riders request a ride, nearby drivers are found and one is matched, and both track the trip live.”

There are two systems hiding in that sentence, and they have opposite characteristics.

Location ingestion is a firehose. Five million drivers each reporting their position every four seconds is over a million writes per second, running continuously, forever. It is by a wide margin the largest stream in the design — larger than trips, payments, and everything else combined.

Matching is the opposite: comparatively rare, but it must answer in about two seconds, and the answer matters. Pick the wrong driver and someone waits eight minutes instead of three.

🎯 The question to ask first

“How often do drivers report location?” It sounds like a detail and it is the largest number in the entire design. Four seconds gives 1.25M writes/sec. Two seconds gives 2.5M. Nothing else you decide moves the infrastructure bill as much.

The property that makes this tractable

Demand is local. A rider in Berlin is never matched with a driver in Lisbon. That sounds trivial and it is the single most useful fact in the design, because it means the system does not have to be one system — it can be a few hundred nearly independent ones, partitioned by geography, with no cross-partition queries in the hot path.

Once you say that, the million writes per second stop being one million-write-per-second problem and become a few hundred manageable ones. Same instinct as everywhere else in this guide: make the constraint local instead of coordinating.

And the part that is genuinely awkward

“Find drivers near this point” is a two-dimensional query, and ordinary database indexes are one-dimensional. An index on latitude finds everyone at the right latitude across the entire planet. An index on longitude does the same the other way. Intersecting them is enormously wasteful for a 3 km radius.

Fixing that — turning two dimensions into one so a normal index works — is the technical core, and it is covered in step 4.

What they are looking for

Do you size the location stream first? It is the dominant cost and the thing most candidates leave until last.

Do you have a real spatial index? “Query by lat/lng range” is not an answer at this scale.

Do you handle the double-booking race? Two riders offered the same driver at the same instant is not hypothetical; it happens constantly at peak.

❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
What is the matching latency budget?
A few seconds allows a global optimisation over a batch; sub-second forces greedy local matching and a worse allocation.
How often do drivers report location?
This dominates total write volume — it is usually the largest number in the whole design.
Is pricing dynamic?
Surge is a separate feedback system with its own stability problems, and it interacts with matching.
One city or global?
Geo-sharding is natural here because demand is local; saying so early earns the partitioning discussion.
Are shared or pooled rides in scope?
Pooling turns matching into a routing optimisation that is NP-hard. Worth scoping out explicitly.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.
📝2. Functional requirements
  • Drivers broadcast location every few seconds while available or on a trip.
  • Riders see nearby drivers moving on a map, within a few kilometres.
  • Request a ride: quote a fare and an ETA up front, then match a driver.
  • Driver accepts or declines within a short window; declining moves on to the next candidate.
  • Trip lifecycle: matched → picked up → in transit → dropped off → paid.
  • No double booking. One driver, one trip.

That last one deserves attention because it is the only strict-correctness requirement in the whole design. Everything else tolerates approximation — a driver's shown position can be four seconds stale, an ETA can be off by a minute, the nearby list can miss someone at the edge. But a driver assigned to two trips is a real-world failure: one rider is standing on a pavement watching a car that is not coming.

Which means one small part of this system needs a genuine transactional guarantee, while the rest of it — including the part handling a million writes a second — does not.

⏱3. Non-functional requirements
RequirementTargetWhat it forces
Location writes~1.25M/secThe dominant number. It rules out writing each ping to a durable, indexed, replicated database.
Nearby query< 100 msRuns on every map refresh for every rider with the app open, which is a much higher rate than ride requests.
Match latency< 2 sFrom request to a driver being offered the trip. This budget decides greedy versus batched matching.
Double bookingZeroThe only hard-correctness requirement here. It needs a real transaction on one row.
Location stalenessSeconds is fineA car shown four seconds behind reality is imperceptible on a map. This tolerance is what lets locations live in memory.
Availability99.99%Per city. A failure in one region should not affect another — which geo-sharding gives you almost for free.

The row that saves the design

“Location staleness: seconds is fine” is worth stating explicitly, because it is what makes a million writes per second affordable.

If every ping had to be durably stored and replicated, you would be running a very large database purely to record where cars were four seconds ago — data that is worthless the moment the next ping arrives. Because staleness is acceptable and history is not required for the live map, current position can live in memory with a short expiry. Losing a node loses a few seconds of positions, and the next round of pings repairs it completely.

Trip history is a separate matter and is written durably. The distinction — ephemeral current state versus durable historical record — is one of the more transferable ideas in this design.

🗂4. Data model and API

The spatial index, which is the real content of this step

The problem: find all drivers within 3 km of a point, fast, from a set of five million that is constantly moving.

The trick is to reduce two dimensions to one. Divide the surface of the earth into a fixed grid of small cells, each with an identifier. A driver's position becomes a cell id. Now “drivers near here” is “drivers in these cells”, which is an ordinary lookup on an ordinary key — no geometry at query time at all.

The grid used here is hexagonal, and the reason is worth a sentence because it comes up. With square cells, the distance from a cell's centre to its edge-neighbours and to its corner-neighbours differ by about 40%, so “the ring of cells around me” is not a consistent distance in every direction. Hexagons have six neighbours all at the same distance, so a ring of hexagons approximates a circle far better. At the resolution used here each cell is a few hundred metres across, which is roughly the granularity of a pickup.

THE QUERY "drivers within 3 km of the rider" rider position → cell 8a2a1072b59ffff | v take that cell + the rings of neighbours out to ~3 km | v GET cell:8a...b59 → { d_101, d_884, d_2277 } plain key lookup GET cell:8a...b5a → { d_443 } one round trip, all cells ... | v a few hundred candidates → filter by exact distance and status

Two dimensions became one key lookup. Exact distance is computed afterwards, on a few hundred candidates rather than five million.

-- Ephemeral Real-Time Geospatial Index (In-Memory Redis / Uber Ringpop H3) -- Redis Geospatial (GEOADD / GEORADIUS) or H3 Hexagonal Cell Sets: KEY: geo:h3:{h3_cell_index} -- e.g. geo:h3:8828308281fffff VALUE: SET of {driver_id} KEY: driver:{driver_id}:state VALUE: HASH { "lat": 37.7749, "lng": -122.4194, "status": "AVAILABLE", "h3_index": "8828308281fffff", "last_ping": 1725682910 } -- Trip State DB (CockroachDB / Cassandra for High Scale + ACID) TABLE trips { trip_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, rider_id UUID, driver_id UUID, status ENUM(requested, matched, arrived, in_progress, completed, canceled), pickup_lat DOUBLE, pickup_lng DOUBLE, dropoff_lat DOUBLE, dropoff_lng DOUBLE, fare_cents INT, created_at TIMESTAMP, updated_at TIMESTAMP }

Note the split in the storage. Live driver positions live in memory, keyed by cell, with a short expiry — a driver who stops pinging simply vanishes from the index, which is exactly the desired behaviour and needs no explicit offline event. Trips live in a real database, because a trip is money and must survive anything.

The API

// 1. Driver Location Broadcast (gRPC Bidirectional Stream) rpc StreamDriverLocation(stream DriverLocationPing) returns (stream LocationAck); message DriverLocationPing { string driver_id = 1; double latitude = 2; double longitude = 3; float bearing = 4; enum DriverStatus { AVAILABLE = 0; DISPATCHED = 1; ON_TRIP = 2; } int64 timestamp = 6; } // 2. Search Nearby Drivers GET /api/v1/drivers/nearby?lat=37.7749&lng=-122.4194&radius_m=3000&ride_type=UBER_X Response: 200 OK { "drivers": [ {"driver_id": "d_101", "lat": 37.7750, "lng": -122.4180, "eta_sec": 180, "bearing": 45.0}, ... ] } // 3. Request Ride (Idempotent Dispatch) POST /api/v1/trips/request Header: Idempotency-Key: {uuid} Body: { "rider_id": "r_901", "pickup_lat": 37.7749, "pickup_lng": -122.4194, "dropoff_lat": 37.7891, "dropoff_lng": -122.4014, "ride_type": "UBER_X", "fare_quote_id": "fq_7723" }

Location updates go over a persistent stream rather than one HTTP request per ping. At this volume the per-request overhead — connection setup, headers, TLS — would dwarf the 100 bytes of actual payload.

And the ride request carries an idempotency key. A rider on a flaky connection who taps twice, or whose client retries, must not end up with two trips and two charges.

📊5. Capacity estimation

The numbers, and the one that dominates.

⚖ Assumptions — and what breaks if each is wrong
Demand is local to a city
Cross-city matching would remove geo-sharding, which is the assumption the whole partitioning rests on.
Drivers report location every 4 seconds
Halving that interval doubles the largest write stream in the system.
Greedy matching is acceptable
If allocation quality mattered more than latency, batched global optimisation would be required.
5M Drivers
Active drivers broadcasting GPS every 4 seconds
1.25M QPS
Continuous location update ingestion rate
100 Bytes
Payload size per GPS ping (driver_id, lat, lng, bearing, status)
125 MB/sec
Ingress location stream network bandwidth
500,000
Simultaneous active trips during peak hours globally
H3 Level 8
Hexagonal spatial indexing resolution (~460m edge length)

Five million drivers pinging every four seconds is 1.25 million writes per second, continuously. Each ping is around 100 bytes, so about 125 MB/sec of ingress — large but not alarming as bandwidth. It is the operation rate that is the problem, not the volume.

Which is why the destination matters so much. Written to a replicated database with a spatial index, 1.25M writes/sec is a very expensive cluster doing work that is discarded four seconds later. Written to an in-memory store partitioned by geography, each shard handles a city's worth — thousands per second, not millions — and that is unremarkable.

The read side is easy to underestimate. Every rider with the app open refreshes the map every few seconds, and there are far more people looking than requesting. Nearby-driver queries therefore outnumber ride requests by a large factor, which is the argument for making that query a plain key lookup rather than anything cleverer.

Trips are the small number: around half a million concurrent globally, with a few thousand starting per second at peak. That is an ordinary transactional workload, and it is the only part of the system that needs one.

⚖6. The key trade-offs

The choices, and their costs.

DecisionChosen ✓Alternative ✗Reasoning
Spatial GridUber H3 Hexagonal GridQuadtree / GeohashHexagons guarantee uniform neighbor distance in all 6 directions, drastically simplifying k-ring spatial smoothing and surge pricing calculations.
Location StorageIn-Memory Redis + TTL (Ephemeral)Persistent RDBMS / Disk DBDriver location pings are only relevant for ~30 seconds. Persisting 1.25M writes/sec to disk is wasteful. History is downsampled and written to cold analytics via Kafka.
Matching ArchitectureCentralized Dispatch (Batch Mini-Auction)Greedy First-Come-First-ServeBatching ride requests every 2-3 seconds achieves global optimization (minimizing total wait time for all riders) rather than greedily assigning the closest car to the first request.

Matching: greedy or batched

This is the trade-off with the most interesting consequences, and it is driven entirely by the latency budget.

Greedy assigns each request to the nearest suitable driver the moment it arrives. It is simple, fast, and locally optimal — and globally it can be poor. Rider A gets the driver who was slightly closer to them, and rider B, requesting a second later, gets one who is six minutes away, when a swap would have served both in four.

Batched waits a few seconds, collects the requests and available drivers in an area, and solves the assignment as an optimisation over the whole batch. Average wait times improve measurably. The cost is the wait itself, plus complexity, plus a much worse failure mode: if the batch solver is slow, everybody waits, whereas a slow greedy match affects one rider.

With a two-second budget, greedy with a few local improvements is the honest answer. Stating that you would instrument average pickup time and revisit if the gap justified it is better than picking either one on aesthetics.

Where the driver's state lives

Position is ephemeral and lives in memory. But availability — is this driver free, offered a trip, or on one? — is not ephemeral, because it is what prevents double booking.

The resolution is to keep them in different places. The spatial index is a fast, lossy, in-memory view used to find candidates. The authoritative availability state is a row in a database, and claiming a driver is a conditional update on that row. The index can be stale and it does not matter, because the index only nominates; the database decides.

🏗7. High-level design
Geospatial matching — and the stale index that matches a driver who has gone
driver locationsride requestcandidates / matchbad match
What is moving: a continuous stream of driver positions into an in-memory H3 cell index, and — occasionally — a rider request that reads one cell plus its ring and greedily matches the best nearby driver. Demand is local, so no query is ever global.
What goes wrong: the location stream is by far the largest write volume in the design, so it is what saturates first. When the index falls behind, matching still works — it just matches against where drivers were 40 seconds ago, producing long pickups and cancellations. Nothing errors. Watch index staleness, not just matcher latency.

Two paths with very different shapes.

THE FIREHOSE 1.25M writes/sec, ephemeral driver app --persistent stream--> LOCATION SERVICE geo-sharded by city | v IN-MEMORY CELL INDEX cell_id -> { drivers }, TTL 10s no durability. the next ping repairs everything. | +--> also to a stream, for trip history and analytics THE MATCH rare, latency-bound, must be correct rider --> request ride idempotency key | v MATCHING SERVICE | +-- 1. rider position -> cell + neighbour rings +-- 2. read those cells -> ~200 candidates may be stale; fine +-- 3. filter: available, right vehicle type, ETA +-- 4. rank -> best driver +-- 5. CLAIM the driver conditional update; this is the only strict step UPDATE drivers SET status='offered', trip=X WHERE id=D AND status='available' 0 rows → someone else got them → try the next candidate +-- 6. offer to the driver; 15s to accept declined or timed out → release the claim, next candidate
The index is allowed to be wrong; the claim is not. A stale index costs one wasted candidate. A missing claim costs a rider standing on a pavement.
🔄8. Workflows — what actually happens
Nina requests a ride in Lisbon
Request to matched driver, end to end.
  1. Nina's position maps to one hexagonal cell. We take that cell plus the rings of neighbours covering about 3 km — a few dozen cells.
  2. One batched read against the in-memory index returns everyone in those cells: 214 drivers. This is a key lookup, not a geometric query.
  3. We filter: available status, right vehicle type, position fresher than 10 seconds. That leaves 38.
  4. For those 38 we compute road-network ETA — not straight-line distance, because a driver 400 m away across a river may be twelve minutes out.
  5. Ranked by ETA with some adjustment for how long each driver has been idle. Best candidate: driver 8817, ETA 3 minutes.
  6. Claim driver 8817 with a conditional update: set status to offered only if it is currently available. One row updated — ours.
  7. The offer goes to their phone. They accept within 15 seconds. The trip is created and both apps switch to tracking.
Total elapsed: well under two seconds, and the expensive part — road-network ETA — ran on 38 drivers rather than five million, because the cell lookup did the cheap filtering first.
Two riders are offered the same driver in the same instant
The race, and the one line that settles it.
  1. Nina and Tomás request rides two blocks apart, within milliseconds. Their requests land on different matching service instances.
  2. Both read the cell index. Both see driver 8817 as available — the index has no idea a claim is in flight.
  3. Both rank them first. Both attempt the claim.
  4. Nina's instance runs the conditional update first. Status was available, so it becomes offered. 1 row updated.
  5. Tomás's instance runs the identical statement a millisecond later. The status is no longer available, so the WHERE clause matches nothing. 0 rows updated.
  6. It reads that zero as “lost the race”, discards 8817, and offers the next-best driver instead. Tomás never knows.
No distributed lock, no coordination service, no consensus. The correctness lives in one conditional update on one row, which is the cheapest real guarantee available — the same move as holding a seat in D19 and the balance check in ch7.
A driver goes through a tunnel mid-trip
Why the design is indifferent to it.
  1. Pings stop. After 10 seconds the index entry expires and the driver disappears from nearby-driver queries.
  2. That is correct behaviour for an on-trip driver anyway — they were not a candidate. Disappearing from the index costs nothing.
  3. The rider's map shows the car's last known position. It stops moving, which is mildly annoying and not a failure.
  4. The trip is untouched. It lives in the database with a status, and nothing about it depended on continuous location.
  5. The driver's app queues its pings locally while offline.
  6. Signal returns. Queued pings are sent, the index repopulates, and the map jumps forward. Within four seconds everything is current again.
Nothing had to detect the outage or recover from it. Expiry handles disappearance and the next ping handles return — which is what you get for choosing ephemeral state with a TTL over durable state that needs reconciliation.
A stadium empties and 40,000 people request rides
Extreme spatial concentration, which is this system's characteristic failure.
  1. All those requests map to a handful of cells. Those cells are served by one shard, and that shard is now doing all the work while its neighbours idle.
  2. The candidate lists explode: a query that normally returns 200 drivers now returns thousands, and ranking gets slower exactly when it is busiest.
  3. Mitigation one: cap the candidate set. Take the nearest few hundred and rank those. A worse match under extreme load is far better than a slow one.
  4. Mitigation two: the 3 km radius adapts. In a dense area, search a smaller radius — there is no shortage of drivers, only a shortage of time to rank them.
  5. Mitigation three: surge pricing, which is a load-shedding mechanism as much as a pricing one. It reduces requests and attracts drivers into the area.
  6. The shard is still hot. Geo-sharding cannot fix a genuinely hot location, and the honest answer is that you split that cell's traffic across replicas and accept that the index is now slightly more stale.
Worth saying plainly: geo-sharding handles uneven load well and concentrated load badly, because the hot spot is a real place and cannot be hashed away. The tools are capping work, shrinking radius and shedding demand — not better partitioning.
🔍9. Deep dives, and what breaks

Why ETA is not distance

Straight-line distance is the obvious ranking function and it is wrong often enough to be a product problem.

A driver 400 m away on the far side of a river, a motorway, or a one-way system can be twelve minutes from the pickup, while one 1.5 km away on a clear road is four. Rank by distance and you regularly send the wrong car.

So ranking uses estimated travel time over the road network, which is a routing query against a graph with current traffic weights — far more expensive than a distance calculation. That cost is exactly why the cell lookup exists: it gets the candidate set down to a few dozen, and only then do you pay for real routing. Cheap filter first, expensive ranking second, on a set small enough to afford it.

What to do when the driver declines

A driver has a short window to accept. Declining or ignoring is common — they are eating, finishing a call, or do not like the direction.

The claim must therefore be released on a timer, not held indefinitely. That is the same lease pattern as D6: a claim with an expiry, so nothing is stuck if the holder never responds.

The cost is the rider's clock. Three drivers each taking their full 15 seconds is 45 seconds of a spinner. The usual mitigation is to offer the trip to two or three drivers simultaneously and give it to whoever accepts first, which cuts the tail latency sharply and means sometimes telling a driver who accepted that the trip is gone. Which annoyance you prefer is a product decision worth naming as one.

Surge as a control loop

Dynamic pricing is usually presented as a revenue feature. In systems terms it is a feedback controller, and it has the stability problems every feedback controller has.

High demand raises the price, which suppresses demand and attracts drivers, which lowers the price, which brings demand back — and if the loop reacts too fast, it oscillates. Riders see the price swing every thirty seconds and stop trusting it.

The dampening is unglamorous and effective: compute over a longer window, limit how fast the multiplier can move, and hold a quoted price for a few minutes so a rider's number does not change while they decide. Naming surge as a control loop with a stability problem, rather than as a pricing rule, is a distinctly staff-level observation.

What breaks

Driver Loses Internet Mid-Trip
Driver app buffers GPS points in local SQLite. Upon reconnection, app uploads buffered breadcrumbs to reconcile route and compute accurate fare.
Dispatch Service Node Crashes during 15s offer
Driver offer is backed by Redis TTL key with an expiring lease. If dispatch node dies, heartbeat supervisor detects pending trip and re-dispatches to another driver.
Surge Traffic Spike (New Year's Eve 10x Load)
Rate limit nearby driver map refreshes from 4s to 8s per rider; drop unneeded background location telemetry while preserving dispatch pipeline.
Redis H3 Shard Failure
Redis Sentinel / Cluster promotes replica in <1s. Lost ephemeral driver pings are replenished within 4 seconds as drivers broadcast.
The dominant constraint

Supply and demand are both intensely local. That is what makes geo-sharding correct here: a rider in one city never needs to be matched against a driver in another, so no query has to be global.

What I would build first

H3 hexagonal indexing over driver locations, with a greedy matcher inside a cell and its ring. It is not optimal, and it is fast enough to be right.

What I deliberately did not build

Pooled rides, which turn matching into an NP-hard routing problem, and dynamic pricing, which is a separate feedback system with its own stability failures.

The biggest risk

Location write volume. Drivers reporting every few seconds is the largest number in the design, and it is what will break first as the fleet grows.

💬 If you get this far, here is what they will push on
Follow-ups an interviewer is likely to ask once the design is on the board. Answers supplied — read the question, answer it out loud, then open it.
“Drivers report location every 4 seconds. Is that write volume a problem?”Answer

It is the largest stream in the system by a wide margin, and it is what breaks first as the fleet grows. A million active drivers at one update every four seconds is 250,000 writes a second doing nothing but overwriting a previous position.

The key realisation is that these writes are disposable. We never need location history for matching, only the current value, so this belongs in memory keyed by driver, not in a durable store.

If history is needed for billing or disputes, that is a separate, much cheaper stream sampled at a lower rate.

“What if a driver's phone loses signal for two minutes?”Answer

Their position goes stale, and stale is dangerous here because the system will happily match a rider to a driver who has since moved or gone offline. Nothing errors; the rider just waits for a car that is not coming.

So every position carries a timestamp and the matcher ignores anything older than a threshold. A driver who stops reporting drops out of the candidate set rather than lingering as a ghost.

Monitor index staleness directly, not just matcher latency, because matching stays fast while quietly getting worse.

“How do you match at an airport where 300 drivers are waiting in one place?”Answer

A dense cell breaks the assumption that a cell contains a handful of candidates. Scanning 300 drivers per request is wasteful, and it also produces unfair outcomes because the same nearby drivers keep winning.

Two adjustments: subdivide dense cells so resolution adapts to density rather than being fixed, and add a queue discipline at known venues so drivers who have waited longest are offered rides first. Airports usually have an explicit queue for exactly this reason.

“Why greedy matching rather than optimal assignment?”Answer

Because optimal assignment needs a batch. To compute a globally best pairing you must hold requests for a window, then solve an assignment problem across all of them, and that window is latency the rider feels.

Greedy matches immediately and is measurably worse in aggregate — slightly longer pickups, slightly more deadheading. Batched matching over a few seconds does better on paper and adds a few seconds to every request.

Which is right depends on the market. Dense cities can afford a short batch window; thin markets cannot, because there is rarely more than one candidate anyway.

Design a Distributed Web Crawler & Search Indexer (Googlebot Architecture)

Difficulty: Hard (Staff Expectation)  •  Target: 45 min
💬 The question, as asked

“Design a web crawler for a search engine. It must fetch billions of pages, discover new ones, refresh what changes, and not overwhelm any site.”

⚡ What makes it hard

Politeness is a per-host constraint, and it is what shapes the whole architecture. Get the partition key wrong and you need a distributed rate limiter you cannot afford.

📋1. Understanding the question

The prompt: “Design a web crawler for a search engine. It must fetch billions of pages, discover new ones, refresh what changes, and not overwhelm any site.”

The instinct is to size the fetching. Four thousand pages a second, a few hundred megabytes of bandwidth — that is a moderate number of machines and it is not where the design lives.

The constraint that shapes everything is the last clause: not overwhelming any site.

🎯 Why politeness is architectural

“At most one request per second to any given host” is a rate limit on a shared resource. Ten thousand crawler machines all potentially wanting the same host means they must somehow agree on who goes when.

Agreeing across ten thousand machines, thousands of times a second, is a coordination problem with no cheap answer — unless you arrange things so it never arises.

And you can. Partition the work by host. Every URL on example.com goes to the same worker. That worker is then the only one that ever touches that host, so the rate limit is a local timer in its own memory — no locks, no coordination service, no shared counters.

This is the single most important decision in the design, it is made before any component is drawn, and it is another instance of the guide's recurring move: make the constraint local instead of coordinating. Pick the wrong partition key — hash the URL, say — and you have signed up for a distributed rate limiter you cannot afford.

The other thing that makes this hard

The web is adversarial and broken, not in the sense of attackers but simply because it is enormous and unowned. A crawler meets:

  • Infinite spaces. A calendar with a “next month” link generates URLs forever. Follow it and one site consumes your entire fleet.
  • Duplicates everywhere. The same article on five mirrors, plus the same page reachable through dozens of URLs differing only by tracking parameters.
  • Servers that hang rather than failing, holding your connections open until you have no workers left.

A crawler that runs for an hour is easy. One that runs for a year without getting stuck is the actual problem.

What they are looking for

Do you partition by host, and can you say why? This is the question.

Do you have a plan for traps? Unbounded URL spaces will find you.

Do you know how big the URL set gets? Two hundred billion URLs is not a set you keep in memory, and “have I seen this?” is asked on every link extracted.

❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
What politeness constraints must we honour?
This is the constraint that shapes the architecture: it forces partitioning by host so the rate limit becomes local instead of coordinated.
Freshness or coverage — which are we optimising?
Recrawling news hourly and archives yearly is a scheduling policy, and you cannot maximise both under a fixed budget.
Do we need to render JavaScript?
Headless rendering costs 10–100× more per page than fetching HTML, and changes your fleet size accordingly.
Exact duplicates only, or near-duplicates?
Exact is a hash. Near-duplicate needs SimHash or MinHash and a similarity threshold someone has to choose.
What is the crawl budget per domain?
Bounds both politeness and the risk of a spider trap consuming the entire fleet.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.
📝2. Functional requirements
  • Crawl from seed URLs, discovering new pages by following links.
  • Extract text and links from each page.
  • Respect robots.txt and per-host rate limits.
  • Deduplicate — both identical content and near-identical content.
  • Recrawl on a schedule that reflects how often a page actually changes.
  • Store the results and feed the index.

Freshness and coverage are in direct competition

Worth stating as a requirement rather than discovering later. With a fixed crawl budget — say four thousand fetches a second — every recrawl of a page you already have is a new page you did not fetch.

Spend the budget on new pages and your index is broad and stale: news from last week, prices that changed, dead links. Spend it on recrawls and your index is current and small.

The answer is not a compromise ratio but a per-page recrawl interval derived from observed change rate. A news homepage changes hourly and earns an hourly recrawl. An academic PDF from 2009 has never changed and earns one a year. Measuring change and letting it drive scheduling is what turns a fixed budget into a good index — and it is a scheduling policy, which means the frontier is the interesting component, not the fetchers.

⏱3. Non-functional requirements
RequirementTargetWhat it forces
Politeness~1 req/sec/hostThe architectural constraint. It dictates the partition key before anything else is decided.
Throughput~4,000 pages/sec10 billion pages a month. Achieved through massive concurrency per machine, not fast individual fetches.
Frontier size~200B URLsFar too large for memory. The “have I seen this?” check is therefore a real design problem.
FreshnessPer-page policyHours for news, months for archives. A single global interval wastes most of the budget.
LivenessRuns for yearsThe genuinely hard one. No deadlocks, no trap consuming the fleet, no host able to stall a worker indefinitely.
Storage~1 PB per cycleParsed text, not raw HTML. Boilerplate stripping pays for itself several times over here.

Why 4,000 pages/sec is not a throughput problem

A page fetch takes maybe 500 ms, nearly all of it waiting for a remote server. Four thousand per second therefore means around two thousand fetches in flight at any moment — and because they are almost entirely idle, one machine with an event-driven fetcher can hold thousands of them.

So the fetching fleet is modest. What is not modest is the bookkeeping: a frontier of two hundred billion URLs, a seen-set of the same size, per-host politeness state, and per-page change history. This is a state-management problem wearing a throughput problem's clothes.

🗂4. Data model and API

Three pieces of state, and the second one is the interesting design problem.

-- URL Frontier State (Distributed Bigtable / Cassandra) TABLE url_frontier { url_hash CHAR(64) PRIMARY KEY, -- SHA-256(canonical_url) url TEXT, domain_hash CHAR(32), status ENUM(discovered, queued, fetching, crawled, error), priority_score FLOAT, -- PageRank + Domain Authority last_crawled_at TIMESTAMP, etag VARCHAR(128), content_simhash BIGINT -- 64-bit SimHash for near-duplicate detection } -- Inverted Index (Distributed Sharded Posting Lists - MapReduce / Lucene) TABLE inverted_index { term VARCHAR(128) PRIMARY KEY, -- e.g. "raft" posting_list BLOB -- Compressed list of (doc_id, term_frequency, [positions]) } -- Example Posting List: -- "raft" -> [Doc#12: TF=5, Pos=[12,45,89]], [Doc#99: TF=2, Pos=[3,120]]

The frontier is not one queue

A single priority queue of URLs would break politeness immediately: the top hundred entries might all be from the same host, and a worker taking a batch would hammer it.

So the frontier is structured in two layers. A front set of queues orders work by priority — how important the page is, how soon it is due for recrawl. A back set has one queue per host, and each back queue carries a timestamp saying when that host may next be touched.

A worker picks the host whose next-allowed time has passed and takes one URL from that host's queue. Politeness is enforced by the structure itself — there is no rate limiter, because the data layout makes it impossible to ask twice too soon.

“Have I seen this URL?” — asked billions of times

Every page yields a hundred links, each needing a membership check against a set of two hundred billion. Even at 20 bytes a URL that set is terabytes, and it cannot be a database round trip on the hot path.

The standard answer is a Bloom filter in front of it. A fixed-size bit array plus a few hash functions gives an approximate membership test in microseconds with no storage per element. Its error is one-sided in the useful direction: it can say “probably seen” about a URL it has not seen, but never “not seen” about one it has.

So a negative is definitive — enqueue it. A positive is checked against the real store. Since the vast majority of extracted links are genuinely duplicates, almost all of the traffic is absorbed by the filter, and the false positives cost you a small number of pages never crawled. At a few billion pages, missing a handful is not a meaningful loss of coverage.

Near-duplicate detection

Exact duplicates are a content hash. Near-duplicates — the same article on five sites with different navigation — need a hash whose output is similar when the input is similar, which ordinary hashes deliberately are not.

SimHash does this: documents differing in a few words produce fingerprints differing in a few bits, so “is this nearly the same as something I have?” becomes a bit-difference comparison against candidates with similar fingerprints. The threshold is a tuning decision somebody has to own, and it is a real one — too tight and the index fills with syndicated copies; too loose and you drop genuinely distinct pages that share a template.

The API
