// URL Frontier Internal RPC Protocol (gRPC) rpc FetchUrlsToCrawl(FetchBatchRequest) returns (FetchBatchResponse); message FetchBatchRequest { string crawler_worker_id = 1; int32 max_urls = 2; // e.g. 500 URLs } message FetchBatchResponse { repeated CrawlTask tasks = 1; } message CrawlTask { string url = 1; string domain = 2; int32 crawl_delay_sec = 3; // parsed from robots.txt int32 depth = 4; } // Inverted Index Search RPC rpc SearchIndex(SearchQuery) returns (SearchResponse); message SearchQuery { string query_text = 1; // "distributed consensus raft" int32 limit = 2; int32 offset = 3; }
📊5. Capacity estimation

The arithmetic, and what it says to build.

⚖ Assumptions — and what breaks if each is wrong
Politeness is defined per host
If it were per IP, hosts sharing an IP would need coordinated rate limiting across partitions.
Most pages are static HTML
If most required JavaScript rendering, fleet cost rises by one to two orders of magnitude.
Near-duplicate detection is good enough
Exact-duplicate-only detection would let templated content flood the index.
10 Billion
Total web pages indexed per monthly crawl cycle
4,000 pages/sec
Average continuous crawl ingestion throughput
10,000 pages/sec
Peak burst crawl throughput
400 MB/sec
Continuous download network bandwidth (at 100 KB/page)
1 Petabyte
Storage required for 10B parsed HTML documents
200 Billion
URLs maintained in URL Frontier queue

Ten billion pages a month is roughly 4,000 per second sustained. At around 100 KB of useful text each that is 400 MB/sec of download — significant, and well within what a modest fleet and ordinary transit can do.

The fetching fleet is small for the reason above: fetches are almost entirely waiting, so concurrency does the work. A few hundred machines running thousands of concurrent connections each is ample.

The costs that actually dominate are elsewhere:

  • The frontier. Two hundred billion URLs with metadata — priority, next crawl time, host — is tens of terabytes of constantly-mutating state.
  • Parsing. Extracting text and links from 4,000 pages a second is real CPU, and it is the largest compute line if rendering is off the table.
  • Rendering, if required. Running a headless browser costs one to two orders of magnitude more per page than fetching HTML. This is why “do we need JavaScript?” is a clarifying question and not a detail — the answer changes the fleet size by 10–100×, and the usual resolution is to render selectively rather than universally.
⚖6. The key trade-offs

The choices, and their costs.

DecisionChosen ✓Alternative ✗Reasoning
URL Seen TestBloom Filter + BigtableRDBMS Unique IndexBloom Filter answers 'seen' checks in 5 nanoseconds from memory, saving 4,000 expensive disk round-trips per second.
Near-Duplicate64-bit SimHash (Cosine distance)MinHash / Jaccard similaritySimHash produces a compact 8-byte fingerprint per document and enables bitwise Hamming distance comparisons with zero decompression.
Crawler StorageSSTable / Bigtable Sparse ColumnRelational DB / PostgresBigtable handles massive append throughput, automatic tablet sharding across petabytes, and compresses sparse web documents efficiently.

Partitioning by host, revisited — because it has a cost too

Hashing the URL would distribute load beautifully and make politeness a distributed coordination problem. Hashing the host makes politeness free and distributes load badly.

Badly, because host sizes are wildly uneven. A large site has hundreds of millions of pages; most have a few dozen. The worker that owns a huge host has years of work; the worker that owns a thousand small ones finishes in an afternoon.

Worse, politeness caps a single host at about one page per second, so a host with a hundred million pages takes over three years to crawl completely at that rate. That is not a bug to fix — it is arithmetic, and the honest response is that you do not crawl such sites exhaustively. You crawl what is important, which turns the problem back into the scheduling policy.

Load imbalance is handled by assigning many host-queues per worker and rebalancing them, rather than by changing the partition key. The partition key is not negotiable; the assignment of partitions to workers is.

Renders or not

An increasing share of the web puts its content behind JavaScript. Fetching the HTML gets you an empty shell.

Rendering everything is unaffordable. Rendering nothing loses real content. The practical answer is a cheap classifier: fetch the HTML, and if the page looks content-free — almost no text, a handful of script tags — queue it for the expensive path. Most pages never go near a browser, and the ones that need it get it.

The general shape is worth naming: a cheap test that decides whether to pay for the expensive one, which is the same structure as the Bloom filter in front of the seen-set and the cell lookup in front of routing in D9.

🏗7. High-level design
Crawl loop — and the spider trap that consumes the whole fleet
URL to fetchpage / contentfingerprinttrap URLs
What is moving: URLs out of per-host queues, pages back, and freshly discovered links returning to the frontier. Partitioning by host is the load-bearing decision: it makes the politeness delay a local constraint instead of a distributed rate limiter.
What goes wrong: a calendar page generates a link to the next month, forever. The frontier grows without bound and the fleet spends itself on one domain producing no new content. Defences: a per-domain crawl budget, a depth cap, and near-duplicate detection before indexing so the trap is visible as thousands of nearly identical pages rather than as growth.

A loop, with the frontier at its centre.

THE FRONTIER two layers — priority, then politeness FRONT QUEUES by priority BACK QUEUES one per host [ high ][ med ][ low ] example.com next_ok 10:00:04 [urls...] news.site next_ok 10:00:01 [urls...] blog.co next_ok 10:00:07 [urls...] politeness is not enforced by a limiter. it is enforced by the shape of the data: one queue per host, one timestamp, one worker owning it. THE LOOP worker (owns hosts H1..H5000) | +-- pick a host whose next_ok has passed +-- take one URL +-- check robots.txt cached per host +-- fetch timeout, size cap, depth cap | +-- set next_ok = now + crawl_delay politeness maintained, locally | v PARSE +-- content hash --> seen exactly? drop +-- SimHash ------> near-duplicate? drop +-- extract text --> document store --> indexer +-- extract links | v for each link: normalise strip tracking params, lowercase host, resolve relative Bloom filter seen? → drop new? → route to the worker owning that host → append to that host's back queue
Normalisation before the seen-check is what stops the same page being crawled forty times under forty URLs that differ only by tracking parameters. It is unglamorous and it is worth an enormous fraction of the crawl budget.
🔄8. Workflows — what actually happens
One page, start to finish
The loop that runs four thousand times a second.
  1. Worker 12 owns about 5,000 hosts. It scans its back queues for one whose next-allowed time has passed. example.com is ready.
  2. It checks its cached robots.txt for that host. The path is allowed and the declared crawl delay is 1 second.
  3. It fetches, with a timeout, a size cap, and a redirect limit. 82 KB of HTML comes back.
  4. It immediately sets example.com's next-allowed time to now + 1 second. Politeness is now maintained — and it took one in-memory write, because no other worker will ever touch this host.
  5. The page is hashed. Not a known duplicate. SimHash puts it near nothing existing. It is genuinely new content.
  6. Text is extracted, boilerplate stripped, and the document is written to storage for the indexer.
  7. 103 links are extracted and normalised. 98 are already in the Bloom filter and dropped. The 5 survivors are routed to whichever worker owns their host and appended to that host's back queue.
Every step is local. No lock was taken, no shared counter was read, and nothing coordinated with another machine except handing off new URLs — which is an append, not a negotiation.
The crawler falls into a calendar
The trap that eats fleets.
  1. A site has an events calendar. Every month page links to the next month. There is no last page.
  2. Each fetch yields a new URL that is genuinely new — the Bloom filter cannot help, because these are not duplicates.
  3. Left alone, this host's back queue grows forever and the crawler keeps finding "new" pages. It will never finish and it is producing nothing of value.
  4. Politeness bounds the damage: one request per second means the trap consumes one host's worth of budget, not the fleet's. The partition key contained the blast radius without anyone designing for it.
  5. The explicit defences are bounds: a maximum crawl depth from any seed, and a per-domain budget of pages per cycle. The calendar hits the budget and stops.
  6. A pattern detector helps too: many URLs from one host, differing only in a numeric path segment, yielding near-identical SimHashes, is a strong signal to deprioritise the whole pattern.
You cannot enumerate every trap in advance — the web will always invent a new one. What you can do is bound everything: depth, per-domain budget, queue length, page size. Unbounded anything is how a crawler dies.
A news homepage and a 2009 PDF
How recrawl scheduling makes a fixed budget useful.
  1. Both pages were crawled a month ago. Both are candidates for recrawl. The budget only affords one of them right now.
  2. The scheduler looks at observed change history. The news homepage has changed on every one of the last 40 crawls. The PDF has changed zero times in three years.
  3. The news page's interval has been driven down to about an hour; the PDF's has been driven up to about a year.
  4. So the news page is recrawled, and it has changed — which confirms the interval and keeps it short.
  5. If it had come back unchanged, the interval would have been extended slightly. The schedule adapts to what the page actually does rather than what anyone assumed.
  6. A conditional request helps further: sending the last modification time lets an unchanged page return 304 Not Modified with no body, costing a round trip instead of 100 KB.
The same crawl budget produces a much better index when spent adaptively. And because the signal is measured rather than configured, nobody has to maintain a list of “sites that change often”.
A host starts hanging on every request
The failure mode that quietly drains a worker.
  1. A server stops failing and starts not responding — connections open, nothing is sent, they stay open.
  2. Without a timeout, each of these permanently occupies a connection slot. A worker with 2,000 slots and one pathological host bleeds capacity until it is doing nothing.
  3. So every fetch has a hard timeout. A hung connection is abandoned after a few seconds and the slot is recovered.
  4. Repeated timeouts on one host trip a circuit breaker: that host is marked unhealthy, its next-allowed time is pushed far out, and its queue is set aside.
  5. Periodically we retry it once. If it responds, the host is restored to normal scheduling.
  6. Meanwhile nothing else on that worker was affected, because the damage was bounded to one host's queue.
Hanging is worse than failing, because failure is fast and visible while hanging is slow and silent. Every outbound request in a system like this needs a timeout, and the absence of one is a bug even when nothing has gone wrong yet.
🔍9. Deep dives, and what breaks

URL normalisation, which is worth more than it sounds

The same page is reachable through an enormous number of URLs: with and without www, with and without a trailing slash, with session ids, with tracking parameters, with fragments, with parameters in a different order.

Without normalisation the crawler treats each as a distinct page and fetches it. On a large site with tracking parameters on every internal link, that is a multiplier on the entire crawl cost for zero additional content.

So before the seen-check: lowercase the host, resolve relative paths, drop the fragment, sort query parameters, and strip known tracking parameters. It is a boring list of string operations that recovers a large fraction of the crawl budget, which is a good reminder that the highest-leverage work in a system is not always the interesting-looking part.

robots.txt, and the caching it needs

Every host's rules must be fetched and honoured, and fetching robots.txt before every page would double the request count — and violate politeness on its own.

So it is cached per host with a refresh interval of hours, which is well within what site operators expect. The file also frequently specifies a crawl delay, which overrides the default and must be respected; a site asking for one request every ten seconds gets that.

The failure cases need explicit answers. If robots.txt cannot be fetched, the polite default is to assume the site does not want to be crawled and back off, rather than to assume permission. If it is malformed, parse what you can and ignore the rest. Getting this wrong is not a performance problem, it is the kind of thing that gets your crawler blocked.

Prioritising the frontier

Two hundred billion known URLs and budget for ten billion a month means the ordering decides what your index actually contains. The frontier's priority function is, in a real sense, the product.

The signals are unsurprising individually: inbound link count and quality, the host's historical content quality, depth from the seed, how long since last crawl, and observed change rate. Combining them is where the judgement lies, and there is no correct formula.

What is worth saying in an interview is the framing: the crawler's quality is decided by its scheduling policy, not by its fetching machinery. Fetching fast is an engineering problem with a known answer. Choosing what to fetch is the open one.

What breaks

Fetcher Worker Freezes (Slow Server Response)
Fetchers use non-blocking asynchronous I/O (epoll/libuv) with hard 5-second socket read timeouts and 2MB response size caps.
DNS Resolution Bottleneck
Local custom caching DNS server with pre-fetching; eliminates 100ms DNS query delay per crawled page.
Frontier Master Node Failure
Frontier queue state is checkpointed to RocksDB / distributed log (Kafka). Standby master restores queue pointers in <5s.
Malicious Spider Trap / Zip Bomb
Decompression stream reader capped at 10MB; immediately aborts and blacklists the URL pattern if exceeded.
The dominant constraint

Politeness is per host, so the partition key must be the host. Making the constraint local instead of coordinated is the entire architectural move; partition by URL and you need a distributed rate limiter you cannot afford.

What I would build first

The Mercator-style frontier with per-host queues and a politeness delay, plus SimHash near-duplicate detection before anything is indexed.

What I deliberately did not build

JavaScript rendering, which costs 10 to 100 times more per page, and the ranking system, which is a different problem entirely.

The biggest risk

Spider traps and infinite URL spaces. Without per-domain budgets and depth caps, one badly behaved site consumes the whole fleet.

💬 If you get this far, here is what they will push on
Follow-ups an interviewer is likely to ask once the design is on the board. Answers supplied — read the question, answer it out loud, then open it.
“A site generates infinite URLs — a calendar with a next-month link forever. What stops you?”Answer

Nothing, unless you build for it, and this is the classic way a crawler wastes an entire fleet. Every page is new, every page yields more links, and none of it is new content.

Three defences together: a per-domain budget so no single site can consume more than its share, a depth cap so you stop following a chain that keeps going, and near-duplicate detection before indexing so the trap becomes visible as thousands of nearly identical pages.

The budget is the important one. The others catch it; the budget bounds the damage while you do.

“How do you decide what to recrawl, and how often?”Answer

You cannot maximise freshness and coverage at once under a fixed budget, so it is a scheduling policy rather than a setting.

The signal that works is observed change rate: crawl a page, compare it to what you had, and adjust its interval. A news homepage changes hourly and earns frequent recrawls. An archived PDF has not changed in three years and does not.

Weight by importance too, because a page nobody ever sees in results is not worth refreshing regardless of how often it changes.

“Why partition by host rather than by URL?”Answer

Because politeness is defined per host. If one host's URLs are spread across every worker, then every worker needs to coordinate to avoid hitting that host too fast, and you have built a distributed rate limiter.

Partition by host and the constraint becomes local: one worker owns that host, applies the delay itself, and needs to talk to nobody.

This is the same move as putting the booking invariant on one row. Choose the partition key so the rule you must enforce lives inside a single partition.

“Do you render JavaScript?”Answer

It depends on how much of the web you are willing to miss, and it is a cost question rather than a technical one. Headless rendering is 10 to 100 times more expensive per page than fetching HTML.

The practical approach is tiered: fetch HTML for everything, and render only pages where it is likely to matter — sites known to be client-rendered, or pages whose HTML is suspiciously empty.

Rendering everything is how a crawler's cost goes up by two orders of magnitude for a modest gain in coverage.

Design a Metrics & Logging Pipeline (Observability at Fleet Scale)

Difficulty: Hard (Staff Expectation)  .  Target: 45 min
💬 The question, as asked

“Several systems emit different kinds of logs and metrics. Design a pipeline that collects them, processes them within a minute, and serves them to dashboards, alerting and ad-hoc search.”

⚡ What makes it hard

Metrics and logs have opposite cost curves — logs are ~20× the bytes for a fraction of the queries — so building them as one system prices metrics like logs. And the thing that kills these systems is not traffic growth.

📋1. Understanding the question

The prompt: “Several systems emit different kinds of logs and metrics. Design a pipeline that collects them, processes them within a minute, and serves them to dashboards, alerting and ad-hoc search.”

The phrase “logs and metrics” is doing something sneaky. It reads as one category of thing. It is two, and they are almost opposites.

🎯 Say this in the first three minutes

Metrics and logs are two different systems, and building them as one is the classic mistake. A metric is a number attached to a name and some labels, sampled on a schedule. A log line is a piece of text somebody wrote, emitted when something happened.

They differ in every dimension that matters for storage: volume, compressibility, query pattern, and how often anyone reads them.

Why the difference is so stark

Take a CPU utilisation metric. It is a name, a few labels, a timestamp and a float. The same series is sampled every ten seconds forever, and consecutive samples are nearly identical. Timestamps are regular, so you can store the difference between them; values move slowly, so the same trick works there. A datapoint that was 16 bytes of structure compresses to somewhere around 1.4 bytes.

Now take a log line. Three hundred bytes of semi-structured text, all different from each other, compressible only in the ordinary way. Roughly a hundred times more storage per event — and there are about as many events.

And the read patterns invert the picture. Every dashboard and every alert rule reads metrics constantly, thousands of times a minute. Logs are read rarely, almost never in bulk, and then suddenly and urgently for twenty minutes during an incident.

So: metrics are small, dense, and read constantly. Logs are large, sparse, and read almost never. Put them behind the same storage engine and you pay log prices for metric access patterns, which is how observability bills get to be larger than the systems being observed.

The thing that actually kills these systems

Not traffic growth. Cardinality.

A metric's cost is not driven by how often it is sampled but by how many distinct label combinations exist. http_requests{method, status} is a few dozen series. Add user_id as a label and it becomes one series per user — potentially millions — each with its own index entry and its own compression state.

One engineer adding one label in one deploy can multiply the system's memory footprint by a thousand in an afternoon. No amount of capacity planning survives that, which is why per-tenant limits appear in this design as a correctness feature rather than a nicety.

What they are looking for

Do you split the two immediately? This is the question.

Do you know about cardinality? Candidates who size by host count have not operated one of these.

Do you protect ingest over query? Not being able to look during an incident is bad. Not having the data to look at is unrecoverable.

❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
Are metrics and logs one system or two?
Ask this first. They have opposite cost curves, and building them as one prices metrics like logs. This question is most of the design.
What is the retention per tier?
Raw for days, rollups for months, is what makes 13-month retention affordable. It is a lossy decision someone must approve.
What query latency do alerting, dashboards and forensics each need?
Three very different budgets. Alerting needs seconds on recent data; forensics can take minutes over cold storage.
Push or pull ingest?
Pull gives free liveness detection but cannot reach short-lived jobs or cross NAT.
Is this multi-tenant, and do we need per-tenant limits?
Without a per-tenant series budget, one team’s cardinality bomb takes down everyone’s monitoring.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.
📝2. Functional requirements
  • Ingest from 100,000 hosts, emitting both numeric time series and semi-structured log events.
  • Queryable within 60 seconds of being emitted — because an alert that fires five minutes late is an alert about history.
  • Serve three consumers with genuinely different needs: dashboards doing range queries over hours, alerting evaluating rules continuously over recent data, and humans searching logs during an incident.
  • Tiered retention: metrics for over a year in downsampled form, raw logs for about a month.

The three consumers are not one workload

Worth separating explicitly, because each has a different latency budget and each fails differently under load.

Alerting re-evaluates the same rules every few seconds over the last few minutes. It is predictable, high-frequency, and it must be fast — it is also the one consumer whose failure is an emergency, because a silent alerting system is indistinguishable from a healthy platform.

Dashboards ask range queries over hours or days, at human pace. They tolerate a second or two. They are bursty, because everyone opens them at once when something breaks.

Log search is rare, unpredictable, and expensive — someone grepping a day of logs for one request id. It can take tens of seconds, and it is the query most likely to be issued during the worst hour of the month.

Which means the same infrastructure must serve a latency-critical steady workload and an occasional enormous one, at exactly the same time.

⏱3. Non-functional requirements
RequirementTargetWhy it is stated this way
Ingest availabilityAbove query availabilityThe most important line in the table. You can tolerate not being able to look; you cannot tolerate losing the data you will need to look at.
Freshness< 60 sSet by alerting. Relax it to five minutes and the whole streaming tier could be a batch job.
Metric retention13 monthsDownsampled. Thirteen rather than twelve so you can compare against the same month last year.
Log retention~30 days rawBounded by cost, not by usefulness. This is a budget decision that someone must own explicitly.
DegradationShed, never collapseUnder overload it must drop work in a controlled way. An observability system that dies during an incident is worse than none, because people trusted it.
CostA design constraintAt this volume storage cost drives architecture as hard as latency does. Saying so is not an excuse; it is the honest framing.

Why ingest outranks query, concretely

A service is failing. Its hosts are emitting the exact metrics and logs that explain why.

If the query path is down, engineers are blind for ten minutes and then the data is there waiting. Painful, recoverable.

If the ingest path is down, those ten minutes never existed. When the system comes back there is a hole precisely where the incident was, and the post-mortem has nothing to work with.

That asymmetry justifies a lot of design: buffering at the agent, generous queue capacity between ingest and storage, and a deliberate choice to shed queries before shedding writes when the system is under pressure.

🗂4. Data model and API

Two storage engines, because the two data types want opposite things.

-- METRICS: the label set IS the identity. Hash it once, store the mapping. TABLE series_index { series_id UINT64 PRIMARY KEY, -- hash(name + sorted labels) metric_name VARCHAR, labels MAP<str,str>, first_seen TIMESTAMP, last_seen TIMESTAMP -- drives churn detection + expiry } -- inverted index: label_name=label_value -> roaring bitmap of series_id BLOCK tsdb_block { -- immutable, 2h of data, columnar series_id, t0, delta_of_delta_ts[], xor_encoded_vals[] } -- ~1.4 bytes/point. Blocks compact 2h -> 1d -> 1w with rollups attached. -- LOGS: index the LABELS only, never the message body. TABLE log_chunk_index { stream_id UINT64, -- hash(stream_labels) t_start TIMESTAMP, t_end TIMESTAMP, object_key TEXT -- gzip chunk in object storage } -- Query = narrow by labels to a few chunks, then brute-force grep them.

Metrics: columnar and delta-encoded

A time series is a name plus a set of labels, and then a long run of (timestamp, value) pairs. The storage exploits everything regular about that.

Timestamps arrive on a schedule, so store the difference between consecutive gaps rather than the timestamps — a perfectly regular series compresses to almost nothing. Values change slowly, so store them XORed against the previous value, which for a slowly-drifting float leaves mostly zero bits.

Together these are what get 16 bytes down to around 1.4. And the effect is not merely storage: a year of one series fits comfortably in memory, so range queries over long windows are fast without a separate aggregation system.

The index is separate and is the part that hurts. It maps label values to series ids, so {service="checkout", region="eu"} resolves to a set. That index is sized by the number of distinct series, not by the number of datapoints, which is exactly why cardinality rather than volume is the binding constraint.

Logs: index the labels, not the text

The tempting design is a full inverted index over log contents, so any word is searchable. It works, and at ten million lines a second the index rivals the data in size and the ingest cost is enormous.

The cheaper model, and the right one at this scale, is to index only the labels — service, host, level, time — and store the log text as compressed chunks. A search then means: use the labels to select a small set of chunks, decompress them, and scan.

Scanning sounds slow and is acceptable because of how logs are actually searched. Nobody greps all of last month. They grep one service, one hour, because they already know roughly where the problem is. Label selection cuts ten million lines a second down to a few hundred thousand lines, and brute-force scanning that is fast enough.

The honest cost: a query with no useful labels — “find this request id anywhere” — degrades to scanning everything, and is slow. That is a real limitation to state rather than hide.

The API

POST /v1/ingest/metrics // protobuf, batched, gzip Body: { series: [{ name, labels{}, points:[{t, v}] }] } Response: 204, or 429 + Retry-After when shedding Note: fire-and-forget from the agent; NO synchronous ack path POST /v1/ingest/logs Body: { stream_labels{}, entries:[{t, line}] } Response: 204 | 429 GET /v1/query_range?q=&start=&end=&step= Response: { series:[{ labels{}, values:[[t,v]] }] } Errors: 422 series_limit_exceeded // reject, never OOM GET /v1/logs/search?selector=&filter=&start=&end=&limit= Response: streaming NDJSON, bounded by scan-bytes budget
📊5. Capacity estimation

The arithmetic, and the number that decides the architecture.

⚖ Assumptions — and what breaks if each is wrong
100K hosts, ~1,000 series each
Cardinality, not host count, is the binding constraint; one bad label can multiply this by the user base.
Sub-minute freshness is required for alerting
Relaxing to five minutes would allow batch ingestion and remove the streaming tier.
Logs are read rarely but urgently
If log search were high-volume, label-only indexing would be too slow and a full inverted index would be justified.
100M
active metric series
10M/s
metric datapoints
10M/s
log lines
3 GB/s
raw log bytes
~14 MB/s
compressed metrics
260 TB
raw logs/day

Metrics: 100,000 hosts with about 1,000 series each at ten-second resolution is 10 million datapoints per second. At 1.4 bytes compressed that is roughly 14 MB/sec — a few terabytes a year, for the entire fleet. That is startlingly cheap, and it is the whole argument for treating metrics as their own system.

Logs: the same hosts at 100 lines a second and 300 bytes a line is 10 million lines and 3 GB per second. Around 260 TB a day raw, and even compressed several times over it is the dominant storage cost in the design by orders of magnitude.

Same event rate. Roughly two hundred times the bytes. That ratio, more than any other number here, is why the two get different engines.

Downsampling is what makes long retention affordable

Keeping ten-second resolution for thirteen months would be most of the storage bill for data nobody looks at that way — nobody examines ten-second granularity from eight months ago.

So raw resolution is kept for days, then rolled up to one-minute aggregates for weeks, then to one-hour aggregates for the remainder. Each step is roughly a 6× reduction, and the year-old data ends up a small fraction of its original size.

It is lossy and irreversible, and that deserves an explicit decision rather than a default. Once you have downsampled to hourly, a two-minute spike from last March is gone forever — the average absorbed it. Storing max and min alongside the average preserves the existence of the spike if not its shape, which is usually the right compromise and is worth naming as one.

⚖6. The key trade-offs

The choices, and their costs.

DecisionChosen ✓Alternative ✗Reasoning
Metrics vs logsTwo storage engines, one ingest pathOne unified storeOpposite cost curves. Logs are ~20x the bytes for a fraction of the queries. A unified store prices metrics like logs and makes 13-month retention unaffordable.
Ingest transportPush, via a durable logPull / scrapePull is simpler and gives free liveness detection, but cannot cross NAT or reach short-lived jobs. The durable log is non-negotiable regardless: it absorbs spikes that would otherwise reach the storage tier.
Log indexLabels only + brute scanFull inverted index~10x cheaper ingest and storage. Searches are almost always already narrowed by service and time window, so the unselective-query penalty is rarely paid.
Under overloadShed at the collector, 429Buffer indefinitelyUnbounded buffering converts an observability degradation into an observability outage, precisely when you need it. Shed low-priority tenants first and keep alerting metrics flowing.
Query safetyReject over series/byte budgetBest-effort executionOne unbounded query must not be able to OOM the node serving everyone's alerts. A fast 422 is a better answer than a slow death.

Push or pull

A genuine fork with no universally right answer.

Pull — the system scrapes each target on a schedule — gives you liveness detection for free: a target that cannot be scraped is down, and you know it without any separate health check. It also centralises the sampling schedule, so nobody can flood you by misconfiguring an interval.

It fails on things that do not sit still. A batch job that runs for eight seconds may never be scraped at all. Anything behind NAT or a firewall cannot be reached. Serverless functions are gone before the scraper arrives.

Push handles all of those, and gives up the free liveness signal — silence now means “down, or misconfigured, or never existed”, which is three different things. It also lets a misbehaving client overwhelm you, so it requires per-tenant rate limits that pull did not.

The practical answer in a large fleet is pull for long-lived services and a push gateway for ephemeral work, and being able to say why both exist is the signal.

The multi-tenant problem, which is the one that bites

One shared observability platform serving fifty teams. One team ships a label containing a user id. Their series count goes from ten thousand to ten million overnight.

Without limits, that team's mistake exhausts the memory of the shared index and everyone's monitoring goes down at once — including, in the worst version, the monitoring you would use to find out why.

So per-tenant limits are load-bearing: a cap on active series, a cap on ingest rate, and a cap on query cost. When a tenant exceeds their series budget, their new series are rejected with a clear error, and everybody else is unaffected.

The general principle is worth stating: in a shared platform, the failure mode you must design against is not your own bug but your noisiest tenant's. Limits are how you convert a platform-wide outage into one team's clear, actionable error message.

🏗7. High-level design
Telemetry ingest — and the cardinality bomb the collector has to stop
metric pointstime serieslog chunksrejected
What is moving: agents batch metric points every 10 s and push them through stateless collectors into a durable log, which is the shock absorber — it decouples a producer spike from consumer capacity. Downstream, the same stream forks into two completely different stores: compressed series for metrics, gzip chunks plus a label index for logs.
What goes wrong: one deploy adds a user_id label to a request counter. Each distinct value becomes its own time series, so one metric becomes millions, and the TSDB’s memory-resident index grows without bound until the process is OOM-killed. Nothing about traffic changed — an application change did this. The defence is a per-tenant series budget enforced at the collector, so the blast radius is one team rather than everyone’s monitoring.

A shared ingest path that forks immediately.

100,000 hosts | v AGENT on each host batches, compresses, buffers to local disk if we are unreachable | v INGEST GATEWAY auth, per-tenant rate limit, cardinality check | reject here, loudly, not silently downstream v BUFFER a durable log this is what makes ingest survive storage being down | +-------------------------------+ v v METRICS PATH LOGS PATH 14 MB/s 3 GB/s | | time-series store object storage, compressed chunks delta + XOR encoded labels indexed, text not ~1.4 bytes/point scan on read | | +-- downsample: raw → 1m → 1h +-- lifecycle: hot → cold → delete at 30d | | v v QUERY SEARCH alerting every 15s, recent "this service, this hour, this string" dashboards ranges, bursty label selection first; brute-force scan second
The buffer between ingest and storage is the single most valuable component. It turns “the storage tier is down” from data loss into a delay, which is the difference between an inconvenience and a hole in your post-mortem.
🔄8. Workflows — what actually happens
A CPU metric from one host to an alert
Sixty seconds, end to end.
  1. The agent on host-4471 samples CPU every 10 seconds. It does not send each sample — it batches a few seconds' worth from all 1,000 of the host's series and compresses them.
  2. The gateway authenticates the tenant, checks their ingest rate and series budget, and appends the batch to the durable buffer. The agent's request is acknowledged here — not after storage.
  3. The metrics consumer reads from the buffer and writes into the time-series store. The new datapoint joins its series, delta-encoded against the previous timestamp and XORed against the previous value. About 1.4 bytes.
  4. It is queryable roughly 15 seconds after it was sampled.
  5. The alerting engine, which re-evaluates every rule every 15 seconds, runs avg(cpu) by (service) > 0.9 over the last 5 minutes.
  6. The average crosses the threshold. The rule has a 2-minute "for" duration, so it does not fire yet — it waits to see whether the condition persists.
  7. It persists. The alert fires, roughly two and a half minutes after the CPU actually rose.
Most of that delay is the deliberate 2-minute wait, not the pipeline. That wait is what stops a single scrape blip from paging someone at 4am, and it is the right place to spend the budget.
An engineer searches logs during an incident
Why label-only indexing is enough.
  1. Checkout is returning 500s. An engineer searches: service=checkout, level=error, last 30 minutes, containing "timeout".
  2. The label index resolves service and level and time to a specific set of compressed chunks. This is the cheap step and it does almost all the filtering.
  3. Out of 10 million lines per second across the fleet, the labels select roughly 200,000 lines — four orders of magnitude less.
  4. Those chunks are fetched and decompressed in parallel across workers.
  5. Each worker scans its chunk for the substring. No index on the text, just a fast scan over a small set.
  6. Results return in a couple of seconds. The engineer sees the timeouts are all to one downstream service.
A full text index would have made this faster and would have cost roughly as much to maintain as the logs themselves. The label index costs almost nothing and does 99.99% of the narrowing, because people always search with a service and a time range — they already know roughly where to look.
A team ships a user_id label
The cardinality explosion, and the limit that contains it.
  1. A well-meaning engineer adds user_id to a request-count metric so they can debug one customer's problem.
  2. That metric had 40 series — a few methods times a few status codes. It now has one series per user who makes a request. Within an hour, 2 million series.
  3. Each needs an index entry and in-memory compression state. Their tenant's memory footprint grows by orders of magnitude in minutes.
  4. Without limits, the shared index exhausts memory and every team's monitoring stops — during which nobody can see that this is what happened.
  5. With a per-tenant series budget, that tenant hits their cap. New series from them are rejected with an explicit error naming the metric and the label.
  6. Their existing series keep working. Every other team is entirely unaffected. The engineer sees the error, removes the label, and it resolves in one deploy.
The limit did not prevent the mistake — nothing prevents that mistake. It converted a platform-wide outage into one team's clear error message, which is the most that can be asked of a shared system.
The storage tier goes down for twenty minutes
Where the buffer earns its existence.
  1. The time-series store becomes unwritable — a bad deploy, a full disk, whatever.
  2. The consumer reading from the buffer starts failing and stops advancing its position.
  3. Ingest keeps working. Agents still send, the gateway still accepts, and the buffer keeps growing. Nothing is lost.
  4. Queries degrade: dashboards go stale and alerting is evaluating data that stops advancing. This is the visible symptom and it is the right one to have.
  5. Alerting needs its own guard here — a rule evaluating on frozen data can silently stop firing. A staleness check on the data itself must page independently.
  6. Storage recovers. The consumer resumes from its position and catches up. Within a few minutes the twenty-minute gap is filled in and nothing is missing.
The twenty minutes of an incident that you most need to see are exactly the twenty minutes that were at risk. The buffer converts a permanent hole into a temporary blindness, which is the entire reason ingest availability is ranked above query availability.
🔍9. Deep dives, and what breaks

Agent-side buffering, and why it is not optional

The buffer at the centre of the pipeline protects against storage failing. It does not protect against the gateway being unreachable — a network partition, a deploy, a regional issue.

So the agent on each host buffers to local disk when it cannot send. It is a small bounded buffer — tens of megabytes, minutes of data — and when it fills, it drops the oldest.

Dropping is the right behaviour and worth saying explicitly. An unbounded agent buffer means that when the pipeline is down, every host in the fleet starts filling its disk, and the observability system becomes the cause of a much larger outage. A component designed to watch the system must never be able to take it down, and bounded buffers with a drop policy are how you guarantee that.

Alerting on data that stopped arriving

The subtlest failure in the whole design, and a genuinely good thing to raise.

A rule says “fire if error rate exceeds 5%”. The pipeline breaks and no data arrives. The error rate is not high — there is no error rate at all. The rule does not fire. Every dashboard is green and nothing is being monitored.

The fix has two parts. Rules need an explicit stance on missing data: treat absence as a firing condition where that makes sense, rather than silently evaluating to false. And more importantly, there must be a separate check on the freshness of the data itself — is the newest datapoint less than two minutes old? — that pages independently of everything else.

That check, ideally, runs somewhere other than this system. A monitoring system that monitors itself has an obvious blind spot, and the usual answer is a small independent watchdog whose only job is to confirm the big one is alive.

What a histogram costs

Percentile latency is the number people actually care about, and percentiles do not average — you cannot combine the p99 of ten hosts into a fleet p99 by taking the mean. So latency is recorded as a histogram: a set of buckets, each a counter.

Counters do combine, so bucket counts sum cleanly across hosts and the percentile is computed at query time from the summed buckets.

The cost is cardinality, again: a histogram with 20 buckets is 20 series, not one. Applied to a metric that already has a few labels, a single latency histogram can be hundreds of series per service. It is usually worth it — but it is the main reason a service's series count is much higher than the number of metrics its developers think they defined.

What breaks

Kafka unavailable
Agents buffer to local disk with a bounded ring (e.g. 1 GB / 15 min) and resume on recovery. Beyond the bound they drop oldest first, because in an incident the newest telemetry is the telemetry you need. Collectors return 429 so agents back off with jitter.
Metrics ingester crashes
The in-memory head block is backed by a write-ahead log on local disk; on restart it replays the WAL to reconstruct the head. Kafka consumer offsets are committed only after the WAL write, so recovery is at-least-once. Duplicate datapoints are idempotent — same series, same timestamp, same value overwrites harmlessly.
Cardinality bomb from one team
Per-tenant series budget enforced at the collector: series beyond the budget are rejected with a named error and an alert to the owning team. Blast radius is one tenant instead of the cluster. This is the single most important safeguard in the design.
Object storage degraded
Recent data is still served from the in-memory head and local blocks, so dashboards and alerting for the last few hours keep working — which is the window that matters during an incident. Historical queries fail fast with a clear error rather than hanging.
The observability system causes an incident
Agents are hard-capped on CPU and memory via cgroups and drop telemetry rather than compete with the application they observe. Ingest endpoints are on separate capacity from query, so a dashboard stampede during an outage cannot block ingestion. This inversion — monitoring taking down production — is common enough that you should raise it unprompted.
The dominant constraint

Metrics and logs have opposite cost curves. Logs are roughly twenty times the bytes for a fraction of the queries, so they get separate storage engines behind one shared, durable ingest path.

What I would build first

The durable log in the middle. It decouples a producer spike from consumer capacity, and everything downstream of it can be rebuilt or restarted without loss.

What I deliberately did not build

Tracing, and per-tenant query isolation beyond a simple budget. Both matter and both are separable.

The biggest risk

Cardinality. One well-meaning application change adding a user_id label can OOM the ingesters, which is why the per-tenant series budget is enforced at the collector rather than reviewed by humans.

💬 If you get this far, here is what they will push on
Follow-ups an interviewer is likely to ask once the design is on the board. Answers supplied — read the question, answer it out loud, then open it.
“A team adds a user_id label to a counter. What happens?”Answer

One metric becomes millions of time series, one per user. Each series carries its own index entry and compression state in memory, so the ingester's memory grows until the process is killed.

Nothing about traffic changed. An application deploy did this, which is why the control cannot be a review process — it has to be a hard limit at ingest.

A per-tenant series budget rejects the new series with a named error and alerts the owning team, so the blast radius is one team rather than everybody's monitoring.

“How do you detect this before it kills you?”Answer

Alert on series churn — new series created per minute — not on absolute series count. Churn moves the instant a bad deploy ships; the absolute count only crosses a threshold once the damage is done.

The absolute count is still worth a dashboard, but as a capacity number rather than an alert.

“Why keep metrics and logs separate? It seems like more work.”Answer

Because they have opposite cost curves. A metric datapoint compresses to about 1.4 bytes; a log line is a few hundred. Logs are roughly twenty times the volume for a fraction of the query traffic.

Store them together and you price metrics like logs, which makes 13-month retention unaffordable. Or you price logs like metrics and cannot keep them long enough to be useful.

They share the ingest path, which is where the operational work actually is. Only the storage engines differ, and that is the cheap part to duplicate.

“An outage starts. Dashboards are down because the system is overloaded. Now what?”Answer

This is the failure mode that matters most, and the answer has to be in the design rather than in the runbook.

Ingest and query run on separate capacity, so a dashboard stampede during an incident cannot starve ingestion. You would rather lose the ability to look than lose the data you will need to look at afterwards.

Alerting evaluates against recent data held in memory, so it keeps working even when historical queries are failing. And agents are capped by cgroup so telemetry can never compete with the application it observes.

Design a Distributed Cache (like Memcached / Redis Cluster)

Difficulty: Hard (Staff Expectation)  .  Target: 40 min
💬 The question, as asked

“Design a distributed cache like Memcached. Ten million requests a second, sub-millisecond, across a ten-terabyte working set.”

⚡ What makes it hard

The first question decides everything: is this a cache or a low-latency store? If the data is reconstructible, you skip replication, durability and consensus entirely. If not, you are building something two orders of magnitude more expensive.

📋1. Understanding the question

The prompt: “Design a distributed cache like Memcached. Ten million requests a second, sub-millisecond, across a ten-terabyte working set.”

Before designing anything, ask one question, because the answer changes the cost of this system by about two orders of magnitude.

🎯 Cache, or low-latency store?

If we lose a node, is the data gone forever, or can it be fetched again from somewhere?

If it can be refetched, this is a cache: no replication, no durability, no consensus, no write path to speak of. Losing a node costs a temporary dip in hit rate.

If it cannot, this is a low-latency database that happens to live in memory, and you now need replication, durability and a recovery story. Everything gets harder and more expensive.

Most candidates assume the first and never say so. Saying it out loud — and naming what it buys — is the highest-value thirty seconds in this round.

What a cache actually does for you

It is worth being precise, because it explains why a cache far smaller than the data can still work brilliantly.

Access is not uniform. In almost every real workload a small fraction of keys accounts for most requests — the popular product, the trending post, the session of someone actively clicking. A cache holding 10 TB in front of a database holding a petabyte still catches the overwhelming majority of reads, because the requests were never spread evenly across that petabyte.

The corollary matters just as much: if access really were uniform, a cache smaller than the dataset would be worse than useless. Every request would miss, and you would have added a network hop and a memory copy to every read in exchange for nothing. Skew is not an incidental property of the workload; it is the precondition for caching to make sense at all.

And the failure that actually takes systems down

Not a cache node dying — that is routine and survivable. The dangerous one is the cache tier coming back empty after a restart, while the traffic that it was absorbing arrives all at once at the origin.

If the database was comfortable at 500K queries per second because the cache was serving 95% of 10M, then a cold cache means 10 million queries per second hitting a database sized for half a million. It does not degrade; it stops. And then it cannot serve the requests that would have refilled the cache, so the system cannot recover on its own.

Designing for that is more important than designing the happy path, and it is covered in the workflows.

What they are looking for

Do you ask the cache-or-store question? Unprompted, in the first minutes.

Do you know the per-entry overhead? It decides whether the design is viable at small value sizes.

Do you have an answer for a cold start? This is where these systems actually fail.

❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
Is this a cache or a low-latency store?
The highest-value question in the round. If we may lose the data freely it is about locality and eviction; if not, you are designing something two orders of magnitude more expensive.
What is the value size distribution?
At 100-byte values, per-entry overhead is more than half your RAM. The fix is to change the workload, not to buy nodes.
How stale may a read be?
Determines whether TTL alone is sufficient or you need an explicit invalidation channel.
What happens if the whole tier restarts?
Forces the conversation about whether the origin survives a 0% hit rate — which is the failure that actually takes systems down.
Single region, or replicated?
Replicating a reconstructible cache doubles cost; that memory usually buys a better hit rate instead.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.
📝2. Functional requirements
  • GET, SET with a TTL, DELETE, plus an atomic INCR for counters.
  • A 10 TB working set spread across the cluster, with values ranging from a hundred bytes to a megabyte.
  • Elastic: add and remove nodes without flushing everything.

That is genuinely the whole interface, and the smallness is the point. The API has no range scans, no secondary indexes, no transactions and no queries. Every operation touches exactly one key, which is what lets the data be partitioned by key with no coordination whatsoever and lets any node answer without consulting any other node.

The moment you add an operation spanning multiple keys, that property is gone and the design becomes an entirely different one. Keeping the interface this narrow is a deliberate choice, not an oversight.

What we are explicitly not building

No strong consistency — a stale read is acceptable. No durability — a restart loses everything and that is fine. No replication — the memory that a second copy would occupy is better spent holding more distinct keys, because a larger cache raises the hit rate and a replicated one does not.

Each of those is a real decision with a real justification, and each one is only valid because of the answer to the cache-or-store question.

⏱3. Non-functional requirements
RequirementTargetWhat it forces
Latencyp99 < 1 msAt the cache, excluding network to the caller. This rules out any disk access on the hot path and any garbage-collection pause of consequence.
Throughput10M QPSAggregate. Divided by per-node capacity, this sets the node count — and per-node capacity is usually limited by network packets, not by CPU.
Working set10 TBAll resident in memory. The RAM per node then determines how many nodes, and the two constraints must be reconciled.
Hit rateAs high as possibleNot a nice-to-have. It is the metric that determines whether the origin survives, so it is a capacity input rather than a performance report.
Data lossAcceptableIndividually. Mass simultaneous loss is not, because of what it does to the origin.
ConsistencyStale reads OKBounded by TTL. If a stale value were unacceptable, this would be a different and much more expensive system.

Hit rate is a capacity requirement

It is usually presented as a performance metric, and here it is better understood as the thing that sizes the database.

At 10M requests per second: a 95% hit rate leaves 500K/sec for the origin. A 90% hit rate leaves one million. Five percentage points doubled the load on the most expensive tier in the architecture.

So hit rate deserves an alert with a threshold, and a drop in it should be treated as an incipient incident rather than a curiosity — it is the leading indicator for the database falling over, and it moves before any database metric does.

🗂4. Data model and API

There is no schema. There is a hash table, a memory allocator, and an eviction policy — and the second of those is where the surprising costs live.

-- Per node: slab allocator, NOT malloc. Fixed-size classes in a -- growth factor (1.25x): 96B, 120B, 152B, 192B ... 1MB STRUCT item { next, prev PTR -- LRU list linkage h_next PTR -- hash chain expiry UINT32 -- lazy: checked on read, not swept nbytes, flags UINT32 cas_id UINT64 -- bumped on every mutation key[], value[] BYTES } -- Rounding to a slab class wastes up to 20% per item. That is the -- price of never fragmenting -- a cache that fragments dies slowly -- over weeks, which is far worse than a fixed 20% tax. -- Ring: 200 physical nodes x ~200 virtual nodes = 40,000 points. -- Virtual nodes are what make removal move 1/N of keys, not half.

The overhead nobody estimates

Every entry carries more than its value. There is the key itself, a hash table slot, pointers for whatever structure tracks recency, the TTL, flags, and allocator bookkeeping. Call it 50 to 120 bytes before your value.

With 1 KB values that is roughly 10% waste, which is unremarkable. With 100-byte values it is more than half your RAM spent on bookkeeping, and buying twice the nodes buys you twice the overhead too.

The right answer when the workload is small values is not more nodes — it is to change the workload. Pack many logical entries into one cache entry: cache a whole user's preference map under one key instead of forty keys of twenty bytes each. One entry's overhead now amortises across forty values, and you also replaced forty round trips with one.

This is a recurring lesson: when per-item overhead dominates, the fix is at the call site, not in the infrastructure.

Why fragmentation matters, and slabs

Values range from a hundred bytes to a megabyte, and entries are constantly allocated and freed. A general-purpose allocator in that situation fragments: free space exists but is scattered in pieces too small to use, and the process grows even though the live data did not.

The standard fix is slab allocation. Memory is divided into pages, each page cut into fixed-size chunks, with a range of chunk sizes available. A value goes into the smallest chunk class that fits it. Freeing returns the chunk to its class's free list, where the next similarly-sized value uses it exactly.

The cost is rounding waste — a 600-byte value in a 1024-byte chunk wastes 424 bytes. In exchange, memory usage is predictable and stable over months of continuous operation, which is worth far more than the waste. It also creates a real operational gotcha: if the workload's size distribution shifts, memory assigned to one chunk class is stranded there, and the cache can start evicting while holding free memory in the wrong class.

The API

// Binary protocol over pooled, pipelined TCP. No HTTP -- header // parsing alone would dominate a sub-millisecond budget. GET key -> value, cas_token | MISS MGET key[] -> values[] // one RTT for N keys, same node SET key value ttl flags -> STORED CAS key value cas_token -> STORED | EXISTS // compare-and-swap: the ONLY concurrency primitive here, // and what makes read-modify-write safe without a lock DELETE key -> DELETED | NOT_FOUND INCR key delta -> new_value // server-side, atomic // Client-side: routing table + consistent hash ring, refreshed // from a config service. The client picks the node -- no proxy hop.
📊5. Capacity estimation

The numbers, and the two independent constraints they set.

⚖ Assumptions — and what breaks if each is wrong
Data is reconstructible from the origin
If it is not, this is a low-latency store and needs replication and durability.
Access is Zipfian
Under a uniform distribution a cache smaller than the working set thrashes and adds latency instead of removing it.
Values average around 1 KB
At 100 bytes, per-entry overhead exceeds the payload and the design must pack entries.
~10B
keys resident
~64 GB
usable RAM/node
~200
nodes (with headroom)
50K
QPS per node avg
~10 GB/s
aggregate value bytes
~1.4 TB
overhead at 120B/key

By memory: 10 TB of values plus per-entry overhead, at around 64 GB usable per node, lands somewhere near 200 nodes with headroom. Headroom matters more than usual here — a cache running at 98% of memory is evicting constantly, and its hit rate falls off before anything looks wrong.

By throughput: 10M QPS across 200 nodes is 50,000 per node, which is comfortable for an in-memory store. The limit in practice is rarely CPU cycles — it is packets. Each request is a small packet with fixed per-packet cost regardless of payload, and a machine that can push a few hundred thousand packets per second is doing well.

The two constraints landing at a similar node count is what you want. If memory said 200 nodes and throughput said 800, you would be buying RAM you cannot use.

And the network sanity check, which people skip: 10M requests at an average 1 KB value is 10 GB/sec of value bytes leaving the tier. Across 200 nodes that is 50 MB/sec each — fine. But a workload with 100 KB values at the same request rate would be a terabyte per second, which no realistic network delivers. Always check the bytes, not just the operations.

⚖6. The key trade-offs

The choices, and their costs.

DecisionChosen ✓Alternative ✗Reasoning
RoutingSmart client, direct connectProxy tierA proxy adds a network hop -- often 0.3-0.5 ms against a sub-1 ms budget -- plus a tier to scale and fail. A proxy wins only when you cannot control the clients or need many languages; then pay the hop deliberately.
PartitioningConsistent hashing + vnodeshash mod Nmod N remaps ~99.5% of keys when one node joins. That is a full flush and a guaranteed origin stampede at exactly the wrong moment.
ReplicationNone, except hot keysReplicate everythingDoubles cost to protect data that is by definition reconstructible. Spend that memory on a larger working set instead -- a bigger cache raises the hit rate, which is worth more than surviving one node loss.
EvictionApproximate LRUStrict LRUStrict LRU requires a lock on the list head per read. The recency ordering it buys was already a heuristic; the lock contention is real.
ConsistencyDelete on write, TTL backstopWrite-through updateUpdating races: two writers can land their cache updates in the opposite order to their database writes and leave the cache permanently stale. Delete has no such race. Ch 9

Where the routing decision lives

Something has to turn a key into a node. There are two places to put that, and the choice has consequences.

In the client. The client library holds the ring and connects directly to the right node. One network hop, minimum latency, no extra tier to run or scale. The cost is that every client must have the current topology, so a node change means propagating it everywhere — and during propagation different clients disagree about where a key lives, which shows up as a brief dip in hit rate.

In a proxy. Clients connect to a proxy that knows the ring. Topology changes are one deployment. The proxy can also pool connections, which matters enormously when ten thousand application servers each want a connection to each of two hundred cache nodes — that is two million connections without pooling.

The cost is a hop, some latency, and a tier that must itself be made highly available.

At this scale, connection pooling usually decides it. The proxy earns its hop back by collapsing the connection count.

Consistent hashing, and why it is not optional

With hash(key) % 200, adding one node changes the modulus and re-maps essentially every key. Every entry in the cache is suddenly on the wrong node. The hit rate goes to zero, and per the failure discussed in step 1, the origin then receives the full 10M QPS.

Adding a node must not be an outage. So keys are placed on a ring and each node owns an arc; adding a node takes over part of one arc and leaves the rest alone. Going from 200 to 201 nodes invalidates roughly half a percent of the keys.

Virtual nodes — giving each machine a few hundred positions on the ring rather than one — are what makes the arcs even, and what makes a departing node's load spread over many neighbours instead of landing entirely on the next one.

🏗7. High-level design
Read path — and what a dead cache node does to the origin
request / hitmiss reaching the origin
What is moving: a key lookup out, and either a cached value back in ~0.2 ms, or — on a miss — a read that continues to the origin. The client hashes the key itself and talks to exactly one node, so there is no coordinator anywhere on this path.
What goes wrong: node B dies and its share of keys is rehashed onto the survivors — where they are not present. Every one of those reads is now a miss travelling to an origin sized for about 1% of read traffic. With consistent hashing that is ~1/N of keys and survivable; with hash mod N it is 99.5% of keys at once, a cold-start stampede the origin will not survive.

Deliberately shallow.

app servers (thousands) | v PROXY / CLIENT LIBRARY holds the ring, pools connections | | key → hash → ring position → one node v CACHE NODES ~200, independent, sharing nothing node-17 node-18 [ hash table ] [ hash table ] [ slab allocator ] [ slab allocator ] [ LRU / LFU chain ] [ LRU / LFU chain ] no replication. no gossip. no coordination. | miss v ORIGIN the database this tier exists to protect sized for ~5% of 10M QPS. it cannot survive 100%. READ the whole hot path hash the key → one node → hash lookup → return no locks, no fan-out, no consensus. this is why it is sub-millisecond. NODE DIES its keys are now unresolvable → they miss → origin serves them with 200 nodes: hit rate drops ~0.5%, origin load rises ~10% survivable. this is why many small nodes beat few large ones.
The last block is the strongest argument for node count. Twenty nodes of 500 GB would mean losing one costs 5% of the cache and a 100% increase in origin load — the same failure, now an outage.
🔄8. Workflows — what actually happens
A read that hits, and a read that misses
The entire hot path, which is deliberately dull.
  1. The app asks for product:88291. The client hashes the key, finds its ring position, and sends the request to node 17. No lookup service was consulted.
  2. Node 17 hashes the key into its table, follows one pointer, finds the entry, and checks the TTL. Not expired.
  3. It bumps the entry's position in the recency structure and returns 1.2 KB. Elapsed: about 100 microseconds, most of it network.
  4. Now a miss: product:99104 is not there. Node 17 returns nothing — and notably does not go and fetch it.
  5. The app reads from the database, gets the row, and writes it into the cache with a TTL.
  6. The next request for that key hits.
The cache never talks to the database. That keeps it a dumb, fast key-value store with no knowledge of schemas, connection pools or query languages — and it means a cache outage degrades the app rather than breaking it, because the app already knows how to read from the origin.
One cache node dies at peak
Routine, and survivable precisely because of the node count.
  1. Node 17 fails. Its 50 GB of entries are gone; there is no replica and by design there was never meant to be one.
  2. Clients detect the failure and remove node 17 from the ring. Its arc is absorbed by its ring neighbours.
  3. Those keys now resolve to nodes that have never seen them, so they miss. Hit rate drops from 95% to about 94.5%.
  4. Origin load goes from 500K to about 550K QPS — a 10% rise, which a database with normal headroom absorbs without noticing.
  5. As those keys are re-read they are populated on their new nodes. Within minutes the hit rate is back.
  6. Node 17 is replaced and takes back its arc, causing a second small, brief dip.
This is the argument for many small nodes rather than few large ones, stated as arithmetic: with 200 nodes one failure is a 10% origin increase; with 20 nodes it is a 100% increase. Same failure, completely different outcome.
The whole cache tier restarts
The failure that actually takes systems down.
  1. A bad configuration push restarts every cache node. All 200 come back healthy, responsive — and completely empty.
  2. Every request misses. The origin, sized for 500K QPS, receives 10 million.
  3. It saturates within seconds. Queries queue, latency explodes, connection pools exhaust, and it effectively stops serving.
  4. Now the trap: the cache cannot refill, because refilling requires successful origin reads and the origin is not completing any. The system cannot recover on its own.
  5. What prevents it, in order of value. Request coalescing at the app: a thousand concurrent misses for the same key become one origin query and 999 waiters. On a skewed workload this alone cuts the stampede by orders of magnitude.
  6. A concurrency limit on origin access: allow only N in-flight queries; beyond that, fail fast or serve degraded. A database doing 500K QPS is far more useful than one doing zero.
  7. Staged restarts: never restart the whole tier at once. Rolling restarts mean the surviving nodes keep absorbing most of the traffic.
Note that all three mitigations live outside the cache. The cache cannot protect the origin from its own absence — the callers must, which is why "what happens if the whole tier restarts?" is a clarifying question rather than an implementation detail.
One key gets a million requests per second
The hot key, which consistent hashing cannot help with.
  1. A celebrity posts, and every request in the system wants the same key. Hashing sends all of them to one node.
  2. That node is now doing a million QPS on its own while 199 others idle. It saturates — usually on packets per second, not CPU.
  3. Adding nodes does nothing. The key has one hash and therefore one home, and no rebalancing changes that.
  4. Fix one: write the value under a few suffixed keys — post:99:1 through :8 — and have clients pick one at random. One hot key becomes eight warm ones on eight nodes.
  5. Fix two, often better: cache it in the application process for a second or two. A million requests per second across a thousand app servers is a thousand per server — served from local memory with no network at all.
  6. The cost of fix two is a second of staleness on the hottest key in the system, and a second of extra staleness on a trending post is invisible.
Worth stating plainly: sharding solves uneven distribution across many keys, and does nothing for concentration on one key. That needs either more copies of the key or a cache layer closer to the caller — the same shape as the stadium problem in D9.
🔍9. Deep dives, and what breaks

Eviction: LRU, and where it fails

Least-recently-used is the default for good reason. It is cheap — a doubly-linked list plus a hash table, all O(1) — and it matches how real access behaves, since something used recently is likely to be used again.

Its known weakness is a large scan. Something walks a million keys once: a batch job, an export, a crawler. Every one of those keys is now the most-recently-used thing in the cache, and they have evicted the genuinely popular entries that had not been touched in the last few seconds. The hit rate collapses and takes minutes to recover.

LFU — evicting the least-frequently used — resists this, because a key seen once does not outrank one seen ten thousand times. Its own weakness is the mirror image: a key that was enormously popular last week keeps its high count and lingers long after anyone wants it, so frequency counts must decay over time.

Practical systems use something in between, often with a small probationary area that scanned keys must survive before entering the main cache at all. The transferable point for an interview: every eviction policy has a workload that defeats it, and knowing which one is worth more than naming the policy.

Invalidation, and why TTL is usually enough

The underlying row changes and the cache still holds the old value. Two approaches.

TTL — entries simply expire. Simple, self-healing, requires no coordination, and bounds staleness to the TTL. The cost is that you are stale for up to that long, and that a short TTL to reduce staleness also reduces hit rate, because entries are discarded while still being requested.

Explicit invalidation — whoever writes the data deletes the cache key. Staleness drops to milliseconds. The cost is a coupling: every writer must know every cache key derived from the data it touches. Miss one code path and you have a permanently stale entry with no expiry to save you, which is one of the more unpleasant bugs to track down.

The pragmatic combination is TTL as the safety net and invalidation as the optimisation: invalidate where it matters and where you are confident, and let the TTL catch everything you forgot. The TTL is what turns a missed invalidation from a permanent bug into a bounded one.

Why not replicate

Replication feels like obvious insurance, and for a cache it is usually the wrong purchase.

A second copy of every entry halves the number of distinct keys you can hold in the same memory. A smaller cache has a lower hit rate, and a lower hit rate means more origin load — continuously, not just during failures.

So you would be accepting a permanently higher database load in exchange for avoiding a brief 0.5% hit-rate dip when a node dies. That trade is clearly bad here.

It becomes good in exactly one circumstance: when the answer to the cache-or-store question was “store”. Then the data cannot be refetched, losing it is real data loss, and replication stops being insurance against a hit-rate dip and becomes the thing keeping the data alive. Everything in this design hangs off that one answer.

What breaks

Single node dies
Its ~0.5% of keys become misses and are refilled from the origin on demand. Clients mark the node down after a short failure-detection window and skip it on the ring. Critically, the origin must have headroom for a 0.5% miss-rate increase -- which it does, because that is a rounding error against the normal miss rate.
Node flapping
Far worse than a clean death: each transition reshuffles key ownership, so keys ping-pong between nodes and the effective hit rate collapses while both copies go stale. Damp it -- require N consecutive failures to eject and a longer, hysteretic interval to re-admit. Slow, stable membership beats accurate, twitchy membership. Ch 1
Whole cache tier restarts
The genuine disaster: hit rate goes to 0% and the origin sees 20-100x its normal load, which is a metastable failure it will not recover from on its own. Mitigate with staggered restarts (never more than 10% of the fleet at once), a concurrency limit on origin fill so the cache cannot forward more than the origin can serve, and load shedding beyond it. Ch 10
Hot key saturates one node's NIC
Count-min sketch detects the key, the control plane promotes it to replicated + client-L1 mode automatically. Detection must be automatic: by the time a human has read the graph, the node has been dropping packets for ten minutes.
Ring disagreement between clients
During a config rollout, two clients may briefly hold different rings and write the same key to different nodes -- producing two divergent copies with no reconciliation. TTLs bound the damage, and the config service versions the ring so a client can detect and refuse a stale topology. This is why membership is the one thing that gets consensus.
The dominant constraint

It is a cache, so the data is reconstructible. That permission is what makes the rest cheap: no replication, no durability, no consensus on the data path, and a node loss costs 1/N of the hit rate rather than any correctness.

What I would build first

Consistent hashing with virtual nodes plus a smart client that connects directly. Consensus is confined to membership, which changes a few times a week.

What I deliberately did not build

Persistence and cross-region replication. Both would double the cost to protect data whose whole point is that losing it is safe.

The biggest risk

The cold-start stampede. If the tier restarts and the origin cannot survive a 0% hit rate, the cache is not an optimisation but an undeclared hard dependency.

💬 If you get this far, here is what they will push on
Follow-ups an interviewer is likely to ask once the design is on the board. Answers supplied — read the question, answer it out loud, then open it.
“The whole cache tier restarts. What happens to the database?”Answer

It takes the full read load with a 0% hit rate, which is typically 20 to 100 times what it is provisioned for. Latency climbs, clients time out and retry, and the retries keep it saturated even after the cache warms — a metastable failure it will not recover from on its own.

Mitigations: stagger restarts so no more than a small fraction of the fleet is cold at once, and put a concurrency limit on origin fills so the cache cannot forward more than the database can serve.

If the database cannot survive a cold cache at all, you do not have a cache in front of a database. You have a database whose availability depends on the cache.

“One key is getting a million requests a second. What breaks?”Answer

The NIC, before the CPU. A million requests a second at 1 KB per value is a gigabyte a second to one node, which saturates an 8 Gbps link. Hot keys are a bandwidth problem first.

The cheapest fix is a client-side L1 with a very short TTL. A key that hot is read constantly, so even a 10 ms TTL collapses a million requests into about a hundred per client.

Beyond that, replicate the key under salted names and have clients pick one at random. Detect which keys need this with a count-min sketch rather than a static list, because static lists are always stale by the time they matter.

“Why consistent hashing rather than hash mod N?”Answer

Because of what happens when N changes. Going from 200 nodes to 201 with mod N remaps about 99.5% of keys, which is a full cache flush and an instant origin stampede — at exactly the moment you were adding capacity.

A hash ring remaps only the keys owned by the node that joined or left, roughly 1/N. Virtual nodes make that share even, so removing a node spreads its keys across all survivors instead of dumping them on one neighbour.

“Should you replicate cache data for durability?”Answer

No, and being able to say why is the point. The data is reconstructible from the origin by definition — that is what makes it a cache.

Replicating doubles your cost to protect data you can regenerate. That memory buys far more as additional cache capacity, because a bigger cache means a higher hit rate, which is worth more than surviving one node loss.

The exception is hot keys, where replication is about spreading load rather than durability.

Design Typeahead / Autocomplete (Search Suggestions at Google Scale)

Difficulty: Hard (Staff Expectation)  .  Target: 40 min
💬 The question, as asked

“Design search autocomplete. As the user types, show the ten most likely completions, fast enough that it feels instantaneous.”

⚡ What makes it hard

It is not a search problem — it is a precomputation problem. Traversing the subtree under a one-character prefix means ranking the entire corpus, which no latency budget survives.

📋1. Understanding the question

The prompt: “Design search autocomplete. As the user types, show the ten most likely completions, fast enough that it feels instantaneous.”

The word “search” is a trap. This is not a search problem.

🎯 The reframe that carries the interview

This is a precomputation problem. You are not searching a corpus when the user types — you are looking up an answer that was computed hours ago.

Once you say that, every other decision follows: the serving path does one lookup and no ranking, and all the interesting engineering moves offline into the pipeline that builds the table.

Why searching at request time cannot work

Consider what the naive version requires. The user types a. To return the ten best completions you must consider every query in the corpus starting with a — tens of millions of them — score each one, and take the top ten.

You have about 50 milliseconds, and you need to do this again on the next keystroke, at around two million requests per second.

The scoring cost is worst exactly where the traffic is heaviest: short prefixes are both the most expensive to answer and the most frequently requested, since every query passes through a before it reaches anniv. There is no index clever enough to rescue that shape.
