  4. Instead, a queue-depth threshold trips. New requests are routed to the fallback model: smaller, CPU-servable, a few points less accurate.
  5. Those requests are answered in about 80 ms with lower confidence. Responses are tagged with the fallback version, so downstream consumers and the logs both know.
  6. Autoscaling adds GPU capacity — slowly, because GPU nodes take minutes to come up. When the queue drains, routing returns to the primary model.
The slow autoscaling is the real reason the fallback exists. GPU capacity cannot appear in seconds, so something has to absorb the gap — and a slightly worse answer now is almost always better than a correct answer after the client gave up.
🔍9. Deep dives, and what breaks

Why batching gives 10×, physically

Worth being able to explain rather than assert, because the reason generalises.

A GPU has thousands of cores and very high memory bandwidth. Running a model means loading its weights from memory and multiplying them against the input. For one small input, loading the weights dominates — the arithmetic is trivial and the hardware spends its time waiting on memory.

With 32 inputs, the weights are loaded once and multiplied against all 32. The memory traffic is nearly unchanged; the arithmetic goes up 32×; and the arithmetic was never the bottleneck. So throughput rises by roughly an order of magnitude while the per-batch time barely moves.

The general principle: when the fixed cost per operation dominates the variable cost, batching wins enormously. It is the same reason Kafka batches produces in D7 and the same reason the cache design packs small values together in D12.

Detecting drift

A model degrades without anyone changing anything, because the world changes. Vocabulary shifts, camera hardware changes, the mix of users moves.

The difficulty is that nothing errors. The service is healthy, latency is fine, and the answers are quietly getting worse.

Ground truth is the definitive signal and usually arrives late or not at all. So the practical monitors are proxies you can compute immediately:

  • Score distribution. If the histogram of outputs shifts, something upstream changed.
  • The uncertain rate. A rise means the model is increasingly encountering inputs it does not recognise, which is the earliest available warning.
  • Input statistics. Image dimensions, text length, language mix — drift here precedes drift in output.

None proves the model got worse. All of them fire before accuracy does, which is what makes them worth having.

Preprocessing must match training exactly

A small-sounding detail that causes real and very confusing incidents.

If training resized images to 224×224 with one interpolation method and normalised with one set of constants, serving must do precisely the same. A different resize filter or a slightly different normalisation produces inputs the model was never trained on, and accuracy drops with no error anywhere — the service is healthy, the model is correct, and the answers are wrong.

The defence is to make preprocessing a versioned artifact that travels with the model, so the serving path cannot use a different one. It is the same instinct as keeping the threshold with the version: anything that must change together should be stored together.

What breaks

GPU fleet saturated
Shed at the gateway with 429 before the request consumes preprocessing, and fail over to a smaller distilled model that runs on CPU. Degraded predictions beat no predictions, provided the response says which model answered.
A model version is bad
Traffic split lives in the registry, not in a deployment, so rollback is a percentage change that takes effect in seconds. This is the reason not to bake the model into the container image.
Model artifact fails to load
The server refuses to report healthy and stays out of rotation. A node serving a partially loaded model silently returns nonsense, which is far worse than a node that is visibly down.
Poisoned or adversarial input
Hard caps on decoded dimensions and duration before the model sees anything — a decompression bomb is a resource attack disguised as an image. Rate-limit per caller on inference cost, not on request count.
Silent accuracy collapse (drift)
Monitor the prediction and confidence distributions continuously, not just latency. Alert on a shift in the uncertain-rate; it moves before any ground-truth label arrives to tell you.
The dominant constraint

Batching economics. Unbatched, this needs roughly ten times the GPUs; every serving decision — the adaptive window, the CPU preprocessing tier, the cache — exists to fill batches without breaking the latency budget.

What I would build first

The preprocessing tier, the batcher and the inference log. The log is not optional: without it you cannot measure drift, and drift is the failure mode with no error message.

What I deliberately did not build

Training and the feature store. Serving and training are separable, and conflating them is how ML systems become impossible to reason about.

The biggest risk

Silent accuracy decay. Nothing alerts, latency stays flat, and the answers quietly stop being right. That is why prediction-distribution monitoring is in the design rather than in a follow-up.

💬 If you get this far, here is what they will push on
Follow-ups an interviewer is likely to ask once the design is on the board. Answers supplied — read the question, answer it out loud, then open it.
“What happens if you remove the batcher?”Answer

You need roughly ten times the GPUs for identical traffic. At 350 requests a second and 40 ms per unbatched inference, that is 14 GPU-seconds of work per second. Batched at 32, the same load is about 1.4.

So batching is not a tuning knob, it is the difference between an affordable system and an unaffordable one.

The window is the dial: longer waits mean fuller batches and lower cost, at the price of tail latency. Make it adaptive to queue depth, because a fixed window is wrong at both ends of the load curve.

“The model's accuracy drops but nothing errors. How would you know?”Answer

This is drift, and it has no error message. Latency is fine, nothing crashes, the answers are just gradually less right because the input distribution moved.

You cannot wait for ground truth, because labels arrive days later if at all. So monitor the prediction distribution and the confidence histogram. If the share of low-confidence results jumps, or the class mix shifts, something changed even before any label confirms it.

That is why the inference log is part of the design rather than an operational afterthought.

“How do you ship a new model without risking a regression?”Answer

Shadow first, then canary. Run the new version on a copy of live traffic, discard its output, and compare its predictions against the current model. Disagreements are where you look.

Offline evaluation only tells you how the model does on data you already had. Shadow traffic tells you how it does on the data you actually get, which is the only question that matters.

Only once the disagreement rate is understood does it start serving anyone, and traffic split lives in a registry so rollback is a percentage change rather than a deploy.

“Where does the confidence threshold come from?”Answer

From the cost of each kind of error, not from maximising accuracy. Accuracy weights false positives and false negatives equally, which is almost never what anybody wants.

For X-ray triage a missed finding is a serious harm and a false alarm costs a few minutes of review, so the threshold should be low and route aggressively to a human. For a landmark-recognition feature a wrong label is mildly embarrassing, so the threshold can be much higher.

It is a product decision, and answering “we would optimise accuracy” is the wrong answer.

Design an ML Experiment & Pipeline Platform (experiment tracking, lineage, and pipeline health metrics)

Difficulty: Hard (Staff Expectation)  .  Target: 40 min
💬 The question, as asked

“Design a platform where researchers track experiments — parameters, metrics, artifacts — compare runs, and trace any deployed model back to the data that produced it.”

⚡ What makes it hard

Three data kinds with nothing in common: kilobyte metadata, a million-point-per-second time series, and gigabyte checkpoints. And the tracker must never be able to kill a forty-hour training run.

📋1. Understanding the question

The prompt: “Design a platform where researchers track experiments — parameters, metrics, artifacts — compare runs, and trace any deployed model back to the data that produced it.”

This reads like a CRUD application with a dashboard. It is not, for two reasons.

🎯 One: three kinds of data with nothing in common
  • Metadata — parameters, tags, code version. Kilobytes per run, queried constantly, needs to be filterable across thousands of runs.
  • Metrics over time — loss at every step. Up to a million points per second across the fleet. This is time-series ingest, not database inserts.
  • Artifacts — model checkpoints. Gigabytes each, written rarely, read rarely.

Putting all three in one store means either a database full of gigabyte blobs or a blob store you cannot query. They get three engines.

🎯 Two: the tracker must never be able to kill a training run

A run has been going for forty hours on expensive hardware. If a call to log a metric blocks, or times out, or throws, and that failure propagates into the training loop — you have destroyed forty hours of GPU time to record a number nobody was going to look at for another day.

The tracker is not on the critical path, and enforcing that is an architectural requirement, not a coding convention.

The scoping question to ask first

Are we tracking experiments, or orchestrating them?

Tracking is a metadata store with a good query layer — substantial, but bounded. Orchestration is a distributed scheduler with dependencies, retries and resource allocation, which is D6's problem in different clothes and is at least as large again.

Conflating them is how you end up designing neither properly. Asking which is meant, out loud, is the cheapest scoping signal available.

What they are looking for

Do you split the three data kinds? This is the question.

Do you make logging fire-and-forget? And do you say why, in terms of the forty-hour run?

Do you understand what lineage actually requires? It is not a field; it is a constraint on everything that produces a run.

❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
Are we tracking experiments, or orchestrating them?
Tracking is a metadata store — comparatively easy. Orchestration is a distributed scheduler with retries and dependencies, which is D6’s problem wearing different clothes. Scope this explicitly.
Must a result be exactly reproducible?
Reproducibility forces you to version code, data, environment and hyperparameters together. Without it you only need to record metrics, which is a far smaller system.
How large are the artifacts?
Metrics are kilobytes; model checkpoints are gigabytes. They belong in different stores, and conflating them is the classic mistake.
How many concurrent experiments, and how chatty?
A training run logging a metric every step at 1 kHz across thousands of runs is a high-rate ingest problem, not a CRUD app.
Who consumes this — researchers, or production?
If production models are promoted from here, the registry becomes a control plane with access control and audit, not a notebook companion.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.
📝2. Functional requirements
  • Record runs: parameters, metrics over time, artifacts, code version, dataset version.
  • Compare runs side by side, and query across them — “best F1 where learning rate below 0.01 and batch size 64”.
  • Full lineage: from a deployed model back to the exact data and code that produced it.
  • Pipeline health: freshness, volume, schema drift and failure rate per stage.

What lineage actually demands

“Trace a model back to its data” sounds like storing a pointer. It is a constraint on the entire system that produces runs, and it is only useful if every link holds.

The chain is: deployed model → the run that produced it → that run's code commit, hyperparameters, environment, and the exact dataset version → how that dataset was built → from which raw sources.

Break any link and the chain is worthless, because the question lineage answers is always adversarial: “this model is behaving badly in production — was it trained on the corrupted batch from the 14th?” A chain that is right most of the time cannot answer that.

The hard link is almost always the dataset version. Code has commits and environments have lockfiles, but “the training data” is frequently a path in object storage that someone overwrites. If the data is mutable, lineage is a record of a thing that no longer exists. Immutable, versioned datasets are therefore a precondition, not a feature — and saying so is the staff-level observation here.

Reproducibility, which is related but stronger

Worth separating in the requirements. Lineage tells you what produced a model. Reproducibility means you can run it again and get the same result, which additionally requires the environment, library versions, and random seeds — and even then GPU non-determinism may prevent bit-identical output.

Asking which is actually needed is a real scoping question, because reproducibility is several times the work.

⏱3. Non-functional requirements
RequirementTargetWhat it forces
Logging impactNever blocks or fails a runThe defining requirement. It makes the write path asynchronous, buffered, lossy and non-throwing — all four, deliberately.
Metric ingest~1M points/sec10K concurrent runs at up to 100 Hz. This is time-series ingest and cannot be rows in a relational table.
Cross-run query< 1 sA dashboard filtering thousands of runs by parameter. Needs an indexed, queryable metadata store.
Metadata retentionYearsSmall and permanent. Lineage is worthless if it expires before the model does.
Artifact retentionLifecycle policyCheckpoints are the storage bill. Most are never read after the run ends — but you cannot tell which in advance.
UI freshnessSeconds of lagResearchers watching a loss curve tolerate a few seconds. That tolerance is what permits buffered writes.

Unpacking "never blocks or fails"

It resolves into four specific properties of the client library, each of which must be deliberate:

  • Asynchronous. The call returns immediately; sending happens on a background thread. A slow network never slows the training loop.
  • Buffered. Points accumulate locally and are sent in batches. Logging at 100 Hz must not mean 100 requests per second per run.
  • Lossy, with a bounded buffer. If the backend is down and the buffer fills, drop the oldest points. An unbounded buffer eventually exhausts the training job's memory, which is exactly the failure we are trying to prevent.
  • Never throws. Any error is swallowed and counted, never propagated. An exception from a logging call that reaches the training loop can end the run.

Losing metric points is genuinely acceptable here. The curve is a diagnostic; a gap in it is a minor inconvenience. Losing the run is not. Getting that priority right is the entire design of the write path.

🗂4. Data model and API

Three stores, because there are three data shapes.

-- Metadata is relational; metrics are time series; artifacts are blobs. -- Three stores, because these three have nothing in common. TABLE runs { run_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, experiment VARCHAR, params JSONB, -- GIN index: query across runs by param code_ref BYTES, -- git sha dataset_ref BYTES, -- content hash of the snapshot env_ref BYTES, -- container digest summary JSONB, -- final metrics, denormalised for sorting status ENUM(running, finished, failed, killed), started_at, ended_at TIMESTAMP } -- Summary metrics are denormalised on purpose: "best F1 in this -- experiment" must not require scanning a time series per run. SERIES metrics { -- in the TSDB, keyed like any other series labels: { run_id, key }, points: (step | ts, value) } TABLE lineage_edges { -- a DAG, not a tree: models beget models child VARCHAR, parent VARCHAR, kind ENUM(trained_from, distilled_from, finetuned_from), PRIMARY KEY (child, parent) }

Metadata — relational, and deliberately so

Runs, parameters, tags, code and dataset versions, artifact references. Kilobytes per run, millions of runs, and the queries are exactly what SQL is good at: filter on parameters, join to metrics, aggregate, sort.

The one awkwardness is that hyperparameters are open-ended — every researcher invents new ones — so they cannot be columns. A key-value table or a JSON column with indexes on the commonly filtered keys handles it. It is not elegant and it works, and reaching for a document database instead usually trades good query support for schema flexibility nobody needed that badly.

Metrics — a time-series store, not a table

A million points per second is about the same ingest rate as the metrics pipeline in D11, and for the same reasons it needs the same treatment: delta-encoded timestamps, XOR-compressed values, roughly two bytes a point.

Writing each point as a row through an ORM would be several orders of magnitude more expensive per point and would produce a table nobody can query at the resolution it was written.

Downsampling applies here too. A forty-hour run logging at 100 Hz produces around 14 million points for one metric — far more than any chart can show. Keep full resolution for recent runs, roll up older ones, because nobody inspects per-step loss from a run six months ago.

Artifacts — object storage, referenced not stored

Checkpoints are hundreds of megabytes to gigabytes. They go in object storage; the metadata holds keys and hashes.

The hash is worth more than it looks. Checkpoints from consecutive epochs of the same run are often substantially similar, and identical artifacts — a base model reused across a hundred fine-tuning runs — are stored once. Content addressing gives that for free, exactly as in D8.

The API

POST /v1/runs Body: { experiment, params{}, code_ref, dataset_ref, env_ref } Response: 201 { run_id } // code_ref/dataset_ref/env_ref are content hashes -- this is // what makes a result reproducible rather than merely recorded POST /v1/runs/{id}/metrics // batched, fire-and-forget Body: { points:[{ key, value, step, ts }] } Response: 202 // client buffers and never blocks training on this call. // A tracker outage must not kill a 40-hour training run. POST /v1/runs/{id}/artifacts -> { upload_url } // direct to object store POST /v1/runs/{id}/finish Body: { status, summary_metrics{} } GET /v1/runs?experiment=&filter=params.lr<0.01&sort=-metrics.f1 GET /v1/models/{version}/lineage -> run, code, dataset, parent models GET /v1/pipelines/{id}/health -> freshness, volume, schema drift
📊5. Capacity estimation

The numbers, and the design conclusions in each.

⚖ Assumptions — and what breaks if each is wrong
10K concurrent runs, 100 metric points/sec each
At 10× this the write path stays but metric storage must become a proper TSDB rather than a relational table.
Artifacts average 500 MB, metrics are kilobytes
If artifacts were small, one store would do and the split would be unnecessary complexity.
Researchers tolerate seconds of lag in the UI
If live training curves had to be real-time, the buffered async write path would need replacing with a streaming one.
1M/s
metric points at peak
~2 bytes
per point compressed
~170 TB/yr
metrics, compressed
~500 MB
average artifact
~50 TB/day
artifact writes at 100K runs
<1 s
cross-run query budget

Metrics. 10,000 concurrent runs at 100 points per second is 1 million points/sec. At ~2 bytes compressed that is only a couple of megabytes a second, or on the order of 170 TB a year — large but tractable. The compression is doing enormous work; uncompressed rows would be hundreds of times that.

Artifacts. At 500 MB average and a hundred thousand runs a day, this is tens of terabytes a day and it is the dominant cost by a wide margin. Which makes lifecycle policy a first-class design element rather than an operational afterthought.

Metadata. Kilobytes per run. Even millions of runs is single-digit gigabytes. It is free, and it is the part that must be kept forever.

The shape that emerges is worth stating: the data you must never delete is tiny, and the data that dominates the bill is mostly never read again. That asymmetry is the whole argument for the three-way split, and it is what makes a sensible retention policy possible — keep lineage forever, and expire most checkpoints.

Which checkpoints to keep

Not all of them, and choosing badly is expensive either way.

A reasonable default: keep the final checkpoint and the best-performing one for every run; keep all checkpoints for runs whose models were promoted to production, forever, because those are the ones lineage will be asked about; expire intermediate checkpoints from ordinary runs after a few weeks.

The failure to avoid is deleting the checkpoint of a run that later turns out to matter. Marking a run as promoted must retroactively pin its artifacts, which means the lifecycle policy has to consult run state rather than age alone.

⚖6. The key trade-offs

The choices, and their costs.

DecisionChosen ✓Alternative ✗Reasoning
Metric ingestReuse the D11 metrics storeA new bespoke store1M points/sec is a time-series problem that is already solved here. Building a second one is duplicated operational burden for no gain.
Client behaviourBuffer and dropBlock and retryA tracker outage must never kill a 40-hour training run. Losing points from a curve is cheap; losing the run is not.
ArtifactsDirect client upload to object storageThrough the APIStreaming gigabytes through a metadata service makes it a bandwidth bottleneck and couples its availability to every checkpoint write.
Summary metricsDenormalised onto the run rowComputed from the series“Best F1 in this experiment” is the most common query. Scanning a time series per run to answer it makes the UI unusable.
ScopeTracking only; orchestration is separateOne combined systemOrchestration is a distributed scheduler with retries and dependencies. Merging them produces a system that does neither well.

Buffered and lossy, versus reliable

The central trade, and it is decided by the forty-hour run.

A reliable write path — acknowledge every point, retry on failure, never drop — means the client must either block when the backend is slow, or buffer without bound. Blocking risks the run; unbounded buffering exhausts its memory and risks the run a different way.

A lossy path drops points when it cannot keep up, and the training run never notices anything happened.

What makes this an easy call is the value asymmetry: a missing point in a loss curve is a cosmetic gap, and a lost forty-hour run is thousands of dollars and a day of someone's time. The cheapest thing in the system is the data the tracker collects; the most expensive is the job it is observing. Any design that risks the second to protect the first has it backwards.

One nuance worth stating: this applies to metrics, not to run completion. The final record — final metrics, artifact references, status — is written with retries and does matter, because losing it means losing the run's result rather than a sample of its progress.

Tracking versus orchestration, revisited

The scope question from step 1, with its consequence.

If the platform only tracks, it is an observer: runs are started elsewhere and report in. It can be down without stopping anybody's work, which is a very comfortable property.

If it orchestrates, it is on the critical path for every experiment in the organisation. It now needs the availability, the scheduling, the retry semantics and the resource accounting of D6 — and when it is down, nobody can train anything.

These usually do get built together, and they should still be separate services with a clear boundary, so that the tracker's failure never becomes the scheduler's failure. Saying that explicitly is worth more than picking one.

🏗7. High-level design
Experiment tracking — and the outage where dropping data is the right answer
metric pointsbatched writemetadatafailed flush
What is moving: metric points at up to 100 Hz per run, buffered in the client and flushed asynchronously; run metadata and the four reproducibility hashes; and gigabyte checkpoints, which the client uploads directly to object storage rather than through the API.
What goes wrong — and why it is fine: the ingest service is down. The client buffers, then drops the points and keeps training. A gap in a loss curve costs nothing; killing a 40-hour run on expensive hardware because a metadata service returned 503 is unacceptable. This is the same inversion as D11: the observability system must never be able to take down the thing it observes.

One client, three stores, and a hard boundary at the top.

training job (40 hours, expensive hardware) | v CLIENT LIBRARY the boundary that protects the run | async — returns immediately | buffered — batches, does not send per point | bounded — drops oldest when full | silent — never throws into the training loop v INGEST | +---------------+---------------+ v v v METADATA METRICS ARTIFACTS relational time-series object storage KB per run 1M points/s GB per checkpoint queried always ~2 bytes/point content-hashed, deduped keep forever downsample old lifecycle, but pin promoted runs | | | +-------+-------+---------------+ v QUERY / UI compare runs, filter by params, plot curves walk lineage: model → run → code + data → sources
The client library is the most important component and the easiest to under-specify. Every property listed on it exists to guarantee one thing: nothing this platform does can end a training run.
🔄8. Workflows — what actually happens
A forty-hour training run, from start to finish
And the moment the tracker goes down in the middle of it.
  1. The run starts and registers: code commit, dataset version, hyperparameters, environment. One small write, and this is the record lineage will depend on.
  2. Training begins. Every step it logs loss and a few other metrics — about 100 points per second.
  3. Each call appends to an in-process buffer and returns immediately. A background thread ships batches every few seconds.
  4. Hour 12: the tracking backend goes down for twenty minutes. Sends start failing.
  5. The client catches every error, increments a counter, and keeps buffering. The training loop does not observe anything. Not a slow call, not an exception, nothing.
  6. The buffer fills after a few minutes and begins dropping the oldest points. About fifteen minutes of loss curve is lost.
  7. The backend recovers, the buffer drains, logging resumes. The chart has a visible gap.
  8. Hour 40: the run finishes. Final metrics, a checkpoint reference and a completed status are written — this write does retry, because it is the result rather than a sample.
Fifteen minutes of curve was traded for forty hours of GPU time. It is not a close call, and it only works because the losing side was chosen deliberately in the client library rather than discovered during an incident.
Comparing two hundred runs
The query that makes the metadata store worth having.
  1. A researcher asks: best F1 among runs on dataset v7 where learning rate is below 0.01.
  2. The filter runs against the metadata store — indexed columns for dataset version, a JSON index for the hyperparameter. Two hundred runs match.
  3. For each, the final value of the F1 metric is needed. Fetching full curves for 200 runs would be millions of points for 200 numbers.
  4. So final and best values are stored as summary fields on the run record at completion. The comparison is a single relational query. Under a second.
  5. The researcher selects five to plot. Only now are full curves fetched from the time-series store, and only for those five.
  6. Downsampled for display — 14 million points cannot render, and 2,000 look identical on a chart.
Two patterns worth taking away: precompute the summaries you filter and sort on, and fetch full resolution only for what is actually being displayed. Together they are the difference between a usable dashboard and a slow one.
A production model starts behaving oddly
Lineage answering the question it exists for.
  1. A deployed classifier is producing more false positives than expected. The question: what is different about it?
  2. The model's registry entry names the run that produced it. One lookup.
  3. The run record names the code commit, the full hyperparameter set, the environment, and the dataset version — v7.
  4. Dataset v7's record names how it was built: which pipeline, which run, and which raw sources with their date ranges.
  5. One of those sources overlaps a known ingestion incident on the 14th, when a schema change silently corrupted a field for several hours.
  6. Cross-checking: the pipeline health metrics show a schema-drift alert on that stage, on that day — which nobody acted on at the time.
  7. Answer found in minutes: the model was trained on partly corrupted data. Retrain from a clean dataset version.
Every link had to hold for this to work, and the fragile one was the dataset version. Had "the training data" been a mutable path that someone overwrote, the chain would have pointed at data that no longer existed and the investigation would have gone nowhere.
An upstream schema change breaks a pipeline quietly
Pipeline health, which catches what nothing else does.
  1. An upstream team renames a field. Their change is correct and nobody tells the ML team.
  2. The feature pipeline still runs. It still succeeds. It emits the expected number of rows.
  3. But that feature is now null for every row. Nothing errors anywhere. Every job is green.
  4. Models trained on this data are missing a signal they relied on. Accuracy drops, and the cause is invisible from any dashboard about job success.
  5. What catches it: per-stage data checks. Null rate for this column jumped from 0.1% to 100% — a distribution alert, not a failure alert.
  6. Also caught by a schema check comparing each run's observed schema to the previous run's.
  7. The alert fires the same day. Without it, this surfaces weeks later as unexplained model degradation.
The lesson generalises past ML: a pipeline that succeeds while producing wrong data is more dangerous than one that fails, because every signal you have says it is healthy. Monitoring the data rather than the jobs is the only thing that catches it.
🔍9. Deep dives, and what breaks

Why the client library is the most important component

Everything else here is a reasonably conventional storage and query problem. The client library is where the platform's defining requirement is either honoured or quietly violated, and it is where a careless implementation does real damage.

Each property has a specific failure it prevents:

  • Async prevents a slow backend from slowing the training loop.
  • Batched prevents 10,000 runs × 100 Hz from becoming a million requests per second.
  • Bounded buffer prevents a long backend outage from exhausting the training job's memory — the failure an unbounded buffer creates while trying to be helpful.
  • Never throws prevents a logging error from ending a run.

All four are needed. Three out of four leaves a real path from “the tracker had a bad day” to “we lost a week of training”.

It also needs to be genuinely cheap per call, because it is invoked inside the training loop. That means no allocation-heavy serialisation on the calling thread — append to a pre-allocated buffer, serialise in the background.

Making datasets immutable

The precondition for lineage, and the place most implementations fall down.

The common practice is a path in object storage that a pipeline overwrites on each run. A run records “trained on s3://data/features/”, and three months later that path contains something completely different. The lineage record is technically accurate and practically useless.

Immutable versioning means each build writes to a new versioned location and registers it with a manifest — the files, their hashes, the row count, the schema, and how it was produced. Runs reference the version, and the version never changes.

The cost is storage, since old versions accumulate. It is worth it: without it, every lineage question about anything older than the current build is unanswerable, which means the platform's headline feature does not work.

Monitoring the data, not just the jobs

Conventional pipeline monitoring asks whether stages succeeded, how long they took, and whether they retried. All useful, and all blind to the most common real failure: a pipeline that succeeds while producing wrong data.

The four checks worth having per stage:

  • Freshness — how old is the newest record? A stage that stopped running looks identical to one that ran and found nothing, unless you check this.
  • Volume — row count against recent history. A 90% drop that did not error is a filter bug.
  • Schema — columns and types against the previous run. Catches the rename above.
  • Distribution — null rates, ranges, category frequencies. Catches the corruption that keeps the schema intact.

These are the observability equivalent of what D11 does for services, applied to data instead of requests — and the reason they belong in this platform is that the person who needs the alert is the person looking at the model, not the person who owns the job.

What breaks

Tracking service is down
Clients buffer, then drop. Training continues and the curve has a gap. This is the correct trade and it should be a stated design property rather than an accident.
Metric write storm from one run
Per-run rate limits at ingest, plus aggregation in the client (log every N steps, not every step). One badly instrumented run must not degrade everyone else’s tracking.
Object storage unavailable
Checkpoint writes fail and the run retries with backoff. Metadata and metrics continue, so the run is still observable even though its artifacts are not being saved.
Dataset snapshot deleted by a lifecycle policy
Lineage records the reference, so this is detectable rather than silent — but reproducibility is lost. Pin datasets referenced by any promoted model, and make deletion of a pinned snapshot fail loudly.
Lineage graph has a cycle or missing edge
Validate on write: a run may only reference artifacts that already exist. A broken lineage graph is discovered exactly when you need it most, during an incident.
The dominant constraint

Three data kinds with nothing in common. Metadata is relational and small, metrics are a 1M-point-per-second time series, artifacts are gigabyte blobs. One store cannot serve all three, and the metrics half is a problem this guide has already solved in D11.

What I would build first

The run metadata store with the four reproducibility hashes, and the buffer-and-drop client. Those two decide whether the platform is trustworthy and whether it is safe.

What I deliberately did not build

Orchestration, and a feature store. Both are frequently bolted on here and both are separate systems that deserve their own design.

The biggest risk

Lineage that is recorded but never exercised. It looks complete until an incident, when you discover the dataset reference points at a mutable table that has since changed.

💬 If you get this far, here is what they will push on
Follow-ups an interviewer is likely to ask once the design is on the board. Answers supplied — read the question, answer it out loud, then open it.
“The tracking service goes down mid-training. What should happen?”Answer

The training run should carry on and the metrics should be dropped. That is the correct behaviour and it should be a stated design property rather than an accident.

A run can last forty hours on expensive hardware. Losing it because a metadata service returned 503 is unacceptable; losing a few points from a loss curve costs nothing.

So the client buffers in memory and drops rather than blocking or retrying forever. Same inversion as D11: the observability system must never be able to kill the thing it observes.

“Someone asks you to reproduce a result from six months ago. Can you?”Answer

Only if you recorded four things, and the one people forget is the data. Code version, environment, hyperparameters and dataset version.

“Trained on the users table” is not a reference, because that table has changed since. The dataset needs an immutable identity: a content hash, a table snapshot, or a time-travel timestamp.

Without it, lineage is decorative. It looks complete right up until somebody actually tries to rerun something.

“A model in production is misbehaving. What do you need to answer?”Answer

The useful query runs backwards: which data produced this model, and what else came from that data?

That is a reverse traversal of the lineage graph, so design for that direction rather than the forward one. And it is a graph rather than a tree, because models beget models through fine-tuning and distillation — one bad dataset can taint a whole subgraph of descendants that all need finding and retiring together.

“What metrics would you actually track for pipeline health?”Answer

Three layers, and naming all three is the signal. System: stage latency, throughput, failure and retry rates, cost per run. Data: freshness, row volume against the same window last week, null rates, schema drift. Model: prediction distribution, confidence histogram, and precision and recall once labels arrive.

Most people give only the first layer, which is the one that tells you least. Nearly every “the model got worse” incident is really an upstream data incident, and the middle layer catches it days before model metrics can.

Design Google Maps for an Uncovered Region (imagery ingestion, map tiles, routing, IP→geo lookup)

Difficulty: Hard (Staff Expectation)  .  Target: 45 min
💬 The question, as asked

“There is a region with no map coverage. Design the system that surveys it, builds the map, and serves tiles and routing to users there.”

⚡ What makes it hard

Building the map and serving it are different systems. Capture produces hundreds of terabytes a day that cannot travel over the air, while serving is latency-bound and cannot wait for it.

📋1. Understanding the question

The prompt: “There is a region with no map coverage. Design the system that surveys it, builds the map, and serves tiles and routing to users there.”

That sentence contains two systems that share a name and almost nothing else.

Building the map is a data pipeline. Vehicles drive around with cameras and GPS, producing hundreds of terabytes a day, which is turned into road geometry and imagery over weeks. It is throughput-bound, it can lag, and nobody is waiting on any individual piece of it.

Serving the map is a read-heavy, latency-bound system. Someone opens the app and expects tiles in under a hundred milliseconds. It cannot wait for anything.

🎯 The number that settles the ingestion design

A thousand capture vehicles producing about 15 MB/s each is roughly 432 terabytes a day.

That cannot travel over a mobile network. Not with better compression, not with a bigger budget. At any plausible cellular uplink, one vehicle's daily output would take longer than a day to upload.

So the data moves physically. Drives are swapped at a depot and shipped. Saying this plainly — rather than drawing an arrow labelled “upload” — is the moment the interviewer knows you did the arithmetic.

And the thing that makes serving tractable

The map is immutable once published. A tile for a given version and coordinate never changes; a new survey produces a new version.

That single property means tiles can be cached forever, at every layer, by every client and every edge, with no invalidation logic at all. A serving system for mutable geographic data would be enormously harder. Making the data immutable is a design decision that removes an entire category of problem.

What they are looking for

Do you do the ingest arithmetic? And conclude that it is physical shipping?

Do you notice the client has no connectivity either? This is a region without map coverage, which usually means it is also a region without good network coverage — so offline packs are a requirement rather than a feature.

Do you know why routing is not just Dijkstra? Running a shortest-path search over a continental road graph per request does not fit in the latency budget.

❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
Are we building the map, or serving it?
Wholly different systems. Capture and conflation is an offline data pipeline; serving tiles and routes is a read-heavy low-latency system. I would scope to both but design them separately.
What is the source of truth for geometry?
Vehicle capture, satellite imagery, or crowd-sourced edits? Each has a different trust model, and crowd-sourcing makes moderation a first-class component rather than an afterthought.
Does routing need live traffic?
Static routing is a precomputable shortest-path problem. Live traffic makes edge weights change every minute and invalidates precomputation.
Offline use on-device?
Users in an uncovered region very likely have poor connectivity, so tile and routing-graph packs must be downloadable — which changes the client design entirely.
What accuracy is required — street level or building level?
Drives capture density, storage, and whether a single pass by one vehicle is sufficient.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.
📝2. Functional requirements
  • Ingest imagery and GPS traces from capture vehicles, and turn them into road geometry and image tiles.
  • Serve map tiles addressed by zoom level and coordinates.
  • Route between two points, with turn-by-turn directions.
  • Resolve a coordinate to an administrative region, and an IP range to a region.
  • Offline packs — downloadable tiles and routing graph for a region.

Why the offline requirement is load-bearing

It follows from the premise. A region with no map coverage is very likely a region with patchy network coverage, and someone navigating there is precisely the person least able to rely on a connection.

That changes the client from a thin viewer into something that holds real data: a tile pack and a routing graph for the area, downloaded while connected. Which in turn changes the server's job — it must be able to produce a bounded, self-contained bundle for a region, not just answer individual requests.

Conflation, which is the hard part of building

Worth naming as a requirement because it is where the real difficulty sits and it has an unhelpful name. Multiple vehicles drive the same road on different days. Their GPS traces disagree by several metres. Satellite imagery suggests a slightly different alignment. A crowd-sourced edit says the road is now one-way.

Producing one road geometry from those disagreeing sources is conflation, and it is the step that actually determines whether the map is any good.

⏱3. Non-functional requirements
RequirementTargetWhy
Tile latencyp99 < 100 msPanning a map fetches dozens of tiles. Any slower and the map visibly tears as you drag it.
Routing latency< 500 msTolerable for a deliberate action, and it is still far too short for a naive graph search over a continent.
Map immutabilityVersioned, never editedThe property that makes caching free. A published tile is valid forever.
Ingest lagDays is fineExplicitly relaxed. It is what allows physical media transport and batch processing.
OfflineRegion packsBecause the users in an uncovered region have poor connectivity by definition.
Coverage accuracyStreet levelDrives capture density — how many passes per road, at what spacing — and therefore the schedule and the cost.

The asymmetry to state out loud

Ingest may lag by days; serving may not lag by a hundred milliseconds. Those two requirements are separated by about six orders of magnitude, which is the clearest possible signal that they are different systems with different hardware, different scaling behaviour, and different on-call concerns.

The only thing connecting them is a publication step: the pipeline produces a new immutable map version, and serving switches to it. Everything upstream of that boundary is batch; everything downstream is online.

🗂4. Data model and API

Three data shapes: tiles, the routing graph, and region boundaries.

-- ROUTING GRAPH: nodes are intersections, edges are road segments. TABLE edges { edge_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, from_node, to_node BIGINT, length_m INT, speed_kph SMALLINT, road_class TINYINT, -- motorway .. residential; drives hierarchy geometry LINESTRING, cell_id BIGINT -- S2/H3 cell: the partition key } -- Partitioned by cell so a route query touches few partitions. -- Long-distance routes cross partitions, which is what the -- hierarchy below exists to avoid. -- IP -> REGION: ranges, not points. The lookup is "which interval -- contains this integer", not an equality match. TABLE ip_ranges { start_ip NUMERIC(39), end_ip NUMERIC(39), -- v4 and v6 as integers region VARCHAR, confidence FLOAT, PRIMARY KEY (start_ip) } -- Ranges are disjoint and sorted, so the lookup is a binary search: -- the largest start_ip <= query. ~500K rows fits in memory; no -- database round trip is needed at all.

Tiles, and why the addressing scheme matters

The world is divided into a pyramid. Zoom 0 is one tile covering everything; each zoom level splits every tile into four. By zoom 20 a tile covers a few tens of metres.

A tile is addressed by (z, x, y) and nothing else. That is the whole lookup: no geometric query, no spatial index at request time — the client computes which tiles it needs from the viewport and fetches them by name.

It is the same move as D13: precompute the answer and make the request path a lookup. Rendering a map region on demand would be far too slow; rendering every tile in advance makes serving a static file fetch.

The count is alarming and misleading. Zoom 0 through 20 is around four trillion tiles worldwide, which at 10 KB each is unstorable. The rescue is that the tile pyramid is only fully populated where there is something to show — oceans and deserts have no detail at zoom 20, so those tiles are never generated. Under 1% of possible tiles exist, and under 1% of those are ever requested.

The routing graph

Intersections are nodes, road segments are edges, and each edge carries a traversal cost derived from length, speed limit, and road class. Turn restrictions live on the connections between edges, not on the edges themselves — which is why the graph is slightly more complex than the obvious model.

It is partitioned geographically, because routing queries are overwhelmingly local and a query rarely needs a graph partition far from either endpoint.

Region boundaries and IP lookup

Two lookups that look similar and are completely different.

Coordinate to region is point-in-polygon against administrative boundaries, which can be complex shapes with islands and holes. Done naively it is expensive; done properly, a spatial index narrows to a handful of candidate polygons first and only those are tested exactly.

IP to region is a longest-prefix match over a table of address ranges — the same operation a router performs, and fast in memory. It is also an approximation of much lower quality than people assume: it locates the network, not the person, and it is routinely wrong for mobile carriers and VPNs. Worth saying so rather than presenting it as a location service.

The API

GET /v1/tiles/{version}/{z}/{x}/{y}.{fmt} Response: 200 image/webp | application/vnd.mapbox-vector-tile Headers: Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable // version is in the PATH, so a new map release is a new URL. // Immutable tiles need no invalidation -- the same trick as // content-hashed asset URLs. This is why the CDN can hold everything. GET /v1/pano?lat=&lng=&heading= -> { pano_id, tiles[], links[] } POST /v1/route Body: { origin, destination, mode, depart_at? } Response: { distance_m, duration_s, legs[], polyline, alternatives[] } GET /v1/geocode/reverse?lat=&lng= -> { country, admin1, locality } GET /v1/geoip?ip= -> { country, region, confidence } POST /internal/ingest/manifest // a depot registers an offloaded drive
📊5. Capacity estimation

The numbers, and the conclusions they force.

⚖ Assumptions — and what breaks if each is wrong
1,000 capture vehicles, 8 hours/day, imagery at ~15 MB/s each
Halving the fleet halves ingest but doubles time to coverage. This is the schedule/cost trade the whole capture plan turns on.
Tiles are pre-rendered, not rendered per request
Vector tiles rendered on the client would cut storage enormously and move cost to the device; a reasonable alternative for modern clients.
Routing is static, without live traffic
Live traffic makes edge weights mutable and rules out full precomputation of shortest paths.
~432 TB

Ingest: the arithmetic that decides everything

A thousand vehicles, eight hours a day, at around 15 MB/s of imagery each. That is roughly 432 TB per day, or about 15 GB/s if it were streamed live.

Fifteen gigabytes per second over cellular is not a hard engineering problem; it is an impossible one. A single vehicle's 430 GB daily output over a good mobile uplink would take well over a day.

So the pipeline starts with physical media. Vehicles return to a depot, drives are swapped, and the full drives are shipped or driven to an ingestion facility. The wire carries only the small things — GPS traces, health telemetry, coverage progress — which are kilobytes and genuinely do travel over the air.

This is worth being comfortable stating. “The data moves on a truck” sounds like a joke and is the correct answer, and it is one of the clearest examples in this guide of an estimate producing an architecture rather than validating one.

Serving: small numbers, easy conclusions

Tiles are about 10 KB and immutable. A user panning a map fetches a few dozen. With caching at the client, the edge, and the CDN, the origin sees a tiny fraction of requests — and because tiles never change, cache hit rates are as high as caching ever gets.

The tile set for a populated region is tens of terabytes. Trivially servable from object storage behind a CDN, with no database in the path at all.

⚖6. The key trade-offs

The choices, and their costs.

DecisionChosen ✓Alternative ✗Reasoning
Imagery uploadPhysical drive shipmentNetwork upload432 TB/day is ~40 Gbps sustained from vehicles on mobile networks. The bandwidth does not exist; a van of drives is the higher-throughput link.
Tile identityVersion in the URL path, immutableMutable tiles + purgeImmutable tiles give a near-100% CDN hit rate and delete cache invalidation from the design. Purging trillions of URLs is not a thing you want to operate.
Deep-zoom tilesRender lazily on first requestPre-render everythingUnder 1% of tiles are ever requested. Pre-rendering the full pyramid is a vast bill for data nobody reads.
RoutingHierarchical / contracted graphPlain DijkstraA continental route over the full graph explores millions of irrelevant residential edges and cannot meet a 500 ms budget.
IP→regionSorted array + binary search, in processDatabase range queryDisjoint sorted intervals make this a few megabytes and a memory access. A database round trip per request is pure waste.

Raster tiles or vector tiles

Raster tiles are pre-rendered images. The server does all the work once; the client just displays pixels. Serving is a static file fetch and any client can render it.

The costs: every style variant — light, dark, satellite, transit — is a complete separate render of the whole world, multiplying storage. Rotating or smoothly zooming looks poor, because you are transforming a bitmap. And text labels are baked in, so a label cannot be re-drawn in another language without re-rendering the tile.

Vector tiles ship the geometry and let the client render. One tile set serves every style, labels can be swapped per language, and rotation and zoom are smooth because the client redraws rather than stretches. Storage drops dramatically.

The cost moves to the device: rendering takes CPU and battery, and old or low-end devices — which is what you should assume in an underserved region — do it poorly.

The honest answer is vector where the device can handle it and raster as a fallback, which is what production systems actually do.

Why routing needs precomputation

A plain shortest-path search from Lisbon to Warsaw explores a large fraction of the European road graph — millions of nodes. Even efficiently implemented, that does not fit in 500 ms, and certainly not at scale.

The standard fix exploits a property of real road networks: long journeys use motorways. So the graph is preprocessed into a hierarchy where important roads form a much smaller upper layer. A long route searches locally at both ends until it reaches the motorway layer, crosses in that small graph, then descends locally at the destination.

The search space collapses by orders of magnitude and the answer is essentially the same route a full search would find.

The cost is preprocessing: the hierarchy takes substantial compute to build and must be rebuilt when the graph changes. Fine here, because the map is immutable and versioned — the hierarchy is built once per map version alongside the tiles. This is why “does routing need live traffic?” is a clarifying question: mutable edge weights invalidate the preprocessing and force a different, much harder design.

🏗7. High-level design
Build and serve the map — and the cold CDN every new version creates
raw captureprocessed data / tilesmap buildorigin fetches
What is moving: 432 TB/day of imagery arrives on physical drives, because that volume cannot go over the air. Conflation turns noisy GPS traces into centrelines, and a build publishes an immutable, versioned tile set that the CDN can cache for a year with no invalidation logic at all.
What goes wrong: immutability has a sting. Because the version is in the URL path, publishing vN+1 changes every tile URL at once — so the CDN is instantly cold and the origin takes the full load. Roll out by region and pre-warm the low zoom levels, which are the overwhelming majority of requests. Ch 9

Two systems, joined only at publication.

BUILD throughput-bound, may lag days capture vehicles 1,000 × 8h × 15 MB/s = 432 TB/day | | this does not go over the air v PHYSICAL MEDIA → depot → shipped → ingestion facility | GPS traces and telemetry do travel over the network — they are KB v CONFLATION many disagreeing sources → one geometry | traces + satellite + prior map + crowd edits | this step decides whether the map is any good v RENDER tiles z0..z20, only where there is detail BUILD GRAPH + road hierarchy for fast routing | v PUBLISH map version v43 immutable from this moment | =======|================================================= v SERVE latency-bound, cannot lag client → CDN → object storage | cache forever — tiles never change | +-- GET /tiles/v43/{z}/{x}/{y} a file fetch. no database. +-- POST /route hierarchy search, <500ms +-- GET /region?lat=&lng= point-in-polygon +-- GET /offline-pack?bbox= tiles + graph, for no connectivity
The version number in the tile path is what makes infinite caching safe. A new survey publishes v44; nothing about v43 is ever invalidated, and clients migrate when they choose.
🔄8. Workflows — what actually happens
A capture vehicle's day, and where its data goes
Following 430 GB from a camera to a published tile.
  1. The vehicle drives assigned routes for eight hours, recording imagery to local drives and logging GPS continuously. About 430 GB by the end of the day.
  2. Over the mobile network it sends only small things: its GPS trace, coverage progress, and health telemetry. A few megabytes. This is what the planning system uses to decide tomorrow's routes.
  3. At the depot, drives are swapped for empty ones. The full drives are shipped to an ingestion facility.
  4. Days later they are ingested. Imagery is decoded, GPS traces are aligned to it, and road geometry is extracted.
  5. Conflation: this road was driven by three vehicles on three days, whose traces disagree by several metres. Satellite imagery suggests a fourth alignment. These are reconciled into one geometry with a confidence score.
  6. Tiles are rendered for the affected area at every zoom level, and the routing graph and its hierarchy are rebuilt.
  7. Map version v43 is published. Tiles land in object storage and the region is live.
The end-to-end latency from driving past a road to it appearing in the app is measured in weeks, and that is acceptable because it was declared acceptable in the requirements. Trying to make it real time would change every decision in the pipeline for no user benefit.
Someone pans the map
Dozens of requests in a second, and almost none reach us.
  1. The client computes which tiles the viewport needs — at this zoom and position, about 20 of them — and requests them by coordinate. No server-side spatial query happens at all.
  2. Most are already in the client's own cache from a moment ago. Perhaps 6 are actually requested.
  3. Those go to the nearest CDN edge. Five are cached there from other users in the same city. One is a miss.
  4. The miss fetches from object storage — a file read, no database — and is cached at the edge for the next person.
  5. The user keeps panning. Every subsequent tile is served from the client or the edge.
  6. Because the version is in the path and the content never changes, the cache lifetime is effectively infinite. There is no invalidation logic anywhere in this system.
Immutability is doing all the work. A design where tiles could be edited in place would need cache invalidation across every CDN edge and every client on earth — and would get it wrong sometimes, which on a map looks like a road that exists in one place and not another.
A 2,000 km route request
Why the hierarchy exists.
  1. Lisbon to Warsaw. A plain shortest-path search would expand outward from Lisbon until it reached Warsaw — exploring millions of nodes across most of Europe.
  2. Instead, the search starts at both ends and works upward through the road hierarchy: local streets, then arterials, then motorways.
  3. Within a few kilometres of each endpoint it reaches the motorway layer, which is a far smaller graph — thousands of nodes rather than millions.
  4. The long middle section is solved entirely in that small upper graph.
  5. The two ends are stitched on, and the result is expanded back down into real turn-by-turn instructions.
  6. Total: well under 500 ms, and the route is the one the full search would have found, because long journeys genuinely do use motorways.
The preprocessing is affordable precisely because the map is immutable — the hierarchy is built once per version. Live traffic would make edge weights change every minute and invalidate it continuously, which is a fundamentally harder problem and worth scoping explicitly.
A user downloads the region for offline use
The requirement that comes free with the premise.
  1. They are about to travel through the newly-mapped region, where they expect little or no signal.
  2. They select an area. The client requests an offline pack for that bounding box at map version v43.
  3. The server assembles the tiles for that area — but not at every zoom. Zoom 0–16 is included; zoom 17–20 would multiply the size for detail rarely needed offline.
  4. It also includes the routing graph for the area, so directions can be computed on the device with no network at all.
  5. The pack is a few hundred megabytes, downloaded once over a good connection.
  6. Offline, the client renders from local tiles and routes from the local graph. Everything works except live search and anything outside the box.
  7. When v44 publishes, the client is told a newer version exists and can download a delta rather than the whole pack.
Versioned immutable data makes the delta possible: the client knows exactly which version it has, and the server can compute precisely what changed between two published versions. With mutable data, "what do I need to update?" has no clean answer.
🔍9. Deep dives, and what breaks

Conflation, and why it is the hard part

Everything else in the build pipeline is mechanical. This step is judgement, at scale.

The inputs disagree by construction. GPS is accurate to a few metres at best and much worse near tall buildings. Three passes of the same road produce three different lines. Satellite imagery offers a fourth opinion with different error characteristics. A crowd-sourced edit claims a change nobody has driven.

The output must be one geometry, and it must be topologically sound: roads meeting at an intersection have to actually connect in the graph, or routing produces impossible detours around a junction that exists in reality and not in the data.

That topological requirement is what makes this hard rather than merely noisy. Averaging three traces gives a plausible line; ensuring the averaged lines still meet correctly at every junction is a different and much harder problem. Confidence scores per feature, and a review queue for low-confidence ones, are what makes it manageable — along with accepting that some areas are simply published at lower accuracy, flagged as such.

Planning the capture

An easy component to overlook and a genuinely interesting one. A thousand vehicles is a scheduling problem: which roads, in what order, and how do you know when a region is covered?

The uploaded GPS traces are the feedback signal. Roads driven are marked covered; a coverage map is maintained and the gaps drive tomorrow's routes. Roads may need multiple passes — different lighting, different lanes, a first pass with poor GPS lock.

Prioritisation matters for the same reason it did in D10: with a fixed capture budget, the order determines what the map actually contains. Population density and road class dominate, so major roads in populated areas come first and the long tail of rural lanes comes later.

What IP-to-region actually gives you

Worth being precise about, because it is commonly overstated.

The lookup itself is straightforward: a table of address ranges mapped to locations, resolved by longest-prefix match. Fast, small, easy.

The data is the problem. It locates the network, not the person. A mobile carrier may route a whole country's traffic through a couple of gateways, so every user appears to be in one city. A VPN relocates the user entirely. Corporate networks appear at headquarters.

So it is fine for coarse defaults — which country's map style, which language, which units — and unsuitable for anything requiring real accuracy. An interviewer asking about this is often checking whether you will overstate what it can do.

Publishing a new version safely

A new map version is an enormous, atomic-feeling change, and it deserves the same caution as a model rollout in D15.

Because versions are immutable and addressed separately, the switch is a configuration change: clients are told which version to request. So it can be staged — a small percentage of users first, then by region, then everyone — and rolled back instantly, since the previous version is still fully present.

What to watch during the stage is not server metrics. The interesting regressions are things like a rise in re-routes, an increase in users abandoning navigation, or a drop in tile requests for an area that suggests something renders wrong. Those are product signals, and they are the only way to detect that a map version is worse rather than merely different.

What breaks

A capture drive is lost or corrupt
Vehicles checksum on write and retain data until the depot acknowledges ingestion. The affected road segments are simply re-queued for a future pass — capture is idempotent by design because roads do not move.
A bad map build is published
Versions are immutable and published atomically, so rollback is repointing clients at the previous version. Gate publication on automated checks: total road length within a few per cent of the prior build, no region losing connectivity, zero unblurred faces in a sample.
Routing service unavailable
Serve tiles regardless — a map you can look at is still useful. Clients that downloaded an offline routing pack keep routing locally, which is why the offline pack is a resilience feature and not only a connectivity one.
Conflation merges two roads wrongly
Detect with topology invariants: a build that creates a dead end where a through road existed, or doubles the road length in a cell, is rejected. Geometry errors are far easier to catch as invariant violations than by inspection.
CDN origin overload after a new version publishes
A new version invalidates every cached tile at once, which is a cold-cache stampede. Stagger the rollout by region and pre-warm the low zooms, which are the overwhelming majority of requests. Ch 9
The dominant constraint

Building the map and serving it are different systems. Ingestion is throughput-bound and may lag days; serving is latency-bound and may not. They share only an immutable published artefact, and coupling them would turn a capture backlog into a user-facing outage.

What I would build first

Immutable versioned tiles behind a CDN. That single decision gives a near-100% hit rate and removes cache invalidation from the design entirely.

What I deliberately did not build

Live traffic, which makes edge weights mutable and fights the precomputation routing depends on, and crowd-sourced edits, which make moderation a whole subsystem.

The biggest risk

Conflation quality. Nothing crashes when traces merge badly; the map is simply wrong, and wrong maps are discovered by users rather than by monitoring. Topology invariants on each build are the only cheap defence.

💬 If you get this far, here is what they will push on
Follow-ups an interviewer is likely to ask once the design is on the board. Answers supplied — read the question, answer it out loud, then open it.
“You publish a new map version. What happens to the CDN?”Answer

It goes cold instantly. Because the version is in the URL path, every tile has a new address, so nothing in the cache matches and the origin takes the full load.

That is the sting of immutability: it removed cache invalidation entirely, and in exchange every publish is a cold-start stampede.

So roll out by region rather than globally, and pre-warm the low zoom levels first — they are a tiny fraction of the tiles and the overwhelming majority of requests.

“Why ship physical drives instead of uploading?”Answer

Because the bandwidth does not exist. A thousand vehicles producing imagery all day is around 432 terabytes daily, which is roughly 40 Gbps sustained from vehicles on mobile networks.

A van of drives has enormously higher throughput than any network those vehicles can reach. Latency is terrible — days — and that is fine, because map building is allowed to lag.

Recognising when the network is not the answer is the point of the question.

“Ten cars drive the same road. How do you turn that into one road?”Answer

This is conflation, and it is where map quality actually comes from. Ten noisy GPS traces have to become one centreline, and next month's pass must merge into the existing geometry rather than creating a parallel road beside it.

It is a clustering and map-matching problem, and it is the part candidates skip. Even mentioning it separates someone who has thought about building a map from someone who has only thought about serving one.

“How do you check a map build is not broken before publishing?”Answer

Topology invariants, because geometry errors are far easier to catch as rule violations than by looking. Total road length within a few percent of the previous build. No region losing connectivity that previously had it. No through-road becoming a dead end.

Plus a privacy gate: zero unblurred faces or plates in a sample. That one blocks the build rather than warning, because a missed blur is a legal incident rather than a bug.

Design a Fleet Upgrade System (“upgrade 5,000 servers” — and the same question on the Moon)

Difficulty: Hard (Staff Expectation)  .  Target: 40 min
💬 The question, as asked

“How would you upgrade 5,000 servers?” — and its harder variant, “how would you upgrade hundreds of thousands of machines on the Moon?”

⚡ What makes it hard

The second version is a latency question in costume. At a 1.3-second one-way light delay, every synchronous control protocol you know stops working, and the fix is architectural rather than a longer timeout.

📋1. Understanding the question

The prompt: “How would you upgrade 5,000 servers?” — and its harder variant, “how would you upgrade hundreds of thousands of machines on the Moon?”

The first version sounds like an operations task and is really a question about blast radius. The second is a latency question wearing a costume, and it is worth recognising that quickly.

The first version

Upgrading one server is trivial. Upgrading 5,000 is not 5,000 times harder — it is a different problem, because the failure you are designing against is not “a machine fails to upgrade” but “the new version is broken and we just put it everywhere.”

🎯 What you are really designing

Not a deployment mechanism — a controlled experiment with an abort condition. Change a small number of machines, watch what happens, and only proceed if nothing got worse.

Which means the interesting components are the health check and the halt logic, not the part that copies a binary.

The Moon version

Light takes about 1.3 seconds to reach the Moon, so the minimum round trip is 2.6 seconds. That is physics; no network engineering reduces it.

Now consider what an ordinary orchestrator does: tell a machine to upgrade, wait for acknowledgement, check health, tell it to proceed. Four round trips is over ten seconds of pure waiting per machine, per step. Across hundreds of thousands of machines, sequenced, the rollout takes years.

The fix is not a longer timeout. It is architectural: move the decision to the machine. Instead of the orchestrator driving each step, it publishes a desired state — “the target version is 4.2, wave 3 should be at it by now” — and an autonomous agent on each machine reads it, decides what to do, does it, verifies locally, and reports asynchronously.

The control loop closes on the machine. The orchestrator observes rather than commands, and the light delay becomes irrelevant because nothing is waiting on a round trip.

That reframing — from imperative orchestration to declarative desired state — is the answer to the Moon question, and it happens to be the better design for the terrestrial version too.

What they are looking for

Do you identify the irreversible steps first? A schema migration or a disk format change cannot be rolled back, and everything else in the plan assumes a rollback exists.

Do you make the orchestrator crash-safe? It will restart mid-rollout, and machines must not be stranded.

Do you ask whether the machines are stateful? It changes what bounds the rate.

❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
Can the service tolerate any capacity loss during the upgrade?
If yes, rolling batches work. If not, you need spare capacity or blue-green, which roughly doubles hardware cost for the duration.
Is the upgrade reversible?
A binary rollback is easy; a schema migration or a disk-format change often is not. Irreversible steps must be identified before the first machine is touched, because they remove the safety net everything else assumes.
Are the machines stateful?
Stateless replacement is trivial. Stateful nodes need data to be drained or re-replicated first, and the upgrade rate is then bounded by re-replication bandwidth, not by machine count.
What is the round-trip latency to the fleet?
This is the Moon variant, and it is a real question. At a 1.3-second one-way delay, no synchronous orchestration protocol works and the agent must be autonomous.
What is the maintenance window, and is there one at all?
A global service has no quiet hour, which forces the design toward continuous safe rollout rather than a scheduled event.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.
📝2. Functional requirements
  • Roll a new version across N machines with a controlled, observable blast radius.
  • Halt automatically on a health regression, and roll back without a human.
  • Track per-machine state: pending, draining, upgrading, verifying, done, failed.
  • Resume correctly after the orchestrator restarts mid-rollout.

Identify the irreversible steps before touching anything

The most important requirement, and the one most often discovered too late.

A binary swap is reversible: put the old one back. A configuration change is reversible. But a database schema migration, an on-disk format change, or a protocol version bump that the old code cannot read is not. Once a machine has upgraded, it cannot go back, and neither can anything that now depends on it.

This matters because the entire rollout strategy rests on “if it goes wrong, roll back”. Where that is false, you need a different strategy — typically splitting the change into reversible stages: first deploy code that can read both formats, then migrate the data, then remove the old path. Each stage is individually reversible even though the sequence is not.

Saying “before I design the rollout, which steps cannot be undone?” is the clearest staff signal in this question.

Crash-safe, which is a real requirement not a nicety

A rollout takes hours. The orchestrator will be restarted during one — a deploy, a node failure, a routine rotation.

If its state lives in memory, a restart means it no longer knows which machines are mid-upgrade. Machines sit drained and out of service with nothing coming to finish them, and the only recovery is manual. The state must therefore be durable and the orchestrator must be able to reconstruct exactly where it was — which makes this a database-backed state machine rather than a script.

⏱3. Non-functional requirements
RequirementTargetWhat it forces
Capacity loss≤ 5% at onceThe core safety constraint. It sets the wave size and therefore the total duration — the two are inversely linked and you cannot improve both.
Duration5,000 in a working dayComfortable at 5% waves. It stops being comfortable at 1%, which is exactly the tension to surface.
Halt on regressionAutomaticNo human in the loop. A rollout at 3am must stop itself, because the alternative is discovering it at 9am.
Orchestrator crashMust not strand machinesDurable state, idempotent steps, and reconstruct-on-restart.
Control latencyUp to 2.6 s round tripThe Moon variant. It rules out synchronous orchestration entirely and forces autonomous agents.
RollbackAutomatic where possibleAnd explicitly identified where it is not, which is the more important half.

The arithmetic linking wave size and duration

At 5% concurrency, 5,000 machines is 250 per wave and 20 waves. At about four minutes per machine, the theoretical minimum is around 80 minutes.

In practice it is several hours, because each wave needs a bake period — time after upgrading to observe whether anything degrades. Problems do not appear the instant a process restarts; a memory leak or a slow resource exhaustion takes tens of minutes to show. Waves that proceed immediately would have all 5,000 machines upgraded before the first bad symptom appears, which defeats the entire purpose.

Now drop to 1% concurrency: 50 machines per wave, 100 waves, and the rollout no longer fits in a day. At that point the answer is not a faster rollout but a different strategy — blue-green, where a parallel fleet is built and traffic switched, at roughly double the hardware cost for the duration. Naming that threshold is better than assuming either approach.

🗂4. Data model and API

The whole system is a durable state machine, and the state table is the design.

TABLE rollouts { rollout_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, artifact TEXT, strategy JSONB, state ENUM(planning, running, paused, halted, rolled_back, done), started_at TIMESTAMP } -- One row per machine. THIS is the crash-safety mechanism: the -- orchestrator holds no rollout state in memory, so it can be -- killed at any moment and resume by reading this table. TABLE machine_state { machine_id VARCHAR PRIMARY KEY, rollout_id UUID, desired_ver VARCHAR, actual_ver VARCHAR, state ENUM(pending, draining, upgrading, verifying, done, failed), wave INT, fencing_token BIGINT, -- monotonic; agent rejects stale orders updated_at TIMESTAMP } -- INDEX: (rollout_id, state) -- "how many are in flight?" is the -- query the concurrency budget is enforced with, every tick.

Every machine has a row with its current state and target version. The orchestrator's job is to move rows through states, and because the state is durable, a restart loses nothing: it reads the table and continues.

The states are worth walking through, because each exists for a reason:

  • pending — not yet in a wave.
  • draining — removed from the load balancer, finishing in-flight work. The step people forget, and the one that turns a rollout into an error spike when omitted.
  • upgrading — the change is being applied.
  • verifying — the machine is up and checking itself before taking traffic.
  • done — serving on the new version.
  • failed — needs attention, and critically, is not retried indefinitely.

Every step must be idempotent

The orchestrator can crash between deciding to do something and recording that it did. On restart it will see a machine in upgrading and not know whether the upgrade happened.

The only safe resolution is for every step to be safe to repeat. “Install version 4.2” on a machine already running 4.2 must be a no-op, not an error and not a reinstall. “Drain” on an already-drained machine likewise.

With idempotent steps the recovery is trivial: re-issue whatever the state says is in progress. Without them it requires reconciliation logic that is almost always subtly wrong.

Desired state, for the high-latency case

For the Moon variant, the orchestrator does not issue commands at all. It publishes a small document: the target version, which wave each machine belongs to, and which waves are cleared to proceed.

Agents poll it on their own schedule, compare it to their local state, and act. Their reports flow back asynchronously and update the table. The 2.6-second round trip affects how stale the orchestrator's view is, not how fast anything proceeds — which is the whole point.

The API

POST /v1/rollouts Body: { target_selector, artifact, strategy:{ batch_pct, bake_s, halt_on:{ error_rate_delta, latency_p99_delta } } } Response: 201 { rollout_id, state:"planning" } POST /v1/rollouts/{id}:pause | :resume | :abort // abort rolls back completed batches; pause freezes in place GET /v1/rollouts/{id} -> { state, waves_done, in_flight, failed[], health_delta } // AGENT-FACING -- pull, not push. This is what makes the design work // across a high-latency link and survive an orchestrator restart. GET /v1/agent/desired?machine_id= -> { version, action, token } POST /v1/agent/report Body: { machine_id, state, version, health, token }
