📊5. Capacity estimation

The numbers, and the trade they expose.

⚖ Assumptions — and what breaks if each is wrong
5,000 machines, ~4 minutes per machine end to end
If a machine took an hour — a large database re-replicating — batch size stops being the limit and data movement does.
Stateless services; capacity is fungible
Stateful nodes make the rate bound re-replication bandwidth, and the whole plan changes.
The fleet can lose 5% of capacity safely
If it can only lose 1%, the rollout takes five times as long, which may exceed the window and force blue-green instead.
250
machines per wave at 5%
20
waves
~80 min
theoretical minimum
~4 h
realistic with bake time
1.3 s
one-way light delay, Moon
~2.6 s
minimum RPC round trip there

Five thousand machines at 5% concurrency is 250 per wave, 20 waves. Four minutes per machine end-to-end — drain, upgrade, restart, verify, return to service — gives a theoretical 80 minutes.

Add a bake period of 10–15 minutes per wave and it becomes four hours or so. That bake time is the majority of the rollout and it is not waste; it is the only thing that makes the safety mechanism work. A rollout with no bake period has a blast radius of 100% regardless of its wave size, because every machine is upgraded before the first symptom appears.

The stateful case changes the bound entirely

The above assumes stateless machines where capacity is fungible. If the machines hold data — database nodes, storage nodes — then taking one out means its replicas carry the load and, if it is out long enough, its data must be re-replicated elsewhere.

Re-replicating a node holding several terabytes takes hours and consumes network bandwidth shared with production traffic. The rollout rate is now bounded by re-replication bandwidth, not by machine count, and a fleet of 500 storage nodes may take longer to upgrade than 5,000 stateless ones.

This is why “are the machines stateful?” is a clarifying question rather than a detail: it changes which quantity you are estimating.

And the Moon

Hundreds of thousands of machines at 2.6 seconds round trip. Sequenced synchronously, at four round trips per machine, the arithmetic gives years.

With autonomous agents, the constraint disappears. Agents act in parallel without waiting for anyone, and the round trip only delays reporting. The rollout duration becomes a function of wave size and bake time, exactly as on Earth — measured in days or weeks because the fleet is larger, not because the link is slow.

⚖6. The key trade-offs

The choices, and their costs.

DecisionChosen ✓Alternative ✗Reasoning
Control directionAgents pull desired stateOrchestrator pushes commandsPull makes the orchestrator stateless and crash-safe, handles offline machines for free, and is the only thing that works at multi-second RTT.
Wave sizingExponential: 1, 10, 100, 250Equal batchesEqual batches risk as much on the first wave as the last, and discard the cheapest information available.
VerificationLocal, on the agentCentral health checkA central check needs a round trip per machine and cannot act during a network partition. Local verification lets a machine roll itself back unattended.
Rollout stateIn a database, one row per machineIn orchestrator memoryIn-memory state means an orchestrator crash strands machines mid-upgrade with no record of intent.
Regression baselineConcurrent not-yet-upgraded machinesYesterday’s metricsComparing against history confuses diurnal patterns and unrelated incidents with a real regression, in both directions.

Rolling or blue-green

Rolling upgrades machines in waves within the existing fleet. It needs no extra hardware and it is gradual, so a problem is caught with a small fraction affected. The costs: the fleet runs mixed versions for hours, which means both versions must interoperate; rollback is another slow rolling operation; and you are always running at reduced capacity.

Blue-green builds a complete parallel fleet on the new version and switches traffic at once. Rollback is instant — switch back — there is no mixed-version period, and the new fleet can be fully validated before it takes any traffic.

The cost is roughly double the hardware for the duration, and the switch is all-or-nothing: if the problem only appears under real production traffic, you have discovered it with 100% exposure rather than 5%.

The choice usually comes down to the capacity budget. If you can only lose 1%, rolling takes too long and blue-green is the answer despite the cost. A canary stage in front of a blue-green switch recovers most of the gradual-exposure benefit.

Version skew, which rolling forces you to handle

For hours, some machines run 4.1 and some run 4.2, and they talk to each other. This is not an edge case; it is the guaranteed state of the fleet during every rolling deploy.

Which means every change must be compatible with the version before it. A new field must be optional. A removed field must be deprecated in one release and removed in the next. A protocol change must be negotiated, not assumed.

The discipline that makes this work is expand then contract: first release code that handles both old and new, deploy it everywhere, then release code that only produces the new form. Two deploys instead of one, and it is what makes rollback possible at every intermediate point.

It is also why irreversible changes are so dangerous: they usually arise from skipping this and doing both halves at once.

🏗7. High-level design
Staged rollout — and the halt that stops 10 machines becoming 5,000
desired versionagent reports OKpullingfailure report
What is moving: the orchestrator writes a desired version into a table and agents pull it — nothing is ever pushed. Waves grow exponentially (1, then 10, then 100) with bake time between them, because the first machine buys the cheapest information you will ever get.
What goes wrong — and is caught: wave 2 shows an error-rate regression against the concurrently running old version. The rollout halts automatically and rolls back the completed waves; wave 3 never starts. Ten machines were affected instead of five thousand — which is the entire purpose of the design. Note the comparison must be against a live baseline, not yesterday, or a diurnal dip reads as a regression.

A state machine, a health signal, and an abort condition.

ORCHESTRATOR holds durable per-machine state; survives its own restart for each wave (5% of the fleet): | +-- 1. DRAIN remove from LB, let in-flight work finish | skip this and the rollout is an error spike +-- 2. UPGRADE apply the change idempotent: already-4.2 is a no-op +-- 3. VERIFY machine checks itself before taking traffic +-- 4. RETURN back into the LB | +-- 5. BAKE 10-15 min, watching fleet health | not machine health — the machine is fine, the version may not be | +--> regression? HALT. roll back this wave. page. +--> healthy? next wave HIGH LATENCY (the Moon) — invert the control flow orchestrator publishes DESIRED STATE: target_version: 4.2 waves cleared: 1, 2, 3 agent on each machine: poll it → am I in a cleared wave and not yet at 4.2? → drain, upgrade, verify locally, deciding for itself → report asynchronously the 2.6s round trip now delays reporting, not progress.
The terrestrial and lunar designs differ only in who holds the control loop. Pushing it to the agent costs you a slightly stale central view and buys immunity to link latency — which is why it is the better design in both cases.
🔄8. Workflows — what actually happens
One machine through one wave
The unit the whole rollout is made of.
  1. Machine 3,041 is selected for wave 13. State goes pending → draining.
  2. It is removed from the load balancer. Existing connections are allowed to finish — typically 30 seconds. Skipping this step is what turns a deploy into an error spike, because in-flight requests are killed mid-response.
  3. State → upgrading. The new binary is installed and the process restarted. The step is idempotent: if it is already at 4.2, this does nothing.
  4. State → verifying. The machine checks itself — process up, port listening, dependencies reachable, a synthetic request succeeding — before accepting real traffic.
  5. Verification passes. State → done, and it re-enters the load balancer.
  6. Total: about four minutes, of which the actual upgrade was thirty seconds.
Drain and verify bracket the change and are where most of the time goes. They are also the two steps most often omitted, which is why so many deploys produce a brief error spike that everyone has learned to ignore.
Wave 3 introduces a memory leak
The failure the whole design exists to catch.
  1. Waves 1 and 2 complete cleanly. 500 machines are on 4.2 and everything looks fine, because a leak takes time to matter.
  2. Wave 3 completes. 750 machines on the new version. Every individual machine reports healthy — the process is up and serving.
  3. During the bake period the fleet-level signal moves: p99 latency on upgraded machines is climbing, and memory use is trending upward on all of them.
  4. The comparison that matters is upgraded versus not-yet-upgraded, on the same traffic, at the same time. The not-yet-upgraded machines are flat. This is a regression, not a traffic change.
  5. The halt condition trips. Wave 4 does not start. 4,250 machines are still on 4.1.
  6. Wave 3 is rolled back automatically. A human is paged with a clear statement of what regressed.
  7. Blast radius: 15% of the fleet, briefly, at 3am, with nobody having to notice.
Two things made this work. The bake period, because the symptom needed time to appear — with no bake, all 5,000 would have been upgraded before the first sign. And comparing upgraded against not-yet-upgraded, which is the only way to distinguish "the new version is worse" from "traffic changed".
The orchestrator crashes mid-wave
Why the state is in a database and every step is idempotent.
  1. Halfway through wave 8, the orchestrator process dies. 120 machines are done, 4 are mid-upgrade, 126 are pending.
  2. If state lived in memory, those 4 machines are now drained, out of service, and abandoned. Nothing is coming to finish them. Recovery is manual and nobody knows to start it.
  3. Because state is durable, the restarted orchestrator reads the table and sees exactly that: 4 machines in upgrading.
  4. It cannot tell whether each upgrade completed before the crash. It does not need to — it simply re-issues the step.
  5. For machines where it had completed, the install is a no-op and verification passes. For the others, the upgrade happens. Both paths converge.
  6. The wave finishes. Nothing was stranded and nothing was upgraded twice in any harmful sense.
Durable state plus idempotent steps means recovery is "re-issue whatever is in progress" rather than a reconciliation algorithm. The alternative — working out what actually happened — is where this kind of system usually has its worst bugs.
The same rollout, 384,000 km away
Where synchronous orchestration stops working entirely.
  1. 200,000 machines, 2.6 seconds minimum round trip. A synchronous orchestrator issuing four round trips per machine would take over ten seconds of waiting per machine, sequenced.
  2. So nothing is issued. The orchestrator publishes a desired-state document: target 4.2; waves 1 through 3 are cleared.
  3. Each machine's agent polls it every few minutes. An agent in wave 2 sees it is cleared and not yet at 4.2.
  4. It drains, upgrades, and verifies entirely locally. No instruction is awaited, and the light delay is irrelevant because nothing is waiting.
  5. If verification fails, the agent rolls itself back and reports. It does not wait 2.6 seconds to be told to — a machine that cannot fix itself autonomously is a machine that stays broken for a round trip.
  6. Reports flow back asynchronously. The orchestrator's view is a few seconds stale, which does not matter, and it clears the next wave when enough of the current one reports healthy.
The design is identical to the terrestrial one except for who holds the control loop. This is worth internalising: the fix for high latency is almost never a longer timeout — it is moving the decision to where the information already is.
🔍9. Deep dives, and what breaks

What the health check should actually measure

The most common mistake is checking whether the machine is up. It is up. The process started, the port is listening, and the version is broken anyway.

Three levels, and each catches something the previous one misses:

  • Liveness — is the process running? Catches crashes and nothing else.
  • Readiness — can it serve a real request end to end, including its dependencies? Catches a service that starts but cannot do its job.
  • Fleet health — are error rate and latency, on upgraded machines compared to not-yet-upgraded ones, unchanged? This is the one that catches the leak, the subtle regression, the change that works perfectly and is 20% slower.

Only the third can distinguish “the new version is worse” from “something else changed”, because it is a controlled comparison: same time, same traffic, two versions. That makes the rollout a genuine A/B test rather than a hopeful sequence of restarts.

How to pick the order

Not randomly, and not alphabetically.

Spread across failure domains. Two hundred and fifty machines in one rack or one availability zone is not 5% of your capacity — it may be 100% of one zone's. The wave must be drawn across racks, zones and regions so that concurrent upgrade never aligns with a correlated failure boundary.

Start with the least important. The first wave should be machines whose failure matters least — a canary region, internal traffic, a low-value tier.

Vary the wave composition. A rollout that upgrades all the machines of one type first will not expose problems that only appear when two types interact. Mixing within waves finds interaction bugs earlier.

Bake time, and the trap of shortening it

It is pure waiting, it dominates the rollout duration, and it is under constant pressure to be reduced.

The correct length is set by how long the problems you are looking for take to appear. A crash appears in seconds. A memory leak takes tens of minutes. A resource exhaustion — file descriptors, connections — can take hours. A daily batch job interacting badly with the new version may take a day.

So there is no single right number, and a useful pattern is graduated bake: long early waves and shorter later ones. The first wave bakes for an hour because it is where problems are most likely and cheapest to catch; by wave 15, most classes of problem would already have surfaced, so ten minutes is defensible.

The thing not to do is shorten the early waves, which is exactly where the pressure is applied.

What breaks

Orchestrator crashes mid-rollout
It holds no state, so a replacement reads machine_state and continues. Agents in flight finish and report; the fencing token stops a resumed agent acting on a superseded order.
A machine fails to come back
It is marked failed, counts against the concurrency budget, and the rollout halts once failures exceed a threshold rather than grinding through the whole fleet. Halting on an absolute count is a common bug: it should be a rate.
The new version is subtly worse
Automatic halt on a health delta against the concurrent baseline, then automatic rollback of completed waves. This is why bake time exists; without it the fleet is upgraded before the regression is visible.
Network partition to a subset of the fleet
Pull-based agents simply do not receive new desired state and keep running the current version, which is the safe outcome. Machines mid-upgrade verify locally and self-roll-back on failure.
An irreversible step has already run
Rollback cannot help, so the design must prevent it: irreversible steps are separated into their own rollout, gated on the reversible one having fully baked, and use expand-and-contract so the old and new forms coexist.
The dominant constraint

The blast radius has to be bounded before speed matters. Everything here — exponential waves, bake time, a concurrency budget, automatic halt — exists to make sure a bad version reaches ten machines rather than five thousand.

What I would build first

The desired-state table with pull-based agents. It makes the orchestrator stateless, survives its own crash, handles offline machines for free, and is the only shape that works at multi-second latency.

What I deliberately did not build

A push-based orchestrator and central health verification. Both are the obvious designs and both fail exactly when the network is the thing that is broken.

The biggest risk

Irreversible steps. Rollback is the safety net the whole design assumes, and a schema change or disk reformat quietly removes it — which is why identifying those first is a clarifying question, not an implementation detail.

💬 If you get this far, here is what they will push on
Follow-ups an interviewer is likely to ask once the design is on the board. Answers supplied — read the question, answer it out loud, then open it.
“Why not just upgrade 250 machines at a time until you are done?”Answer

Because equal batches risk as much on the first wave as the last, and throw away the cheapest information you will ever get.

Start with one machine. That catches “the binary does not start”. Then ten, which catches “it starts and is broken”. Then a hundred, which catches problems that only show under real traffic mix.

Each stage buys confidence proportional to what it risks, and the small early waves cost minutes against a rollout measured in hours.

“How do you know the new version is actually worse?”Answer

Compare upgraded machines against machines that have not been upgraded yet, serving the same traffic at the same moment.

Comparing against yesterday is the common mistake: a diurnal dip or an unrelated incident reads as a regression, and a real regression during a quiet period reads as fine. A concurrent baseline removes both.

You also need bake time between waves, because memory leaks, pool exhaustion and cache warm-up effects take minutes to appear. A rollout with no bake is a fast way to break the whole fleet with confidence.

“The orchestrator crashes halfway through. What state are you in?”Answer

Recoverable, because it holds no state. Every machine's desired and actual version lives in a table, so a replacement orchestrator reads it and carries on.

Agents in flight finish what they were doing and report. The fencing token stops a resumed agent acting on an order that has since been superseded.

If rollout state lived in orchestrator memory, its crash would strand machines mid-upgrade with no record of intent — which is the actual argument for pull-based agents.

“What about a change you cannot roll back, like a schema migration?”Answer

Rollback is the safety net everything else assumes, so an irreversible step quietly removes it. Those steps have to be identified before the first machine is touched, which is why it is a clarifying question rather than an implementation detail.

Then separate them: ship the reversible parts first, let them bake, and do the irreversible step as its own rollout. Use expand-and-contract so old and new forms coexist — add the column, dual-write, migrate readers, and only drop the old column much later.

Design a Reservation & Booking System (airline seats, parking bays, tickets — inventory under contention)

Difficulty: Hard (Staff Expectation)  .  Target: 40 min
💬 The question, as asked

“Design a reservation and payment system — a parking garage, an airline, a ticket sale. Users hold an item, pay, and confirm.”

⚡ What makes it hard

One invariant that cannot bend: a seat is sold at most once. Plus an external payment call that can time out ambiguously, leaving you unable to tell whether the customer was charged.

📋1. Understanding the question

Here is the prompt you get: “Design a system where people reserve something and pay for it — a parking bay, an airline seat, a concert ticket.”

It sounds small. It is not, and the reason is worth saying up front.

Almost every design in this book can be wrong for a second and recover. A stale feed, a late metric, a cache that lags — nobody is harmed. This one is different. If two people are sold seat 14A, somebody gets turned away at the gate. You cannot patch that later, and no amount of eventual consistency makes it acceptable.

So the whole design is organised around one sentence:

🎯 The one rule

A seat is sold at most once. Everything else — search, caching, the waiting room, the payment flow — can bend. This cannot.

What the interviewer is actually looking for

Three things, and only the first is technical.

Do you find the one invariant? Plenty of candidates spend ten minutes on search, caching and sharding before anyone mentions double-selling. The seat is the whole problem.

Do you keep it simple? This is the trap. The instinct is to reach for a distributed lock, or two-phase commit, or a consensus service. You do not need any of them, and reaching for them is the most common way to fail this question. One database row does the job.

Do you handle the payment timeout? Payments go through someone else — Stripe, a bank — and sometimes the call just times out. You do not know whether the card was charged. Most candidates never mention it. It is the most interesting part of the problem.

❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
Is the inventory fixed and identified, or interchangeable?
A named seat 14A is a distinct row with its own invariant. Twenty identical parking bays are a count, which is a different and slightly easier problem — you decrement rather than claim.
How long is a hold, and what happens when it expires?
The hold duration is the whole checkout experience. Too short and people lose seats mid-payment; too long and inventory sits unsellable during a sell-out. It also decides whether you need a reaper or can expire lazily on read.
Is overselling ever acceptable?
For airlines, deliberately yes — they oversell and compensate. For a concert, absolutely not. This changes whether the invariant is hard or a business rule with a tolerance, and it is worth asking rather than assuming.
What does the payment provider guarantee on a timeout?
If they support an idempotency key, a retry is safe and the ambiguity resolves itself. If they do not, you need reconciliation, and that is a background system rather than a code path.
Is there a queue or waiting room for high-demand events?
A stadium on-sale is a thundering herd against a few thousand rows. A waiting room converts that into a controlled admission rate, and it is a separate system worth scoping explicitly.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.
📝2. Functional requirements

What the system has to do. Nothing exotic:

  • Search availability. “What seats are free on flight BA117 on 3 May?”
  • Hold a seat. Alice picks 14A and gets a few minutes to pay, during which nobody else can take it.
  • Confirm with payment. The hold becomes a booking once the money clears.
  • Release it. Either Alice cancels, or her few minutes run out and the seat goes back on sale automatically.

The hold is the interesting one. Without it, Alice types her card details for two minutes and discovers at the end that the seat went to someone else. With it, we have to track a seat that is neither free nor sold, and remember to free it if she wanders off. That in-between state is where most of the bugs live.

⏱3. Non-functional requirements

Now: how well does it have to do those things?

RequirementTargetWhy this number
Never double-sellAbsoluteNot a percentage. Not five nines. Zero. This is the requirement the design exists to satisfy.
Search latency< 200 msPeople browse before they buy, so search gets far more traffic than booking. It is allowed to be slightly out of date.
Booking latency< 1 sSlower than search, and that is fine. A booking is a considered action, not a scroll.
Survive a rush100K at onceConcert on-sales are the hard case: tens of thousands of people hitting the same few hundred seats in the same second.
Money and seats agreeAlways, eventuallyNobody charged for a seat they did not get. Nobody flying on a seat they did not pay for.

Notice the asymmetry in that list. Search can be stale and nobody minds. Booking cannot be wrong and everybody minds. That split — a relaxed read path and a strict write path — is what lets the system scale at all.

🗂4. Data model and API

The data model is where this design is won, so it is worth going slowly.

Here is the key idea: we put the rule on a single row. One row per seat. That row knows whether the seat is free, held, or sold. Because it lives in one place, the database can settle any argument about it on its own, without asking anybody else.

TABLE seats { seat_id VARCHAR PRIMARY KEY, -- "BA117-2026-05-03-14A" state ENUM(available, held, booked), hold_id UUID, -- who is holding it, if anyone hold_expires TIMESTAMP -- and until when } TABLE bookings { booking_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, seat_id VARCHAR UNIQUE, -- <-- the safety net user_id UUID, idempotency_key VARCHAR UNIQUE, -- makes retries safe payment_ref TEXT }

Two things in there are doing real work.

The UNIQUE on bookings.seat_id is a belt-and-braces guarantee. Even if every piece of logic above it is buggy, the database physically cannot store two confirmed bookings for the same seat. It will reject the second one. That is a nice property to have when the cost of being wrong is somebody standing at a gate.

The idempotency_key is how we survive a flaky network. Alice's phone generates a random string before it sends anything. If her connection drops and the app retries, the second request carries the same key, and we recognise it as the same booking rather than making a new one.

The API

GET /v1/availability?flight=BA117&date=2026-05-03 → { seats: [...], as_of: "10:04:12Z" } // as_of is honest: this might be a few seconds old POST /v1/holds Idempotency-Key: req-8f2a { seat_id: "BA117-2026-05-03-14A", user_id: "alice" } → 201 { hold_id, expires_at: "10:14:00Z" } → 409 seat_unavailable // somebody beat you. Normal, not an error. POST /v1/holds/{id}/confirm Idempotency-Key: req-8f2a // same key, safe to retry { payment_token: "tok_..." } → 200 { booking_id } → 410 hold_expired → 402 payment_declined

That 409 is worth a comment. Losing the race for a seat is not a system failure, it is Tuesday. The app should show “sorry, that one just went” and offer another seat, not an error screen.

📊5. Capacity estimation

Some quick numbers, mostly to show which parts are actually hard.

⚖ What I am assuming, and what changes if I am wrong
People browse far more than they book — roughly 100 searches per booking
If it were 1:1, caching search results would stop being worth it and the whole read path would look different.
Each event has hundreds of seats, not millions
Millions of units per event would make one-row-per-unit expensive and push us toward counters.
Payment can take seconds and can time out
If payments were instant and reliable, we would not need the hold at all — one transaction would do.
100K/s
availability searches
~2K/s
booking attempts
100K/s
on the same rows in a rush
10 min
hold window
~30%
holds that expire unpaid
1
row the rule lives on

Look at the third number. In a concert on-sale, 100,000 people want the same few hundred seats in the same second. Every one of those requests wants to write the same handful of rows.

This is worth sitting with, because it changes what “scaling” means here. Adding application servers does nothing. A hundred servers all trying to update row 14A just means a hundred servers queueing behind each other. The contention is on the data, not on the compute. You cannot scale your way out of it; you can only control the rate at which requests reach the row.

⚖6. The key trade-offs

Four decisions matter. Here they are, with what I rejected and why.

DecisionWhat I would do ✓What I would not ✗Why
How to stop double-sellingOne conditional UPDATE on the seat rowA distributed lock (Redis, ZooKeeper)The rule is naturally about one row, and the database already settles races on one row atomically. A lock takes a local problem, makes it distributed, and adds a component that can fail on its own.
How holds expireCheck the clock when someone claimsA timer per holdMillions of timers is a lot of machinery, and a timer that fails to fire silently locks up a seat forever. Checking on claim cannot be missed.
Payment timeoutDo nothing; let the hold lapseGuess either wayGuess “paid” and you give away a seat for free. Guess “not paid” and you charge someone for nothing. Doing nothing is genuinely the right move.
Concert rushA waiting room in frontMore serversMore servers make the pile-up on the row worse, not better. A queue turns 100,000 simultaneous writers into a rate the database can actually absorb.

If you take one thing from this design, take the first row. The instinct when you hear “two people must not get the same thing” is to reach for a lock. You almost never need one. Ask instead: can I put this rule on a single row? If the answer is yes, the problem stops being a distributed systems problem.

🏗7. High-level design
Hold, pay, confirm — and the timeout where doing nothing is correct
booking requestinventory / resultpaymentambiguous
What is moving: the request takes a hold via a single conditional UPDATE on one row — that one statement settles every race atomically — then calls the payment provider with an idempotency key, and only confirms once payment succeeds.
What goes wrong: the payment call times out. You do not know whether the card was charged (Ch 1). Confirming risks giving away a seat nobody paid for; releasing risks charging someone who gets nothing. The correct action is to do neither — leave the hold to expire and reconcile against the provider afterwards. If the charge did land, refund it: a refund is recoverable, a double-sold seat is not.

Now the picture. There are two paths through this system and they have completely different jobs.

THE BROWSING PATH fast, cached, allowed to be slightly wrong Alice → CDN → availability service → read replica a few seconds stale, and that is fine THE BOOKING PATH slower, exact, allowed to say no Alice | Idempotency-Key: req-8f2a v HOLD SERVICE | | one conditional UPDATE, on one row v PRIMARY DATABASE 1 row changed = you win. 0 rows changed = someone else did. | v hold granted, 10 minutes on the clock | v PAYMENT someone else's system. Slow. Can time out. | | paid → confirm: seat becomes booked | declined → release the seat now | timed out → do nothing. Let the hold lapse. v RECONCILE later against the payment provider's records DURING A RUSH a waiting room admits N people per second so the database sees a steady rate instead of a wall
Search is a cache and is allowed to lie. The hold is the only place where truth is decided. Keeping those two apart is what lets the read path scale without putting the one rule at risk.
🔄8. Workflows — what actually happens

This is the part that usually gets skipped, and it is the part that makes a design click. Let us walk through what actually happens, with real people and real times.

Alice books seat 14A
The ordinary case. Nothing goes wrong.
  1. 10:04:00 — Alice searches for seats. She gets a list from a read replica. It is about four seconds out of date, and the response says so.
  2. 10:04:09 — She taps 14A. Her app makes up a random string, req-8f2a, and sends it with the request. That string is how we will recognise a retry later.
  3. The hold service runs one statement: set seat 14A to held, but only if it is currently available. The database reports 1 row changed. Alice has it.
  4. She gets back a hold that expires at 10:14:00. The app starts a countdown.
  5. 10:06:30 — She enters her card. We call the payment provider, passing req-8f2a along so that they can spot a duplicate too.
  6. Payment succeeds. In one transaction we set the seat to booked and insert the booking row. Both happen or neither does.
Alice has seat 14A. It took about two and a half minutes, and the seat was locked to her for all of it.
Alice and Bob both want 14A, at the same instant
The race. This is the one the whole design is built for.
  1. 10:04:09.000 — Both tap 14A. Both saw it as free, because both were looking at a slightly stale list.
  2. Two requests arrive, possibly at two different servers, possibly in the same millisecond. Neither server knows about the other.
  3. Both run the same statement: set 14A to held, only if it is available.
  4. The database processes them one at a time, because that is what databases do to a single row. Alice's runs first and changes 1 row.
  5. Bob's runs second. By now the seat is no longer available, so his condition does not match. The database changes 0 rows.
  6. Bob's server sees “0 rows changed”, and that is the whole answer. It returns 409, and the app says “sorry, 14A just went — how about 14B?”
One seat, one owner. No lock, no coordination, no extra services. The database did it in the ordinary course of doing its job.
The payment times out
The hard one. We genuinely do not know what happened.
  1. 10:06:30 — Alice's hold is good until 10:14. We send the charge to the payment provider.
  2. 10:06:55 — Twenty-five seconds pass and we hear nothing. The call times out.
  3. Here is the problem. A timeout tells us the reply never arrived. It tells us nothing about whether the charge happened. Maybe her card was charged and the response was lost. Maybe it never reached them at all. From here, those look identical.
  4. If we confirm the booking, we might be giving away a seat nobody paid for.
  5. If we release the seat, we might have charged Alice for nothing.
  6. So we do neither. We leave the hold exactly as it is and let it expire at 10:14. The seat goes back on sale on its own.
  7. Separately, a job compares our records against the provider's. If the charge did land, we refund it.
A refund is an annoyance. A double-sold seat is somebody standing at a gate with a valid ticket and no seat. When you cannot tell which happened, choose the mistake you can undo.
Alice wanders off
Where the lazy expiry idea pays for itself.
  1. 10:04:09 — Alice takes the hold, then closes her laptop. Nothing tells us she has gone.
  2. 10:14:00 — The hold expires. Notice that nothing runs at this moment. No timer fires. No job wakes up.
  3. 10:21:00 — Bob tries for 14A. His statement says: set to held if the seat is available or it is held and that hold has expired.
  4. The seat is held, but by an expired hold. The condition matches. 1 row changed. Bob gets the seat.
Expiry cost nothing and cannot be forgotten. There is a background job tidying up old rows, but only so the dashboards look right — if it stopped running tomorrow, nothing would break.
🔍9. Deep dives, and what breaks

Why one row is enough

The thing that makes this work is not clever. It is that a database updating a single row does so one writer at a time. That is not a feature we asked for, it is how they work.

So when two requests race, we do not need to arrange who goes first. We ask the database to change the row only if it still looks the way we expect, and then we look at how many rows changed. One means we won. Zero means somebody else did. There is no third answer, and no ambiguity to resolve.

Compare that to the alternative. A distributed lock needs a separate service. That service can be unreachable. Its leases can expire while you are in the middle of something, so now you need fencing tokens. It can be slow, so now you need timeouts. You have added a whole component and several failure modes to solve a problem the database was already solving.

This is the most useful habit in system design, and it comes up constantly: before you coordinate, check whether you can rearrange the problem so that coordination is not needed. Put the rule on one row, one shard, one owner. You will see the same move in D4, where messages are partitioned by conversation, and in D10, where the crawler is partitioned by host.

The concert rush

A hundred thousand people, a few hundred seats, one second. More application servers will not help — they will all end up queueing for the same rows, and everybody gets a timeout instead of an answer.

The fix is a waiting room. Let people in at a rate the database can handle, show everyone else their place in the queue, and be honest about the wait. It is a worse experience than instant access. It is a much better experience than the site falling over, which is the actual alternative.

What breaks, and what happens

Two people claim the same seat
The conditional update settles it: one gets 1 row changed, the other gets 0 and a clean 409. The UNIQUE constraint on bookings is a second line of defence in case the hold logic ever has a bug.
Alice's phone retries after a dropped connection
The idempotency key means the retry returns her original booking instead of making a second one. Without it, a bad signal gives one person two seats and two charges.
The payment provider is down
Holds are granted but cannot be confirmed, so they expire and the seats come back automatically. “You cannot buy right now” is acceptable. Losing inventory is not.
The database fails over mid-hold
Holds are ordinary rows, so they survive. In-flight requests fail and the app retries with the same key. Nothing is stranded, because expiry is a condition rather than a scheduled job.
The cleanup job stops running
Nothing breaks. Expired holds are already treated as claimable by the claim itself. The job only tidies rows so reports are accurate.
If you remember one thing

A seat is sold at most once, and that rule lives on a single database row. One conditional update settles every race, with no lock and no coordination.

What I would build first

The hold, with expiry checked on claim and idempotency keys on both steps. That is the correctness core. Search, caching and the waiting room all sit on top of it.

What I would leave out

Distributed locks, and strongly consistent search. Both are the instinctive answers, and both add cost and failure modes without buying any correctness.

The thing that will bite you

The ambiguous payment timeout. It is rare, it is the one case where doing nothing is right, and it is where real systems quietly double-sell or charge for seats nobody got.

💬 If you get this far, here is what they will push on
Follow-ups an interviewer is likely to ask once the design is on the board. Answers supplied — read the question, answer it out loud, then open it.
“Why not use a distributed lock to stop double-selling?”Answer

Because you do not need one, and adding it makes things worse. The rule is about a single row, and a database already settles single-row updates one writer at a time.

A lock service is a separate component that can be unreachable. Its leases expire while you are mid-operation, so now you need fencing tokens. It adds a network round trip to every booking.

You have taken a local problem, made it distributed, and acquired several new failure modes — to solve something a conditional UPDATE already solved.

“100,000 people hit the on-sale at the same second. Do you just add servers?”Answer

No, and this is the trap. The contention is on the rows, not the CPU. A hundred servers all trying to update seat 14A means a hundred servers queueing behind each other, and everybody gets a timeout instead of an answer.

The fix is a waiting room in front: admit people at a rate the database can absorb, show everyone their position, and be honest about the wait.

Sharding the inventory works when units are interchangeable — any parking bay — and not when they are not, because seat 14A exists in exactly one place.

“How long should a hold last?”Answer

It is a product decision with a direct inventory cost, and it is worth framing it that way. Too short and people lose the seat while typing their card. Too long and inventory sits unavailable for customers who would have bought it.

Ten minutes is common for tickets, two or three for a high-demand on-sale where inventory turnover matters more than convenience.

The number to watch is what fraction of holds expire unpaid. If it is very high, the window is too long or checkout is too slow.

“What if the payment succeeds but your confirm step crashes before writing the booking?”Answer

The customer has been charged and has no seat, which is the worst outcome, so this is worth designing for rather than hoping about.

The hold expires and the seat returns to sale. Separately, reconciliation compares your bookings against the provider's charges and finds a charge with no booking.

At that point you either issue the booking if the seat is still free, or refund. Either is recoverable. The reason this works is the idempotency key: the customer retrying does not create a second charge.

Design Collaborative Editing (Google Docs, and the same engine for a shared canvas or photo editor)

Difficulty: Hard (Staff Expectation)  .  Target: 45 min
💬 The question, as asked

“Design collaborative editing — Google Docs, or the same engine for a shared canvas or photo editor. Multiple people edit simultaneously and everyone converges.”

⚡ What makes it hard

Concurrent edits do not commute. Two people inserting at position 5 cannot both simply apply their change, and there is no way around it — only two families of solution with very different costs.

📋1. Understanding the question

The prompt: “Design collaborative editing — Google Docs, or the same engine for a shared canvas or photo editor. Multiple people edit simultaneously and everyone converges.”

The whole difficulty fits in one example, and it is worth walking through slowly because everything else follows from it.

🎯 Two edits that cannot both just be applied

The document says HELLO. Two people edit at the same moment.

Priya inserts X at position 5. Dev deletes the character at position 2.

If Priya's edit is applied first: HELLOX, then delete position 2 gives HLLOX. If Dev's is applied first: HLLO, then insert X at position 5 lands past the end — the document is now shorter than Priya thought it was.

Same two edits, different order, different results — and in the second case, an operation that does not even make sense any more.

This is not a bug to fix. Concurrent edits expressed as positions genuinely do not commute, because a position is a statement about a document state that the other edit has already changed.

The two families of answer

There are exactly two known approaches, and they differ in where they put the difficulty.

Transform the operations. Keep positions, but before applying a remote edit, adjust it against every concurrent edit you already applied. Dev's delete at position 2 happened before Priya's insert point, so Priya's insert becomes “insert at position 4”. Both clients now reach HLLOX.

This is operational transformation, and it works. The cost is that the transformation function must be correct for every pair of operation types, and it needs a server to impose a single order, because transforming against a set everyone agrees on is far easier than against sets that differ.

Stop using positions. Give every character a unique, permanent identifier, and express edits as “insert this character after that one” rather than “at position 5”. There is now nothing to invalidate: the character Priya is inserting after still exists regardless of what Dev did, unless Dev deleted it — in which case it is marked deleted rather than removed, so it is still there to anchor against.

These are CRDTs. Operations commute by construction, so no server ordering is needed and offline editing merges naturally. The cost is that every character carries an identifier, so the document's in-memory representation is many times its text size, and deleted characters linger as tombstones.

Which one, and why

For live collaboration with a handful of editors and a server in the middle, transformation is simpler and lighter, and having an authoritative sequencer removes most of the hard cases. For heavy offline editing or peer-to-peer, CRDTs are clearly right because they do not need a central order at all.

Which is why “must offline editing merge?” is the clarifying question that decides the design.

What they are looking for

Do you produce the non-commuting example? Concretely, with positions.

Do you know local edits must apply instantly? Typing that waits for a round trip is unusable, and that requirement is what creates the divergence in the first place.

Do you handle undo correctly? It is the requirement that catches people out.

❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
Text, or a spatial canvas?
This changes the data model completely. Text is a sequence where concurrent inserts must not scramble order; a canvas is a set of objects where concurrent moves are usually independent and far easier.
Must offline editing merge, or is live-only acceptable?
Live-only lets a server serialise everything, which is dramatically simpler. Offline merge is what forces CRDTs or a robust transform, and it is the hardest requirement in the design.
How many concurrent editors per document?
Five is a different system from five hundred. Above roughly fifty, broadcasting every keystroke to everyone becomes the bottleneck and updates must be batched.
Is full edit history required?
Undo needs recent operations; legal or compliance history needs all of them forever, which changes storage from a buffer into an archive.
Does the server need to read the content?
Server-side search, spell-check and thumbnails all require plaintext, which rules out end-to-end encryption. This is a product decision with a large architectural consequence.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.
📝2. Functional requirements
  • Multiple users edit one document simultaneously and converge to the same state.
  • Remote cursors and selections shown live.
  • Undo affects only your own edits, not whatever happened most recently.
  • Reconnect and merge after a disconnection without losing work.

Why undo is harder than it looks

In a single-user editor, undo is a stack: reverse the last thing that happened. In a shared document that is wrong, and obviously so once you see it.

Priya types a paragraph. Dev, elsewhere in the document, deletes a sentence. Priya presses undo. She expects her paragraph to disappear. A naive stack would undo Dev's deletion — reversing a change she cannot see, made by someone else, in a part of the document she is not looking at.

So undo must be per user: find my most recent operation, and apply its inverse transformed against everything that has happened since. That transformation step is essential — if my insert was at position 10 and three characters were since deleted before it, the inverse must target position 7.

This is one of the clearest examples in the design of why the operation model has to be principled rather than ad hoc. Undo is not a feature layered on top; it is the same transformation machinery pointed backwards.

⏱3. Non-functional requirements
RequirementTargetWhat it forces
Local edit latencyZero — instantTyping must never wait for a server. This is what creates divergence, and therefore the entire problem.
Remote edit latency~200 msFast enough that collaboration feels live. Slower and people start editing over each other.
ConvergenceNon-negotiableNo sequence of concurrent edits may leave two clients with different documents. Not “rarely” — never.
Concurrent editors~10 typicalBounded. Hundreds would require batching and a fan-out tier this design does not need.
Offline mergeSupported, rareSupported because people close laptops. Rare, which is what makes server authority viable.
HistoryRecent, for undoFull permanent history is a different requirement — an archive rather than a buffer — and worth scoping explicitly.

The first row is the source of the problem

It is worth making the connection explicit, because it explains why this cannot be designed away.

If typing waited for the server, there would be no problem at all: the server would order every edit, there would be exactly one document state, and nothing would ever diverge. It would also be unusable — a 100 ms round trip on every keystroke feels broken, and on a poor connection it feels dead.

So edits apply locally and immediately, which means the local document is ahead of the server, and every other client's is ahead in a different direction. Divergence is not a failure mode; it is the normal, continuous state of a working system, and the design's job is to guarantee that it always resolves.

🗂4. Data model and API

The document is not stored as text. It is stored as a sequence of operations, with the text as a derived view.

-- The op log is the source of truth; snapshots are an optimisation. TABLE operations { doc_id UUID, version BIGINT, -- server-assigned, gapless, per document client_id UUID, client_seq BIGINT, -- dedup on client retry op JSONB, -- {insert, pos, text} | {delete, pos, len} | {move,...} created_at TIMESTAMP, PRIMARY KEY (doc_id, version) } -- (doc_id, version) is a total order per document. That total order -- IS the definition of the document -- everything else is derived. TABLE snapshots { doc_id UUID, version BIGINT, content BYTES, PRIMARY KEY (doc_id, version) } -- Load = latest snapshot + ops after it. Without snapshots, opening -- a year-old document means replaying millions of operations. -- Cursors are NOT stored. They are ephemeral presence state, they -- are worthless one second later, and persisting them would be a -- far higher write rate than the edits themselves.

Each operation records what was done, by whom, and where it sat in the order. Replaying them from the beginning reconstructs the document, which is what makes history, undo and crash recovery all the same mechanism rather than three features.

Replaying from zero on every open would be slow for a document with a million operations, so periodic snapshots are stored: the full text at operation 900,000. Opening means loading that snapshot and replaying the remainder. The same idea as a database checkpoint, and the same trade-off — snapshot frequency against replay cost.

The sequence number is what makes the server authoritative

Each operation gets a monotonically increasing number when the server accepts it, and that ordering is the single source of truth. Every client applies operations in that order and therefore reaches the same state.

Crucially, a client also tracks which server operation its local state was based on. When it sends an edit it says “this was made against version 41”, which tells the server exactly which concurrent operations to transform it against — everything from 42 onward.

Without that, the server would have no way to know what the client had seen, and transformation would be guesswork.

Presence is not part of this

Cursors, selections and who-is-here change constantly — a cursor moves on every keystroke — and are worthless the moment they are stale.

So they travel on a separate, ephemeral channel that is never persisted and never sequenced. Putting them through the operation log would multiply its volume for data with no durability requirement at all, and would mean the document's history filled up with cursor movements.

Same instinct as presence in D4: ephemeral high-rate state and durable low-rate state should not share a pipeline.

The API

// WebSocket per open document. HTTP only for load and snapshot. GET /v1/docs/{id} -> { snapshot, version, participants[] } WS /v1/docs/{id}/stream -> { type:"op", client_id, base_version, ops:[...] } <- { type:"ack", client_seq, server_version } <- { type:"op", from, server_version, ops:[...] } // transformed <- { type:"cursor", from, range } // ephemeral, never persisted <- { type:"resync", snapshot, version } // client too far behind // base_version is what makes this work: the server knows exactly // which document state the client was looking at, and therefore // which concurrent ops it must transform against. POST /v1/docs/{id}/snapshot // internal: compact the op log
📊5. Capacity estimation

The numbers, and why they are reassuring.

⚖ Assumptions — and what breaks if each is wrong
Typical document has fewer than 10 concurrent editors
Hundreds of editors forces update batching and a fan-out tier, which this design does not need.
Live collaboration; offline merge is supported but rare
If most editing were offline, CRDTs become clearly correct and the server-authority design stops being viable.
The server may read document content
End-to-end encryption would remove server-side search, thumbnails and transform, and force all merging onto clients.
~50/s
ops per busy document
~500/s
fan-out messages per document
~200 ms
remote-edit budget
~100 B
per operation
~1 KB/s
per active editor
1
authoritative sequencer per doc

A busy document with ten active editors at around five operations per second each is 50 operations per second per document. Each must be broadcast to the other nine, so about 500 messages per second of fan-out. Operations are around 100 bytes.

That is tiny, and saying so is useful: per document, this is a trivial workload. A million active documents is a scale problem in aggregate, but it partitions perfectly, because documents never interact. One document's editing session has no relationship to another's.

So the scaling model is straightforward: route all editors of a document to the same server instance — the sequencer for that document — and spread documents across instances. No coordination between instances, ever.

That routing requirement is the only awkward part, and it is the same one as D4: all participants must reach the one machine holding the authoritative state for their document. It makes the tier stateful, which means a registry and a reconnection story.

The number worth watching is operations per document, not documents. The design holds comfortably to tens of concurrent editors. Past roughly fifty, broadcasting every keystroke to everyone becomes the bottleneck and updates must be batched — which is a different design, and knowing where the threshold sits is better than claiming it scales indefinitely.

⚖6. The key trade-offs

The choices, and their costs.

DecisionChosen ✓Alternative ✗Reasoning
Merge algorithmOT with a server sequencerCRDTWith a live server there is a natural total order, and OT’s operations are far smaller. The moment strong offline merge is required this flips to CRDTs.
Ordering authorityOne session owner per documentConsensus across replicasSingle-writer-per-document makes ordering trivial. Consensus is needed only to decide ownership, which changes rarely, not for every keystroke.
Local editsApply immediately, rebase on ackWait for server confirmationA round trip per keystroke is unusable. The cost is client-side rebase complexity, which is the price of the feature existing at all.
CursorsEphemeral, never persistedStored with the documentCursor updates are a higher write rate than edits and are worthless a second later. Persisting them buys nothing and costs everything.
LoadingSnapshot + tail of opsReplay the full logA long-lived document has millions of operations. Replaying them all to open a file is an unbounded cost that grows with the document’s age.

Transformation or CRDT, in detail

Operational transformation keeps operations small — an insert is a position, a character and an author — and the document in memory is roughly the size of its text. That efficiency is why it is used for large documents with many collaborators.

The cost is correctness effort. You need a transformation function for every pair of operation types, and it must satisfy properties that are easy to state and notoriously easy to get subtly wrong. Published algorithms have had bugs found years after deployment. The central server helps enormously — transforming against a single agreed order is far more tractable than the peer-to-peer case — which is why nearly every production OT system has one.

CRDTs make operations commute by construction, so there is nothing to get wrong in the same way and no central authority is required. Offline merge works naturally: reconnect, exchange operations in any order, converge.

The cost is size. Every character carries a unique identifier, so the in-memory representation can be several times the text. Deleted characters remain as tombstones because other operations may anchor to them, and a heavily-edited document accumulates them. Garbage-collecting tombstones requires knowing every participant has seen the deletion, which is its own coordination problem.

Modern CRDT implementations have narrowed the gap considerably, and for a design discussion the right answer is to state the trade rather than to declare a winner.

Text or canvas

Worth asking early, because a canvas is a much easier problem and it is easy to over-engineer it.

Text is a sequence. Every element's position depends on every element before it, so an insert at the start shifts everything — which is exactly what makes concurrent edits interfere.

A canvas is a set of objects, each with its own position. Two people moving two different shapes do not interfere at all; the operations are independent and both simply apply. Even two people moving the same shape has an acceptable resolution — last write wins on that shape's position — because the shape ends up somewhere sensible and nothing is scrambled.

So a canvas needs far less machinery than a document. Reaching for full OT on a drawing tool is a real over-engineering risk, and noticing that the data model changes the difficulty is the useful observation.

🏗7. High-level design
Concurrent edits — and the split brain that silently forks a document
local editsordered oprebased op
What is moving: two edits authored against the same document state. Each applies locally first — typing never waits for a round trip — then the session owner assigns a sequence number, transforms the second against the first, and broadcasts the rebased operation. One sequencer per document turns a distributed consensus problem into a single-threaded one.
What goes wrong: a network blip and two nodes both believe they own the document. Now there are two total orders, and clients converge to different documents with no error anywhere. This is why ownership needs a fenced lease rather than a best-effort lock: the stale owner’s writes must be rejected at the log, not merely discouraged. Ch 6

One authoritative sequencer per document.

Priya's browser Dev's browser | | | edit applies instantly locally | same | and is queued to send | v v SEQUENCER for this document — all editors route here | | 1. receive op, tagged "based on version 41" | 2. transform it against ops 42..47 everything it had not seen | 3. assign sequence 48 | 4. append to the operation log | 5. broadcast to every client v OPERATION LOG the document, as a sequence of ops | +-- periodic snapshots so opening does not replay a million ops SEPARATE CHANNEL presence: cursors, selections, who is here never persisted, never sequenced — worthless once stale RECONNECT client: "my last server version was 41, and I have 3 unsent ops" server: here are 42..60, and your 3 are now 61..63 (transformed) nothing is lost; the client just did what it always does, later
A client's local state is always ahead of the server, and the server's order is always the truth. Reconciling those two continuously — not occasionally — is the entire job.
🔄8. Workflows — what actually happens
Priya and Dev type at the same moment
The example from step 1, resolved.
  1. The document is HELLO, and both clients are at server version 41.
  2. Priya inserts X at position 5. It appears on her screen instantly — she sees HELLOX. The operation is queued, tagged "based on 41".
  3. Dev deletes position 2 at the same moment. He sees HLLO instantly. Also tagged "based on 41".
  4. Dev's operation reaches the server first. Nothing concurrent to transform against, so it becomes version 42 and broadcasts.
  5. Priya's arrives, tagged 41. The server sees it was made without knowledge of 42, so it transforms it: a delete at position 2 occurred before position 5, so her insert becomes "insert X at position 4". It becomes version 43.
  6. Priya receives version 42 — the delete. She applies it to her local HELLOX, transformed against her own pending insert, giving HLLOX.
  7. Dev receives version 43 and applies it to HLLO, giving HLLOX.
  8. Both show HLLOX. Neither ever saw a character jump or a cursor move unexpectedly.
Both clients were briefly wrong, in different ways, and both converged without either user noticing. That is the standard the whole design is held to: divergence is continuous and invisible.
Priya closes her laptop and edits on a plane
Offline, then reconnection.
  1. She goes offline at server version 41. Her client keeps working entirely locally — nothing about editing requires the server.
  2. Over two hours she makes 400 operations. All apply immediately; all queue, tagged "based on 41".
  3. Meanwhile Dev and two others take the document to version 380.
  4. She reconnects. Her client says: I last saw 41, and I have 400 operations based on it.
  5. The server sends 42 through 380. Her client applies them, transforming each against her pending queue so her own edits stay put relative to the text around them.
  6. Her 400 operations are then sent, each transformed against the 339 server operations she had not seen, and appended as 381 onwards.
  7. Everyone converges. Her two hours of work is intact and interleaved sensibly with everyone else's.
Note that reconnection is not a special path — it is the ordinary algorithm with a larger backlog. A design where offline is a distinct code path is one where offline is broken, because that path is exercised rarely and tested less.
Priya presses undo
Where the naive stack gives an obviously wrong answer.
  1. Priya typed a paragraph at version 300. Since then Dev deleted a sentence elsewhere (310) and Sam reformatted a heading (315).
  2. A single-user undo stack would reverse the most recent operation — Sam's. Priya would watch a heading she never touched change back.
  3. Instead, undo finds Priya's own most recent operation: her insert at 300.
  4. Its inverse is "delete the text I inserted". But the document has changed since — Dev's deletion removed characters before her insertion point.
  5. So the inverse is transformed against operations 301 to 315, landing on the correct current positions.
  6. The transformed inverse is submitted as an ordinary operation, version 316, and broadcast like any other edit.
  7. Priya's paragraph disappears. Dev's and Sam's changes are untouched.
Undo is not a separate mechanism — it is an inverse operation run through the same transformation machinery as everything else. Which is exactly why the operation model has to be principled: an ad-hoc one cannot express its own inverse correctly.
The sequencer for a document crashes
Stateful routing, and why nothing is lost.
  1. Four people are editing. The server instance holding the authoritative order dies.
  2. All four sockets drop. Their clients keep working locally — typing still applies instantly — and queue operations.
  3. The routing layer picks a new instance for the document. Clients reconnect there.
  4. The new sequencer loads the latest snapshot from durable storage and replays the operations after it, reconstructing state at, say, version 380.
  5. Operations the old sequencer accepted but had not yet durably appended are lost. Those clients still have them queued and re-send.
  6. Each client says what version it last saw and sends its pending queue. Everything is transformed and applied.
  7. The interruption shows as a brief "reconnecting" indicator. Nothing typed is lost.
This works because the client keeps its own pending operations until the server confirms them, and because durability lives in the log rather than in the sequencer's memory. The sequencer is authoritative about order, not about data — which is what makes it replaceable.
🔍9. Deep dives, and what breaks

Why a server at all, given CRDTs exist

A fair question: if CRDTs converge without coordination, the sequencer looks like unnecessary centralisation.

It earns its place for reasons that have little to do with convergence. The server is where access control is enforced, where the document is durably stored, where history and snapshots live, where server-side search and thumbnails are generated, and where a client that has been gone for a month can be caught up efficiently rather than by exchanging a month of operations peer to peer.

And with a server present, OT's hard cases largely disappear, because there is one order to transform against.

The honest framing: CRDTs remove the need for a coordinator to achieve convergence, not the need for a server to run a product. Peer-to-peer collaborative editing is a real thing and it is a different product with different properties.

Routing every editor to the same instance

The awkward operational consequence of having one sequencer per document.

It is the same shape as the connection registry in D4: a mapping from document to the instance that currently owns it, consulted on connect. The difference is that here it must be correct, not merely helpful — two sequencers for one document would produce two divergent orders, which is the one failure the design cannot tolerate.

So ownership needs a lease with a fencing token, exactly as in D6: an instance holds the document for a bounded period, renews while healthy, and a new owner can only take over with a higher token. An old owner that wakes up after a pause finds its writes to the log rejected.

This is a good moment to notice how often the same primitive recurs: a lease plus a monotonically increasing token is the standard answer to “exactly one owner” in an asynchronous system.

The operation log is three features

Storing operations rather than text looks like extra work and pays for itself three times.

History is free: any past state is a prefix of the log. Undo is a transformed inverse operation, as above. Crash recovery is a snapshot plus a replay.

Storing only the current text would give you none of these, and each would have to be built separately — a version table, an undo stack, a recovery mechanism — that could drift out of agreement with each other.

The cost is that the log grows forever and must be compacted behind snapshots, and that reconstructing state is replay rather than a read. Both are manageable; the three features are not, separately.

What breaks

Session owner node dies
Another node acquires the document lease with a fencing token, replays from the last snapshot plus the op log, and resumes. Clients reconnect and resync from their last acknowledged version, replaying their pending queue. Ch 6
Client reconnects after being offline
It sends its pending operations with their base_version; the server transforms them against everything that happened meanwhile. If it is too far behind to transform economically, the server sends a full resync instead — correct, and occasionally visible as a jump.
Two nodes both believe they own a document
This is split-brain, and it is the failure that silently corrupts documents by producing two divergent orderings. The fencing token makes the stale owner’s writes rejected at the log rather than merely discouraged.
Op log write fails after broadcasting
Ordering must be decided by the log, not by the broadcast: assign the version and persist before fanning out. Broadcasting first is faster and lets clients converge on state the server cannot reproduce after a crash.
A malformed op corrupts the document
Validate operations against the current document state before assigning a version, and keep snapshots immutable so any point in history can be recovered. The op log is the audit trail that makes corruption diagnosable rather than mysterious.
The dominant constraint

Concurrent edits do not commute. Everything in the design exists to impose a total order on operations that were authored against different states, and then to make each client’s local view converge to that order.

What I would build first

One authoritative session per document with an append-only op log and periodic snapshots. That converts a distributed consensus problem into a single-threaded one and makes ordering trivial.

What I deliberately did not build

Offline-first merge and end-to-end encryption. Either would force CRDTs and move all merging onto clients — a legitimate design, and a different one.

The biggest risk

Split-brain on document ownership. Two sequencers means two orderings and silently divergent documents, which is why ownership needs a fenced lease rather than a best-effort lock.

💬 If you get this far, here is what they will push on
Follow-ups an interviewer is likely to ask once the design is on the board. Answers supplied — read the question, answer it out loud, then open it.
“Two people type at the same position at the same instant. What does each see?”Answer

Both edits apply locally first, so each person sees their own character appear immediately — waiting for a round trip per keystroke would be unusable.

The server assigns an order, transforms the second edit against the first, and sends the rebased operation back. Each client then reconciles its local state with the server's order, which may mean adjusting a character it already drew.

The result is that both converge to the same document, and neither person felt any lag while typing.

“Should you use OT or CRDTs?”Answer

It depends on one requirement: how strong is offline editing? With a live server sequencing everything, OT is simpler and its operations are much smaller on the wire.

CRDTs give every character an immutable identity so operations commute and merge without any server. That is what you need for peer-to-peer or for merging after days offline, and you pay for it in per-character metadata and tombstones that never go away.

The strong answer names the condition: OT with a server for live editing, CRDTs the moment serious offline merge is required.

“The server holding a document crashes. What happens to people editing it?”Answer

Another node takes ownership, replays the operation log from the last snapshot, and rebuilds the document. Clients reconnect and resync from their last acknowledged sequence number, replaying anything they had pending.

Because operations are appended to the log before being acknowledged, nothing acknowledged can be lost.

The dangerous case is two nodes both believing they own the document, which produces two orderings and silently forks the file. That needs a fenced lease, not a best-effort lock.

“How does undo work when someone else has edited since?”Answer

Undo means “invert my last operation”, not “revert the last thing that happened” — otherwise you would undo a colleague's work, which is the bug people actually hit.

So you take your operation, construct its inverse, and transform that inverse against everything that has happened since.

If a colleague deleted the text you are undoing an edit to, the transformed inverse becomes a no-op rather than resurrecting the text. That is the correct outcome and it falls out of the transform.

Design a Denylist / Request Blocking Service (deny service to banned IPs from a third-party feed)

Difficulty: Medium-Hard  .  Target: 35 min
💬 The question, as asked

“A third party publishes a feed of banned IP addresses. Design a system that denies service to requests from them, across your entire edge.”

⚡ What makes it hard

The naive design puts a network call on 100% of traffic and makes an auxiliary protective component able to take the whole site down. The dataset size is the thing that unlocks the real answer.

📋1. Understanding the question

The prompt: “A third party publishes a feed of banned IP addresses. Design a system that denies service to requests from them, across your entire edge.”

The obvious design is a denylist service that the edge asks about each request. It is wrong in two ways, and both are worth stating before anything else.

🎯 What the obvious design costs you

A network call on 100% of traffic. Every request now waits for a round trip to ask whether it is allowed. At 500,000 requests per second that service is the busiest thing you own, and it has added latency to every single request in the system.

An auxiliary component that can take the site down. If it is slow, everything is slow. If it is down, you either block everyone or trust no one. A protective mechanism has become your largest availability risk.

The number that unlocks the real answer

A million denylist entries, mostly CIDR ranges, stored in a compact structure, is about eight megabytes.

Eight megabytes fits in the memory of every edge process you have. Which means the check does not need to be a service call at all — it can be a lookup in local memory, in microseconds, with no network, no dependency and no failure mode.

The denylist service stops being a request-path component and becomes a distribution component: its job is to get the current list to every edge node and then get out of the way.

This is the whole design, and it comes entirely from doing one size estimate early. It is one of the cleanest examples in the guide of an estimate changing the architecture rather than confirming it.

The second question to ask

Fail open or fail closed? If the list cannot be loaded or refreshed, do we admit everyone or reject everyone?

For abuse prevention, fail open: letting some bad traffic through for a few minutes is much better than blocking all your real users. For a sanctions or fraud list, possibly closed — and that is a business and legal decision, not an engineering one. Surfacing it as a question rather than assuming is the point.

What they are looking for

Do you avoid the per-request network call? This is the question.

Do you distrust the feed? An upstream that publishes 0.0.0.0/0 would block the entire internet. You are ingesting someone else's data into your request path.

Do you know CIDR is an interval problem? A set of addresses and a set of ranges need different structures.

❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
How fast must a new ban take effect?
Seconds versus minutes is the whole design. Seconds means pushing updates to every edge; minutes allows ordinary polling and a much simpler system.
Fail open or fail closed?
If the denylist service is unavailable, do we admit everything or reject everything? For abuse prevention, fail open. For a sanctions or fraud list, possibly closed — and that is a business decision, not an engineering one.
How large is the list, and is it ranges or individual addresses?
A million individual IPs is a set membership problem. CIDR ranges are an interval problem and need a different structure entirely.
Is the third-party feed trusted?
An upstream feed that suddenly contains 0.0.0.0/0 would take the site down. Feed changes need sanity limits before they are applied.
Do we need to explain or appeal a block?
Auditability turns a stateless filter into a system that must record why each decision was made, which is a meaningfully larger design.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.
📝2. Functional requirements
  • Ingest a third-party feed of banned addresses and CIDR ranges, plus internal manual bans.
  • Decide allow or deny for every inbound request, at the edge.
  • Temporary bans with expiry, and an allowlist that always overrides.
  • Record every block for audit and appeal.

The allowlist is not symmetric with the denylist

It looks like the mirror image and it has a different role: it is the escape hatch for when the denylist is wrong.

Third-party feeds contain mistakes. A shared NAT gateway for an entire office, a mobile carrier, or a cloud provider's egress range gets listed because of one bad actor behind it. Suddenly a large customer cannot reach you, and the cause is a data file from someone else.

So the allowlist must be checked first and must win unconditionally, and adding an entry has to take effect in seconds — because it is used during an incident, by someone who has just discovered that a legitimate customer is being blocked.

Why audit is a real requirement

Someone will ask why they were blocked, and “a file said so” is not an answer that survives contact with a customer or a regulator.

So every block records which rule matched, which feed version that rule came from, and when. That turns a stateless filter into something with a durable output, which is a meaningfully larger system — worth acknowledging rather than glossing over, because at 500,000 requests per second the block log is itself a data pipeline.

⏱3. Non-functional requirements
RequirementTargetWhy
Check latency< 1 ms, ideally µsIt runs on 100% of traffic. A millisecond added here is a millisecond on every request the company serves.
Propagation< 30 s globallyA new ban should take effect quickly. Note this is the only requirement that needs a distribution mechanism at all.
Availability impactCannot take the site downThe defining constraint. It rules out a synchronous dependency and dictates fail-open.
List size~1M entries, ~8 MBThe estimate that makes in-process lookup possible. Everything else follows.
Allowlist effectSecondsIt is used during an incident, to undo a wrongful block.
False positivesExpectedShared NATs and carrier ranges guarantee them. The design must assume the list is wrong sometimes.

"Cannot take the site down", made concrete

Worth spelling out what it eliminates, because it eliminates a lot.

No synchronous call to another service. No database read on the request path. No dependency that can be slow. No shared resource that can saturate.

What is left is a read from a local in-memory structure, which cannot fail in any way that matters: it cannot time out, it cannot be partitioned away, and it does not care whether the rest of the infrastructure is healthy.

The failure mode that does remain is a stale list — if distribution breaks, edges keep enforcing yesterday's list. That is a clearly acceptable degradation, and stating the difference between “fails safely” and “cannot fail” is more honest than claiming the latter.

🗂4. Data model and API

The interesting part is the data structure, because CIDR ranges are not a set membership problem.

TABLE rules { cidr CIDR PRIMARY KEY, -- v4 and v6 action ENUM(deny, allow), -- allow always wins reason TEXT, source ENUM(feed, manual, automated), expires_at TIMESTAMP, -- NULL = permanent created_at TIMESTAMP } -- EDGE REPRESENTATION: a binary radix trie over address bits. -- Longest-prefix match, so a /32 allow beats an enclosing /8 deny -- for free -- specificity is structural, not a rule engine. -- root -- +- 0... -> ... -- +- 1... -> 10.0.0.0/8 DENY (feed) -- +- 10.1.2.3/32 ALLOW (manual override) -- Lookup walks at most 32 (v4) or 128 (v6) bits: constant time. TABLE block_events { -- sampled, not every block: 500K/s of audit ts TIMESTAMP, ip INET, matched_rule CIDR, edge VARCHAR } -- rows would dwarf the traffic being protected

Why a hash set does not work

If the list were individual addresses, a hash set would be perfect: hash the address, look it up, done.
