But an entry like 192.168.0.0/16 covers 65,536 addresses. Expanding ranges into individual entries turns a million entries into billions, and a single /8 would be sixteen million on its own.

The question is not “is this address in the set?” but “is this address inside any of these intervals?”, which is a different operation.

A prefix trie, which is what routers use

An IP address is a sequence of bits, and a CIDR range is a prefix of those bits. 192.168.0.0/16 means “any address whose first 16 bits are these”.

So the structure is a binary tree over the bits. Walk down from the root, one bit at a time; if you pass a node marked as a denylist entry, the address is covered by that range.

Three properties make this the right choice:

  • Bounded work. At most 32 steps for IPv4, 128 for IPv6, regardless of list size. A million entries costs the same as a hundred.
  • Overlapping ranges are natural. 10.0.0.0/8 and 10.1.0.0/16 simply sit at different depths on the same path, and the longest match wins — which is exactly the semantics you want when a specific allow sits inside a broad deny.
  • Compact. Compressed, a million entries is around 8 MB.

It is the same structure a router uses for forwarding, for the same reason, which is a satisfying thing to be able to point out.

What lives where

The edge holds only the compiled trie: an immutable snapshot with a version number, loaded into memory. Nothing is written on the request path.

The control plane holds the editable state: feed entries with their source and expiry, manual bans, the allowlist, and the history of compiled versions. This is an ordinary database doing an ordinary amount of work, because it is nowhere near the request path.

The API

// CONTROL PLANE -- low volume, ordinary REST POST /v1/bans Body: { cidr, reason, expires_at?, source } DELETE /v1/bans/{cidr} POST /v1/allowlist Body: { cidr, reason } // always wins over a ban GET /v1/bans/check?ip= -> { blocked, matched_rule, source } // for support and appeals, NOT the hot path // DATA PLANE -- edges pull versioned snapshots, they are never pushed to GET /v1/snapshot/latest -> { version, url, sha256, entry_count } GET /v1/delta?from= -> { version, added[], removed[] } // Pull means an edge that was offline catches up on its own, and // the control plane holds no per-edge state. // The hot path has NO API. It is a function call into local memory.
📊5. Capacity estimation

The numbers, and the single one that decides the architecture.

⚖ Assumptions — and what breaks if each is wrong
~1M denylist entries, mostly CIDR ranges
Tens of millions of individual addresses would push from an in-memory structure toward a probabilistic filter with a confirmation lookup.
Feed updates arrive every few minutes, not continuously
A high-frequency feed would need streaming updates rather than periodic snapshot rebuilds.
Blocking is best-effort abuse prevention, not a legal control
If it were a sanctions list, fail-open would be unacceptable and the availability calculus reverses.
500K/s
requests checked
~1M
denylist entries
~8 MB
compressed trie in memory
<1 µs
per lookup, in process
~30 s
global propagation target
0
network hops on the hot path

The list fits in memory. A million entries, compiled into a compressed trie, is about 8 MB. On an edge node with gigabytes of RAM this is negligible — smaller than a typical service's own code.

That single fact is the design. Compare the two options directly:

  • Remote check: ~1 ms added to every request, a service handling 500,000 QPS, and a new hard dependency in the request path.
  • Local check: under a microsecond, no service, no dependency, no failure mode.

Three orders of magnitude of latency, and an entire availability risk removed, because the data was small enough to copy everywhere.

Distribution is the only real traffic

Two hundred edge nodes each fetching an 8 MB snapshot is 1.6 GB per full rebuild. Doing that every thirty seconds would be pointless waste.

So the steady state is deltas: what changed since version N, which is typically kilobytes. A full snapshot is fetched only on startup or when a node has fallen too far behind to apply deltas.

Worth noting how small this problem is. The hard-sounding part — checking every request — turned out to be free, and what remains is distributing a few kilobytes to two hundred machines every thirty seconds. That is an unremarkable engineering problem, which is the sign the design is right.

⚖6. The key trade-offs

The choices, and their costs.

DecisionChosen ✓Alternative ✗Reasoning
Check locationIn-process, local memoryCall a denylist serviceA network call on 100% of traffic adds latency and creates a dependency that can take the site down. 8 MB replicates everywhere for free.
StructureRadix trie, longest-prefix matchHash set of addressesA hash set cannot express CIDR ranges or specificity. The trie gives override semantics structurally rather than through rule ordering.
DistributionEdges pull versioned snapshotsControl plane pushesPull removes per-edge state, handles offline edges automatically, and keeps working when the control plane is down.
On failureFail open, keep the last snapshotFail closedA protective component must not be able to cause a larger outage than the abuse it prevents. A legal control is the deliberate exception.
AuditSample high-volume, keep manual blocksLog every decision5,000 rows/sec of audit is a bigger data problem than the traffic being protected, and almost none of it is ever read.

Fail open or fail closed

The question is what happens when an edge node cannot get a fresh list, or has none at all.

Fail open — allow everything — means some blocked traffic gets through during the outage. Given that this is abuse prevention, that is a few minutes of unwanted requests, which is a cost you can absorb.

Fail closed — reject everything — means a distribution failure becomes a total outage. The protective mechanism has caused a far worse incident than the thing it protects against.

For abuse prevention, fail open, clearly. For a sanctions list where serving a prohibited party is a legal violation, the calculus genuinely reverses — being down may be preferable to being non-compliant.

The staff-level move is not picking one. It is recognising that the answer depends on what the list is for, and that this is a business decision to surface rather than an engineering default to assume.

Trusting the feed — and not

You are ingesting a third party's data directly into the path of every request you serve. Treating it as trusted is a serious mistake with an obvious failure mode: a feed that accidentally publishes 0.0.0.0/0 takes your entire site down, instantly, globally, and the cause is in someone else's system.

The guards are all sanity checks applied before compilation, and they are cheap:

  • Reject over-broad prefixes. Nothing broader than a /8 without explicit human approval.
  • Bound the rate of change. If a feed update changes more than a few percent of entries, halt and alert rather than apply.
  • Protect known-good ranges. Your own infrastructure, your monitoring, and major customer ranges are permanently allowlisted and cannot be denied by any feed.
  • Stage the rollout. New versions go to a few edges first, with block-rate monitored, before going everywhere.

That last one turns “the feed was wrong” from a global outage into a small anomaly on a handful of nodes, and it is the same staged-rollout instinct as D18.

🏗7. High-level design
Denylist distribution — and the upstream feed that could ban everyone
feed dataaccepted deltasnapshotrejected
What is moving: a feed of banned ranges is validated, diffed and compiled into a signed radix trie of about 8 MB, which every edge pulls. The hot path never appears here at all — the actual check is a local memory lookup with zero network hops.
What goes wrong: the upstream feed malfunctions and publishes an over-broad range. Applied faithfully, that blocks everyone. Treat the feed as untrusted input: reject any delta banning more than a small fraction of address space, or removing most existing rules, and never accept a prefix broader than a configured maximum. Edges keep the last good snapshot indefinitely, so a rejected feed is an alert, not an outage.

A control plane that distributes, and a data plane that never calls anyone.

CONTROL PLANE nowhere near the request path third-party feed ----+ manual bans ----+---> VALIDATE allowlist ----+ reject prefixes broader than /8 halt if >N% of entries changed never deny our own ranges | v COMPILE → trie snapshot v812 ~8 MB | v DISTRIBUTE staged: a few edges first, watch block rate DATA PLANE 200 edge nodes each node: trie v812 resident in process memory polls for deltas every ~10s KB, not MB request arrives | +-- 1. allowlist? → ALLOW checked first; always wins +-- 2. denylist trie → ≤32 bit-steps, no network | match → DENY + async audit record | no match → ALLOW | sub-microsecond. no I/O. no dependency. cannot time out. DISTRIBUTION BROKEN edges keep enforcing the last list they have a node with no list at all: fail open for abuse prevention
The control plane can be entirely down and every request is still served correctly — just against a slightly older list. That separation is what satisfies “must never take the site down”.
🔄8. Workflows — what actually happens
A request arrives and is checked
The hot path, in full, which is shorter than its description.
  1. A request lands at an edge node with source address 203.0.113.45.
  2. The allowlist trie is checked first. No match, so the denylist is consulted.
  3. The address is walked bit by bit through the denylist trie. At depth 24 it passes a node marked as an entry — 203.0.113.0/24 is on the list.
  4. Denied. Elapsed: well under a microsecond. No network call, no lock, no allocation.
  5. A 403 is returned. An audit record — address, matching rule, feed version, timestamp — is written to a local buffer and shipped asynchronously, off the request path.
  6. A request from an unlisted address walks the same 32 steps, finds nothing, and is allowed. The cost is identical either way.
The check costs the same whether the list has a thousand entries or ten million, because the work is bounded by address length rather than list size. That property is what lets the list grow without anyone re-examining the latency budget.
A new ban is published and takes effect
Thirty seconds, globally, without touching the request path.
  1. The third-party feed publishes an update: 400 new ranges, 120 expired.
  2. The control plane validates it. Nothing broader than a /8; the change is 0.05% of entries, well inside the limit; none of our own ranges are affected.
  3. It merges with manual bans and the allowlist, compiles a new trie, and publishes it as version 813.
  4. Rollout is staged: five edge nodes first. Their block rate is compared against the rest of the fleet for a minute. It moves by a fraction of a percent — normal.
  5. The remaining 195 nodes poll, receive the delta from 812 to 813 — a few kilobytes — and apply it.
  6. Each swaps the new trie in atomically: build alongside, flip a pointer. No request ever sees a half-updated structure.
  7. Total from publication to global effect: about 30 seconds.
The atomic pointer swap is the same immutable-snapshot pattern as the prefix table in D13 and the map version in D17. Building alongside and flipping is the general answer to "update a live in-memory structure safely".
The feed publishes a range that blocks a major customer
The false positive that is guaranteed to happen.
  1. A large customer's office NAT gateway appears in the feed, because one machine behind it was compromised weeks ago.
  2. Every employee at that company is now blocked. From their side the site is simply down, with no explanation.
  3. Support escalates. The audit log answers the question immediately: blocked by rule 198.51.100.0/24, from feed version 813, at 14:22.
  4. An engineer adds that range to the allowlist.
  5. A new version compiles and distributes. Because the allowlist is checked first and wins unconditionally, those requests are allowed regardless of the feed.
  6. Within a minute the customer is working again, and the allowlist entry survives every future feed update.
Two things made this a minor incident rather than a long one. The audit log turned "why can't we reach you?" into a precise answer in seconds, and the allowlist gave a fix that does not require the third party to correct their data — which they may never do.
The feed publishes 0.0.0.0/0
The failure that would have been catastrophic.
  1. An upstream bug emits an entry covering every address on the internet.
  2. Applied naively, every edge node would block every request worldwide within thirty seconds. A total outage, caused by someone else's data, with the fix requiring a new deployment.
  3. Instead the validation stage rejects it: prefixes broader than /8 require explicit human approval.
  4. A second guard also fires — this update would change effectively 100% of matching behaviour, far past the rate-of-change limit.
  5. The update is halted entirely, not partially applied. Edges continue enforcing version 813.
  6. An alert names the offending entry. A human confirms the upstream bug and the feed is quarantined until it is fixed.
The general lesson is worth stating: any third-party data entering your request path is untrusted input, and needs bounds on how much it is allowed to change behaviour in one step. The guard is a few lines of validation and it is the difference between an alert and a global outage.
🔍9. Deep dives, and what breaks

Why the audit log is harder than it looks

“Record every block” sounds trivial until you consider the volume. A denial-of-service attempt can produce hundreds of thousands of blocks per second — the blocked traffic is, by definition, the traffic with the highest rate.

Writing each one synchronously would make the block path slower than the allow path, which is exactly backwards: an attacker could then degrade the edge by sending traffic they know will be blocked.

So blocks are buffered locally and shipped asynchronously, and under extreme load they are sampled and aggregated — one record per (range, minute) with a count, rather than one per request. The individual records are indistinguishable anyway.

The property to preserve is that every distinct rule that fired is recorded, which is what audit and appeal actually need. Recording every individual request is a volume problem with no corresponding benefit.

IPv6, which changes the arithmetic

The trie handles it — 128 bits instead of 32, so at most 128 steps, still bounded and still fast.

What changes is the blocking strategy. An IPv4 address is scarce enough that banning one means something. In IPv6 a single customer is routinely allocated a /64, which is more addresses than the entire IPv4 internet. Banning one IPv6 address is meaningless — the sender simply uses the next one.

So IPv6 bans operate on prefixes, typically /64 or /48, treating the allocation rather than the address as the unit of identity. Getting that wrong produces a denylist that grows without bound and blocks nothing.

Expiry, and why it is a compile-time concern

Temporary bans need to lapse, and the edge must not be checking timestamps per request — that is work on the hot path, and it would mean the trie contains entries that are present but inactive.

Instead expiry is resolved when the snapshot is compiled: expired entries are simply not included. The trie contains only currently-active rules, so the lookup stays a pure structural match with no time comparison at all.

The consequence is that expiry granularity equals rebuild frequency. A ban expiring at 14:30:15 is actually lifted at the next compile after that, up to thirty seconds later. Entirely acceptable, and worth stating rather than implying precision the design does not provide.

When the list stops fitting in memory

The whole design rests on 8 MB. It is worth being explicit about where that stops holding, because an interviewer may push on it.

At tens of millions of individual addresses — not ranges — the structure grows past what is comfortable to hold in every process. The answer then is the same shape as D10's seen-set: a Bloom filter in memory as a cheap negative test, with a confirming lookup for the small fraction that the filter says might match.

Most traffic is not on the denylist, so most requests are settled by the filter with no I/O. Only possible matches pay for the confirmation, and a false positive costs a lookup rather than a wrong decision.

That preserves the important property — no network call on the common path — while relaxing the memory requirement. Naming the threshold and the next design is better than claiming the current one scales forever.

What breaks

Control plane entirely down
Edges keep serving the last good snapshot indefinitely. Bans stop getting fresher, which is a degradation nobody notices for hours — the correct behaviour for an auxiliary system.
Third-party feed publishes garbage
Sanity limits reject the delta before it is built into a snapshot, and the previous snapshot stays live. Alert loudly: a rejected feed is a real incident even though nothing broke.
A legitimate large network is banned
The allowlist overrides by longest-prefix match and propagates in one poll interval, so the remedy is fast. This is why manual allow entries exist separately from feed data and are never overwritten by it.
Snapshot is corrupt or truncated
Snapshots are content-hashed and the edge verifies before swapping. A failed verification means keeping the current trie — never load a partially parsed denylist, which would silently allow or block arbitrarily.
Edge memory pressure from IPv6 growth
IPv6 tries are deeper and larger. Cap entries, prefer aggregated prefixes over individual /128s, and alert on snapshot size growth — an OOM on the edge is an outage caused by the protective system itself.
The dominant constraint

The dataset is small enough to live everywhere. A million rules compress to about 8 MB, so the check is a local memory lookup rather than a network call — which removes both the latency and the dependency that the obvious design would add to 100% of traffic.

What I would build first

The radix trie and the pull-based snapshot distribution. Together they make the hot path zero-hop and make control-plane availability irrelevant to serving.

What I deliberately did not build

Per-request auditing and real-time streaming updates. Both sound thorough and both add cost far out of proportion to their value here.

The biggest risk

The upstream feed. It is untrusted input with the power to block everyone, and the sanity limits on ingestion are the only thing standing between a bad publish and a total outage.

💬 If you get this far, here is what they will push on
Follow-ups an interviewer is likely to ask once the design is on the board. Answers supplied — read the question, answer it out loud, then open it.
“Why not just call a denylist service on each request?”Answer

Because it puts a network round trip on 100% of traffic and creates a dependency that can take the whole site down — for a component whose entire job is protective.

A million CIDR rules compress to about 8 MB as a radix trie, which fits in every edge process's memory. So the check becomes a function call with zero network hops.

Recognising that the dataset is small enough to replicate everywhere is the whole answer to this question.

“The feed publishes a rule that blocks the entire internet. Then what?”Answer

Applied faithfully, you have taken your own site down with somebody else's data. So the feed is untrusted input and ingestion is a validation step, not a copy.

Reject any delta that would ban more than a small fraction of address space, or that removes most existing rules, or that contains a prefix broader than a configured maximum. Subtract the allowlist last.

Edges keep the last good snapshot, so a rejected feed is an alert rather than an outage.

“Should it fail open or fail closed?”Answer

Fail open, almost always, and the reasoning is blast radius. Failing closed means an outage in an auxiliary protective component becomes a total outage of your service, which is a far bigger harm than a window of unblocked abuse.

The exception is when the block is a legal control — a sanctions list — where serving a blocked party is the greater harm.

That is a business decision and should be surfaced as one rather than assumed by the engineer.

“How do you audit blocks without drowning in data?”Answer

At 500,000 requests a second, even a 1% block rate is 5,000 audit rows a second, which is a bigger data problem than the traffic you are protecting.

So sample the high-volume automated blocks, and keep every block that came from a manual rule, because those are the ones a human will be asked to justify.

Per-rule counters give you the operational picture without a row per event.

Design a Distributed Sort (“the data set does not fit in memory and you have many workers”)

Difficulty: Medium-Hard  .  Target: 35 min
💬 The question, as asked

“You have a data set far too large to fit in memory on one machine, and many workers. How do you sort it?”

⚡ What makes it hard

Real keys are always skewed, so an evenly divided key space sends most rows to one worker and the job takes as long as that worker does. The fix costs minutes and is the step people skip.

📋1. Understanding the question

The prompt: “You have a data set far too large to fit in memory on one machine, and many workers. How do you sort it?”

This is the most algorithmic question in the guide, and it still turns on a systems judgement rather than an algorithm.

Start with one machine

Before distributing anything, solve the smaller version: how does one machine sort 100 GB with 16 GB of RAM?

You cannot load it, so you sort it in pieces. Read 16 GB, sort it in memory, write it out. Repeat until you have several sorted files on disk. Then merge them: read a little from the front of each, repeatedly take the smallest, and write out a single sorted stream.

The merge is the clever part, because it needs almost no memory. You only ever hold the front of each run, so merging seven 16 GB files uses a few megabytes of buffer. That is external sorting, and the distributed version is the same idea with the network in the middle.

The distributed version, and where it goes wrong

With 100 workers, the obvious plan: give each worker a range of the key space, have everyone send each row to the worker owning its range, and let each worker sort what it received. Concatenate the outputs and the whole thing is sorted.

It is correct, and it fails in practice for one reason.

🎯 Real keys are always skewed

Divide the key space evenly and you have assumed the data is spread evenly across it. It never is.

Sort by surname and the worker holding S–T gets far more than the one holding Q–R. Sort by country and one worker gets China. Sort by customer and one worker gets your largest account. Sort by URL and one worker gets an entire domain.

The job then takes as long as the most loaded worker. Ninety-nine workers finish in ten minutes and one runs for three hours. You have 100 machines and the throughput of one.

The fix is to look at the data before deciding the ranges: sample a small fraction, see where the keys actually fall, and choose boundaries that give each worker an equal share of rows rather than an equal share of key space.

It costs a few minutes and it is the step people skip. Everything else here is mechanical.

What they are looking for

Do you raise skew unprompted? This is the question.

Do you know the merge is memory-bounded? It is what makes external sorting work at all.

Do you ask what “sorted” means? Globally ordered output is much stricter than sorted files in order, and downstream consumers usually only need the latter.

❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
Does the whole result need to be globally sorted, or only partitioned?
A globally ordered single output is much stricter than “each output file is sorted and files are in order”. Downstream consumers usually only need the latter, and it is far cheaper.
What is the key distribution?
Uniform keys make range partitioning trivial. Skewed keys — and real keys are always skewed — are the entire difficulty, because one reducer gets everything.
Is this one-off or recurring?
A recurring job justifies sampling, tuning and a stored partition map. A one-off should use the simplest thing that finishes.
Where does the data live and where must the output go?
If input and output are the same object store, network shuffle is the cost. If workers have local disks, spilling changes the arithmetic.
Are duplicate keys significant, and must the sort be stable?
Stability constrains how you merge and rules out some parallel shortcuts.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.
📝2. Functional requirements
  • Sort a data set far larger than any machine's memory, by a specified key.
  • Produce globally ordered output across partitions.
  • Tolerate a worker dying mid-job without restarting from scratch.

What "globally ordered" is allowed to mean

Worth pinning down, because the two readings differ enormously in cost.

Strict: one output stream, fully ordered end to end. Producing it means a final merge through a single point, which is a serial step that undoes much of the parallelism you just bought.

Practical: N output files, each internally sorted, where every key in file 3 is less than every key in file 4. Reading them in order gives a globally sorted stream, and each was written in parallel with no final merge at all.

Almost every real consumer is happy with the second, because reading files in order is trivial. Asking which is needed can remove a serial bottleneck from the design, which is precisely the kind of question worth asking.

Fault tolerance, which changes the job structure

A ten-thousand-worker-minute job will lose a worker. If that restarts everything, long jobs never finish — the probability of completing without a failure falls as the job grows.

So work is divided into independently retryable tasks whose outputs are written durably. A dead worker's tasks are re-run on another machine and everything else is untouched. That requirement is what makes the intermediate shuffle output something you materialise rather than stream — a real cost, paid deliberately.

⏱3. Non-functional requirements
RequirementTargetWhat it forces
Memory per workerBoundedThe job must never depend on fitting in RAM. This is what makes it external sorting rather than sorting.
Skew toleranceNo worker dominatesThe requirement the naive design fails. It is why sampling exists.
Scaling~Linear in workersUntil the network saturates. The shuffle is the wall.
Worker failureRe-run one taskNot the job. Requires durable intermediate output.
Shuffle volume~Input size, onceEvery row crosses the network exactly once. That is the floor, and it sets the minimum runtime.

The shuffle floor

The one piece of arithmetic worth doing early, because it bounds everything.

Every row must travel from the worker that read it to the worker that will sort its range. That is the entire data set crossing the network, once. Ten terabytes over a hundred workers at 10 Gbps each is roughly two hours, and no amount of algorithmic cleverness reduces it.

So the network, not the CPU, is the bottleneck, and the optimisations that matter are the ones that move fewer bytes: compress the shuffle, drop unneeded columns before shuffling, and combine locally first where the operation allows it.

Establishing that the job is network-bound in the first two minutes is what stops the discussion drifting into comparison-sort micro-optimisation.

🗂4. Data model and API

There is no schema. There is a partition map, and it is the only shared state in the job.

-- The partition map is the artefact that decides whether this job -- finishes in two hours or twenty. It is built by SAMPLING, not -- by assuming a uniform key space. TABLE partition_map { job_id UUID, partition INT, key_start BYTES, -- inclusive key_end BYTES, -- exclusive est_bytes BIGINT, -- from the sample PRIMARY KEY (job_id, partition) } -- Boundaries are chosen so est_bytes is roughly EQUAL per partition, -- not so the key ranges are equal. Equal key ranges on skewed data -- is exactly how one reducer ends up with 80% of the rows. TABLE tasks { job_id UUID, task_id INT, kind ENUM(map, merge), attempt INT, worker VARCHAR, state ENUM(pending, running, done, failed), output_prefix TEXT, -- includes attempt: .../task7/attempt2/ PRIMARY KEY (job_id, task_id, attempt) } -- Attempt-scoped output paths are what make retries safe: a -- zombie worker writes to a path nobody will ever read.

The partition map is a list of key boundaries: keys below B go to worker 0, B to F to worker 1, and so on. Every worker holds the same copy, so routing a row is a local decision — a binary search over a hundred boundaries — with no coordination.

It is tiny. A hundred boundaries is kilobytes. And it is the entire mechanism that makes the output globally ordered: because the ranges are disjoint and increasing, concatenating the workers' outputs in order gives a sorted result.

Choosing the boundaries by sampling

The boundaries are not chosen by dividing the key space. They are chosen by looking at the data.

Read a small random sample — a fraction of a percent is plenty — sort it, and take evenly spaced values from the sorted sample as the boundaries. If 12% of the sample falls below “B”, roughly 12% of the data does too, so the first boundary lands where 1% of the sample sits rather than at an arbitrary letter.

The result is equal numbers of rows per worker, not equal key ranges. Which is exactly the property that makes the job finish in the time of the average worker rather than the worst one.

The sample must be random across the whole input, not the first N rows. Input files are frequently already ordered by something, and sampling the head of the data gives boundaries that describe one corner of it — a mistake that produces worse skew than not sampling at all.

What the intermediate output looks like

Each map task writes one file per partition: a hundred small sorted files. A reduce task then reads its own file from every map task — ten thousand small reads in total for a hundred-by-hundred job.

That fan-out is why shuffle is operationally painful, and why the number of small files, not the bytes, is often what actually limits a large job.

The API

POST /v1/sorts Body: { input_prefix, output_prefix, key_spec, order, workers, sample_rate } Response: 201 { job_id, state:"sampling" } GET /v1/sorts/{id} Response: { state, phase:"sample|map|shuffle|merge", partitions:[{ id, bytes, state, worker }], skew_ratio } // max partition / mean partition // skew_ratio is the number to watch: above ~3 the job is // waiting on one straggler and the partition map was wrong. // WORKER-FACING POST /internal/tasks/claim -> { task_id, kind, inputs[], attempt } POST /internal/tasks/report Body: { task_id, state, output_refs[] } // tasks are idempotent and write to attempt-scoped paths, so a // duplicate execution is harmless -- see the fault table
📊5. Capacity estimation

The numbers, and the two conclusions they force.

⚖ Assumptions — and what breaks if each is wrong
10 TB input, 100 workers with 16 GB RAM each
Total RAM is 1.6 TB against 10 TB of data, so the data cannot be held in memory even collectively. That is what forces external sorting.
Keys are skewed, as real keys always are
Uniform keys would make fixed-range partitioning correct and sampling unnecessary.
The network is the bottleneck, not the CPU
On very fast interconnects, comparison cost can dominate instead and merge strategy matters more.
10 TB
input size
1.6 TB
total cluster RAM
~100 GB
per worker share
~6×
spill passes at 16 GB
10 TB
bytes crossing the network once
~2.2 h
shuffle floor at 10 Gbps

The data does not fit, even collectively. Ten terabytes against a hundred workers with 16 GB each is 1.6 TB of total RAM — about a sixth of the data. So this is external sorting not just per worker but cluster-wide, and every stage must be designed to spill to disk.

Each worker's share is around 100 GB against 16 GB of memory, which means roughly six sorted runs per worker and a merge over them. Six is a comfortable merge width; a thousand would not be, which is where multi-pass merging becomes necessary.

The shuffle sets the floor. Ten terabytes crossing the network once, at 10 Gbps per node, is about two hours if the network is perfectly utilised — and it never is. That is the minimum runtime, and it is worth stating before anyone optimises the comparison function.

How many partitions

A real decision with a trade on both sides.

Too few and each partition exceeds what a worker can handle efficiently, forcing deeper spilling, and there is no room to rebalance if the sample was slightly off.

Too many and the small-file problem dominates: a thousand-by-thousand shuffle is a million intermediate files, and the per-file overhead swamps the actual data movement.

A few times the worker count is the usual answer. It keeps per-partition size manageable and gives the scheduler room to hand extra partitions to workers that finish early — which is, incidentally, a second and cheaper defence against mild skew.

⚖6. The key trade-offs

The choices, and their costs.

DecisionChosen ✓Alternative ✗Reasoning
PartitioningRange partition from a sampleEqual key ranges, or hashEqual ranges collapse on skewed data. Hash partitioning balances beautifully but destroys order, so the output is not globally sorted.
Sort strategyExternal merge sort with spillsSort in memoryThe data is larger than total cluster RAM. Any design that assumes it fits is answering a different question.
Global orderFalls out of partition boundariesA final merge of all partitionsA single final merge is a serial bottleneck through one machine. Ordered partitions give the same result with no coordination.
RetriesAttempt-scoped output pathsLocking a task to one workerA slow worker is indistinguishable from a dead one. Idempotent output makes duplicate execution harmless instead of dangerous.
StragglersSpeculative duplicate tasksWaitThe last few tasks dominate tail runtime, and duplication is cheap once tasks are idempotent.

Sampling: a few minutes against hours of straggler

The central trade, and it is lopsided enough to be easy.

Sampling costs a pass over a small fraction of the input — minutes on a ten-terabyte job. Skipping it risks one worker receiving many times its share and running for hours after everyone else has finished.

The reason anyone skips it is that it adds a serial stage: everyone waits while the sample is collected and the boundaries computed. On a job that would otherwise start immediately, that feels like pure overhead, and on uniformly distributed keys it is.

The rule worth stating: sample unless you have measured the distribution and know it is uniform. Assuming uniformity is how you end up with the 99-idle-workers outcome, and the assumption is almost never true of real keys.

Materialise the shuffle, or stream it

Materialising — map tasks write their partitioned output to disk, reduce tasks read it — means a dead reducer simply re-reads the data that is still sitting there. Recovery is cheap and local.

The cost is a full write and read of the entire data set: significant I/O, and the reduce phase cannot begin until the map phase finishes, so the two do not overlap.

Streaming — map tasks send rows directly to reducers — avoids that I/O and overlaps the phases, so the job is meaningfully faster. But if a reducer dies, the data it was receiving is gone, and the map tasks that produced it must be re-run.

The failure probability is what decides it. A ten-minute job on twenty workers can afford to stream and occasionally redo everything. A six-hour job on a thousand workers will lose a worker, so materialising is the only structure that finishes.

This is a general pattern worth naming: checkpointing trades throughput for recoverability, and the right amount depends on the expected number of failures during the job.

🏗7. High-level design
External sort — and the key skew that makes one reducer the whole job
boundariesshuffled datamerged outputskewed partition
What is moving: a small random sample first, to choose partition boundaries with roughly equal bytes per range; then the data itself, sorted in memory, spilled as runs, and shuffled to the reducer that owns its range. Ordering falls out of the boundaries — no reducer ever compares against another.
What goes wrong: skip the sample and split the key space evenly, and a skewed distribution sends most rows to one reducer. The job’s runtime becomes that single worker’s runtime. Worse, if a single key value exceeds a partition’s budget, no boundary choice helps — it cannot be split without breaking the sort, and needs special handling or an accepted straggler.

Three phases, and one of them is optional-looking and essential.

PHASE 0 — SAMPLE the step people skip read ~0.1% at random from across the whole input sort the sample take evenly spaced values as boundaries | v PARTITION MAP kilobytes, identical on every worker keys < "B" → worker 0 "B" .. "F" → worker 1 equal ROWS, not equal key ranges ... PHASE 1 — MAP parallel, one task per input split read split → for each row, binary-search the map → route → buffer per partition → sort each buffer, write one file per partition 100 map tasks × 100 partitions = 10,000 intermediate files PHASE 2 — SHUFFLE + REDUCE the network floor lives here reducer 7 fetches its file from all 100 mappers | v MERGE 100 sorted streams → one sorted output holds only the head of each stream: megabytes, not gigabytes | v output-00007 sorted, and every key < those in output-00008 concatenating outputs 0..99 in order = globally sorted
No final merge step exists, and that is the point: because the partition ranges are disjoint and increasing, the parallel outputs are already in order relative to each other.
🔄8. Workflows — what actually happens
Sorting 10 TB of web logs by URL
The whole job, end to end.
  1. Sample. Each worker reads a random 0.1% of its assigned splits — about 10 GB total. These are collected and sorted centrally: a small, fast job.
  2. Ninety-nine boundaries are picked at evenly spaced points in the sorted sample, producing 100 partitions with roughly equal row counts. The map is broadcast to every worker.
  3. Map. Each worker reads its 100 GB share. For every row it binary-searches the partition map and appends to the right in-memory buffer.
  4. When a buffer fills, it is sorted and written out. Each worker ends up with 100 sorted files — one per partition.
  5. Shuffle. Reducer 7 fetches file 7 from all 100 mappers. This is where the two-hour network floor is spent.
  6. Merge. It merges those 100 sorted streams into one output, holding only the head of each — a few megabytes of buffer for 100 GB of output.
  7. Every reducer does the same in parallel. The 100 output files, read in order, are a globally sorted 10 TB data set.
Notice there is no final merge. The partition map guaranteed the ordering between files before a single row moved, which is what keeps the last phase fully parallel.
The same job without sampling
What the skipped step costs.
  1. Boundaries are chosen by dividing the key space evenly — for URLs, by splitting the alphabet into 100 equal slices.
  2. Map runs normally. Nothing looks wrong; the phase completes in the usual time.
  3. Shuffle begins and the imbalance appears. One partition covers a range containing a handful of enormous domains and receives 4 TB instead of 100 GB.
  4. Ninety-nine reducers finish their 100 GB in about ten minutes.
  5. Reducer 43 is still merging. With 4 TB against 16 GB of memory it needs many more spill passes, so it is not 40× slower — it is worse than that.
  6. It may not finish at all: if the partition exceeds its local disk, the task fails, is retried on another worker, and fails there too. The job is stuck, and retrying cannot help because the problem is the partitioning.
The failure is not graceful. It is not "the job is a bit slower" but "one task cannot complete and retrying it changes nothing" — which is why sampling is worth a few minutes on any job where the distribution is unknown.
One key is 30% of the data
Where sampling is not enough.
  1. Sorting by customer id, and one customer accounts for 30% of all rows.
  2. Sampling detects this correctly — the boundaries will try to give that key its own partition.
  3. It does not help. A single key cannot be split across partitions without breaking the sort, so one reducer gets 3 TB no matter how the boundaries are drawn.
  4. This is the limit of range partitioning, and recognising it is the point: no choice of boundaries fixes a single dominant key.
  5. One escape: if the sort key is composite — customer then timestamp — the heavy key can be split on the secondary field, giving multiple partitions with ordered sub-ranges.
  6. Another: handle that key separately. Route it to a dedicated set of workers that sort it among themselves, and merge the result back at the correct position.
  7. And sometimes the right answer is to question the requirement. If downstream only needs rows grouped by customer, sorting within each customer independently is a much cheaper job.
Worth being able to say plainly: sampling fixes uneven distribution across keys and does nothing for concentration on one key. That distinction — the same one as the hot key in D12 and the stadium in D9 — recurs throughout distributed systems.
A worker dies during the reduce phase
Why the intermediate output was written to disk.
  1. Reducer 43 is 70% through merging when its machine fails.
  2. Its partial output is discarded — it was never complete and cannot be resumed from the middle.
  3. But its inputs still exist: the 100 intermediate files written by the map tasks are sitting in durable storage, untouched.
  4. The scheduler assigns partition 43 to another worker. It fetches the same files and redoes the merge.
  5. Cost: one reducer's work, perhaps ten minutes. The other 99 partitions are unaffected and the map phase is not re-run.
  6. Had the shuffle been streamed rather than materialised, those 100 map tasks would have had to re-run to regenerate the data — an hour of work instead of ten minutes.
This is the recoverability that the materialised shuffle was paid for. On a short job the extra I/O is not worth it; on a job long enough that a failure is likely, it is the difference between finishing and restarting.
🔍9. Deep dives, and what breaks

Why the merge needs so little memory

The property that makes external sorting possible, and it is worth being able to state precisely.

To merge N sorted streams you only need the current front element of each. Take the smallest, emit it, advance that stream, repeat. At no point do you hold more than N elements — plus whatever buffer you use to read efficiently.

So merging a hundred 100 GB files needs a few megabytes, not ten terabytes. Memory is proportional to the number of streams, not their size.

Which is also why merge width matters. With a thousand streams, the per-stream read buffer shrinks until reads become inefficiently small, and you are better off merging in two passes — groups of thirty, then thirty results — reading more data twice but reading it in larger chunks. The crossover depends on the storage, and knowing that it exists is the useful part.

Stragglers, and speculative execution

Even with perfect partitioning, one task will be slow: a degraded disk, a noisy neighbour, a machine that is simply worse.

Since the job finishes when its last task does, one slow task extends everything. The standard answer is speculative execution: when a task is running far slower than its peers, start a second copy elsewhere and take whichever finishes first.

It costs a small amount of duplicated work and removes the long tail. It only works because tasks are idempotent — running the same partition twice and discarding one result must be harmless, which it is here because the output is deterministic and written atomically.

It also cannot fix a partition that is genuinely too large. Speculating a task that is slow because it has 4 TB of data just runs two slow tasks, which is a useful diagnostic: if speculation does not help, the problem is data, not hardware.

Compressing the shuffle

Since the job is network-bound, the highest-leverage optimisation is moving fewer bytes.

Compressing intermediate output typically trades a little CPU — which is idle, since the bottleneck is the network — for a substantial reduction in bytes. On text-like data a 3–4× reduction is ordinary, which turns a two-hour shuffle floor into well under an hour.

The fast-but-weak compressors are the right choice here rather than the strong-but-slow ones: the goal is to keep the network busy, not to minimise size. A compressor that halves the bytes at negligible CPU cost beats one that quarters them while becoming the new bottleneck.

Dropping columns before the shuffle is even better where the sort only needs a subset — bytes never sent cost nothing at all.

What breaks

A worker dies mid-task
Its task is reassigned and rerun from the input split. Only that task’s work is lost, not the job — which is the whole reason for splitting work into independently retryable units.
A worker is slow but alive
Speculative execution starts a duplicate; the first to finish commits. Attempt-scoped outputs mean the loser’s bytes are inert rather than corrupting.
Partition skew discovered mid-job
Monitor the skew ratio during shuffle. A badly skewed map is worth aborting and resampling early; discovering it at the merge phase means the job has already paid the shuffle cost.
Disk fills during spilling
Bound the number of runs per worker and merge intermediate runs early to reclaim space. Running out of disk mid-merge fails the task late, after the most expensive phase.
Coordinator fails
Task state is in a durable store, so a replacement resumes from it. In-flight tasks complete and report; the coordinator holds no state that cannot be rebuilt.
The dominant constraint

The data is bigger than the cluster’s total memory. That forces an external sort — spill sorted runs, then merge with bounded buffers — and it means at least one full pass of the data across the network, which is the floor on runtime.

What I would build first

The sampling phase and the partition map. Minutes of work that decide whether the job finishes in hours or hangs on one straggler for a day.

What I deliberately did not build

A globally strict single output file, and hash partitioning. The first serialises the job through one machine; the second balances perfectly and destroys the ordering the job exists to produce.

The biggest risk

Key skew that sampling cannot fix. A single value larger than a partition budget cannot be split, and no amount of boundary tuning helps — it needs special handling or an accepted straggler.

💬 If you get this far, here is what they will push on
Follow-ups an interviewer is likely to ask once the design is on the board. Answers supplied — read the question, answer it out loud, then open it.
“Why sample first? It sounds like wasted work.”Answer

It costs minutes and routinely saves hours. Dividing the key space into equal ranges assumes a uniform distribution that real data never has.

If 40% of keys share a prefix, one reducer receives 40% of the data and the job takes as long as that single worker. Reading a small random sample and choosing boundaries at its quantiles gives partitions of roughly equal size, which is what actually matters.

Skipping the sample is the single most common way this question is answered badly.

“What if one key alone is bigger than a partition?”Answer

Then no boundary choice helps, and saying so is better than pretending sampling solves everything. A single key cannot be split across partitions without breaking the sort.

The options are to handle that key specially — sort its records separately and concatenate, since they are all equal on the sort key anyway — or to accept the straggler.

It is the same hot-key problem as Ch 5, with the same shape: partitioning distributes keys, not load.

“A worker is slow but not dead. Do you wait?”Answer

No. Near the end of a phase, when most tasks are done and a few are lagging, start duplicate copies of the slow ones and take whichever finishes first.

This is cheap precisely because tasks are already idempotent: each attempt writes to its own output path and the coordinator records which one won, so the loser's bytes are inert.

It protects against the far more common cause of a slow task, which is a degraded machine rather than skewed data.

“Why not hash partition? It balances perfectly.”Answer

It does, and it destroys the ordering that the job exists to produce. Hashing scatters adjacent keys across unrelated partitions, so the output is sorted within each partition but the partitions have no relationship to each other.

Range partitioning is what makes the global order fall out of the boundaries: each partition is sorted independently, and concatenating them in order gives a sorted result with no cross-worker comparison at all.

Design Degrees of Connection (“is this profile 1st, 2nd or 3rd degree?” at LinkedIn scale)

Difficulty: Hard (Staff Expectation)  .  Target: 40 min
💬 The question, as asked

“On a professional network, a search results page must instantly show whether each profile is a first-, second- or third-degree connection.”

⚡ What makes it hard

The arithmetic kills the obvious approach: at 500 connections each, third degree is about 125 million people per viewer. It cannot be precomputed and cannot be cached.

📋1. Understanding the question

The prompt: “On a professional network, a search results page must instantly show whether each profile is a first-, second- or third-degree connection.”

Do the arithmetic before anything else, because it eliminates the two designs everyone reaches for first.

🎯 The numbers that decide the design

With an average of 500 connections per member:

  • First degree: 500 people. Trivial — a set lookup.
  • Second degree: 500 × 500 ≈ 250,000. Large, and storable — a few megabytes as a compact set.
  • Third degree: 500 × 250,000 ≈ 125 million. For one viewer. Across a billion members that is not storable by any margin.

So third degree cannot be precomputed and cannot be cached. Whatever answers it has to work differently.

The insight that makes it possible

You do not need to enumerate the third-degree neighbourhood. You need to answer a yes/no question about one specific person.

And “is P within three hops of V?” can be answered without exploring 125 million people, because of a simple observation: if there is a path of length 3 from V to P, then somewhere along it there is a midpoint. Specifically, V's second-degree set and P's first-degree set must intersect.

Both of those are small. V's second-degree set is 250,000 — a set we can hold. P's connections are 500 — a list we can fetch. Testing 500 members against a 250,000-element set is 500 cheap lookups.

That is the whole design: meet in the middle, from both ends, so neither side ever grows large. The expensive set is never built.

And the constraint that makes it harder

This is not one lookup. It renders inline with a page of search results, so it is 25 answers in one request, in under 50 milliseconds. That changes the per-item budget to about two milliseconds, and it rules out doing 25 independent graph traversals.

The saving grace is that all 25 share the same viewer, so V's second-degree set is fetched once and reused for every profile on the page.

What they are looking for

Do you do the 125-million arithmetic? Early, and conclude precomputation is out?

Do you find the meet-in-the-middle? This is the question.

Do you handle the members with 30,000 connections? Their neighbourhoods break every assumption above.

❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
How many degrees do we need — and is 3 the maximum?
This is the whole design. Degrees 1 and 2 are cheap; degree 3 is where the neighbourhood explodes and precomputation stops being possible.
Is this shown on a profile view, or on a search results page?
One profile is a single query. A results page needs the degree for 25 profiles at once, which is a batch problem with a much tighter per-item budget.
Is the answer allowed to be slightly stale?
A connection made five seconds ago not yet showing as 1st degree is almost always acceptable, and that tolerance is what makes caching viable.
Do we need the connecting path, or just the number?
“You are connected via Priya” is a much more expensive query than “2nd degree”, because it needs an actual path, not just its existence.
What is the degree distribution at the top end?
A user with 30,000 connections has a second-degree neighbourhood in the tens of millions. Those users break every naive approach and must be handled explicitly.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.
📝2. Functional requirements
  • Given a viewer and a profile, return 1, 2, 3, or “out of network”.
  • Answer for a page of about 25 profiles in one request.
  • Reflect new connections within seconds.

The asymmetry in what a wrong answer costs

Worth stating because it shapes every caching decision that follows.

Showing someone as further away than they are — 3rd degree when they are actually 2nd — is a missed opportunity. The user does not notice; nothing looks broken.

Showing someone as closer than they are — 2nd degree when there is no such connection — is visibly wrong. The user clicks through expecting a shared contact, finds none, and now distrusts the feature.

So staleness must err outward. A connection made five seconds ago not yet showing as 1st degree is fine. A connection removed five seconds ago still showing as 1st degree is not. Which means removals need to invalidate promptly while additions can propagate lazily — an asymmetry worth building in deliberately rather than discovering later.

Path or just the number?

A clarifying question with a large consequence. “2nd degree” requires only proving an intersection exists. “You are connected via Priya” requires producing an actual path and then fetching and ranking the shared contacts.

The first is a boolean; the second is a query. Scoping to the number for the results page — and computing the path only on the profile page, where there is one target and a larger budget — is the right split.

⏱3. Non-functional requirements
RequirementTargetWhat it forces
Batch latencyp99 < 50 ms for 25Renders inline with search results. About 2 ms per profile, which rules out 25 separate traversals.
Scale1B members, ~500 edgesAround 500 GB of edge data compressed — large, but distributable across memory.
2nd-degree set~250K per memberStorable. This is the number that makes the design work.
3rd-degree set~125M — unusableThe number that rules out precomputation and forces meet-in-the-middle.
FreshnessSecondsAnd asymmetric: removals must propagate faster than additions.
Error directionToo far, never too closeStale in the safe direction. An inflated degree is invisible; a deflated one is a visible bug.

Why the batch requirement is the hard part

A single lookup in 50 ms would be comfortable. Twenty-five in 50 ms is not, if each is independent.

What rescues it is that they share a viewer. The expensive object — V's second-degree set — is built or fetched once and then used 25 times. The per-profile work drops to fetching one connection list and doing 500 set lookups, which is well under a millisecond.

This is a generally useful framing: when a batch shares a parameter, find the work that depends only on that parameter and hoist it. Here it turns an impossible per-item budget into a comfortable one.

🗂4. Data model and API

Two things to store: the edges, and the derived second-degree sets.

-- Adjacency, sharded by member. Both directions are stored, because -- "who is connected to X" must be answerable without a scan. TABLE edges { member_id BIGINT, peer_id BIGINT, created_at TIMESTAMP, PRIMARY KEY (member_id, peer_id) } -- Partition key is member_id, so one member's whole adjacency list -- is a single-shard read. This is the one access pattern that must -- never fan out. -- 2nd-degree set, cached as a compressed bitmap / roaring set. -- ~250K member IDs compress to a few hundred KB, which is small -- enough to fetch and intersect in single-digit milliseconds. CACHE second_degree { key: member_id value: RoaringBitmap(member_ids), built_at, edge_version ttl: hours, invalidated on connection change } -- No 3rd-degree cache exists. 125M IDs per member is ~500 MB per -- user even compressed; storing it for 1B members is absurd. -- Degree 3 is COMPUTED, never stored.

Edges, stored as sorted integer lists

The connection graph is symmetric — connections are mutual — so each member has one list of neighbours. A billion members at 500 connections is 500 billion directed edges.

Stored naively as 8-byte ids, that is terabytes. Two things shrink it dramatically: member ids are integers, and each list can be kept sorted, so consecutive ids can be stored as small deltas rather than full values. The same delta-encoding idea as the time-series stores in D11, applied to ids rather than timestamps.

Sorted lists also make intersection cheap — a linear merge rather than a nested loop — which matters for the path queries.

Second-degree sets, and why they are approximate

The 250,000-member second-degree set is fetched on almost every request, so it wants to be small and fast rather than exact.

Stored as explicit ids it is around 1 MB — workable, but a lot to ship per request. Stored as a Bloom filter it is a few hundred kilobytes with a small false-positive rate, and membership testing is a handful of hash computations with no allocation.

The false positives are acceptable only because of the error asymmetry stated in step 2 — wait, in the wrong direction. A Bloom filter false positive says “this person is in your second-degree set” when they are not, which is the unsafe direction: it shows someone as closer than they are.

So the filter is used as a cheap first pass, not as the answer. A negative is definitive and settles the vast majority of profiles immediately. A positive triggers an exact check against the real set, which is rare enough to afford. Same structure as the crawler's seen-set in D10: cheap probabilistic filter in front, exact confirmation behind.

The API

POST /v1/degrees:batch Body: { viewer_id, target_ids:[ ...up to 100... ] } Response: 200 { results:{ target_id: { degree: 1|2|3|null, via?: [member_id] } } } // batch by construction: a search results page needs 25 at once, // and 25 separate round trips cannot fit a 50 ms budget GET /v1/connections/{member}?cursor= -> paged 1st-degree list POST /v1/connections Body: { a, b } // creates an undirected edge // invalidates the 2nd-degree cache for a, b and all their // 1st-degree neighbours -- the expensive part of a write

The API is deliberately batch-first. A single-profile endpoint would invite callers to loop, and looping is precisely what the latency budget cannot afford.

📊5. Capacity estimation

The numbers, restated as design conclusions.

⚖ Assumptions — and what breaks if each is wrong
1B members, ~500 connections average
At 50 average the second-degree set fits comfortably and the whole design simplifies.
Answers may be seconds stale
Strict freshness would remove caching and force every query to hit the graph store.
Degree 3 is the maximum required
Degree 4 makes the neighbourhood approach the whole graph and the question stops being answerable this way.
1B
members
~500
average connections
~250K
2nd-degree neighbourhood
~125M
3rd degree — unusable
~500 GB
edge list, compressed
50 ms
p99 for a batch of 25

First degree: 500. Fetch the list, check membership. Nothing to design.

Second degree: ~250,000. A megabyte as explicit ids, a few hundred kilobytes as a filter. Cacheable per member, rebuildable in milliseconds from the edge store. This is the number that makes everything work.

Third degree: ~125 million. Per viewer. At a billion members, storing these would be more data than exists in the rest of the product by orders of magnitude. Not large — impossible, and saying so plainly is what forces the better approach.

The edge data overall is around 500 GB compressed. Too much for one machine, comfortable across a sharded in-memory tier — and partitioned by member id, since every query starts from a member.

The degree distribution is the real risk

All of the above uses the average, and a social graph's degree distribution is extremely skewed.

A member with 30,000 connections has a second-degree neighbourhood in the tens of millions rather than 250,000. Every assumption above fails for them: the set is not cacheable, the filter is not small, and building it is not a millisecond operation.

They are rare and they are also disproportionately likely to appear in results and to be doing searches. Designing for the average and discovering the tail in production is the standard failure here, which is why “what is the degree distribution at the top end?” belongs in the clarifying questions.

⚖6. The key trade-offs

The choices, and their costs.

DecisionChosen ✓Alternative ✗Reasoning
Degree 3Meet in the middle (2 from viewer + 1 from target)Expand 3 hops from the viewerThree hops is ~125M members. Bidirectional search gives the identical answer for a few hundred operations.
2nd-degree setCached compressed bitmapComputed per requestRecomputing 250K members per query cannot meet 50 ms, and the same set is reused across all 25 targets on the page.
High-degree membersExpand from the smaller sideCache everything uniformlyA 30K-connection member has a tens-of-millions neighbourhood. Symmetry of the relation lets you choose the cheap end instead.
InvalidationLazy, version-stampedEager recompute on every edgeOne new connection dirties ~1,000 cached sets, most of which will never be read before changing again.
FreshnessStale additions, immediate removalsUniform TTLDegree gates profile visibility, so being one degree too far is harmless and being too close is a privacy incident.

Precompute, traverse, or meet in the middle

Precompute everything. Store each member's full third-degree set and make queries a lookup. Ruled out by arithmetic — 125 million entries per member, a billion members.

Traverse at query time. Breadth-first search from V until you reach P or exhaust three hops. Correct, and it explores the full 125-million neighbourhood in the worst case, which does not fit in 50 milliseconds for one profile, let alone 25.

Meet in the middle. Search two hops from V and one hop from P, and test whether the two sets intersect. The work is 250,000 (held once, reused) plus 500 per profile.

The general principle is worth naming because it recurs: a bidirectional search meets at depth d/2 from each end, and neighbourhood size grows exponentially with depth, so two searches of half the depth are vastly cheaper than one of full depth. Here it is the difference between 125 million and 500.

Caching, and which direction staleness must go

Second-degree sets are expensive enough to want caching and change often enough to go stale.

The resolution follows from the error asymmetry. A cached set that is missing a recent addition reports someone as 3rd degree when they are 2nd — invisible, acceptable, self-correcting on the next rebuild. A cached set that still contains a removed connection reports someone as 2nd degree when they are not — visibly wrong.

So the two events are treated differently. Additions propagate lazily, picked up whenever the set is next rebuilt. Removals invalidate eagerly, pushing an invalidation for both endpoints' sets and for the sets of everyone connected to them.

That second part is a real fan-out — removing one edge invalidates up to 1,000 cached sets — and it is worth it, because removals are far rarer than additions and the failure they cause is the visible one.

🏗7. High-level design
Degree lookup — and the high-degree member who breaks the arithmetic
batch of profilesadjacency / resultcached 2-hop setuncacheable
What is moving: the viewer’s cached second-degree set — ~250K IDs as a compressed bitmap, a few hundred kilobytes — intersected against each target’s ~500 first-degree connections. Third degree is 2 + 1, computed by meeting in the middle rather than by expanding three hops to 125 million members.
What goes wrong: a viewer with 30,000 connections has a second-degree neighbourhood in the tens of millions — too large to cache and constantly invalidated. Because the relation is symmetric, the fix is to expand from whichever side is smaller: compute from the target instead. Without that check, a handful of users dominate the cluster’s load.

Two shards' worth of data and one clever query.

THE ARITHMETIC everything follows from this 1st degree ~500 a set lookup 2nd degree ~250,000 storable: ~1 MB exact, ~300 KB as a filter 3rd degree ~125,000,000 per viewer. not storable. not cacheable. MEET IN THE MIDDLE "is P within 3 hops of V?" V --hop--> --hop--> [ V's 2nd-degree set ] | | do these intersect? | [ P's connections ] <--hop-- P 250,000 vs 500 500 set lookups. not 125 million. A BATCH OF 25 ~50 ms total 1. fetch V's connections once 2. fetch/build V's 2nd-degree set once — this is the hoisted work 3. for each of the 25 profiles: in V's connections? → 1st in V's 2nd-degree filter? → confirm exactly → 2nd fetch P's connections, intersect with V's 2nd? → 3rd otherwise → out of network V HAS 30,000 CONNECTIONS 2nd degree is now tens of millions — every assumption above fails handle explicitly: cap, or invert the query and search from P instead
Step 2 is the whole trick. It depends only on the viewer, so it is paid once per page rather than once per profile — which is what turns a 2 ms per-item budget from impossible into comfortable.
🔄8. Workflows — what actually happens
A search page renders 25 profiles
The batch, and where the time goes.
  1. Viewer V's connection list is fetched — 500 ids, a few kilobytes. Sub-millisecond from the in-memory tier.
  2. V's second-degree filter is fetched from cache. A few hundred kilobytes, once for the entire page.
  3. Profile 1: its id is in V's connection list. 1st degree. Done in microseconds.
  4. Profiles 2 through 9: not 1st. Tested against the second-degree filter — each returns negative, which is definitive. Out to 3rd-degree checking.
  5. Profile 10: the filter says possible. An exact check against the real set confirms it. 2nd degree.
  6. Profiles 2 through 9 now need the third-degree test: fetch each one's connection list — 500 ids — and test each against V's second-degree filter. A hit means a path of length 3 exists.
  7. Six are 3rd degree, two are out of network. Total for the page: about 35 ms, most of it fetching the eight connection lists.
The second-degree set was built once and used 25 times. Had each profile triggered its own traversal, the page would have taken 25× as long — which is the difference between a batch API and a loop over a single-item one.
Why the third-degree test does not explode
The arithmetic, run both ways.
  1. The naive question: is P in V's 125-million-member third-degree neighbourhood? Answering it directly means building that neighbourhood.
  2. Building it would mean, for each of V's 250,000 second-degree contacts, fetching their 500 connections — 125 million fetches. Not in 50 ms; not in 50 seconds.
  3. The reformulation: a path V → a → b → P exists exactly when b is in both V's second-degree set and P's connection list.
  4. So fetch P's 500 connections — one fetch — and test each against V's second-degree filter.
  5. 500 hash computations. Under a millisecond. No traversal from V's side at all beyond the set we already had.
  6. A single hit proves a path exists, which is all the question asked for.
125 million operations became 500, by asking the question from the other end. The general move — search from both endpoints and meet in the middle — works because neighbourhood size grows exponentially with hop count, so halving the depth is worth far more than halving the work.
The viewer has 30,000 connections
Where the averages stop applying.
  1. A recruiter with 30,000 connections. Their second-degree neighbourhood is roughly 30,000 × 500 = 15 million, not 250,000.
  2. The filter for that set would be megabytes, and building it means fetching 30,000 connection lists — far outside the latency budget.
  3. Caching helps only partially: the set is large, expensive to build, and invalidated constantly because 30,000 people's connections change often.
  4. Mitigation one — invert the query. Instead of building V's huge second-degree set, build P's and test V's 500 connections against it. P is an ordinary member, so their set is the normal 250,000.
  5. Mitigation two — cap the expansion. Build the second-degree set from a bounded sample of V's connections. The answer becomes approximate, and it errs by saying "3rd" where the truth is "2nd" — the safe direction.
  6. Mitigation three — for the most extreme accounts, degrade to a simpler answer: 1st degree exactly, and "in network" rather than a precise 2 or 3.
Inverting the query is the elegant one and it works because the relation is symmetric: a path from V to P is a path from P to V, so you may always start from whichever end is cheaper. That is a nice property to notice out loud.
Someone removes a connection
The invalidation that must not be lazy.
  1. Priya removes her connection to Dev. The edge is deleted from both their lists immediately.
  2. First-degree answers are now correct — they read the edge list directly.
  3. But cached second-degree sets are wrong. Everyone connected to Priya had Dev in their second-degree set because of her, and everyone connected to Dev had Priya.
  4. Left stale, those people see Dev as 2nd degree when he is not — the visible failure. They click expecting a shared contact and find none.
  5. So removal triggers eager invalidation: the cached sets of Priya, Dev, and everyone connected to either of them are dropped. Up to 1,000 entries.
  6. Those sets are rebuilt lazily on next use, from the now-correct edge lists. A rebuild is milliseconds.
  7. An addition, by contrast, invalidates nothing. The new connection shows as 1st degree immediately from the edge list, and second-degree sets pick it up whenever they next rebuild.
Two events, two policies, chosen by which direction the error runs. It is a small amount of extra machinery and it converts the one user-visible failure mode into an invisible one.
🔍9. Deep dives, and what breaks

Why degree 4 is not on the table

Worth having an answer ready, because it is the obvious follow-up.

Fourth degree would be roughly 500 × 125 million — tens of billions, which is more than the entire membership. At that point almost everybody is within four hops of almost everybody, and the answer stops carrying information.

That is the small-world property, and it is the real reason the product stops at three: not that four is expensive to compute, but that four is meaningless. A label that applies to 95% of the network tells the user nothing.

Meet-in-the-middle would still work mechanically — two hops from each end — but there is no reason to build it.

Producing the path, not just the number

The results page needs a number. The profile page wants “connected via Priya and two others”, which is a different query.

For second degree it is the intersection of two connection lists — both sorted, so it is a linear merge of two 500-element lists. Fast, and it yields the shared contacts directly.

For third degree it is harder: you need an actual path, not just proof that one exists. The meet-in-the-middle structure gives you the midpoint b from the intersection test, and then you need one more hop back from V to find the a connecting them.

There may be many such paths and the useful ones are ranked — a strong shared contact beats a distant one. That is a ranking problem on top of a graph problem, which is why it belongs on the profile page where the budget is larger and there is one target rather than 25.

Sharding the graph, and why it is awkward

Five hundred gigabytes of edges must be distributed, and graphs partition badly.

The natural choice is by member id, so each shard holds the connection lists for its members. Fetching one member's connections is then a single shard hit, which is what the hot path needs.

The awkwardness is that building a second-degree set means fetching 500 members' lists, and those 500 are spread across every shard. It is a scatter-gather, and its latency is the slowest shard's — the tail-latency problem that fan-out queries always have.

Which is precisely why second-degree sets are cached rather than computed per request. The cache is not an optimisation on an already-fast path; it is what keeps the scatter-gather off the request path entirely.

Partitioning by community rather than by id would keep connected members together and reduce the fan-out, and it introduces rebalancing and hot-partition problems that are usually worse than the scatter. Naming that trade is better than asserting either.

What breaks

2nd-degree cache is cold or unavailable
Fall back to computing from adjacency lists for the batch, with a reduced target set and a slower response. Degrading to “connection degree unavailable” on a search page is acceptable; failing the page is not.
A viewer has an enormous connection count
Detect by degree at query time and switch to expanding from the target side. Without this check, one member’s query can consume orders of magnitude more resources than everyone else’s combined.
A connection is removed
Removals must invalidate immediately rather than lazily, because a stale bitmap would show a closer degree than the truth and expose profile data the viewer should no longer see.
Graph shard unavailable
Adjacency is partitioned by member, so an outage affects a subset of members rather than everyone. Return “unknown” for affected targets instead of guessing a degree.
Cache stampede on a popular member
Many viewers connected to the same hub can miss the same bitmap simultaneously after an invalidation. Coalesce the rebuild so one request computes and the rest wait. Ch 9
The dominant constraint

Third degree is 125 million members and cannot be materialised. Everything follows: cache what is affordable at two hops, and answer three hops by meeting in the middle rather than by expanding further.

What I would build first

The compressed second-degree bitmap and the bidirectional intersection. Together they turn the expensive query into a handful of set operations and let one cached set serve all 25 targets on a page.

What I deliberately did not build

Returning the connecting path, and any degree beyond three. The path needs an actual traversal rather than a set intersection, and degree 4 approaches the whole graph.

The biggest risk

High-degree members. They break the neighbourhood arithmetic the whole design rests on, and without an explicit switch to expand from the smaller side, a handful of users can dominate the cluster’s load.

💬 If you get this far, here is what they will push on
Follow-ups an interviewer is likely to ask once the design is on the board. Answers supplied — read the question, answer it out loud, then open it.
“Why not precompute everyone's third-degree set?”Answer

At around 500 connections each, third degree is roughly 125 million people per viewer. Even as a compressed bitmap that is hundreds of megabytes per user, and storing it for a billion members is absurd.

It also changes constantly: every new connection anywhere in the network invalidates it.

So third degree is computed, never stored — by expanding two hops from the viewer, which you can cache, and one hop from each target, which is tiny, then intersecting.

“A viewer has 30,000 connections. Now what?”Answer

Their second-degree set is in the tens of millions, which is too large to cache and constantly invalidated. The design's central assumption has broken for them.

The fix uses symmetry: if V is within three hops of P, then P is within three hops of V. So when the viewer is a high-degree member, compute from the target's side instead, where the neighbourhood is ordinary.

Choosing which end to expand from based on degree is the most valuable optimisation here, and without it a handful of users dominate the cluster.

“Someone makes a new connection. How much cache does that invalidate?”Answer

More than you would like. It changes the second-degree set not only for the two people involved but for everyone connected to either of them — roughly a thousand cached sets per new connection.

Eagerly recomputing them is wasteful because most will change again before anyone reads them. So invalidate lazily: stamp each bitmap with the edge version it was built from and rebuild on read when it is stale.

That trades a slower first read for far less write amplification, which the staleness tolerance permits.

“Is it acceptable to show the wrong degree?”Answer

In one direction only, and the asymmetry matters. Showing 3rd where the truth is now 2nd is harmless — the data is just a little stale.

Showing 2nd where the truth is 3rd is a privacy problem, because degree gates what profile information is visible.

So the cache may only ever miss new edges, never invent them. Additions can lag; removals must be applied immediately.

Design a Central iOS Push Notification Service (APNs-style: many publishers, many apps, one device)

Difficulty: Hard (Staff Expectation)  .  Target: 45 min
💬 The question, as asked

“Design a central push notification service for iOS. Many app publishers send notifications; each app has many users; and one phone has many apps installed.”

⚡ What makes it hard

The connection model is the whole design, and it is decided by battery rather than by throughput. Forty apps holding forty sockets on one phone is a cost users answer by turning push off.

📋1. Understanding the question

The prompt: “Design a central push notification service for iOS. Many app publishers send notifications; each app has many users; and one phone has many apps installed.”

That last clause is the question. Everything else is scaffolding.

🎯 One connection per app, or one per device?

A phone has forty apps that want push. If each holds its own connection to the service, that is forty TCP connections, forty TLS sessions, and forty independent keepalives on one device.

Each keepalive wakes the radio. Waking the radio is by far the largest battery cost on a phone, and it costs roughly the same whether you send one byte or a thousand. Forty apps each poking the radio on their own schedule means the radio is almost never allowed to sleep.

Users answer battery drain by turning push off, which makes the product worthless. So: one connection per device, multiplexing every app's traffic, with a single keepalive.
