That decision is why this service is central at all. If each app could run its own push infrastructure well, there would be no need for a shared one. The whole reason it exists is that the radio is a shared resource that no single app can manage responsibly.

What the decision costs

Having chosen one connection per device, you inherit a set of problems:

  • You are now holding hundreds of millions of simultaneous connections, which is a fleet sized by idle sockets rather than by traffic.
  • Every app's notifications flow through your infrastructure, so one misbehaving publisher must not be able to degrade any other.
  • You need an addressing scheme — the device token — that identifies a device-and-app pair without becoming a cross-app tracking identifier.

And the requirement to push back on

Is this a durable queue? Publishers will assume it is. Real push services are explicitly best-effort, and that is a deliberate choice rather than a limitation.

Durable at-least-once delivery to a billion devices means a per-device queue, acknowledgements and retries — and a phone offline for a week returning to four thousand queued notifications, which is a worse user experience than having missed them. Saying “best effort, and here is why” rather than promising durability is the honest answer.

What they are looking for

Do you ask per-app or per-device? First, and do you justify it by battery?

Do you isolate publishers? A shared service's defining risk is a noisy tenant.

Do you treat the token as a privacy object? It is the piece most candidates get casually wrong.

❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
Is the persistent connection per app or per device?
Ask this first — it is the whole design. Per app means a phone with 40 apps holds 40 TCP connections and dies of battery drain. Per device means one connection multiplexing every app’s traffic, and everything else follows from that.
What delivery guarantee do publishers get?
Best-effort at-most-once needs almost no storage. At-least-once needs durable per-device queues and acknowledgement, which is a far larger system. Real push services choose best-effort and say so.
What happens to notifications for a device that is offline for a week?
If you retain everything, a returning phone gets 4,000 notifications. If you coalesce to the latest per app, it gets 40. That single decision changes storage by orders of magnitude.
Can a publisher broadcast to all its users, or must it address devices individually?
Individual addressing pushes fan-out onto the publisher. Topic broadcast means we own the fan-out, and a 50-million-device topic becomes our capacity problem.
Is the device token stable, and is it tied to a user?
It must be per (device, app), opaque, and rotatable — not a user ID. Otherwise the token becomes a cross-app tracking identifier and a privacy incident.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.
📝2. Functional requirements
  • Authenticated publishers submit a notification addressed to a device token.
  • Deliver immediately if connected; otherwise hold briefly and deliver on reconnect.
  • One device, one connection, carrying every installed app's traffic.
  • Report invalid and expired tokens back to publishers so they stop sending.

What a device token has to be

It is the address, and getting it wrong is a privacy incident rather than a bug.

It must be per (device, app), not per device and not per user. If two apps on the same phone received the same token, any publisher could correlate their users with any other publisher's — a cross-app tracking identifier handed out by the platform.

It must be opaque. Nothing derivable about the device, the user, or the app should be inferable from the bytes, because tokens end up in publishers' databases and logs.

It must be rotatable. A reinstall, a restore from backup, or a device transfer should invalidate the old token. Which means publishers must handle tokens going dead, which is exactly what the feedback requirement exists for.

Why the feedback channel matters more than it looks

Without it, a publisher keeps sending to tokens for apps that were uninstalled a year ago. Those notifications are pure waste — they can never be delivered — and over time they become a large fraction of a publisher's volume, which is your capacity being consumed for nothing.

So invalid tokens are reported back, and publishers are expected to remove them. It is a small API and it is what keeps the system's load proportional to real users rather than to historical installs.

⏱3. Non-functional requirements
RequirementTargetWhat it forces
Concurrent connections~400MThe defining number. Sized by idle sockets, not by messages — they cost memory at 3am when nothing is being sent.
Delivery latencyp95 < 1 sPublisher accept to device, for a connected device. Push that arrives late is push that arrives after the user looked.
Delivery guaranteeBest effortExplicitly not a durable queue. Stated as a requirement so it is a decision rather than an omission.
Publisher isolationStrictOne publisher's burst or bug must not affect another's delivery. This is the defining risk of any shared service.
Battery costFirst-classWhich is unusual and correct. The device's radio budget constrains the server design.
Token privacyPer (device, app)Opaque and rotatable. A design constraint, not an implementation detail.

The keepalive interval, which is the most consequential constant

The connection must survive carrier NAT timeouts, which on mobile networks can be as short as a couple of minutes. So something must send a byte periodically or the connection dies silently and notifications stop arriving with no error anywhere.

Too frequent and you are waking the radio on hundreds of millions of devices more often than necessary — the exact cost the whole design exists to avoid. Too infrequent and connections die, delivery becomes unreliable, and devices reconnect constantly, which is worse for battery than the keepalives would have been.

The refinement that matters: the interval should adapt to the network. Wi-Fi tolerates much longer gaps than cellular, and different carriers differ substantially. A client that learns the longest interval its current network survives is doing more for battery life than any server-side optimisation.

🗂4. Data model and API

Three pieces of state, and only one of them is large.

-- Where is this device connected RIGHT NOW? Read on every notification, -- so it must be an in-memory lookup, never a database query. TABLE device_sessions { -- sharded KV, in memory device_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, gateway_id VARCHAR, -- which box holds the socket connected_at TIMESTAMP, lease_expires TIMESTAMP -- gateway heartbeats; stale rows expire } -- The token is per (device, app). It is opaque and rotatable so it -- cannot be used as a cross-app identifier for the same person. TABLE device_tokens { token BYTES PRIMARY KEY, device_id UUID, bundle_id VARCHAR, -- the app state ENUM(active, unregistered), rotated_at TIMESTAMP } -- INDEX: (device_id) -- one device, many apps, many tokens -- Offline holding area. NOT a queue: at most ONE row per -- (device, app, collapse_id). This is the capacity trick. TABLE pending { device_id UUID, bundle_id VARCHAR, collapse_id VARCHAR, payload BYTES, expires_at TIMESTAMP, PRIMARY KEY (device_id, bundle_id, collapse_id) } -- An UPSERT here means a week offline yields ~1 notification per app, -- not thousands. Storage is bounded by DEVICES x APPS, not by traffic.

The connection registry

Maps each connected device to the gateway holding its socket. Written on every connect, read on every notification.

It is the same component as D4's registry and it is allowed to be wrong in the same way. A stale entry means a notification is sent to a gateway that no longer has that device; the gateway says “not mine” and the notification is dropped or retried once.

Because delivery is best-effort, a stale entry costs one lost notification rather than a correctness problem — which is precisely what allows it to be an in-memory store with a TTL rather than anything more expensive.

The token table

Maps each opaque token to a device and an app, with validity state. A billion devices times several apps each is billions of rows, but they are tiny and the access is a point lookup by token — a sharded key-value store with no interesting queries.

The important column is the validity state, because it is what drives the feedback channel. A token becomes invalid on uninstall, on reinstall (which mints a new one), and after a long period with no device contact.

The pending buffer, which is deliberately small

For a device that is not connected, notifications are held briefly — and coalesced to the latest per app, not queued.

The arithmetic justifies it plainly. A device offline for a week, at ten notifications a day across forty apps, would accumulate on the order of four thousand messages. Delivering all of them on reconnect is a terrible user experience, a large storage cost, and a burst of load at exactly the moment a device is reconnecting.

Coalescing to the most recent per app turns four thousand into forty. The user sees what is current, which is almost always what they wanted, and storage per device is bounded by app count rather than by time offline.

The API

// PUBLISHER-FACING (HTTP/2, one stream per notification) POST /3/device/{device_token} Headers: authorization: bearer <provider JWT> apns-topic: com.example.app // which app apns-expiration: <unix ts> // 0 = deliver now or discard apns-collapse-id: <string> // COALESCING KEY -- newer // replaces older with same id apns-priority: 10 | 5 // 5 = power-considerate Body: { aps: { alert, badge, sound }, custom... } // <= 4 KB Response: 200 { apns-id } 410 Unregistered // app deleted -- STOP SENDING to this token 429 TooManyRequests // per-publisher quota // DEVICE-FACING (one persistent TLS connection per DEVICE, not per app) device -> { type:"hello", device_id, topics:[bundle ids...] } device <- { type:"push", topic, apns_id, payload } device -> { type:"ack", apns_id } // lets us drop the stored copy device <-> keepalive on a long interval // radio wake-ups cost battery
📊5. Capacity estimation

The numbers, and the one that sizes the fleet.

⚖ Assumptions — and what breaks if each is wrong
1B registered devices, ~400M concurrently connected
If concurrency were 10× lower this stops being a connection-management problem and becomes an ordinary API.
~10 notifications per device per day
A 10× increase makes fan-out CPU, not connection count, the binding constraint.
Payloads are small — 4 KB cap
Large payloads would force a fetch-on-notify design where the push carries only a pointer.
Offline retention coalesces to the latest per app
Retaining every notification instead would multiply storage by roughly the number sent during the outage window.
400M
concurrent connections
~400
gateway nodes at 1M conns
~116K/s
notifications average
~350K/s

~10 KB
kernel + app memory per conn
~4 TB
connection state across the fleet

Connections dominate. Four hundred million concurrent sockets, at perhaps 50,000 per machine with tuned buffers and an event loop, is around 8,000 gateway machines whose primary job is holding connections open.

Note what that number is not derived from. It is not messages per second — it is idle sockets. Those machines cost the same at three in the morning with zero notifications flowing.

Messages are comparatively easy. A billion devices at ten notifications a day is about 115,000 per second average, a few times that at peak. Payloads are small. As a throughput problem this is unremarkable; it is the connection count that makes the system large.

The keepalive traffic is worth computing. Four hundred million devices each sending a small packet every few minutes is on the order of a million packets per second of pure overhead — comparable to the notification traffic itself. Which is a good argument for making the interval as long as the network tolerates, on both the battery and the server side.

The worst load this system sees

Not a notification burst. A mass reconnection.

A gateway deploy, a regional network blip, or a load balancer change causes hundreds of thousands or millions of devices to reconnect simultaneously. Each reconnection is a TCP handshake, a TLS handshake, an authentication, and a registry write — all far more expensive than delivering a notification.

Sizing for steady state and not for reconnection storms is the standard way this kind of system falls over, and the defences are the ones you would expect: staged deploys, client-side reconnect backoff with jitter, and connection rate limits at the gateway.

⚖6. The key trade-offs

The choices, and their costs.

DecisionChosen ✓Alternative ✗Reasoning
Connection modelOne per device, multiplexedOne per appForty sockets and forty keepalive timers per phone is a battery and radio cost users will not accept. The multiplexing hop is worth its complexity.
Delivery guaranteeBest-effort, at-most-onceDurable at-least-onceDurable per-device queues for 1B devices is a vastly larger and more expensive system. Push is a hint to open the app; the app fetches the truth.
Offline handlingCoalesce to latest per appQueue everythingQueuing makes storage grow with traffic × outage length and delivers hundreds of stale alerts. Coalescing bounds storage by devices × apps.
Session lookupIn-memory sharded registryDatabase queryIt is read on every notification at 350K/sec. A database round trip on that path is a self-inflicted bottleneck.
Publisher fan-outPublisher addresses devices individuallyWe own topic broadcastIndividual addressing keeps our fan-out bounded and predictable; owning broadcast means a single publisher action can become a 50-million-device write.

Best effort, and what durable delivery would cost

The trade to state clearly, because publishers will push on it.

Durable at-least-once means a persistent per-device queue, acknowledgement tracking, and retries. For a billion devices with several apps each that is an enormous amount of state whose whole purpose is to serve devices that are not there.

It also produces a bad product. The returning phone gets its four thousand notifications, most of them about things that are no longer true — a match that ended, a sale that finished, a message already read on another device.

Best effort with coalescing means storage bounded by app count, no acknowledgement machinery, and a returning device seeing what is currently true.

The honest framing: a notification is a hint that something changed, not a message. The authoritative content lives in the app, which fetches it on open. Once you accept that, best-effort delivery is not a compromise — it is the correct semantics, and durability would be solving the wrong problem expensively.

Isolating publishers

The defining risk of a shared service. One publisher with a bug — a retry loop, a broadcast to their entire user base at once — must not delay anyone else's notifications.

The defences are the standard multi-tenant set, and it is worth naming all three because each catches a different failure:

  • Per-publisher rate limits at ingest, so excess is rejected with a clear error rather than absorbed into shared queues.
  • Separate queues per publisher, so a backlog is their backlog. A shared queue means one publisher's million-message burst sits in front of everyone else's traffic.
  • Fair scheduling at the gateway, so a device with one app generating heavy traffic does not starve its other apps' notifications.

This is the same lesson as the cardinality limits in D11: in a shared platform, design against your noisiest tenant, not against your own bugs.

🏗7. High-level design
Push delivery — and the reconnect storm when a gateway dies
notificationrouting / storedelivery to devicereconnects
What is moving: a notification addressed to an opaque device token. Ingest authorises it and applies the publisher’s quota, the router looks up which gateway holds that device, and the gateway pushes it down one connection shared by every app on the phone. If the device is offline the router upserts into the pending store, keeping at most one notification per app.
What goes wrong: a gateway holding a million connections dies. All million devices notice at once and reconnect — and if they reconnect immediately they arrive as a synchronised wall of TLS handshakes that knocks over whichever gateway they land on next. Devices must back off with jitter, and the tier must carry enough headroom to absorb a whole node’s worth of reconnections. Ch 10

Two halves: accepting from publishers, and holding sockets.

PUBLISHER SIDE publisher --> INGEST authenticate, validate token, per-publisher rate limit reject here, loudly | v PER-PUBLISHER QUEUE a backlog is THEIR backlog, not everyone's | v lookup token → device lookup registry → which gateway? DEVICE SIDE phone ---- ONE connection for ALL 40 apps ----> GATEWAY one TLS session ~50K devices each one keepalive adaptive: longer on wi-fi ~8,000 machines delivery: notification → multiplexed down the device's single socket tagged with which app it belongs to DEVICE OFFLINE registry has no entry | v PENDING BUFFER coalesce to latest per app 4,000 notifications over a week → 40 on reconnect bounded by app count, not by time offline TOKEN DEAD (uninstalled, reinstalled, expired) → feedback to the publisher: stop sending without this, dead tokens become a large share of a publisher's volume
The single socket per device is the design. Everything above it — queues, registry, coalescing — exists to feed that one connection without letting any publisher monopolise it.
🔄8. Workflows — what actually happens
A message arrives for an app on a connected phone
The happy path, and note how little of it is per-app.
  1. A publisher posts a notification addressed to a device token. Ingest authenticates them, validates the token's format, and checks their rate limit.
  2. It is accepted and placed on that publisher's queue. The publisher gets a 202 — accepted, not delivered, which is an important distinction to make in the API.
  3. The token is resolved to a device and an app. The registry says the device is on gateway 4,412.
  4. The notification is forwarded there. The gateway writes it down the device's single existing socket, tagged with the app it belongs to.
  5. The operating system on the phone routes it to the right app. No new connection was opened, and the radio was already awake for this socket.
  6. Total: about 300 ms from publisher accept to device.
The per-app cost of this delivery was a tag in a message header. That is the payoff of the per-device connection: the fortieth app costs almost nothing, where forty separate sockets would cost forty keepalives forever.
A phone is off for a week
Coalescing, and the four-thousand-notification problem it avoids.
  1. The device disconnects. Its registry entry expires within a minute.
  2. Notifications keep arriving — roughly 10 a day across 40 apps, so about 2,800 over the week.
  3. Each one lands in the pending buffer, where it replaces the previous pending notification for that same app rather than joining a queue behind it.
  4. Storage for that device stays at roughly 40 entries regardless of how long it is away.
  5. The phone comes back. It reconnects, authenticates, and the registry is updated.
  6. The gateway delivers the 40 pending notifications — one current item per app.
  7. The user sees what is true now, rather than a week of history most of which is obsolete.
This is what "best effort" buys, stated as a product outcome rather than a limitation. Durable delivery would have been more storage, more machinery, and a visibly worse experience on reconnect.
A publisher broadcasts to 50 million users
Isolation doing its job.
  1. A publisher sends a campaign to their entire install base. Fifty million notifications arrive over a few minutes.
  2. Their rate limit caps the accept rate. Beyond it they get explicit 429 responses telling them to slow down — rejected clearly rather than absorbed silently.
  3. What is accepted goes onto their queue, which grows to millions deep.
  4. Every other publisher's queue is untouched. A small app's notification sent during this window is delivered in its usual 300 ms, because it never waited behind anything.
  5. Delivery workers drain the large queue at a controlled rate. The campaign takes ten minutes rather than arriving instantly.
  6. At the gateway, fair scheduling ensures a device receiving this campaign still gets its other apps' notifications promptly — the campaign does not monopolise its socket either.
Three layers of isolation, each catching a different failure: the rate limit bounds what enters, the separate queue bounds who waits, and fair scheduling bounds what monopolises a device. A shared queue would have made this one publisher's campaign into everybody's outage.
A gateway is deployed and 50,000 devices reconnect
The worst load this system sees.
  1. A gateway is taken out of service for a deploy. Its 50,000 sockets drop at once.
  2. Every one of those devices immediately tries to reconnect. Each reconnection is a TCP handshake, a TLS handshake, an authentication and a registry write — far more expensive than delivering a notification.
  3. If they all retry at once and land on the same few gateways, those gateways are overwhelmed, drop the connections, and the devices retry again — a reconnection storm that feeds itself.
  4. Defence one: clients use randomised backoff. Reconnections spread over tens of seconds rather than arriving in one burst.
  5. Defence two: gateways enforce a connection rate limit, rejecting excess with a signal to retry later rather than accepting and collapsing.
  6. Defence three: deploys are staged, so a small fraction of the fleet is cycling at any time.
  7. Notifications arriving for those devices during the gap go to the pending buffer and are delivered on reconnect.
This system's peak load is a control-plane event, not a traffic event — which is easy to miss when capacity planning from message rates. A fleet sized by idle connections is stressed by connections churning, and that is the number to design against.
🔍9. Deep dives, and what breaks

Holding 400 million sockets

The engineering here is about making idle cheap, since the overwhelming majority of these connections are doing nothing at any instant.

A thread per connection is immediately out. It is an event loop with non-blocking I/O, where one thread services tens of thousands of sockets and does work only when one has bytes.

Then per-connection memory. Default socket buffers are sized for throughput; here the traffic is tiny messages, so buffers should be small — 50,000 connections times a few hundred kilobytes is an entire machine spent on buffers. File descriptor limits and ephemeral port ranges both need raising well past their defaults, which assume servers holding hundreds of connections rather than tens of thousands.

And TLS session state per connection is not free. Session resumption matters enormously here, because it turns a reconnection from a full handshake into a cheap one — which directly reduces the cost of the reconnection storms described above.

Why the notification should carry almost nothing

There is constant pressure to put content in the payload — the message text, the order status — so the app can display it without a fetch.

Three arguments against, and they compound.

Staleness. A notification delivered from the pending buffer may be minutes or hours old. Its embedded content may already be wrong, and the user sees the stale version.

Privacy. Payload content passes through and may be briefly stored by a central service that has no business reading it. Minimising what it carries minimises what can leak.

Size. Multiplied across billions of notifications, payload size is real bandwidth on constrained mobile networks.

So the notification is best understood as a wake-up with an identifier. The app opens, fetches current state from its own backend, and displays something true. This is the same conclusion D4 reaches from a different direction — there because encryption makes server-side content impossible, here because staleness makes it undesirable.

Why the token cannot be a user id

It is tempting: a stable per-user identifier would simplify addressing enormously.

It would also mean that every publisher who has ever received a push token for a user could correlate that user across every other app, because they would all see the same identifier. That is a cross-app tracking capability handed out by the platform itself — the kind of thing that becomes a regulatory matter rather than a bug report.

Per (device, app) tokens mean two apps on the same phone see unrelated opaque strings and can learn nothing about each other's users. The cost is that a user with three devices is three tokens per app, and that publishers must handle tokens changing — both of which are small prices.

Worth stating out loud in the interview. Privacy properties of identifiers are a genuine staff-level concern and one candidates rarely raise unprompted.

What breaks

A gateway holding 1M connections dies
One million devices detect the drop and reconnect. Without jittered backoff they arrive together and knock over the next gateway — a synchronised reconnect storm. Devices must reconnect with randomised delay, and the tier needs headroom to absorb a whole node’s worth of reconnections. Ch 10
Session registry unavailable
Notifications for connected devices cannot be routed. Degrade by writing to the pending store instead of failing the publisher — the device collects on its next reconnect. Best-effort delivery is what makes this degradation acceptable rather than a data-loss event.
One publisher floods the ingest tier
Per-publisher quota rejects with 429 at the door, before the notification consumes routing or gateway capacity. Quotas must be per publisher and per topic, since one publisher may own many apps.
A device is offline for weeks
The pending store holds one coalesced notification per app with an expiry; expired entries are dropped rather than delivered. Delivering a two-week-old alert is worse than delivering nothing.
Token continues to be used after app deletion
Return 410 Unregistered and mark the token dead. Publishers that ignore it get their quota consumed by traffic that cannot succeed, which is the correct incentive.
The dominant constraint

Four hundred million idle connections. This is a presence system that occasionally carries a message, so the gateway tier is sized by concurrent connections rather than throughput, and one connection per device — not per app — is what makes it viable on a battery.

What I would build first

The device-multiplexed connection and the coalescing pending store. Those two decide the battery cost and bound the storage; everything else is routing.

What I deliberately did not build

Durable delivery. A guaranteed per-device queue for a billion devices is a different and far more expensive system, and push is a hint to open the app rather than the payload of record.

The biggest risk

The reconnect storm. Losing one gateway means a million devices reconnect at once, and without jittered backoff and real headroom that cascades through the tier faster than it can absorb.

💬 If you get this far, here is what they will push on
Follow-ups an interviewer is likely to ask once the design is on the board. Answers supplied — read the question, answer it out loud, then open it.
“A phone has 40 push-enabled apps. How many connections?”Answer

One. That is the decision the whole design rests on, and it is made for battery rather than throughput.

Forty connections means forty TLS handshakes, forty sets of keepalives and forty radio wake-ups, and on a mobile network the radio is the dominant power cost. Users answer that by turning push off, which is a product failure.

So the connection belongs to the device, each notification carries a topic identifying the app, and the phone demultiplexes locally. The session registry and the routing hop exist to support that.

“A gateway holding a million connections dies. What happens next?”Answer

A million devices notice within seconds and reconnect. If they reconnect immediately they arrive as a synchronised wall of TLS handshakes and knock over whichever gateway they land on next, which cascades.

So devices must back off with randomised delay, and the tier needs enough headroom to absorb a whole node's worth of reconnections.

This is the same synchronised-retry problem as Ch 10, and jitter is what turns a wall into a ramp.

“A phone is off for a week. How many notifications does it get on reconnect?”Answer

About one per app, not thousands. Notifications for offline devices are upserted into a pending store keyed by device, app and collapse id, so a newer one replaces the older.

That bounds storage by devices times apps — a fixed quantity — rather than by traffic times outage length.

It is also better product behaviour. Nobody wants 400 “you have a new message” alerts; they want the latest one.

“One publisher has a bug and sends ten million notifications a second. Who notices?”Answer

Only that publisher, if the design is right. A per-publisher quota at ingest rejects the excess with 429 before it consumes routing or gateway capacity.

Quota at the door is the cheapest place to shed, because the notification has not cost anything yet.

Without it, one app's bug consumes capacity shared with every other app, and the failure looks like a platform outage rather than a customer problem.

Design a Two-Player Browser Game (matchmaking queue, live play, reconnect, and game history)

Difficulty: Hard (Staff Expectation)  .  Target: 45 min
💬 The question, as asked

“Design an online two-player browser game. Players wait in a queue, get matched, play, and can review their game history afterwards.”

⚡ What makes it hard

It is not a scale problem — all the concurrent state fits in a few hundred megabytes. It is stateful routing plus durability, which is the opposite of every other design in this book.

📋1. Understanding the question

The prompt: “Design an online two-player browser game. Players wait in a queue, get matched, play, and can review their game history afterwards.”

The first useful thing to do is size it, because the answer reframes the entire question.

🎯 This is not a scale problem

A million daily players, ten games each, five minutes per game, gives around 35,000 concurrent games. At a few kilobytes of state per game, that is roughly 180 megabytes — all the live state in the entire system, comfortably inside one machine's memory.

So none of the usual instincts apply. There is nothing to shard for capacity, no hot partition, no throughput wall.

What is hard instead is stateful routing and durability, which is the opposite of most designs in this guide. Two specific players must reach the one process holding their game, and that process must not be able to lose the game by dying.

The second thing that shapes everything: who owns the state

The tempting design has each client track the game and tell the server the result. It is simple, it halves the server's work, and it is completely broken the moment anything is at stake.

A browser client can be modified. If the client computes the outcome, a player can make it compute any outcome they like. Cheat detection after the fact is a losing game — you are trying to spot a modified client from its outputs, which is a permanent arms race.

So the server is authoritative: clients send intents — “I want to place a piece at C4” — and the server validates against the rules and the current state, and decides what actually happened. A modified client can send illegal moves; it cannot make them legal.

Cheating becomes structurally impossible rather than detected, which is a much better place to be.

And the thing you cannot solve

A player disconnects mid-game. You cannot tell whether their connection dropped or they quit because they were losing — from the server, the two are identical, and this is the fundamental limit from ch1.

So it is a product decision rather than an engineering one: a reconnection window, then a forfeit timer. Getting the interviewer to agree the numbers is better than picking them silently.

What they are looking for

Do you size it and notice it is small? The candidates who shard this have not.

Do you make the server authoritative? And explain why detection is not enough?

Do you find the move log? It solves three problems at once.

❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
Turn-based or real-time?
The single biggest fork. Turn-based means a few messages per minute and a relaxed latency budget. Real-time means a fixed tick rate, client prediction and server reconciliation — a fundamentally harder system.
Is the server authoritative, or do we trust the client?
If the game is competitive or has any stake, the server must own the state and clients may only send intents. A client that computes its own outcome is a client that can be modified to win.
Skill-based matchmaking, or first-come-first-served?
FIFO is a queue. Skill-based needs rating buckets and a search window that widens over time, or high-rated players wait forever.
What happens when a player disconnects mid-game?
You cannot distinguish a rage-quit from a dropped connection (Ch 1), so this is a product decision: a reconnect window, then a forfeit timer.
Is history a list of results, or a replayable game?
A result row is trivial. A replayable game means storing the full move log — which you probably want anyway, because it is also how you rehydrate a crashed session.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.
📝2. Functional requirements
  • Join a matchmaking queue and be paired with an opponent.
  • Play a turn-based game with server-validated moves.
  • Reconnect mid-game and resume from the current state.
  • View past games, with the move history, and replay them.

The move log, which is three features for the price of one

Worth pulling out, because noticing it is the nicest observation in this design.

Storing the game as a list of moves rather than as a board state gives you:

  • History and replay. Step through the moves to reconstruct any point in the game. That is the feature the requirement asked for.
  • Crash recovery. If the process holding a live game dies, replay its moves from the durable log and the game is back exactly as it was.
  • Dispute resolution and anti-cheat auditing. Every move, with its timestamp and who made it, is on the record.

One dataset, three requirements. A design that stores current board state instead would need a separate history table, a separate recovery mechanism, and would still have nothing to audit — and those three could drift out of agreement with each other.

It is the same structure as the operation log in D20, and for the same reason: storing what happened, rather than what is, makes several features fall out for free.

⏱3. Non-functional requirements
RequirementTargetWhat it forces
Queue waitMedian < 10 s, never unboundedThe second clause is the hard one. A skill-based queue that never widens leaves top players waiting forever.
Move round trip< 150 msComfortable for turn-based play. Real-time would need a fixed tick rate, client prediction and reconciliation — a much harder system.
Crash safetyNo game lostA process failure must be recoverable, which is what the durable move log provides.
CheatingStructurally impossibleNot detected afterwards. Server authority is the only version of this that holds.
Concurrent state~180 MBThe number that says this is not a scale problem.
DisconnectionWindow, then forfeitA product decision, because the server genuinely cannot distinguish a drop from a quit.

Why "never an unbounded wait" is the interesting half

Median wait is easy: most players are near the middle of the rating distribution and there are always opponents available.

The problem is the tails. A player rated far above everyone else has very few valid opponents, and a strict rating window means they may wait indefinitely — while the queue is full of people they are not allowed to play.

So the window widens over time. Start with a tight rating band, and expand it every few seconds the player waits. Eventually it is wide enough to match somebody.

The trade is explicit and worth stating: match quality against wait time. A widening window says that after some number of seconds, an imperfect match is better than continuing to wait — which is almost always true, because a player who waits two minutes usually leaves.

🗂4. Data model and API

Two kinds of state, and the distinction between them is the design.

-- LIVE: in memory on the owning server, checkpointed on every move. STRUCT live_game { game_id, players[2], board_state, turn, clocks, move_seq, -- monotonic; dedupes client resends owner_server, epoch -- epoch fences a resurrected old owner } -- DURABLE: the move log is the source of truth. Board state is -- derived from it, which is why a crashed game can be rebuilt. TABLE moves { game_id UUID, seq INT, player UUID, intent JSONB, applied_at TIMESTAMP, PRIMARY KEY (game_id, seq) } -- Append-only. Replay + history + crash recovery are the SAME data. TABLE games { game_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, p1 UUID, p2 UUID, result ENUM(p1_win, p2_win, draw, abandoned), started_at, ended_at TIMESTAMP } -- INDEX: (p1, started_at DESC) and (p2, started_at DESC) -- so "my recent games" is one sequential read, not a scan. SORTED SET queue:{mode}:{bucket} -- rating bucket -> waiting tickets

Live game state — in memory, on one process

The current board, whose turn it is, both players' clocks. A few kilobytes, held by the single process that owns this game.

One process, deliberately. Two processes holding the same game could accept conflicting moves and produce two divergent boards, which is the one failure this design cannot tolerate. Single ownership means move validation is a local operation with no locking and no coordination — and it is what makes a move round trip fast.

The move log — durable, append-only

Every validated move is appended: game id, sequence number, player, the move, timestamp.

The ordering rule that matters: a move is appended to the log before it is acknowledged to either player. If the process dies a millisecond later, the move is not lost, and both players' views remain consistent with the record.

Doing it the other way — acknowledge, then persist — means a crash can leave two players having seen a move that the recovered game does not contain. That is the worst kind of bug, because the players remember something the system does not.

Matchmaking state

Players waiting, with their rating and the time they joined. Tiny, and ephemeral — a player who disconnects while queued simply stops being in the queue, with no cleanup needed.

The API

POST /v1/queue Body: { mode, rating } Response: 202 { ticket_id } // matched asynchronously WS /v1/play <- { type:"queued", position, est_wait_s } <- { type:"matched", game_id, opponent, color, server_hint } -> { type:"move", game_id, seq, intent:{ from, to } } // the client sends an INTENT, never a resulting state. // seq makes a resend idempotent after a flaky reconnect. <- { type:"state", game_id, seq, board, turn, clocks } <- { type:"invalid", seq, reason } // server rejected the move <- { type:"ended", result, reason:"checkmate|resign|timeout|forfeit" } GET /v1/games?player=&cursor= -> paged history GET /v1/games/{id} -> { players, result, moves[] } // the move log IS the replay -- no separate recording exists

Note the shape of the move message: it carries an intent, not a result. The client says where it wants to play; the server says what happened. That asymmetry is the anti-cheat design expressed in the protocol.

📊5. Capacity estimation

The numbers, and why they are reassuring rather than alarming.

⚖ Assumptions — and what breaks if each is wrong
1M daily players, 10 games each, ~5 minutes per game
Ten times the players changes nothing structurally — games are independent, so this scales horizontally almost perfectly.
Turn-based, roughly one move every 5 seconds
Real-time play at 30 ticks/second multiplies message volume by ~150 and forces client prediction.
Games are short and self-contained
Multi-day asynchronous games would move the design from live sessions toward a persistent store with notifications.
10M
games/day
~35K
concurrent games
~70K
concurrent players
~14K/s
moves at peak
~5 KB
state per live game
~180 MB
all live game state

A million daily players, ten games each, is ten million games a day. At five minutes each, roughly 35,000 concurrent games and 70,000 connected players.

Moves at one every five seconds across 35,000 games is about 14,000 per second at peak. That is an ordinary write rate for an append-only log, and the validation per move is trivial CPU.

All live state is around 180 MB. Worth saying out loud: the entire concurrent state of this system fits in the memory of a laptop.

What that means for the architecture

It means the scaling story is boring, which is the correct outcome. Games are completely independent — no game's state affects another's — so this shards perfectly by game id, and ten times the players is ten times the machines with no structural change.

What does not scale automatically is matchmaking. A single shared queue is a coordination point, and splitting it into independent queues fragments the pool and makes match quality worse. Fortunately the queue is small — a few thousand waiting players — so one process handles it easily for a long time. Regional queues are the natural split when it stops being enough, and they align with latency requirements anyway.

The storage that grows without bound is the move log. Ten million games a day at a few hundred bytes each is modest per day and accumulates, so history gets a retention policy — recent games in full, older ones as results only.

⚖6. The key trade-offs

The choices, and their costs.

DecisionChosen ✓Alternative ✗Reasoning
AuthorityServer-authoritative, clients send intentsTrust client-computed stateClient authority makes cheating trivial and undetectable. Validation on the server makes an edited client capable only of sending moves that get rejected.
Durable artefactAppend-only move logPeriodic board snapshotsThe log serves replay, history and crash recovery from one dataset. Snapshots give recovery but neither replay nor history, so you build all three separately.
MatchmakingRating buckets with a widening windowStrict rating match, or pure FIFOStrict matching gives unbounded waits at the tails; FIFO gives fast but lopsided games. Widening trades a little fairness for a bounded wait.
Game placementOne owning server per game, stickyStateless with shared state storeA per-move round trip to a shared store cannot meet a 150 ms budget, and two servers holding the same game is a correctness bug, not a scaling win.
Live stateIn memory, checkpointed per moveDatabase as the live storeAll concurrent state is ~180 MB. Keeping it in memory is both faster and simpler; the log gives durability without putting the database on the move path.

Server-authoritative, and what it costs

The alternative is trusting the client, and the trade is worth spelling out rather than dismissing.

Client-authoritative is less server work, lower latency (no round trip to see your own move applied), and it works offline. For a single-player game or a friendly puzzle, it is fine.

For anything competitive it is unusable, because a browser client is under the player's control. They can modify it to make illegal moves, see hidden information, or simply report that they won. Detecting that from the outside is an arms race you do not win.

Server-authoritative costs a round trip per move and a server process per game. In exchange, a modified client can send whatever it likes and the server rejects anything the rules do not permit.

The framing worth using: you are choosing between preventing cheating and detecting it, and prevention is strictly cheaper over the life of the product. At 150 ms per move in a turn-based game, the latency cost is not noticeable.

Disconnection, which has no correct answer

The server cannot distinguish “their wifi dropped” from “they quit because they were losing”. This is not an implementation gap; the information does not exist.

So it is a policy, and the policy has to balance two unfairnesses:

  • Forfeit too quickly and a player with a brief connection blip loses a game they were winning. Unfair, and it makes the product feel hostile on mobile networks.
  • Wait too long and the opponent of someone who rage-quit sits staring at a timer for minutes. Also unfair, and more common.

The workable shape is a reconnection window — 30 to 60 seconds, during which the game is held and the opponent is told what is happening — followed by a forfeit. Repeated disconnections by the same player are tracked, because the pattern is distinguishable even when the individual event is not.

Being explicit that this is a product decision, and that no amount of engineering resolves it, is the right answer here.

🏗7. High-level design
Matchmaking, play and recovery — why the move log is the whole design
queue joinmatchmove / replayrehydration
What is moving: two players join a rating-bucketed queue whose search window widens over time, get paired onto one authoritative game server, and then exchange intents — “move e2 to e4”, never “the board is now X”. Each validated move is appended to a durable log, which is simultaneously the replay, the history and the recovery record.
What goes wrong — and is survivable: the game server dies mid-game. A new owner is assigned and replays the move log to rebuild the board; both clients reconnect and resync from their last applied sequence number. Because the log is appended before the move is acknowledged, no acknowledged move can be lost. The real hazard is two servers both believing they own the game — which the epoch fence at the log rejects.

A queue, a set of game processes, and a durable log.

MATCHMAKING one small process; a few thousand waiting players player joins → { rating 1450, joined 14:02:11 } | v search for an opponent within the current window t=0s rating ±50 tight; best match quality t=10s rating ±150 widen — an imperfect match beats waiting t=30s rating ±400 t=60s anyone | v pair found → create game → assign to a game server tell both players where to connect LIVE GAME exactly one process owns it player A ---ws---> GAME PROCESS <---ws--- player B | | state in memory: board, turn, clocks ~5 KB | move arrives: an INTENT, not a result | +-- is it this player's turn? no → reject +-- is the move legal? no → reject +-- APPEND TO DURABLE LOG before acknowledging +-- apply to state +-- broadcast the result to both | v MOVE LOG append-only, per game = history + replay + crash recovery + audit PROCESS DIES → new process reads the move log → replays → game restored PLAYER DROPS → 30-60s reconnect window → then forfeit timer
Appending before acknowledging is the ordering that makes recovery correct. Acknowledge first and a crash can leave two players remembering a move the restored game has never heard of.
🔄8. Workflows — what actually happens
Two players are matched and play a move
The path, with the anti-cheat design visible in it.
  1. Ana joins the queue at rating 1450. The window starts at ±50 and no opponent is available.
  2. Eight seconds later Bo joins at 1490. Within Ana's current window, so they are paired.
  3. A game is created and assigned to a game server. Both players are told where to connect, and both open a socket to that same process.
  4. Ana sends a move: place at C4. This is an intent — she is not telling the server what the board now looks like.
  5. The server checks it is Ana's turn and that C4 is legal given the current state. Both pass.
  6. The move is appended to the durable log as sequence 1. Only after that is it applied to the in-memory board.
  7. The resulting state is broadcast to both players. Round trip: about 60 ms.
Ana's client could have been modified to send any move at all. It could not have made an illegal one legal, because the validation is on the side she does not control — which is what "structurally impossible" means in practice.
Bo's laptop sleeps mid-game
Reconnection, and the judgement call at the end of it.
  1. Bo's socket drops. The server cannot tell whether he quit or his machine slept — and it never will.
  2. The game is not ended. It moves to a disconnected state and a 45-second reconnect window opens.
  3. Ana is told what is happening — "opponent disconnected, waiting" — with a visible countdown. Silence here is worse than bad news.
  4. Bo's laptop wakes at 30 seconds. His client reconnects, presents its game id and session token, and is routed back to the same process.
  5. It receives the current state and the moves it missed. His board is correct within a second of reconnecting.
  6. Play resumes. Bo's clock was running while he was away, which is the fair resolution — the alternative lets a losing player buy thinking time by pulling a cable.
  7. Had he not returned by 45 seconds, the game would be forfeit, and the repeated-disconnection counter on his account would tick up.
Every number here is a product decision dressed as a technical one. The engineering just implements the policy; the value of naming it as a policy is that it gets chosen deliberately rather than inherited from a timeout somewhere.
A game server crashes with 400 live games on it
Where the move log earns its second job.
  1. The process dies. Four hundred games' in-memory state is gone, and 800 players' sockets drop simultaneously.
  2. Nothing is actually lost, because every validated move was appended to the durable log before it was acknowledged.
  3. The routing layer reassigns those game ids to other servers.
  4. Each new owner reads its games' move logs and replays them. A five-minute game is around 60 moves — replay is milliseconds.
  5. Players reconnect, are routed to the new owner, and receive the current state. The interruption shows as a few seconds of "reconnecting".
  6. A move that was mid-validation when the process died was never logged and never acknowledged, so neither player saw it. The client re-sends it.
Recovery is replay, not reconciliation. There is no question of "what state was it in?" because the log is the state — which is exactly why storing moves rather than boards was worth doing.
A top-rated player joins the queue
The tail case that a fixed window handles badly.
  1. Kai is rated 2400. In the whole queue there are perhaps two players above 2200, and neither is waiting right now.
  2. With a fixed ±50 window, Kai waits indefinitely while thousands of players queue and match around him.
  3. Instead the window widens on a schedule: ±50, then ±150 at ten seconds, ±400 at thirty.
  4. At 22 seconds the window reaches down to 2250 and a 2280-rated player is available. They are matched.
  5. The match is less balanced than ideal. It happened, which for a player who would otherwise have left is unambiguously better.
  6. The rating system handles the imbalance afterwards: an expected win gains Kai almost nothing, and an upset costs him a lot.
The widening window is a small piece of logic that converts an unbounded wait into a bounded one at the cost of some match quality. Worth noticing that the rating system already absorbs the imbalance, which is what makes the trade cheap.
🔍9. Deep dives, and what breaks

Routing both players to the same process

This is the awkward operational part, and it is the same problem as D4 and D20: a stateful tier where a specific request must reach a specific machine.

A registry maps game id to the owning server, consulted on connect and on reconnect. Unlike the push registry in D24, this one must be correct rather than merely helpful — two processes owning the same game would accept conflicting moves and produce two boards.

So ownership is a lease with a fencing token: a server holds a game for a bounded period, renews while healthy, and a new owner can only take over with a higher token. A paused process that wakes up finds its log appends rejected.

Worth noticing how often this primitive recurs: it is the same mechanism as the job scheduler's claim in D6 and the document sequencer in D20. A lease plus a monotonically increasing token is the standard answer to “exactly one owner” in an asynchronous system.

What real-time play would change

Worth having ready, since it is the obvious follow-up and it changes the design substantially.

Turn-based play sends a few messages a minute and tolerates 150 ms. Real-time play runs at a fixed tick rate — say 30 per second — which multiplies message volume by more than a hundred and makes latency directly visible in the gameplay.

At that point you cannot wait for the server to confirm your own action; the character would lag behind the controls. So the client predicts: it applies your input immediately and simultaneously sends it to the server. When the server's authoritative state arrives, the client reconciles — if the prediction was right, nothing visible happens; if it was wrong, the client corrects, which is the rubber-banding players occasionally see.

Server authority is preserved, which is the important part. The client is guessing at what the server will say, not deciding it. But the machinery is considerably more complex, which is exactly why “turn-based or real-time?” is the first clarifying question.

Rating, and why it belongs in this design

Matchmaking quality depends entirely on having a meaningful number to match on, so the rating system is not a separate product feature — it is an input to the queue.

The standard approach updates both players after each game based on the difference between the result and what was expected from their ratings. Beating a much stronger player moves your rating a lot; beating a much weaker one moves it barely at all.

Two refinements matter for the queue. New players should have a high-uncertainty rating that moves quickly, so they reach their true level in a handful of games rather than a hundred — otherwise their first opponents get unfair matches. And ratings should decay slowly with inactivity, so a player returning after a year is not matched against current form they no longer have.

What breaks

Game server crashes mid-game
A new owner is assigned, replays the move log for that game, and rebuilds the board. Both clients reconnect and resync from their last applied sequence number. Because the log is appended before the move is acknowledged, no acknowledged move can be lost.
Both players disconnect simultaneously
The game is checkpointed and idle. A reaper ends games with no connected player after a timeout and records the result as abandoned — otherwise abandoned games accumulate in memory forever, which is a slow leak nobody notices until it is large.
Two servers both believe they own a game
This is split brain, and it produces two divergent boards. The epoch number fences it: the move log rejects an append from an older epoch, so the stale owner cannot corrupt the game even though it thinks it is in charge. Ch 6
A client resends a move after a flaky reconnect
The sequence number makes it idempotent: a move at a seq already applied is acknowledged without being replayed. Without this, a poor connection produces double moves, which is indistinguishable from cheating.
Matchmaker restarts with players queued
Queue state lives in a shared sorted set rather than in matchmaker memory, so a restart loses nothing and players keep their position. Clients also re-announce on reconnect, so a lost ticket self-heals rather than stranding someone in an invisible queue.
The dominant constraint

This is not a scale problem. All 35,000 concurrent games fit in about 180 MB. It is a stateful routing and durability problem: both players must reach the same authoritative process, and that process must be able to die without losing the game.

What I would build first

The append-only move log and server-side validation. The log collapses replay, history and crash recovery into one dataset, and validation makes cheating structurally impossible rather than something you detect afterwards.

What I deliberately did not build

Real-time play with client prediction and rollback, and spectators. Both are legitimate and both are considerably harder than what was asked for.

The biggest risk

Split-brain ownership of a game. Two servers holding the same game produce two boards and no error, which is why ownership needs an epoch fence at the log rather than a best-effort lock.

💬 If you get this far, here is what they will push on
Follow-ups an interviewer is likely to ask once the design is on the board. Answers supplied — read the question, answer it out loud, then open it.
“How do you stop a modified client from cheating?”Answer

Structurally rather than by detection. The client sends intents — “move this piece to e4” — and the server validates against the rules and computes the result.

An edited client can then only send illegal moves, which get rejected. If instead the client sent “the board now looks like this”, no amount of anomaly detection reliably saves you.

The same applies to information: never send a player state they should not see. In a game with hidden information, possession of the opponent's cards is the vulnerability, even encrypted.

“A player's connection drops mid-game. What happens?”Answer

You cannot tell a rage-quit from a train entering a tunnel, so this is a product decision rather than a technical one.

The game continues to exist on the server. There is a grace window during which their clock keeps running but the game waits, then a forfeit.

Running the clock is what stops disconnection being used as a stalling tactic — the mechanism has to be designed against the adversarial case, not the sympathetic one. On reconnect they resync from their last applied sequence number.

“Why does each game need a single owning server?”Answer

Because ordering moves is trivial with one writer and genuinely hard with two. A single authoritative process assigns sequence numbers and validates in order, with no coordination at all.

A shared state store instead would put a round trip on every move, which cannot meet a 150 ms budget, and two servers holding the same game is a correctness bug rather than a scaling win.

Consensus is needed only to decide who owns a game, which changes rarely, not for the moves themselves.

“Top players wait ten minutes for a match. Why, and what do you do?”Answer

Because a strict rating match has almost nobody to match them with at the tails. A narrow window is easy to specify and produces unbounded waits for exactly the players who care most.

So widen over time: start at roughly ±25 rating and relax toward ±400 over thirty seconds. Almost everyone matches quickly and fairly, and the tail matches slightly unfairly rather than waiting forever.

Expose the widening curve, because it is the dial between match quality and wait time and product will want to move it.

Design an Ad Impression Counting & Billing System (Google TV: millions of TVs, exactly-once billing, fully auditable)

Difficulty: Hard (Staff Expectation)  .  Target: 50 min
💬 The question, as asked

“TVs already send playback logs to a backend. Design the system that ingests them, decides which are valid billable impressions, aggregates them, and produces billing an advertiser can audit — never charging twice for the same impression.”

⚡ What makes it hard

Five billion events a day and every one is money. Devices duplicate, arrive days late and lie about the time, so you need exactness from a fundamentally unreliable input stream.

📋1. Understanding the question

The prompt: “TVs already send playback logs to a backend. Design the system that ingests them, decides which are valid billable impressions, aggregates them, and produces billing an advertiser can audit — never charging twice for the same impression.”

Five billion events a day, and every single one is money. That combination is what makes this different from every other pipeline in this guide.

A metrics pipeline that loses 0.01% of events is fine. A billing pipeline that loses 0.01% of events has under-charged by 0.01%, and one that duplicates 0.01% has over-charged — which is a refund, a disclosure, and a conversation with someone's legal team.

🎯 Ask this before anything else

Does the TV mint a stable impression id that survives a retry?

If the TV generates an id once and reuses it on every retry, then three copies of the same event all carry the same id, and deduplication is a GROUP BY.

If the server mints the id on arrival — or the TV re-mints on each retry — then those three copies are three distinct events. Nothing downstream can tell them apart. Not a clever algorithm, not a human reviewing the data, not a forensic audit six months later. The information required to distinguish them never existed.

This is the one decision in the design with no recovery path, and it lives in the device contract rather than in your backend.

Why the TVs retry at all

They are on domestic internet connections, and they get switched off mid-upload. So a TV batches events locally, sends them, and keeps them until it sees an acknowledgement. If the acknowledgement is lost — which is far more common than the request being lost — it sends the batch again.

That is correct device behaviour and it is why duplicates are the normal case here rather than an anomaly. The design does not try to prevent them; it makes them harmless.

The second thing that shapes everything

“It played” is not a definition of a billable impression. Two seconds of video? Screen on? Not muted? Not a screensaver? Enough of the ad visible?

Each of those rules changes the number an advertiser is charged. Which means the rules are data, not code: they need a version, and every billed number must record which version produced it. Otherwise a rule change silently alters last month's figures and nobody can reconcile anything.

What they are looking for

Do you ask where the id is minted? First, before designing anything.

Do you separate fast from correct? You cannot be exact at 250,000 events per second on the write path, and you do not have to be.

Do you know which direction to err? Under-billing and over-billing are not symmetric.

❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
Does the TV generate a stable impression ID that survives a retry?
Ask this before anything else — the entire design depends on the answer. If the ID is minted on the TV once and reused on every retry, deduplication is a GROUP BY. If the server mints it, or the TV re-mints on retry, the same impression arrives as three distinct events and no amount of downstream engineering can tell them apart.
What exactly makes an impression billable?
“It played” is not a definition. Two seconds of video? Screen on? TV not muted and not a screensaver? Each rule changes the number an advertiser is charged, so the rule set needs a version and must be an input to the pipeline, not code buried in it.
How long may billing lag reality?
This is the close window, and it is a product decision. Real-time billing is impossible when a TV can be offline for a week. Something like T+72h then the period closes makes the problem tractable.
What happens to an event that arrives after its period closed?
Silently dropping it under-bills and destroys trust when someone reconciles. The workable answer is to bill it in the next period as an explicit adjustment, with an audit record.
Which is worse — over-billing or under-billing?
They are not symmetric. Under-billing costs revenue you can recover next month. Over-billing is a trust and legal problem and may require refunds and disclosure. That asymmetry says: when uncertain, do not charge.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.
📝2. Functional requirements
  • Ingest playback logs from millions of TVs that already batch and retry.
  • Store every raw event immutably, for audit.
  • Apply a versioned validity rule set to decide which events are billable.
  • Deduplicate so one impression is counted exactly once.
  • Aggregate by advertiser, campaign, creative, TV, network and period.
  • Produce a billing number that can be explained and reproduced line by line.

"Reproducible" is the requirement that shapes the storage

An advertiser disputes an invoice from four months ago. They want to know why they were charged for 1,847,221 impressions rather than 1,840,000.

Answering that means being able to re-derive the number from the raw events, with the rule set version that was in force at the time. Which means the raw events must still exist, unchanged, and the rules must be identifiable by version.

So the raw log is not a staging area to be cleaned up after processing — it is the evidence, and it is retained for the full dispute window. Everything downstream is a derived view that can be thrown away and recomputed.

Late events are normal, not exceptional

A TV offline for four days arrives with four days of events. This is not an edge case; with fifty million devices it happens constantly.

Which raises a question that must be answered explicitly: what happens to an event that arrives after its billing period closed? Silently dropping it under-bills and destroys trust the moment anyone reconciles. The workable answer is to bill it in the next period as an explicit adjustment, with an audit record — visible, explainable, and reconcilable.

⏱3. Non-functional requirements
RequirementTargetWhat it forces
Ingest rate~250K/sec peakPrime time. Too fast for per-event transactions, which is why the write path validates nothing.
Double billingNeverThe defining requirement. It depends entirely on where the impression id is minted.
Late and duplicate dataThe normal caseStated as a requirement rather than a failure mode, because with 50M devices it is continuous.
ReproducibilityMonths laterRaw events retained immutably; rules versioned; jobs versioned.
Billing lag~T+72h then closeA product decision. Real-time billing is impossible when a device can be offline for a week.
Error directionUnder, never overWhen uncertain, do not charge. See below.

Why under-billing and over-billing are not symmetric

This is the judgement that should drive every ambiguous decision in the design, and it is worth stating explicitly rather than leaving implicit.

Under-billing costs revenue you can recover. The impression is in the raw log; next month's adjustment picks it up; the advertiser is charged correctly, slightly late. An internal accounting problem.

Over-billing is a trust problem and potentially a legal one. Refunds, disclosure, an audit, and an advertiser who now checks every invoice you send them forever. The money is recoverable; the credibility is not.

So wherever the system is uncertain — a malformed event, an ambiguous validity signal, a suspected duplicate it cannot confirm — the rule is do not charge. Log it, flag it, and leave it out of the invoice.

And the two numbers advertisers see

Advertisers want a live dashboard. Billing needs exactness. These cannot be the same number.

So there are two, and every number is labelled with which kind it is: a provisional figure from the streaming path, available in seconds and approximately right; and a final figure from the batch path, available after the close window and billable.

Showing a single unlabelled number is how you end up explaining to an advertiser why their dashboard said one thing and their invoice said another.

🗂4. Data model and API

Three layers, and the relationship between them is the design: raw is evidence, aggregates are derived, the ledger is money.

-- 1. RAW: immutable, append-only, partitioned by ARRIVAL hour. -- Partition by arrival, not event_time: the device clock is -- untrusted and a wrong clock must not scatter rows across months. TABLE raw_events { -- object storage, columnar (Parquet) impression_id BYTES, -- the dedup key, from the TV device_id UUID, ad_id, campaign_id, creative_id, network_id VARCHAR, event_time TIMESTAMP, -- device clock, for attribution arrival_time TIMESTAMP, -- server clock, for windowing played_ms INT, screen_on BOOL, viewport_pct INT } -- NEVER updated, NEVER deleted inside retention. This table is the -- evidence: every invoice must be re-derivable from it alone. -- 2. AGGREGATES: derived. Keyed so a re-run REPLACES, never adds. TABLE billable_hourly { campaign_id, creative_id VARCHAR, hour TIMESTAMP, ruleset_version VARCHAR, -- which rules produced this count job_version VARCHAR, -- which code produced it impressions BIGINT, computed_at TIMESTAMP, PRIMARY KEY (campaign_id, creative_id, hour, ruleset_version) } -- UPSERT on this key. Re-running an hour is therefore IDEMPOTENT -- -- the single most important property in the whole design. -- 3. LEDGER: append-only money. Corrections are new rows, not edits. TABLE ledger { entry_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, invoice_id UUID, campaign_id VARCHAR, period DATE, impressions BIGINT, amount NUMERIC, kind ENUM(charge, adjustment, credit), supersedes UUID, -- lineage for a correction UNIQUE (invoice_id, campaign_id, period, kind) } -- You never rewrite an invoice. You issue an adjustment against it.

Partition raw events by arrival time, not event time

A detail that looks arbitrary and prevents a real disaster.

The event_time comes from the TV's clock, which is untrusted. A device with a badly wrong clock — not rare, across fifty million consumer devices — can report events dated 1970 or 2038.

Partition by event time and those rows scatter across partitions spanning decades, creating tiny partitions in periods that are already closed and cannot be reprocessed.

Partition by arrival time, the server's clock, and every event lands in the hour it actually arrived. The device clock is kept as a field and used for attribution, where being wrong is a data-quality issue rather than a structural one.

The aggregate key is what makes re-runs safe

The single most important property in the design, and it is expressed entirely in a primary key.

Aggregates are keyed on (campaign, creative, hour, ruleset_version) and written as an upsert. Re-running an hour therefore replaces that hour's row rather than adding to it.

Which means re-running is idempotent: safe to do once, twice, or fifty times. And re-running is exactly what you do when a job fails halfway, when late data arrives, or when a bug is found in the rules. A design where re-running double-counts is a design where nobody dares fix anything.

The ledger is append-only, because money is

You never rewrite an invoice. If a figure was wrong, you issue an adjustment — a new row referencing the one it corrects.

That is not a technical preference; it is how accounting works. An invoice that silently changes value is unauditable, and the whole point of this system is auditability. The correction history is itself part of the record.

The API

// TV-FACING -- batched, retried, and idempotent by construction POST /v1/impressions:batch Headers: authorization: bearer <device attestation token> Body: { device_id, batch_id, events: [ { impression_id, // MINTED ON THE TV, stable across retries ad_id, campaign_id, creative_id, network_id, event_time, // device clock -- untrusted, for attribution played_ms, screen_on, muted, viewport_pct } ] } Response: 202 { accepted: 500, batch_id } // 202, not 200: we have DURABLY LOGGED them, not validated // or billed them. The TV may now delete its local copy. Errors: 429 backoff 413 batch too large // ADVERTISER-FACING GET /v1/reports?campaign=&from=&to=&granularity=hour Response: { rows:[{ period, impressions, state }] } // state: "provisional" (streaming) | "final" (batch, billable) // NEVER show one number without saying which kind it is GET /v1/billing/{invoice_id}/lineage Response: { ruleset_version, job_version, input_partitions[], computed_at, adjustments[] } // this endpoint IS the auditability requirement

Note the 202 on ingest. It means durably logged, not validated and not billed. That is precisely what the TV needs to know before deleting its local copy, and promising anything more would be a lie the write path cannot support at this rate.

📊5. Capacity estimation

The numbers, and the two conclusions they force.

⚖ Assumptions — and what breaks if each is wrong
50M TVs, ~100 impressions each per day
Ten times the volume changes nothing structurally — every stage partitions by a hash. It changes the storage bill, not the architecture.
TVs batch events and retry until acknowledged
If TVs sent fire-and-forget with no retry, you would trade duplicates for silent loss — which for billing is the worse failure.
A TV may be offline for days
If devices were always online, the close window could be minutes and the late-data machinery would be unnecessary.
Raw events are retained 90 days for audit
Shorter retention means an invoice can be disputed after the evidence is gone, which defeats the point of the system.
5B
impressions/day
~58K/s
average ingest
~250K/s
prime-time peak
~2 TB
raw per day
~500 GB
compressed per day
~45 TB
90-day audit store

Fifty million TVs at around a hundred impressions a day is 5 billion events daily — about 58,000 per second on average and 250,000 at prime time. At 400 bytes each, roughly 2 TB of raw data a day, or 500 GB compressed. Ninety days of audit retention is around 45 TB, which is unremarkable storage.

Conclusion one: you cannot be correct on the write path

At 250,000 events per second there is no room for a transaction per event, a uniqueness check per event, or a validity evaluation per event. Any of those would need a coordinating store doing a quarter of a million serialised operations per second, and it would be the least available component in the system.

So stop trying. Accept events fast and unvalidated into an immutable log, and compute the billable number afterwards as a derived view. Ingest's only job is to not lose anything.

Conclusion two: deduplication must be exact, which rules out the obvious trick

The instinct for “have I seen this id?” at this scale is a Bloom filter, as in D10. Here it is wrong, and the arithmetic says so clearly.

A filter covering 5 billion keys a day at a 1% false-positive rate is around 6 GB — and a false positive means the filter says “already seen” about an impression it has never seen. One percent of 5 billion is 50 million real impressions dropped, a 1% under-bill, every day.

Probabilistic structures are fine for a dashboard and unacceptable for an invoice.

Exact deduplication comes from sorting the day's partition and taking the distinct set — which a batch job does trivially and a streaming system cannot, because it would need unbounded state to remember every id it has ever seen. That difference is the whole argument for having a batch layer at all.

⚖6. The key trade-offs

The choices, and their costs.

DecisionChosen ✓Alternative ✗Reasoning
Impression identityMinted on the TV, stable across retriesMinted on the server at arrivalServer-minted IDs make retries indistinguishable from genuine impressions. Deduplication becomes impossible, permanently — this is the one decision with no recovery.
Billing sourceBatch layer, after closeStreaming countsStreaming dedup is bounded by its state window, so a TV returning after days double-counts. Exact dedup needs a full sort, which batch does trivially.
Aggregate writesUPSERT keyed by (campaign, creative, hour, ruleset)INSERT, or incrementReplacement makes a re-run idempotent. Incrementing means every job retry inflates the bill — the exact failure the system exists to prevent.
Late eventsAdjustment in the next periodRetro-insert, or dropRetro-inserting mutates a sent invoice; dropping under-bills silently and cannot be reconciled. An adjustment keeps the ledger immutable and the loss visible.
Windowing clockarrival_time (server)event_time (device)A TV with a wrong clock would scatter its rows across arbitrary months. Device time is kept for attribution, never for deciding the billing period.
Validity rulesVersioned data, an input to the jobLogic inside the pipelineRules change. If they live in code, last month's numbers stop being reproducible the moment the code moves on — which breaks the audit requirement.

Two layers: fast and approximate, slow and exact

The structural decision, and it exists because no single system can do both jobs.

Streaming gives numbers within seconds. It cannot deduplicate exactly, because that would require remembering every impression id forever, and it cannot handle data that arrives three days late without holding windows open for three days. Its output is provisional and it feeds dashboards.

Batch runs after the close window over a complete, bounded set of data. It sorts, deduplicates exactly, applies the versioned rules, and produces the number that goes on the invoice. Its output is final and it feeds billing.

The cost is running two implementations of the same logic, which can drift apart — the standard criticism of this shape. The mitigation is to compare them continuously: a persistent gap between provisional and final figures is a bug in one of them and should alert.

The reason to accept that cost is that the alternatives are worse. Streaming alone cannot be exact. Batch alone means advertisers see nothing for three days.

Where the close window goes

A period stays open for late data, then closes. Choosing when is a product decision with real consequences on both sides.

Close early — say T+6h — and you bill quickly, and a meaningful volume of genuine impressions from offline devices arrives afterwards and must be handled as adjustments.

Close late — T+7d — and you capture nearly everything, and advertisers wait a week for an invoice while you carry a week of unbilled revenue.

Around T+72h captures the large majority of late arrivals while keeping billing reasonably prompt. And crucially, closing is not a deadline after which data is discarded. Events arriving later are still ingested, still deduplicated, and billed in the next period as explicit adjustments. The window decides when a number becomes final, not when data stops mattering.

🏗7. High-level design
Impression ingest — and the retry that must not become a triple charge
impression eventslogged / dedupedbilledduplicate identities
What is moving: batched impression events, each carrying an impression_id minted on the TV and reused on every retry. Collectors accept fast and validate nothing; the log partitions by hash of that id so every copy lands on one partition. The batch layer sorts, takes the distinct set, and bills once — no matter how many times the TV resent.
What goes wrong: if the id were minted on arrival instead, a TV that never saw its 202 and resends three times produces three distinct events. They are not duplicates in any detectable sense — nothing downstream can tell them apart — and the advertiser is charged three times for one impression.
